People came out after it.

The choir first. Then graduates helping graduates. Then Tank carrying the woman with the cane while Rosa and Mercedes pushed two overturned benches out of the way. Porsche had a fire extinguisher in each hand and was shouting at niggas like she personally owned oxygen.

I got out and ran back up the steps.

Knox met me at the opening with Mercer beside her. Shawna came behind them, one hand over her mouth, the other holding my graduation cap.

"Baby!"

I caught her.

She hit my shoulder with the cap, then put it on my head herself.

"You almost forgot something."

"Nigga, I was making an entrance."

"You made an exit."

"A great man does both."

She kissed me while the whole courtyard watched.

Behind us, the fire crews arrived. Knox's people brought the surviving attackers out in handcuffs. One of them looked at the Lamborghini and shook his head.

"We burned the building."

"And the nigga still came through it," his partner said.

"With a police car."

"Nigga, I saw."

I heard them. Of course I heard them. They'd come to ruin my graduation and now they were reviewing the best part of it together.

I straightened my cap.

"Principal. You got a microphone out here?"

***

They brought the lectern into the courtyard.

Mercer stood beside it still crying. Halcyon put a hand on his back. Professor Lorne looked at the smoke coming out of the auditorium and then at me with the expression of a man whose roof calculation had just acquired a personal reason to live.

The graduates gathered in front of us. Some had soot on their gowns. Some were holding shoes. Everybody had somebody by the hand.

I stepped up to the microphone.

"Aight. Where we at?"

The laughter rolled across the courtyard, wild and relieved. Tank stood behind Shawna with his arms folded and his face shining. Marcellus had one hand on Rosa's shoulder. Mercedes lifted her camera.

"Niggas, I ain't gonna lie. I wasn't here much."

The laughter got louder.

"You were not here at all!" somebody shouted.

"And look what happened the morning I came. You welcome."

They cheered. A man in the third row took off his cap and waved it over his head.

I looked out at them. All those people. All those grown men and women who'd come back to a classroom after life had given them plenty of reasons to leave it alone. They were looking at me like I could tell them something worth taking into tomorrow.

Nigga, I could do that too.

"You came for your name," I said. "Some of you worked all night and came anyway. Some of you had people telling you this wasn't your kind of room. Some of you got somebody missing today who should've been here making too much fucking noise."

Shawna looked down at her watch. Then back at me.

"But you here. And when the doors caught fire, niggas started carrying each other. I saw that. That part belongs to you. Keep it. Don't let anybody make you little enough to forget it."

I put my hand on the cross.

"Three letters on this. D. B. M."

Tank's eyebrows lifted. Shawna began smiling before I said the words.

"Damn, boy. Magnificent."

The courtyard erupted.

"That's you too," I told them. "Men, women, every grown motherfucker standing here with a cap and a dream. You look in the mirror tomorrow, say it properly. Don't mumble greatness in your own house."

Mercedes shouted, "Say it again!"

"Damn!"

The whole courtyard answered, "Boy!"

I spread my arms.

"Magnificent!"

They shouted it back so loudly the pigeons left the roof of Aiden Hall together.

Mercer put the diploma in my hand while he was still crying. I had driven through a burning auditorium and finished my valedictorian speech before the principal finished his first fucking breakdown.

Nigga, education was going beautifully.

***

Knox stepped up beside me before anybody could start the next hymn.

Two officers brought a blue velvet box. Another brought a dark uniform jacket with gold braid on its shoulders. The whole courtyard went quiet in stages as people realized the police had come to offer me more than a ride.

"Aiden," Knox said, "you've been making this offer difficult to postpone."

"Chief, I been busy graduating."

"You've also saved my officers' lives, protected this city's people, and demonstrated a relationship with automobiles I have never seen in any man who still has all his limbs."

Porsche applauded first.

Knox opened the box.

A gold captain's badge lay inside.

Not honorary. Not a souvenir. The chief told the entire courtyard that before any nigga could get confused and make me explain it with a siren later.

"Captain Aiden," she said. "Las Vegas Police Department. Actual command. Actual badge. Actual trouble for anyone who thinks otherwise."

Tank bent forward with his hands on his knees.

"Nigga."

Rosa caught his arm.

"You all right?"

"This nigga's a cop."

"I heard."

"My nigga's the police."

"Stand up before he arrests your posture."

Knox held out the badge.

"Raise your right hand."

I did.

The oath she gave me was short. Keep faith with my people. Stand when somebody needed standing for. Use the authority of the badge with my whole name behind it. I spoke every word in front of the chief, the officers, the graduates, and the woman I wanted beside me for the rest of my life.

Then Knox pinned the badge inside my jacket.

"Captain."

I looked down at the gold.

Nigga, my mother would've had to sit down twice.

Shawna came up the steps. Took my face in both hands. Kissed me slowly enough that the police officers started applauding before the students did.

"My man," she whispered.

"Your captain."

"Still my man."

I could've stood there forever letting her settle the rank.

Knox gave me the Lamborghini's keys again. One door had a scratch from the auditorium. The hood smelled like smoke. The siren still worked, because God wasn't going to give a nigga that much greatness and then get petty over wiring.

"It's yours," she said.

"I noticed."

She leaned close enough that only I could hear.

"Red's people used to believe they owned every uniform that mattered in this city. Let him see yours."

I looked at her.

She smiled.

"I know exactly who I recruited, Captain."

We left the college with my diploma on Shawna's lap and the badge inside my jacket. Tank followed in the original Mercedes. The rest of the convoy came behind him, horns sounding all the way to the gates.

Every graduate turned to watch the Lamborghini pass.

At the fountain, Marcus raised his cap and shouted, "That's our nigga!"

His friend shouted, "That's our captain!"

I hit the siren once for both of them.

Shawna put her hand on my leg as the campus disappeared behind us.

"What you doing tomorrow?"

I looked at her. Looked at the road. Let the car stretch its legs beneath us.

"Baby, niggas better not schedule anything they can't afford."

## 9. Forty Million and One Woman

The morning after my graduation, a nigga tried to rob a casino while I was buying coffee in uniform.

That was his first mistake.

His second was parking in front of my Lamborghini.

I stood outside the coffee shop with two cups in my hands. Shawna sat in the passenger seat wearing sunglasses and my captain's jacket over her dress. She'd taken it off me because she said the gold braid felt good against her wrists. Nigga, the department hadn't had time to miss it yet.

Across the street, four men came out of a casino carrying bags. Behind them an alarm rang. One man had a gun pointed backward toward the doors. Another had a bleeding lip and a look that suggested he had expected the morning to involve less resistance.

Their van stood across my bumper.

I looked at the coffee. Looked at the van. Looked at Shawna.

"Baby, hold these."

She took both cups.

"You getting involved?"

"Nigga involved me when he parked."

The driver saw me coming and laughed.

"Keep walking, pretty boy."

I opened my shirt enough for him to see the badge.

His laugh changed shape.

"Police?"

"Captain."

"You don't look like police."

"Nigga, police improving. Move the van."

The man behind him raised his pistol.

I caught the van's open door and drove it into his arm. The shot went into the street. I hit him against the side panel and took him down while the driver tried to get back behind the wheel.

The van lurched forward.

Its rear doors were still open. Bags of money tumbled out. The driver shouted at his partner to pull them in, and I caught the door handle as the van gathered speed.

"Aiden!" Shawna shouted.

"Coffee!" I shouted back.

I wasn't going to let some nigga make her spill eight dollars on a police uniform.

The van dragged me past the corner. My shoes hit the curb, found it, lost it. I got one foot on the rear step and pulled myself up while the man inside tried to kick me off.

"Nigga, let go!"

"You let go!"

"It's my van!"

"Then your nigga should've moved it!"

I came through the doors and hit him into the pile of bags. The driver looked back. That was enough to put the van halfway onto the sidewalk. A newspaper stand exploded against the windshield. Papers flew everywhere, yesterday's miracles suddenly competing with the one hanging out of a moving fucking robbery.

The man on the floor reached for his gun.

I put my foot on his wrist.

"Don't."

He looked up at me.

"You're Aiden."

"Nigga, you would've had a easier day remembering that at the coffee shop."

The driver turned into a parking structure. Concrete closed over us. Tires screamed on the first ramp. The van tipped, caught, and kept climbing.

I could hear my Lamborghini outside before I saw it.

Shawna came through the entrance behind us with the siren on.

My jacket was back over the seat. The coffee cups sat upright in the holders. My woman was chasing a van full of criminals while saving my breakfast, and nigga, every good thing I'd ever believed about marriage started taking notes.

We hit the second floor. Then the third.

The driver shouted, "She's still behind us!"

"She's thorough," I told him.

"Nigga, who the fuck asked you?"

"You brought me."

At the next turn, Shawna swung the Lamborghini across the ramp above us and stopped.

The driver braked. The van slid. I caught the front seat before I went through it, and the two men behind me hit the bags of money in a way that sounded financially painful.

Shawna got out with her silver pistol in her hand.

"Everybody out."

The driver stared through the windshield.

"She's police too?"

"Nigga, she's worse. She's disappointed."

He put up his hands.

Knox's officers found us on the third floor ten minutes later. Four men on the ground. The stolen money in the van. My Lamborghini blocking the ramp like the city had finally bought itself a beautiful fucking answer.

A sergeant with a gray mustache shook my hand so hard I had to tell him about the coffee.

"Captain, we have been after that crew for months."

"Niggas parked wrong."

He looked at the van, then back at me.

"We should've tried that."

Shawna handed me my cup. Still warm. Not one fucking drop on the seat.

The sergeant saluted her too.

"Ma'am."

"You can call me Shawna."

"Yes, ma'am."

Nigga, respect sometimes refused to take a suggestion.

The casino owner came to the station before lunch. He brought two gold watches and an envelope. I gave the watches to the two employees the robbers had knocked down, kept the envelope because gratitude ought to reach its address, and bought the whole shift lunch with it.

Knox watched from her office doorway while officers took pictures beside my car.

"How's your first morning?"

"Need a bigger cup holder."

She laughed.

"Anything else?"

"Nigga wants a raise."

"You've been here four hours."

"And look what the four hours did for you."

By evening every officer in the station knew my name. By the next afternoon, when I went to buy the suit for Red's gala, half of them had volunteered to wait outside the Saint in case my night needed company.

I told them to stay close to Knox. Red liked surprises. I intended to give the nigga one wearing a badge.

***

I bought a white suit for the robbery because I wanted Red to see who ruined his fucking life.

The tailor tried to sell me black. Then he tried to sell me dark blue. He had Shawna on a little velvet chair behind me, drinking champagne and telling him I looked handsome in everything, which meant she hadn't looked up from her phone once.

“Nigga, white,” I told him. “I want the whole room seeing who came.”

“Your injury—”

“Nigga, is the suit going to heal me?”

The nigga stopped talking about the injury.

Tank stood beside the door in a black suit we had bought forty minutes earlier. He had already torn it reaching for a peppermint. The tailor was pretending not to notice. I wasn't.

“Get the nigga another one too.”

“A larger size?”

“Get that nigga whatever size a cathedral is.”

Tank put the peppermint back.

“Nigga, eat. We rich enough for the candy and whatever seam your ass takes with it.”

Shawna laughed then. She lifted her eyes, and for a second I had her. No dead husband. No diamond. No Red waiting for his chance. Just my woman laughing because I was standing in a thousand pins threatening to buy a church-sized suit for the biggest motherfucker in Nevada.

My nigga, I would've bought the actual church to keep her laughing.

Between graduating, becoming a captain, and chasing a van through a parking garage, I had still found time for the three days before the gala to do something terrible to me. I could take a bullet. I could bury a man who called himself my father. But sitting beside Shawna while she told Red over the phone that she missed him had me walking around my own house like I was looking for somebody to rob.

I knew the plan. Nigga, I had agreed to the plan. I had nodded while she explained it and said some shit about trusting her. Then she had put Red on speaker and called him baby, and all that intelligent shit left my body.

“You don't have to say it to that nigga like that,” I told her afterward.

“Like what?”

“With your mouth.”

She stared at me.

“Aiden.”

“Nigga got a name. Use the name.”

She hung up on the argument by kissing me. I let her. The second night I made the same complaint, and she kissed me again. By the third, she knew exactly what I was doing and told me to come over there without starting a fight first.

Now the tailor knelt beside my shoes while she answered another message.

“That nigga again?”

“Rosa.”

“Let me see.”

She turned the screen. Rosa had sent a picture of six gowns thrown across a bed and the words *Your nigga paying for all this?*

“Tell her your nigga said yes.”

“You don't know how much it is.”

“Tell her yes in capital fucking letters.”

Shawna put her phone away. Then she stood and walked around the tailor to straighten my collar herself.

“You know you're allowed to be scared tonight.”

“I'm not.”

“Okay.”

“You are?”

“Yes.”

I caught her wrist before she could step away. Dante's watch slid down against my fingers. I let it.

“Then your nigga scared too.”

She kissed the uncut corner of my mouth.

“Good. Maybe you'll listen.”

I listened to every fucking thing she said. I just sometimes decided the whole world was wrong after I heard it.

***

At the house, Rosa had turned our bedroom into a kingdom of women getting dressed. There were shoes on the chairs, perfume in the air, and a bottle of champagne standing in the sink beside my toothbrush. Somebody had moved my gun to make room for a heated hairbrush. Nigga, I owned the house, and they asked me why I was in there.

“Nigga, because I sleep here.”

“Not while we're busy,” Rosa said.

She was wearing red, diamonds at her throat, and an expression that told me she had already decided who was going to disappoint her that night.

“I need Shawna.”

“Your nigga needs patience,” Rosa told Shawna.

“Nigga, I bought patience. They said it'll be here tomorrow.”

Rosa picked up a shoe. A nigga left.

Downstairs, Marcellus sat by the windows in a gray suit. Somebody had polished his shoes until they looked wet. The disguise was supposed to make him a wealthy old jeweler, which mostly involved getting him a better jacket and telling him not to look like he wanted Red dragged behind a car.

My nigga still looked like that.

On the table in front of him lay Celeste's letter. The folds were so worn they looked ready to separate. He wasn't reading it. He had laid one hand across the paper like somebody might reach down from heaven and take it back.

“My nigga, tell me you ready,” I said.

“I have been ready for years.”

“Nigga, that's not what I asked.”

He looked up, and for the first time since I met him, the old man almost smiled.

“Yes, Aiden.”

I sat across from him. My side objected. That bullet had settled into my life like it intended to pay rent. Every time I forgot it, the pain came back to tell me who had put it there.

Marcellus glanced at the way I lowered myself.

“Does she know how much that hurts?”

“She knows everything.”

“Does she?”

I looked toward the stairs.

“Nigga, she knows enough.”

He folded Celeste's letter and put it in his inside pocket.

“The stone cannot love you back,” he said.

“I got somebody for that.”

“Then remember which one you came for.”

Before I could answer, Tank walked in holding two phones. He turned one facedown as soon as he saw us.

“Niggas, the cars ready.”

“What nigga calling you?”

“Nobody.”

“Nigga, then why you got two phones?”

“In case somebody does.”

I would've laughed on any other night. That night I watched him put both in his pocket, and something in my stomach moved. I thought about asking again. Then I heard Shawna on the stairs.

My nigga, everything in me turned around.

She wore blue. Dark blue, cut close to her body, with a train dragging behind her like even the floor wanted to hold on. Diamonds touched her ears. Dante's watch was on her wrist. Her hair was up, and that little scar above her eyebrow stood out plainly. I loved the scar. I loved knowing the exact place on her face where the world had tried some shit and failed.

“Rosa's dress,” she said when she saw me looking. “She never wore it.”

“Nigga, I said I'd buy you anything.”

“I wanted this one.”

Rosa lifted the train off the last stair.

“And I want it back. Both of you hear me?”

“Yes,” Shawna said.

I should've heard how softly she said it.

Rosa came down behind her carrying a small envelope.

“I've got the watch paper,” she said. “The original. Nobody gets it off me.”

The order hidden in Dante's watch was inside. Red's words. Red's decision. All the grief he had handed Shawna while pretending he was helping her carry it.

Shawna had made a copy for tonight. Rosa would keep the original safe, along with the truth if none of us came back.

I didn't like thinking about that second part, so I stood up.

“Turn around for your nigga,” I told Shawna.

She did.

“Again.”

“Aiden.”

“Nigga, I'm trying to remember whether there's anybody left alive I need to thank.”

She slipped her little silver pistol into her purse, then came over and put both hands against my chest.

“If you tear this dress, I'm killing you before Red gets the chance.”

“Your nigga will buy the factory.”

“I'll kill you in the factory.”

I kissed her. I kissed her until Tank cleared his throat, then I kissed her again because that nigga did not determine the length of my happiness.

***

We went to the Saint in four cars. I drove Shawna in the dark-blue police Lamborghini. Tank kept the original black Mercedes behind us. Rosa drove Marcellus, and Porsche brought Mercedes in the green Bentley.

I wanted six. Tank said we only had enough people for four. I told him to put one nigga in each of the other two, and he asked who was driving. Apparently the man had chosen tonight to become a fucking mathematician.

Four cars pulled under the Saint's canopy. Four cars full of my niggas. It still looked like a palace somebody had built with all the money they should've used to raise their children. Gold everywhere. Flowers as tall as men. A fountain full of coins that were worth less than one button on the security guard's jacket.

Red had made the gala white tie. Nigga thought if he dressed his sins in enough silk, God might mistake them for somebody else's.

I came out in my white suit with the cross against my chest, the captain's badge inside my jacket, and Shawna beside me. Cameras started flashing.

My nigga, that surprised me. I had expected guns.

“Keep walking,” she whispered.

I kept walking like I had paid for the fucking sidewalk.

A photographer asked us to stop against a wall of white roses. Shawna put her hand on my shoulder. I put mine at her waist. A man with a microphone asked whether I was taking over Big T's interests.

“Every nigga that owes them anything owes me,” I said.

“And your relationship with Mr. Redmond?”

Redmond. Nigga had a government name tonight.

“Ask me at the end.”

Rosa stepped between the reporter and us before I could make it worse. Tank followed so closely I felt his jacket brush mine. For a second his hand touched my arm.

“Anything happen tonight,” he said, “you stay with me.”

“Nigga, that was already the idea.”

The nigga didn't answer.

Inside, a staircase curved around a statue of a naked woman holding a bowl of fire. Red had put real flames in the bowl. I respected that nigga for that one thing. If you were going to waste money, make the building itself nervous.

Women in jewels walked past women who had sold them drugs in the bathroom. Men greeted men they had paid to have killed and had not yet heard back about. A preacher I recognized from television stood beside a man whose entire fortune came from stolen cars. The preacher had the bigger watch.

There was a private lounge full of cocaine and champagne. Somebody called my name from inside. I looked over and saw a man I had spent a filthy weekend with before I ever met Shawna, sitting between two women I had met the same weekend.

He lifted his glass.

“Aiden! You disappear when you fall in love?”

“Nigga, I got promoted.”

The women laughed. Shawna looked at all three, then at me.

“All of them?”

“Your nigga had a long weekend.”

“You nasty motherfucker.”

“You love me.”

She squeezed my hand hard enough to hurt.

“Don't get confident.”

I got confident. I got so fucking confident that when Red came down the far staircase in a dark green jacket, I smiled at him like he had arrived at my party.

He wasn't looking at me.

He was looking at Shawna.

***

“There she is,” Red said. Nigga sounded like she had come out of his own prayers.

He held out both hands. She gave him one. He kissed it above Dante's watch.

Nigga, I saw the whole murder happen in my mind. His head through the flower arrangement. His green jacket on fire. Me standing over him while the preacher told God to mind His business.

Instead I smiled.

“Nigga, you throw a good party. Shame about your future.”

Red finally looked at me.

“Captain,” Red said, and the word came out like a bone he had to swallow. “You clean up well.”

“You still talking.”

Shawna's fingers tightened against my arm.

Red laughed softly, as if I was a child who had threatened to buy his own house.

“We should get a photograph. All three of us.”

Before anybody could object, he called the photographer over. He put Shawna in the middle. Then he rested a hand against her upper arm. On that hand he wore a broad dark ring with a blue stone set almost flush into it.

Marcellus, a few feet behind us, went perfectly still at the sight of Red holding Shawna. The ring was half-hidden against the green sleeve.

The flash went off.

The nigga asked for another.

I stared straight into the lens. If that photograph ever hung in a museum, people would know which motherfucker had come there to kill somebody.

An attendant brought glossy little copies while Red greeted Rosa. Rosa took two. She tucked them into her purse with a smile I knew cost her real effort.

“Now,” Red said, holding out his arm to Shawna, “I promised this woman a dance.”

Shawna looked at me.

I remembered every word of the plan. I remembered agreeing. I remembered her saying she needed him close and foolish and thinking he had already won.

I also remembered that I had hands.

“One dance,” I said.

Red smiled.

“Let's see what she wants.”

Then he took my woman onto the floor, and I followed them with my eyes like a nigga watching his own heart get carried through traffic.

## 10. Blue Mercy

The band started playing a song Shawna knew.

I knew she knew it because her face changed before the singer got to the first word. Red saw the change too. He said something against her ear, and she looked down at their hands.

Nigga, I wanted to rip the song out of the speakers.

They turned beneath a chandelier that probably cost enough to feed everybody I had grown up with until the end of time. Red held her close. Not too close for a ballroom. Too close for me.

Tank brought me a drink.

“Nigga, this one for drinking. Don't throw it.”

“Nigga, then why you bring it where I got hands?”

“Nigga might surprise me once. I keep hoping.”

I swallowed half. My side burned. Across the room Marcellus spoke to an older woman wearing a necklace so heavy she looked like she was being slowly arrested by it. He looked ordinary. Harmless. I knew he had a dead wife folded over his heart and a fury older than mine.

That made two of us watching the same dance for different ghosts.

Red turned Shawna. Her blue dress swung around his legs. She smiled at something he said.

“Nigga,” I told Tank.

“Nigga, I see.”

“Nigga.”

“I know.”

“No, you don't.”

My nigga drank his whole glass.

***

The nigga who came to interrupt my misery wore six championship rings and a gold mouthguard on a chain.

"Captain Aiden."

I looked up.

"Depends who's bleeding."

"Rex Crown."

Tank's eyes moved from the rings to the man's shoulders. Rex was forty-five, built like he'd spent twenty years eating other men's excuses. I knew the face from fight posters outside casinos. Heavyweight champion twice. Ex-champion three times. Nigga had made a whole career out of getting his crown back.

"I know you," I said.

He smiled.

"Heard you think you can fight."

"Nigga, I heard you get paid to. We can both have a nice night."

"Not what I'm asking."

Behind him a little crowd had gathered. Men holding drinks. Women looking from his shoulders to my face. Mercedes stood among them with Porsche beside her, both of them smiling in a way Rex hadn't learned to fear yet.

"He asked you something," one of Rex's friends said.

"And my nigga answered," Mercedes told him. "Try listening with the part of your head you ain't drinking through."

Porsche laughed into her glass.

Rex looked at her. Then at me again.

"Five thousand says I put you down before your woman finishes her dance."

Across the floor Red turned Shawna beneath the lights. The green jacket moved against the blue dress. I watched them for one second too long.

Then I put my drink down.

"Nigga, that's a cheap way to become a story."

Rex spread his hands.

"Twenty."

"You looking for my price or your dignity?"

"A hundred thousand."

The people behind him made a noise. Somebody said his name like they wanted him to think about his children, his savings, his whole fucking future. Rex kept smiling.

I looked at Tank.

"Hold my jacket."

"Your side."

"Hold it on the good side."

He took it reluctantly. The badge flashed inside the lining. Rex looked at the gold, and for half a second I saw him wonder whether he'd challenged a man or an entire department.

Then his friends started cheering, and the nigga chose stupidity with witnesses.

We moved into a little clear space beside the ballroom's tall windows. Nobody stopped the music. Red saw us, saw Rex take off his jacket, and smiled as if he'd just learned his dinner came with entertainment.

Shawna didn't smile.

She looked at me over his shoulder and shook her head once.

I lifted one finger.

One.

She shut her eyes like she was trying to love me without laughing at the size of the task.

Rex rolled his shoulders. Took the mouthguard off his chain. Put it in.

"Nigga brought jewelry he can chew," Tank murmured.

Mercedes bent double laughing.

Rex swung.

Not wild. Not drunk. The nigga knew exactly what he was doing. His fist came at my face with all the years behind it, all the ropes and bells and men who'd already discovered what those hands could make of a morning.

I moved.

His punch went past my cheek. I felt the air on the cut Shawna had cleaned days earlier. I stepped inside his reach and hit him once beneath the ribs.

The sound wasn't loud.

His reaction was.

Rex folded forward. I caught the back of his collar before he fell into the champagne table and held him there with one hand. He tried to straighten. Couldn't. Tried to get enough breath to say something impressive. Couldn't do that either.

The crowd went quiet.

Then Porsche whispered, "Nigga."

Mercedes answered, "Nigga."

Tank looked down at Rex and nodded.

"That's about the whole sentence."

I set the champion gently in a chair.

His friends stared at me. One of them looked at his watch as if time might explain what strength hadn't.

"You said before the dance," I told Rex. "Nigga, you still got two verses. Enjoy them."

The ballroom erupted.

People came over from the far tables. A man pushed a phone toward me. A woman touched my shoulder and said she had watched every one of Rex's title fights and had never seen him sit down so respectfully.

Rex finally got air into his chest.

"Again," he said.

"Nigga, breathe first."

"Again."

"You want a rematch or a hospital bracelet?"

He looked up at me. The anger went out of his face slowly, leaving something almost peaceful behind it.

"What the fuck are you?"

I took my jacket from Tank.

"Her man."

I looked toward Shawna when I said it. Everybody looked with me.

She stood beside Red at the edge of the dance floor. Her hand was still in his, but her face belonged entirely to me. She was smiling now. Proud enough that she couldn't hide it even with the whole plan hanging from her wrist.

Red saw that too.

His smile vanished.

Rex took out a checkbook with hands that still weren't steady. Wrote the amount. Signed it. Held it up.

"I don't welch."

I gave it to Mercedes.

"For you and Porsche. You got my car out of that first night."

She looked at the number, then at me.

"Nigga, that's a hundred thousand dollars."

"You want it smaller?"

"Don't you fucking dare."

She kissed my cheek. Porsche kissed the other one. The whole little crowd laughed, and Rex sat in the middle of it looking at me like a man who'd paid a great deal for a lesson and hated how much he'd learned.

Then somebody behind him pulled a gun.

A thin man in a silver jacket. One of his people. He'd been watching the money change hands with the kind of face men make when another nigga's humiliation starts feeling like their own.

"Give it back," he said.

Mercedes stepped behind me.

I looked at the gun. Looked at Rex.

"Your nigga?"

Rex got up out of the chair.

"Put it away, Silas."

"He made you look—"

"He beat me. Put it away."

Silas didn't.

I caught his wrist as Tank caught his shoulder. The shot went into the ceiling. Crystal rained from a small chandelier above us. People screamed and ducked.

Silas hit the floor with both of us over him.

The gun slid away. Porsche kicked it under an empty table and kept her heel on it. Mercedes put the check inside her purse and then hit Silas with the purse for making her bend down.

Rex stood over his friend, furious.

"Nigga, you pull a gun because I lost?"

Silas looked up at him.

"I was helping."

"You was ruining my fucking reputation twice."

Two of Knox's officers came from the lobby. They'd been outside with the cars. They saw my badge before they saw Silas and immediately changed the direction of their attention.

"Captain?"

"This nigga's evening is over."

They took him away while the band, after one frightened pause, found the song again.

Rex offered his hand.

"You ever need somebody in your corner."

I shook it.

"Stay out of mine first."

He laughed. Carefully, because it hurt. Then he bowed his head once, champion to captain, and went to find a drink he could lift without remembering me.

I turned back to the floor.

Shawna was dancing with Red again.

Nigga, I'd beaten a heavyweight, made two friends a hundred thousand dollars, and arrested a fool in less than a song. None of it had solved the one thing I was looking at.

***

Shawna told me later what Red said during that dance. She told me every word because I asked her every word, and because some nights loving a woman means hearing the part that makes you want to break your own furniture.

He began with the song.

“You used to sing this upstairs.”

“I sang a lot of things.”

“Before Dante.”

“I had a life before all of you.”

Red drew her a little closer. To everybody else, they looked beautiful. Two people moving together at a party full of people who believed beauty was the best possible excuse.

“You could have that life now.”

“Could I?”

“Whatever you want.”

She looked at the ring on his hand. Blue against the green sleeve. He noticed her looking and turned his hand away to bring her through another step.

“I want him left alone,” she said.

“Already thinking about that nigga?”

“His name is Aiden.”

“I know what the nigga's name is.”

Red smiled for somebody passing them. Shawna had to smile too.

“You said you were tired of running,” he said when they were alone inside the music again.

“I am.”

“You said you wanted to come home.”

“I said I wanted somewhere I could sleep.”

“My bed was never the problem.”

She almost pulled away then. I had seen it from across the room: the small hard line her shoulder made beneath his hand.

He held on.

“Don't do that tonight, Shawna.”

“Then don't talk to me like that.”

For a moment he stopped guiding her. They stood with couples turning on either side.

“Do you know what it felt like?” he asked. “Standing there while he put that ring on you? Paying for a room where you were going to spend the night with him?”

“Dante was your friend.”

“Nigga knew.”

“Knew what?”

“That his nigga saw you first.”

Shawna looked him in the face.

“You all keep saying that like I was a fucking parking space.”

His fingers tightened. Then loosened. He gave another careful smile to the room.

“I could've given you everything.”

“Then give me the diamond.”

The song carried on without them.

“That's what tonight is for,” she said. “You said you wanted me to know how serious you were. Show me.”

“And Aiden?”

“You let him walk out.”

Red looked across the floor at me.

“Will he?”

Shawna put her hand against his cheek.

“He will if I tell him to.”

That was the part of the dance I could see. Her touching his face. His eyes going soft. My woman telling another man something that made him look at me like I was already gone.

I finished my drink.

Nigga, I should've broken the glass in my own hand. It would've been less stupid than what I did next.

***

Nigga, I went onto the floor.

Tank said my name. Rosa stepped toward me. I kept moving.

I told myself I would only take Shawna aside for a second. Ask if she was all right. Let Red know that whatever he imagined was happening, there was a living nigga standing right there with a say in it.

“Nigga, your dance over,” I said.

Red didn't stop.

“Nigga, you hear the band? The band's still playing.”

I put a hand on his shoulder.

Now he stopped.

Shawna looked at my hand. Then my face. She was trying to tell me something without making a sound, and I was trying so hard to prove I loved her that I stopped listening.

“Nigga, that hand comes off me,” Red said quietly.

“Nigga, yours comes off her first.”

Three men in dark jackets moved from the edge of the room. Tank moved too. The singer saw what was happening and missed a word. The band kept playing under it.

Shawna stepped between us.

“Aiden. Go sit down.”

I stared at her.

“What?”

“You're embarrassing me.”

Nigga, I knew it was supposed to be a lie. I knew we had agreed she might have to hurt my feelings in front of him. Nobody had explained that my feelings were going to show up with fucking guns.

“You mean that about your nigga?”

We had agreed on the slap that afternoon, standing in front of our bedroom mirror. She had refused twice. I had said I could take one slap if it got her close enough to finish the plan. Now she gave me the one we had promised each other.

The sound cracked across the music. The whole room seemed to turn on the same neck.

I looked back at her. Her hand was shaking.

“I told you,” she said, her eyes bright with fury that wasn't all pretend, “to listen to me.”

Red watched us like somebody had just handed him a country.

I stepped back.

For one second, Shawna's face begged me to understand. Then she covered it and turned toward Red.

“Let's finish our dance.”

They moved away together.

I stood there with the whole fucking gala looking at me, and I had never needed a gun less or wanted one more.

Tank caught my sleeve.

“Come on.”

“Don't.”

“Come on.”

He brought me to the side of the room. I let him because I couldn't see where to put my feet.

Rosa came up beside us.

“She just kept you alive,” she said.

“I know.”

“Then act like you know.”

I looked at the floor. My cheek burned where she had hit me. My side burned where T had shot me. Apparently every nigga I loved came with a different place to hurt.

Across the ballroom, Red kissed Shawna's hand again.

This time I stayed where I was.

***

At nine, Red had the music stopped.

He walked onto a low stage with Shawna beside him. Behind them, attendants opened a curtain. A glass case stood under a white light.

Inside lay Blue Mercy.

I had spent three days hearing about that diamond. Forty million dollars. A marriage. A prison. Dante bleeding in the desert because he had come too close to the truth. Nigga, I expected the thing to stand up and say my name.

Nigga, it was smaller than I expected.

My nigga, that made it worse.

A little blue light in a velvet cradle, and all those lives wrapped around it. I looked at Marcellus. The old man's face went slack. Whatever he had prepared himself to feel, it hadn't been enough.

Red took the microphone.

“Some things wait a long time to come home.”

He looked at Shawna when he said it. People clapped. Nigga had spent his life hurting people and learned to pause in the places where strangers would congratulate him.

“Tonight isn't an auction,” he said. “Nobody in this room can afford what this means to me.”

A man in the front laughed too loudly. Red didn't look at him.

“Tonight is a promise.”

He held Shawna's hand up for the room. Dante's watch slid toward her elbow.

I heard Tank say something under his breath. I didn't ask what.

Marcellus moved forward with the jeweler's case we had brought for him. Red's men let him approach the stage. A name was given. A profession. The old man inclined his head as if he had spent his entire life attending evenings like this without wanting to burn one down.

Red watched him closely.

“You approve?”

Marcellus looked at the glass.

“I would like to see it closer.”

“Later.”

“A piece of this age deserves—”

“Later,” Red repeated.

His ring flashed blue when he lowered the microphone.

Marcellus looked at his hand again.

Then Shawna turned. She found me in the crowd and held my eyes. The plan was still moving. She needed me to move with it.

I nodded once.

Nigga, it felt like swallowing a knife.

***

An attendant came for me after the presentation.

“Mr. Redmond would like you upstairs.”

“Nigga can come get me.”

Tank touched my arm.

The attendant waited.

I looked toward Shawna. She was speaking to Rosa beside the stage. Rosa had a hand at her back. Both of them looked over when the attendant repeated the invitation.

Shawna nodded.

Fine. Nigga wanted a private conversation, I would give him a private conversation. I was tired of standing under expensive lights while he performed his ownership of everything I wanted alive.

Tank came with me. So did Marcellus. The attendant objected to the old man, and I told him if his boss was giving away forty million dollars, he could let a jeweler look at it before everybody left.

Red's office was above the ballroom. You could hear the party through the floor. The doors opened onto dark wood, city windows, and a desk big enough to lay a king out on.

Red stood behind it. Shawna was already there, having come through another door. She held a small blue box.

“I thought you might prefer privacy,” Red said.

“For what?”

“The end.”

Shawna took a step toward me.

Red put his hand on her shoulder.

“Tell him.”

Her face was pale. I didn't know how much of it was acting anymore.

“Aiden, take the box.”

“Come here to your nigga.”

“Take it.”

She held it out. I took it because her hand was shaking, and because for a moment all I could think about was making that stop.

Inside lay the blue stone from the ballroom.

Red watched my face.

“Forty million,” he said. “Enough to start over anywhere.”

I looked at him.

“Nigga, you think I'm selling her?”

“I think she just sold you.”

Marcellus stepped forward. Red lifted one finger. Two men appeared beside the door.

The old man stopped.

Shawna's eyes moved from Red to the men, then back to me.

Something had changed. We had come to steal the diamond and take the truth. Red was handing me the diamond. He had stopped asking questions. He looked like a man standing in a grave he had dug for somebody else.

He opened a drawer.

“And since your friends are so interested in history.”

He put a flat leather folder on the desk.

DANTE was written across a white label.

Shawna made a sound I had never heard from her before.

I reached for the folder.

Red let me take it.

That was when I knew we were in serious fucking trouble.



Red opened the wide drawer in his desk and pushed a folder toward me.

“Captain wants evidence,” he said. “Let the captain read.”

I took it.

## 11. The Money at the Bottom

The first page had a date. The second had numbers. On the third, beside Valentino's name, somebody had written *settled* in red ink.

Under it was a copy of the order we had found in the watch.

Red had kept his own.

I looked up at him.

“Nigga, you sick motherfucker.”

“Nigga, careful where you point that mouth.”

Shawna snatched the pages from my hand. She found the order. Read it. Turned the page like there might be something on the other side that could make it less real.

She already knew what it said. I had watched her read the original. Knowing didn't make her ready to see it sitting in a drawer under the man's desk, waiting beside his good pens.

“You kept this?” she asked.

Red didn't answer her directly.

“T believed in records. Nigga kept everything.”

“You're sitting behind the desk.”

“Shawna.”

“You're sitting behind the fucking desk.”

She threw the order at him. It struck his chest and fell across the edge of the blotter.

He looked down at it. Then at me.

“I was going to make this generous.”

“Nigga, shut your mouth.”

Tank moved closer to me. The men at the door moved with him.

Red noticed. His expression changed into something almost happy.

“Maybe you should ask your man what generosity looks like.”

Tank went still.

I turned toward him.

“What the fuck is this nigga talking about?”

“Aiden.”

“Nigga. What?”

Red picked up a remote from the desk. A screen on the wall lit up.

An empty swimming pool filled it.

For a second I was back at the motel. T's gun against my side. Shawna on the balcony. Cash blowing across blue tiles while I tried to keep another man from deciding whether I got to breathe.

Then I saw Tank climbing down into the pool.

On the recording, our Mercedes was already gone.

Tank had a bag.

He began putting the money inside.

***

I watched until I couldn't.

“Nigga, you heard enough breathing in this room. Turn it off.”

Red left it playing.

Onscreen, Tank went back for another bag. The nigga stepped around the same place where T had fallen, leaned over, and picked up a loose bundle beside his shoe.

“Nigga. Turn it the fuck off.”

Red pressed the remote.

The office became quiet enough that I could hear Shawna breathing.

“Three million,” Red said. “All of it. Your friend is thorough.”

Tank looked at me. He didn't look away when I turned on him.

“Nigga, you took her money?”

“Nigga, I took it out the pool. I'm standing here saying that.”

“Don't play with me.”

“I'm not.”

“You watched her hold me together. You saw her drive off with me bleeding. And you went back for the fucking money?”

His jaw moved.

“Yes.”

I hit him.

I couldn't even remember deciding to. My fist caught the side of his face. Pain went through my ribs so hard my knees almost followed it. Tank stayed where he was.

I hit him again.

He took that one too.

“Nigga, look at me and hit me back.”

“No.”

“Hit me the fuck back.”

Shawna caught my arm. Tank's mouth was bleeding. He looked at her, then at me.

“I'm not hitting you.”

Red leaned against his desk.

“This is touching.”

I turned so fast Shawna tightened her grip.

“You say one more word—”

“And what? You'll die rich?”

He glanced at the blue box in my hand.

I had forgotten I was holding it. Forty million dollars, and I wanted to throw it through his fucking face.

Marcellus stepped closer to the desk. His eyes moved over the stone under the lamp. The look on his face stopped me.

“Aiden,” he said.

Red looked at him.

The old man didn't stop looking at the box.

“Close it.”

“What?”

“Close the box.”

I did.

He raised his eyes to mine.

Whatever he had seen, he didn't want Red hearing it yet.

***

Tank wiped his mouth with the back of his hand.

“It's at your house. Back of my closet. I moved it when we moved in.”

Shawna stared at him.

“All of it?”

“Every fucking dollar.”

“Why didn't you tell us?”

He looked down at the floor. Then he looked back up because I had stepped toward him again.

“Because I thought you was going to leave.”

That stopped me for half a breath.

“Nigga, what?”

“You got her. T was dead. You had the car. You was talking about water and houses and taking her anywhere. I thought you was gone.”

“Nigga, I was fucking dying.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

His eyes filled, which made me angrier. Tank was not supposed to do that. Tank was supposed to be something solid I could hit until the rest of the world made sense.

“I thought if you left, I'd have something,” he said. “That's it. That's the whole thing.”

Red shook his head.

“Tell the nigga the rest.”

Tank looked at Red.

“You called me.”

“And you answered.”

“You sent me that video.”

“And you answered again.”

Shawna let go of my arm.

“You told him where we were?”

“No.”

“Tank.”

“No, Shawna. I didn't tell him about the house by the lake. Didn't tell him what you was doing. He knew you were coming here because you fucking told him.”

Red's smile thinned.

“I offered him his place back.”

I looked at Tank.

“What place?”

“Yours,” Red said.

The room seemed to move farther away from me. All those nights with Tank outside my door. The spare phone. The way he watched when I called men who used to answer to T and heard them answer to me instead.

“You want it?” I asked him.

Tank said nothing.

“Nigga, I'm standing right here. You want it?”

He looked at my white suit. At the red mark coming through near my side. I hadn't noticed it before.

Then he shook his head.

“Nigga, I wanted you to ask me to stay. Me. Not whoever drove the car.”

I didn't have an answer ready for that. Nigga, I had an answer ready for a hundred different betrayals. That one caught me with my hands empty.

Red opened another drawer. Took out a car key and tossed it onto the desk.

“You can still make the intelligent decision,” he told Tank. “Bring me my money. Walk out of here with a future.”

Tank looked at the key.

He picked it up.

My whole body went cold.

Then the nigga threw it through Red's window.

The glass cracked under the impact without breaking apart. The key bounced down onto the carpet.

Tank looked at the window. Then at Red.

“Fuck your car too.”

***

Everything happened close.

One of Red's men caught Tank by the shoulder. Tank turned and drove him into the wall hard enough to knock a framed picture sideways. The other man reached inside his jacket.

Shawna grabbed the desk lamp and smashed it across his arm.

The room flashed white as the bulb burst. Red caught her from behind. I went toward them, and the man beside the door hit me in the side with something heavy.

Nigga, the whole world left my lungs.

I fell against the desk. Papers slid beneath my hands. Red dragged Shawna toward the inner door while she fought him, her shoes scraping the floor.

“Let her go.”

It came out barely louder than breathing.

I tried again.

“Let her fucking go.”

Tank tore the man away from me. Marcellus caught my sleeve and pulled me upright. I had the blue box in one hand and Dante's folder under the other. I don't know why I held on. Maybe because letting go of one more thing felt like the end of the whole fucking world.

A gun went off.

The sound filled the room. A piece of wood jumped from the desk beside my hand. Somebody downstairs screamed, then more people screamed, then the party stopped pretending to be beautiful.

Red had Shawna in front of him by the inner doorway.

The gun was against her.

I stopped.

Tank stopped.

For one second, everybody did exactly what Red wanted.

“There,” he said. “You can learn.”

Shawna's hair had come down. One earring was gone. She stared at me over his arm, and I could see her trying not to cry because she thought that would make me do something stupid.

Nigga, I was already past stupid. I was standing in the place where I would've paid for my next breath with every life in the building if it let me reach her.

“Take me,” I said.

Red looked almost offended.

“Nigga, I don't want you.”

“Let her walk. I'll stay.”

“I heard you.”

Shawna shook her head. Just once. Hard.

“Aiden.”

I couldn't look away from the gun.

“Aiden, take it and go.”

“I'm not leaving you.”

“Go.”

The inner door opened wider. Another man stood behind Red. Shawna saw him before I did. Something in her eyes changed, and she used the last second she had to look straight at Tank.

“Get him out.”

Then Red pulled her through the door.

I went after them.

Tank caught me around the chest. I fought that nigga harder than I had fought anybody the night they jumped me in. I hit him in the face. In the shoulder. I told him I would kill him. I meant it. He kept pulling me away while a man behind us shouted and another shot struck the wall.

Marcellus was at the outer door. Rosa appeared beyond him with her red dress gathered in one fist. Her face changed when she saw Shawna wasn't with us.

“Where is she?”

“He has her,” Marcellus said.

Rosa tried to go past him.

The old man caught her hand.

“Not this way.”

Tank dragged me into the hall.

I could still hear Shawna on the other side of the office.

Then I couldn't.

***

We reached the ballroom stairs just as one of Red's men pulled the front doors shut.

Nigga, he actually put his back against them. A whole room full of people trying to leave, and this motherfucker decided the most important thing in the building was the fact that his boss hadn't said they could.

"Open them!" Rosa shouted.

He raised his gun.

Tank pulled me behind the banister as the shot struck the wall above us.

I could still hear Shawna's voice in my head. *Take it and go.* I had taken the box. I had taken the papers. Nigga, I had left the only thing in that room I wanted, and now a man was pointing a gun at Rosa because he thought the evening still had instructions.

I put the blue box inside my jacket. The folder went under my belt. My badge lay against both of them.

"Put me down."

Tank tightened his grip.

"Aiden—"

"Nigga, I ain't going back upstairs. I'm getting these people out. Put me on my fucking feet."

He did.

The room stopped tipping after one terrible second. I caught the rail. Got enough breath to remember I had lungs. Then I looked down at the man by the doors.

"Police!"

He laughed.

I opened my jacket.

The gold badge caught the light.

"Captain, nigga. Try your joke with the right title."

His eyes moved from the badge to my gun.

For half a second I thought he might be intelligent.

Then he fired again.

I went over the lower banister and hit the carpet beside a table. Tank came down the stairs behind me, firing toward the door. People crawled away from us. A woman in diamonds grabbed my sleeve and asked if we were going to die.

"Not with that nigga shooting," I told her. "Get behind the table."

She went. Her husband followed so closely he lost a shoe and didn't even look back for it.

A second guard came through the side corridor. He saw me crouched beside the table and tried to get his gun around the corner.

Rex Crown hit him from behind.

The two men crashed into a champagne tower. Glass fell like a crystal fucking waterfall. Rex held on, driving the guard into the wall with all the strength he'd been saving for a better ending to his night.

"Captain!" he shouted.

I fired past him toward the front door. The guard there dropped behind a planter. Tank reached the doors and pulled one open while the people closest to him ran into the lobby.

Rex wrestled the second man to the floor. The guard hit him across the face with the gun. Rex went sideways, stunned, and the man rolled free.

I crossed the room before he could stand.

He raised the weapon at Rex.

I hit him with the heavy blue box through my jacket.

Forty million dollars made a solid fucking sound against his head. Later I'd find out it wasn't worth forty million. At that moment it was worth exactly one living boxer.

The man went down. I took his gun away and kicked it under the bar.

Rex looked up at me with blood running from his eyebrow.

"Twice," he said.

"Nigga, you keeping score now?"

"You beat me. Then you saved me."

"Keep up. Night ain't over."

He got up laughing, blood on his teeth, and put his huge shoulder under my good arm. Together we went toward the doors while Tank held them and Rosa pushed Marcellus ahead of her.

Above the staircase, the statue's bowl of fire tipped.

Something had struck its base. I never saw what. I heard metal grind, looked up, and saw burning liquid spill down the bronze woman's arms. Flame ran over the flowers beneath her. The statue leaned toward the people in the passage below.

Mercedes stood directly underneath it pulling a man off the floor.

"Move!" I shouted.

She looked up.

The bronze woman fell.

I got to Mercedes as the statue struck the banister. Bronze snapped wood. The bowl flew one way, the statue another, and I drove both her and the man through the open passage before the whole staircase's broken lower section hit the carpet behind us.

Heat rolled over my back.

My side went white with pain.

Mercedes caught my face in her hands when we stopped sliding.

"Nigga. Nigga, you got me?"

"I got you."

"You sure?"

"Baby, count your fucking legs."

She looked down at herself. Two legs. One shoe. A dress she was going to mention for the rest of my natural life.

Then she kissed my forehead so hard I thought the bullet might come out from gratitude.

"You beautiful, stupid, magnificent motherfucker."

I tried to get up. Couldn't the first time. Rex and Tank reached me together and lifted.

The people behind us had found their way through. Porsche stood outside holding the lobby door open with one leg and shouting directions nobody dared ignore. The woman in diamonds I'd spoken to stopped beside me, caught my hand, and pressed her wedding ring into it.

"For saving us."

I pushed it back.

"Nigga, keep your husband nervous. I got a woman waiting."

She laughed through her tears.

My own woman wasn't waiting outside.

That thought hit as soon as the cold air touched my face. All the people I'd brought out moved around me, alive and calling me Captain, and the one voice I needed wasn't among them.

I turned toward the stairs again.

Tank caught my shoulder.

"Not that way."

The look on his face stopped me harder than his hands.

"She told me to get you out. Nigga, you alive enough to go get her somewhere else. That's what we got left."

I let him take me to the car.


Rosa went with Marcellus to another car. Before she got in, she pushed one of the gala photographs through my open window.

“She gave me this,” she said.

The picture showed Shawna between me and Red. His hand against her arm. His ring under the lights. My hand at her waist like I thought holding her in a photograph meant the world couldn't take her anywhere.

Rosa's voice broke.

“She told me to keep one for when you two got married.”

I stared at it.

Then Tank drove. The police Lamborghini stayed with Knox's officers at the Saint; they would bring it back when the road was clear.

***

We didn't get far before Marcellus called.

I put him on speaker. My fingers had gone sticky against the blue box.

“The stone,” he said. “Aiden. Listen carefully. The stone you have is the duplicate.”

Tank looked at me.

I opened the box beneath the dashboard light.

Blue looked back at me.

“You sure?”

“Nigga, I made it.”

I shut the lid.

Nigga. We had gone in with Shawna and come out with a fucking lie in velvet.

“Does Red know?” Tank asked.

Marcellus didn't answer right away.

“He expected you to take it.”

The road lights passed across the windshield. One. Another. Another. I counted them because if I stopped looking at something in front of me, I saw Red's arm across Shawna's chest.

Rosa took the phone.

“We still have the original order. And you have his papers.”

I looked at the folder against my leg. The corners were bent. On one page, a line of red ink lay beneath Valentino's name. On another was a list of payments tied to the old jewel transaction. Evidence of the life Red had built out of other people's bodies.

“I don't want his fucking papers.”

“I know.”

“I want her.”

“I know, Aiden.”

Tank drove faster. Not wild. Just like every second now had somebody's hand around its throat.

My phone lit up with an unknown number.

I answered before the first ring finished.

“Shawna?”

Red breathed into the line.

“I wondered how long it would take you to notice the gift.”

I put the phone against my ear so hard it hurt.

“Let me hear her.”

“Your friend has my three million. You have papers that belong in my desk. And somewhere, somebody is holding a very old note.”

“Let me hear her.”

A sound came through. Movement. A door. Then Shawna.

“Baby.”

I closed my eyes.

“I'm here.”

“I know.”

“I'm coming.”

“I know.”

Red took the phone away.

“The unfinished casino in the desert. Midnight. Bring the money. Bring the papers. Bring the original.”

I looked at the clock on the dashboard.

We had less than three hours.

“If you hurt her—”

“Then come before I get bored.”

The call ended.

Tank kept his eyes on the road.

For a while neither of us spoke. I held the photograph in one hand and the worthless blue box in the other. My white suit was ruined. My cheek still held the heat of Shawna's slap. Every place she had touched me that night felt like the only part of my body still alive.

“Take me to the money,” I told Tank.

“Yeah.”

“All of it.”

“Yeah.”

I put the photograph inside my jacket, over the cross.

I had walked into the Saint thinking I could steal a fortune and a future in one night. Now that nigga had my future locked in a room somewhere, and all the money in Vegas couldn't make the next red light change.

“Tank.”

“What?”

“After we get her.”

He glanced at me.

“Nigga, we are getting her.”

I looked out at the city.

“After we get her, there isn't going to be enough desert left to hide what we do to him.”

## 12. Everybody Bring Your Heart

At nine forty, I put my fist through the glass door of the house and cut myself for a woman who wasn't there to tell me to stop.

Tank caught my wrist before I could do it again.

“Aiden.”

I swung on him.

My nigga took it. His head went sideways, and his hand stayed around my wrist. There was blood on his lower lip. I hit him again, harder, and something in my wounded side pulled so sharp that my knees almost went.

“Nigga, let go.”

“No.”

“Nigga, you had the money.”

“Yeah.”

“This whole fucking time.”

“Yeah.”

I tried to drag him into the broken door with me. He turned his body and held me against the wall instead. Tank weighed enough to end an argument by falling asleep on the other person. I was hurting too bad to move him, and I hated that he knew it.

“Nigga, you let me walk in there thinking I knew what was mine.”

“I know.”

“You let him stand there and laugh at me.”

His face changed then. The shame had been sitting on him like sweat, but now something deeper came up. He looked past me into the house.

“I heard him,” Tank said. “I was standing right there.”

I shoved him once more. He let me go.

The front room still looked like a place where money went to get drunk. Two bottles of champagne sat in silver buckets. A woman I didn't know had left one red heel under the piano. Somebody had put a little pile of cocaine on a photograph of me and Shawna because there wasn't enough table in the whole fucking house. Her face was under it.

I swept everything onto the floor.

“Get these niggas out.”

There were only four men left inside, and all four were already moving.

“Everybody,” I said.

One of them had a woman's handbag slung over his shoulder. He looked down at it like he'd just discovered a child. He went back toward the hall, remembered my face, and left with it.

Tank shut the ruined door as well as it could be shut.

“You want me gone too?”

I looked at him. His jacket was torn. He'd lost a cuff link at the Saint. There was blood on his hands that wasn't mine or his, and he'd followed me out anyway.

“Get the money.”

He went upstairs.

I sat on the piano bench because it was the nearest thing and because my legs had started shaking. Shawna had been sitting there that afternoon. She'd played three notes, missed the fourth, and told me the piano was cheap. I'd offered to buy her another one. She'd asked if I was going to buy a different instrument every time she made a mistake.

I'd told her yes.

Nigga, I'd meant it. We would've had a fucking orchestra by Christmas.

Now her perfume was still in the room and Red had her.

I put my head down. For one ugly second I saw him kissing her. I saw the dance again, her hand on his shoulder, the way she'd leaned close because we'd agreed she had to. I'd said I could take it. I'd stood there dressed like a king and discovered I couldn't take shit.

The case upstairs hit something with a heavy thump.

“Don't you drop her money,” I shouted.

“I got it.”

“You been saying that.”

He came down carrying the money in two bags. No silver case. He'd saved the cash and left the case broken in the pool, just like he'd left the rest of us thinking it was all gone.

He opened the bags on the dining table.

Three million dollars filled the space between two candles Shawna had bought because she said the house smelled like men lying to each other.

Tank stood back.

“All of it.”

“You count it?”

“More than once.”

“That make you feel good?”

He shook his head.

I picked up a bundle and threw it at him. It hit his chest and broke against the floor.

“There's your fucking tip.”

He watched the bills settle.

“Nigga, look at me.”

He did.

“What did you think was gonna happen?”

“Nigga, I thought you were gonna die.”

The room got quiet enough for me to hear the refrigerator.

Tank rubbed both hands over his head.

“That morning, before she drove off. You were bleeding all over the seat. She leaned through the open door and kept asking you to look at her. You kept saying the same shit about a house. Water. A room for singing. Nigga, you weren't answering her half the time. I thought you were already gone.”

“So you went shopping.”

“So I went back.”

His voice rose. He looked ashamed of that too, but he kept going.

“T was there. The money was there. I looked at that nigga on the ground, and I thought about all the years I stood behind him. Every room. Every car. Every time somebody said his name wrong, I was the nigga who got up.”

“You loved that nigga.”

“Yeah.”

I stared at him.

“Say it again.”

“I loved him. You want me to lie about that too?”

His lip was bleeding down his chin. He didn't wipe it.

“You knew him one night. I knew him ten years. He was a piece of shit. I know. He'd give you something with one hand and keep the other around your neck. I know that too. But when I got there, I still wanted the nigga to get up.”

I looked down at the money.

“And when he didn't?”

“I took what was left.”

That was the first thing he'd said that didn't make me want to put him through a window.

It didn't make me forgive him either.

“That nigga Red got to you after.”

Tank nodded.

“Said he knew. Said the money bought him whatever he asked for.”

“And you believed that nigga.”

“For a while.”

“Until when?”

Tank looked straight at me.

“Until he put his hand on her and you stopped breathing.”

I felt the room tilt.

“Nigga, don't.”

“I'm telling you.”

“Don't tell me what I looked like.”

“You looked like you did in that car.”

I picked up a candle and threw it into the fireplace. The glass broke. Tank didn't move.

“I ain't dying in another fucking car.”

“Then let your nigga drive. Let me get one fucking thing right.”

The lights outside went blue.

For one stupid second I thought they had brought Shawna home. I was on my feet before I heard the cars stop. Tank moved toward the front window, then turned back with a look I didn't like.

"Not ours."

A man came through the broken door wearing a police uniform and the kind of confidence that had never learned what a door could mean to the man behind it.

Captain Wade Frost. Forty-six. Silver hair. Pink face. Two officers behind him, both younger, both looking at the money on the table as if the room had just asked them a very personal question.

Frost looked at my blood, then the bags, then my badge.

"Take it off."

I stared at him.

"Nigga, you selling shirts now?"

"The badge."

Tank stepped between him and the table.

"You got an appointment?"

"Move."

"Nigga, this a house. Ask like you walked into one."

Frost put his hand on his gun. The two officers behind him looked at each other. Neither moved closer.

I came around Tank.

"What you want?"

"Redmond filed a complaint. Theft. Assault. Armed men at his property. A woman being held against her will."

I felt my face go cold.

"He got that last part right."

"We're here to recover the money and suspend your authority until this is settled."

"Nigga, who sent you?"

"You don't question me."

"That's interesting. I'm doing it beautifully."

He took a folded paper from his pocket and held it toward me.

I didn't take it.

"Knox sign that?"

"The chief has larger concerns."

"Nigga, the chief bought me a Lamborghini yesterday. She thinking about me plenty."

One of the younger officers looked at the paper again. A Black woman, thirty-one, name of Bell on her chest. She'd been at the station when I brought the robbers in. She had eaten the lunch I bought. I could see her trying to fit that morning into the room she was standing in now.

Frost noticed her hesitation.

"Bell. Collect the bags."

She didn't move.

"I said collect them."

I put my phone on the table and called Knox.

Frost stepped toward it.

Tank caught his wrist.

"Nigga, let the telephone ring."

Knox answered on the second ring.

"Aiden. Tell me you have her."

For half a second I couldn't speak. The fact that she knew. The fact that her first question wasn't about the money or the fire or the badge she had pinned on a criminal's chest the morning before.

"Not yet. You send Frost?"

Silence.

Then her voice changed.

"Put me on speaker."

I did.

"Wade," she said.

Frost stopped pulling against Tank's hand.

"Chief. We're securing—"

"You at his house?"

"We have evidence of—"

"You at his house, Wade?"

He looked at the phone.

"Yes."

"Then you listen carefully. Captain Aiden retains his command. You have no order from me. You bring whatever Redmond put in your hand to my office, and you bring your own badge with it."

The room went quiet enough for me to hear Bell breathe out.

Frost's face changed. Whatever authority he had brought through the door began leaving him through his eyes.

"You choosing this thug?"

I tilted my head.

"Nigga, you can say Captain while you cry."

Knox didn't laugh.

"I'm choosing the officer who carried people out while your friend locked the doors. Get out of his house."

Frost's hand jerked toward the phone.

Tank let go of his wrist just as I came forward. The man stumbled into the table, knocking a candle over. One of the money bags slid toward the edge. He reached for the bag with one hand and his gun with the other.

I hit him before either hand got what it wanted.

The table rocked. Money flew across the floor. Frost went backward into the chair and took it down with him. His gun skidded under the piano.

Bell already had her weapon out. It was pointed at Frost.

"Stay down, sir."

He looked up at her in disbelief.

"You're taking his side too?"

"I'm following my chief."

"Nigga," I said, "people keep making this clear for you."

Frost tried to get up anyway. Tank put a hand on his shoulder and returned him to the carpet with the calm of a man correcting where a heavy box belonged.

I picked up the folded paper.

Red's handwriting sat across the bottom. Three short lines. The money back. Aiden disarmed. Shawna's name used like a rope around both requests.

I held it toward Bell.

She read it. Her mouth tightened.

"He sent you for her rescue money," she said.

Frost didn't answer.

She put him in cuffs.

The other officer picked up the paper, folded it carefully, and stood beside her. He looked at me before they left.

"Captain, where do you need us after this?"

I looked at the floor. At Shawna's million-dollar future scattered beside the leg of a chair. At Tank kneeling to gather the bills before anybody stepped on them.

"With Knox. Make sure nobody else comes here in a uniform they borrowed from Red."

He nodded.

"Yes, Captain."

They took Frost out through the door he hadn't bothered knocking on. The police lights moved across the ceiling, then went away.

Knox was still on the phone.

"Aiden."

"I'm here."

"I have officers at the Saint. He's moved her. Your car's safe. We can bring it to you."

"Keep the roads open. Keep my people from getting stopped on the way to that unfinished casino. That's where he's taking her. Midnight."

"I'll hold the outside when you get there."

"Chief."

"What?"

I looked at the badge inside my ruined white jacket.

"Nigga doesn't forget this."

Her voice softened just a little.

"Then bring your wife home, Captain. Give me something worth remembering too."

The call ended.

Tank put the last bundle back into the bag. Every dollar stayed. He set the fallen candle upright and looked at me.

"Nigga, you really are the police."

"We discussed that at graduation."

"I heard the words."

"You seeing the picture now?"

He nodded slowly.

Then, for the first time since Red opened that drawer, my brother smiled at me without looking ashamed of the fact that he wanted to.


The front door moved behind us.

Rosa came in wearing a man's coat over her gala dress. One earring was gone. She had Marcellus by the arm. Tank brought the decoy's box in from the Mercedes and handed it to the old man, who took it like he was being given the head of somebody he used to know.

My phone rang again before Rosa reached the table.

Rex Crown.

I almost didn't answer. Then I remembered the man coming out of the champagne with a stranger's gun in his face and took the call.

“Captain.”

“Busy.”

“I know. Your woman.”

I shut my eyes.

“Nigga, everybody knows?”

“Everybody who saw you get those people out. They're still outside saying your name.”

“I don't need my name. I need her.”

“Then tell me where.”

I looked at Tank. At the bags. At my own hand bleeding into the towel Rosa had put down for me.

“You hurt?” I asked Rex.

“My pride's in worse shape than my face.”

“Then stay with it.”

“Nigga, you think I called to get sent home?”

I didn't answer.

“You beat me in front of everybody,” he said. “Could've let me get killed in front of the same people. You came back. I ain't carrying that around owing you forever. Give me somewhere to bring it.”

I looked toward the dark windows.

“Unfinished casino. Desert. Midnight.”

He repeated it once.

“I'm there.”

“Rex.”

“What?”

“Your friend with the gun—”

“Not coming. I got better friends.”

I laughed once, and it hurt enough that Rosa looked up sharply.

“What?” she asked.

“Nigga making sense.”

Rex heard her. His voice got louder.

“Tell those women their money's good. Tell them I don't stop being a gentleman because a beautiful motherfucker rearranged my afternoon.”

Rosa took the phone from me.

“Then bring your gentleman ass ready to help.”

“Yes, ma'am.”

She handed it back after he hung up.

“Another one?”

I looked at her.

“Another what?”

“Man who'd walk into a fire because you remembered he was in it.”

I didn't have anything clever ready.

She touched my good shoulder.

“Use them, baby. Let the people who love you do something.”

“Which one of you stupid niggas broke the door?” Rosa asked.

Nobody answered.

She saw my hand.

“Of course.”

She came straight to me, took my wrist, and looked at the cuts. Her fingers were shaking. She hadn't been shaking when she crossed the room.

“Where is she?”

“Red.”

“I know fucking Red. Where is that nigga?”

“He's bringing her to that casino in the desert. Midnight.”

“Then why are you bleeding on the furniture?”

I started to speak. Rosa gripped harder.

“You can be angry after she gets here. You can buy a mountain and fight the whole mountain. Right now I need you standing.”

“Don't talk to me like I'm a kid.”

“Then quit making me.”

Tank turned his face away. I looked at him.

“Something funny?”

“No.”

“Good.”

Rosa sat me down and went to get a towel. Marcellus stayed by the table. He looked at the money, then at me, then at the floor where the first bundle had come apart.

“Yours?” he asked.

“Hers.”

He nodded as though that settled a price we'd been fighting over.

When Rosa came back, she had my phone. It was vibrating in her hand.

Red had sent a picture.

Shawna sat in a white chair. Her dress was torn at the shoulder. Her hair covered one side of her face. Red stood behind her with his hand resting under her chin, his blue ring turned toward the camera.

I got up so fast the bench fell over.

Rosa caught my shirt.

“Aiden.”

“I'm gonna kill that nigga.”

“Look at her.”

“I am looking.”

“No. Her.”

I made myself stop staring at his hand.

Shawna was looking into the camera. Her mouth was swollen a little on one side. Her eyes were open and furious. She wasn't looking away from whoever would see it.

Under the picture, Red had written four words.

*She remembers this room.*

I called him.

He answered on the first ring.

“Nigga,” I said, “if you touch her again—”

“She's sitting right here.”

“Put her on.”

“Ask nice.”

I couldn't get air into my chest.

Rosa squeezed the back of my neck. I felt every finger.

“Please,” I said.

Red laughed softly.

Then Shawna was there.

“Aiden?”

“Baby.”

“Are you hurt?”

I closed my eyes.

“No.”

“Don't lie to me.”

“I'm here.”

There was a little noise on her end. Fabric moving. A breath that stopped too early.

“Tell Rosa I ruined her dress.”

Rosa pressed a fist against her mouth.

“She don't give a fuck about the dress, baby.”

“She does. Tell her I'll pay for it.”

Rosa took the phone out of my hand.

“You owe me a fucking earring too, bitch.”

Shawna laughed once.

That one little laugh made the whole room stand still.

Then Red came back.

“Midnight. Bring whatever you stole tonight. Bring my money. Come ready to apologize.”

I took the phone.

“You want me on my knees?”

“Now you're listening.”

“Nigga, you keep her alive. You can see me any way you want.”

He hung up.

I stood there holding the dead call. Tank picked up the bench and set it behind me. I didn't sit.

Marcellus held out his hand.

“Let me see that photograph.”

I gave the old nigga the phone because I had run out of things to break that would make Red feel it.

The old man enlarged the picture.

His thumb stopped on the ring.

“There you are,” he whispered.

I looked up.

Marcellus had begun to smile, and there wasn't a happy thing in it.

## 13. What She Told Me After

Shawna told me what happened in that room later. She told it sitting beside me with her bare feet under my leg, stopping whenever she wanted water and starting again wherever it hurt. I asked her the same questions until she threatened to throw the glass at me. Some parts she could give me word for word. Some parts she wouldn't give anybody.

This is what she told me.

Red took her back through the Saint after we'd gone, with two men behind her and one hand around her arm. The party hadn't completely emptied. A few people were still holding drinks because nobody had personally told them the good time was dead.

She saw a woman by the elevators lift a phone.

“Get my good side,” Shawna said.

Red pulled her harder.

The woman lowered the phone.

“You always gotta do that?” he asked.

“Look good?”

“Make a fucking scene.”

“You dragged me out of one.”

He took her into a private room she knew. White chairs. White carpet. A huge painting of a horse coming out of the ocean. Red loved that painting. He'd once spent twenty minutes explaining the horse to her while she tried to work out whether she could leave without him noticing.

Tonight the carpet had somebody else's blood on it.

One of the men had brought her purse from the office. Red took it from him and put it on the table. Then he shut the door and told the men to wait outside.

Shawna said that was when she first got scared enough to feel cold.

Not at the gunfire. Not at his hand on her arm. At the little click of the door and the fact that he wanted no one else to hear him talk.

“Sit,” he said.

She stayed standing.

“Shawna.”

“Give me a cigarette.”

He went to the table and took one from a silver box. He lit it before he handed it to her, like he was bringing her flowers.

“I could've killed that nigga,” he said.

She took the cigarette.

“Nigga, you tried.”

“Nigga ran.”

“My nigga's coming back.”

Red laughed.

“They always come back for the money.”

“Then put me outside and see.”

He didn't answer that. He poured a drink, missed the glass a little, and wiped the spill with his sleeve. Shawna noticed because Red never cleaned anything. He would wait for somebody to come across a whole room to pick up a thing beside his shoe.

He was angry enough to forget who he thought he was.

“You think that nigga loves you?”

She smoked.

“I asked you something.”

“I heard you.”

“That nigga loves winning. You're what he stole. Soon as you're just a woman in his house, watch what happens.”

She looked at the painting instead of him. The horse had its mouth open. She'd always thought it looked surprised to be swimming.

“He begged, you know,” Red said.

She kept looking at the horse.

“Dante. That nigga begged us to look after you.”

“Us.”

Red stopped with the bottle in his hand.

Shawna turned toward him.

“You were standing there?”

“I didn't say that.”

“Then who told you?”

He put the bottle down too carefully.

“Everybody knew what happened.”

“I didn't.”
