He looked toward the door. She watched him do it. Shawna said she would've given anything to have the old letter and the order in her hand right then, to lay them in his lap and make him touch what he'd done. All she had was the watch. She turned it around her wrist.

“What did he call me?” she asked.

“What?”

“When he begged. What name did he use?”

“Your fucking name.”

“Which one?”

“Shawna, I don't remember every—”

“Dante called me Trouble.”

He stared at her.

“Miss Trouble if he was happy. Mrs. Trouble when I was mad at him. He'd come in and say, Mrs. Trouble, I fucked up, and I'd know I had to sit down before that nigga finished talking.”

She laughed, and that made Red angrier than anything she'd said. She couldn't help it. She was remembering Dante coming into their little apartment with a whole bumper in his hands. He'd taken it off the car he'd borrowed for their honeymoon. He'd brought the bumper upstairs because he thought she might be less mad if he hadn't left any of it behind.

“Nigga carried it like flowers,” she told me later. She laughed then too. I hated the dead nigga for making her laugh with something he'd done years before I met her, and I wanted to hear it again anyway.

In Red's room, she wiped her eyes with the back of her wrist.

“You don't know how he talked to me.”

“I know what he was.”

“Then talk about that. Talk about your dead nigga. You don't get to talk about mine.”

Red came close enough that she could smell the drink.

“You keep making him a saint.”

“No. I'm remembering my husband. That nigga stole money, lied badly, and left his socks in the bed. I loved him. You think telling me he was a bad man changes something?”

She touched the watch again.

“Tell me something I don't fucking know.”

“That nigga Dante said the same shit,” Red went on. “A house. A different life. Music. That nigga was gonna buy you a microphone and call himself a husband.”

Shawna turned back.

“That nigga was my husband.”

“I paid for the wedding.”

“You paid for the room.”

“I paid for everything.”

“Then you should've kept the receipts. Maybe the preacher would've married you.”

Red threw the glass.

It hit the wall beside the horse and broke. Shawna said she didn't move, which she was proud of until she told me why. Her legs had gone stiff. She couldn't move.

He came toward her.

“You used to know how to talk to me.”

“I used to need you to stop talking.”

He caught her face in one hand. That's where the picture came from. He called one of his men in and told him to take it while he held her there.

Shawna stared into the phone.

“He'll see you touching me,” she said.

“That's the point.”

“I know.”

The man took the picture and left. Red's ring dragged against the edge of her jaw when he let go.

She looked at it.

“You wearing it now?”

His hand closed.

“Wearing what?”

“All that money, and you still want somebody to notice.”

He put his hand in his pocket.

A telephone rang outside the room, and Red's face changed when the man at the door told him who was calling.

“Frost?” Shawna asked.

Red looked at her.

She knew the name. Had heard it in enough penthouse conversations to recognize which uniform Red meant when he said the city would be reasonable.

The man at the door whispered something.

Red took the phone so hard the man stepped backward.

“What do you mean arrested?”

Shawna leaned back in the white chair.

Nigga, when she told me this part later, she made me listen twice. Said the first time I'd smiled so much I hadn't heard the whole sentence.

Red kept listening.

“Knox said what?”

Shawna lifted her cigarette.

“My captain?”

He covered the phone.

“Shut up.”

“I'm just wondering which nigga finally made your policeman nervous.”

He went into the hallway to finish the call. Left the door open three inches. Left the man who'd taken the picture inside with her.

The man looked tired. Thirty-eight, name of Arlo, a little gray beginning in his beard. She knew him too. He'd once carried her groceries upstairs when the elevator broke and then apologized because Red heard him asking whether she was all right.

“You don't have to stand in here,” she told him.

He looked at the door.

“It's my job.”

“Nigga, your job's turning into a funeral.”

He didn't answer.

She stood up with the cigarette in one hand. He moved toward her. She lifted the other hand as if she only wanted him to stop crowding her.

Then she threw the heavy silver cigarette box into his face.

Arlo went back against the wall. She ran through the door, past Red with the telephone still against his ear, and into the corridor before either man understood that waiting quietly had ended.

Red shouted her name.

She kept running.

Her borrowed dress caught the corner of a table. She pulled free and left a strip of blue silk behind her. At the far end, the service doors were open. Light came through from a stairwell. She could hear men below, radios, a woman crying.

She hit the door with her shoulder and nearly fell over a waiter sitting on the landing.

He was holding his wrist. Blood marked his white cuff. Beside him stood a young-looking woman who told Shawna she was twenty-four when Shawna asked if she could lift him. Both of them had been trying to get past the men downstairs.

“Where's the outside door?” Shawna asked.

“Two floors,” the woman said. “But they won't let us—”

“Get him up.”

They lifted the waiter together. Shawna took his good side. The woman took the other. They started down the stairs, three people moving awkwardly, the blue dress dragging through dust and somebody else's dropped flowers.

Behind them, Red came through the service door.

“Shawna!”

She didn't look back.

“Nigga, if you want to help, get his fucking feet.”

Red caught her at the next landing. The woman with the waiter stopped. He pointed toward the stairs below.

“You two. Go.”

They stared.

“Go!”

Shawna held on to the waiter until the woman had him steady. Then she let them pass. She watched them reach the lower door, watched the woman look up at her once, watched them disappear into the light.

Red grabbed her arm.

“You made me run.”

“You should try it more.”

He pulled her toward him.

“Think you're him now?”

She looked at his hand, then his face.

“Nigga, I know exactly who I am. That's what's upsetting you.”

He tried to drag her back up the stairs. She planted her feet and hit him with Dante's watch across the wrist holding her. He swore and loosened his grip. She drove an elbow into his chest, got one step away, and nearly reached the lower door.

Arlo stood in it.

One eye was swelling. Blood ran from his nose. He looked at Shawna, looked at Red behind her, and for one second she thought he might move.

Then he raised his gun.

She stopped.

He couldn't make himself look at her while he pointed it.

“I'm sorry,” he said.

“Then get better at it.”

Red pulled her back upstairs. Her shoulder struck the rail. She bit the inside of her cheek to keep from giving him a sound he could enjoy.

When he put her back into the white chair, the room looked different. The cigarette box lay on the floor. The little patch of carpet where it had stood was clean and bright amid the mess.

Red bent over her.

“You get one more fucking idea—”

She looked up at him.

“I got several. You're gonna need a longer night.”

He stepped away.

Shawna told me her hands were shaking after that. She put them under her thighs so he wouldn't see. She had failed to get out. Two other people had made it.

She held on to that while he paced in front of her.

When I asked what she'd been thinking, she put her feet beneath my leg and looked at me like the answer ought to have been obvious.

“What my nigga would've done,” she said. “Only in a better dress.”


At the house, I didn't know any of this yet. Marcellus was still looking at the same photograph, holding my phone so close to his face I thought he might press his forehead through it.

“It's the stone,” he said.

“Nigga, tell me you sure.”

“Yes.”

“Nigga, we were sure at the party.”

He looked at me over the top of the phone.

“You were.”

I wanted to throw him through the rest of the door. I also wanted him to be right more than I'd wanted anything besides hearing her voice.

“Tell me,” I said.

He set the decoy on the table. In that room it looked worth forty million dollars. It looked worth killing for. Red could've shown it to a king, and the king would've started moving money.

Marcellus looked at it like an old sin.

“Nigga changed the setting on the original. Put dark stones around it. Made it look smaller by giving you other things to see.”

“Nigga, you can read forty million through my phone?”

“I can tell you he didn't do a good job.”

His hands had steadied. For the first time that night, he was somewhere he'd spent more years than prison. He turned the picture toward the light.

“I saw the ring at the gala. Only from the side. I thought I recognized the shoulder of the mounting. Here.”

He touched the screen.

“The nigga kept that part.”

“Because it's gold?” Tank asked.

“Because that nigga's an idiot.”

Rosa let out a breath through her nose.

“Finally, some good fucking news.”

Marcellus showed us where the blue metal curved under the stone. Not a secret map. Not a number to somebody's money. The old curve of a mounting he had shaped himself. Red had reused one tiny part when he changed the necklace into a ring. Marcellus knew the work the way I knew the sound of Shawna coming down our stairs.

“He has her stone under his finger,” he said.

Nobody spoke for a moment.

Then I said, “We'll get it.”

He looked at me.

“Will we, my nigga? Say the whole promise.”

“Yeah.”

“If that nigga says her or the diamond?”

“Her.”

I didn't wait to see how that felt to him.

“If that nigga says burn the letter?”

“I burn it.”

“If he says give him back the proof of what he did?”

“Then he gets it. You want me to make you a promise, I'll make you one. I'm bringing her home. Everything else better find a way to come with us.”

Marcellus nodded. His mouth tightened once.

“Dante said something very much like that.”

I grabbed the edge of the table.

“Nigga, I'm not Dante.”

“I know.”

“Then stop putting that nigga between me and every fucking thing I do.”

Rosa said my name.

I shook my head.

“No. I love her. Right now. Me. I'm the nigga standing here bleeding. I'm the nigga going out there. You can remember him all you want, but when her phone rings, I want her to know who's calling.”

My voice had gone loud enough to shake. I hated all three of them hearing it.

Marcellus took the papers we had brought out of the gala and laid them beside Celeste's old letter. Rosa handed him the original order from Dante's watch, still inside its envelope. He kept the different pages apart. One held a dead woman's handwriting. The others held proof that Red had wanted another man dead. They'd cost more nights than I could count, and I would have set them all on fire if it got Shawna through that door.

“Then give her something to answer,” he said.

He slid my phone back to me.

I opened her name.

The last message I'd sent before the gala was still there.

*You look good as fuck.*

She had sent back a picture of one eye, half her forehead, and her middle finger. She'd been trying to take a photograph of the whole dress and got mad at the phone.

I stared until the screen blurred.

Rosa stood beside me.

“She sent me six of those,” she said quietly. “Bitch got the bathroom ceiling in one.”

I wiped my face with the heel of my hand.

“Nigga,” I whispered, though I wasn't talking to anybody now.

I started typing.

*I'm coming. Wear whatever you want.*

Then I deleted the second sentence. She couldn't choose what she was wearing. She couldn't choose where she was sitting. Red would read it first, and I wanted to take his head off for being between us even inside a fucking phone.

I sent only the first two words.

At the Saint, Shawna said Red watched the message arrive. He held the phone where she could see it and smiled.

“Nigga thinks he's in a love song.”

“Then don't stand in the chorus.”

He took the phone away.

She asked for her purse. He laughed at that. She asked for water instead, and he brought it because he wanted to look like the kind of man who brought water.

“Tell me you were lying to that nigga,” he said.

She drank.

“About what?”

“All of it.”

“That's a lot of lying.”

“You lied to Valentino.”

She set the glass down.

“Yeah.”

“You lied to me.”

“Yeah.”

“Then tell me you lied to that nigga.”

He waited so hard that Shawna could see him believing her before she even opened her mouth. She said that was the ugliest thing in the room. He'd hurt her, trapped her, scared her, and still wanted her to make his heart feel better.

She almost gave him what he wanted. Not because it was true. Because she knew how to do it. She knew exactly how soft to make her voice. She could've called him baby and watched his shoulders come down.

Instead she said, “I told Aiden I wasn't scared.”

Red leaned closer.

“There you go.”

“I told him I didn't think about Dante when we were together.”

He smiled.

“And?”

“I told him I didn't like that stupid fucking cross.”

“You see? You see what I'm saying?”

She looked straight at him.

“I told him I could live without him.”

His smile went away.

She said his name then. Not mine. Red's. She wanted him to know he was the one hearing it.

“That was a lie.”

He knocked the water out of her hand.

For a second she thought he was going to hit her again. He stood there breathing, staring at the wet front of her dress. Then he picked up his jacket.

“Get up.”

“Where?”

“You wanna see your nigga so bad, let's go see him.”

He opened her purse and took out the little silver pistol. He looked at it, then at her, and put it in his jacket.

“Taking this too,” he said.

He took her back into the hall. She left the cigarette burning in his silver box. She told me that part twice. Of everything he'd taken away from her that night, she wanted me to know he'd forgotten to make her put it out.

At ten thirty-seven, he sent me another message.

*On our way. Don't disappoint her.*

I looked around the room at Tank, Rosa, Marcellus, and the three million dollars that had already buried too many people.

“Call everybody,” I said.

Tank picked up his phone.

“Everybody?”

“Everybody who ever called me brother.”

## 14. Ten Toes, Thirty Engines

By eleven, the street outside the house was full of cars.

Niggas came in leather. Niggas came in silk. One came wearing the pajama shirt his woman had bought him, with a gold chain lying against the little white moons. He'd put on shoes and brought everything else he thought he needed. Another had a fresh haircut with shaving foam still behind his ear.

Nobody asked if I was serious.

They looked at the money and started asking who had to die.

I knew some of those niggas would have asked the same question in Red's house. I wasn't stupid. I was in love. People kept confusing the two, and tonight I had enough money to make them stop.

There were men there I'd drunk with, fought with, watched betray women who were still sending them plates from home. There were men there who'd carried T's coffin and called me boss before the flowers died. I wanted every rotten heart that would come when I called it.

The world could ask for better men in the morning.

I wanted mine now.

Tank stood at the dining table, putting the three million where everybody could see it. He didn't hide behind me. He waited until the room filled and then he spoke.

“This is the money from the motel.”

A few heads turned.

“I took it.”

One man beside the piano said, “Nigga, what?”

Tank kept his eyes on the room.

“I took all of it. I let Aiden think it was gone. Red knew. He tried to use it against him tonight.”

“Tried?” somebody asked.

“Tried.”

The man beside the piano looked at me.

“Nigga, and this nigga still breathing?”

Tank's jaw moved once.

I walked between them.

“Look at me when you say that.”

The man did.

“Tank's standing with me.”

“I'm just saying—”

“Say he stole it. He did. Say he's a lying motherfucker. He was. Say you're gonna touch him tonight, and you can find out how fucking fast I can forget your name.”

The room went still.

Tank looked at the back of my head. I could feel it.

The man by the piano lifted his hands.

“Your house.”

“Yeah.”

I let that sit.

“My house. My money on the table. My girl with Red. If any of that bothers you, the door already fucking broke. You ain't gotta worry about hurting it.”

Nobody left.

Rosa stood by the staircase in the borrowed coat. She watched every face. Marcellus sat behind her with the decoy in its box and the papers inside his jacket. The old nigga looked tired enough to disappear if you let your eyes move too fast, but he hadn't asked to lie down.

I put my hand on the cash.

“Some of you came because you owe me. Some of you came because Red owes you. Some of you just heard there was gonna be money.”

One man in the back said, “All three.”

I looked at him.

He didn't apologize.

I nodded.

“Good. Nigga knows why he came.”

I started giving it away.

Not throwing it in the air. I wanted every nigga who touched it to look into my face while he did. I wanted him to feel the weight of it and know the woman we'd left behind had carried it out of a room full of killers before any of us had the nerve.

Stacks went into hands. Into coats. Into the pajama shirt, where the buttons strained so hard I thought the little moons were gonna fly off.

“Nigga, put that in a bag,” Tank told him.

“I'm good.”

“You look pregnant.”

“I'm good.”

I kept paying.

Some of them laughed. Some counted. One man held the money without doing either, and I remembered he'd been sitting in a hospital hallway two nights earlier with his head in his hands. Tonight he kissed the stack and tucked it inside his coat.

I didn't ask which part of his life I'd just bought.

I had one woman to bring home. The whole city could put its heart on the fucking table.

When two million had left the bags, I stopped.

The last million stayed together. I pulled the bag shut and set it aside.

“That's hers.”

Nobody argued.

Tank hadn't taken anything. I picked up a share from the two million I'd already laid out and held it toward him.

He shook his head.

“No.”

“Nigga, take it before I have to love you louder.”

“Aiden.”

“Nigga, poor and guilty? I'm letting you have one bad feeling. Pick one.”

His eyes flicked toward the men around us.

“Nigga, I don't want it.”

“Then spend it on somebody who does.”

I pushed the money against his chest until he took it.

He looked down at it. Then he put it on the table beside the million I was keeping for Shawna.

“For her,” he said.

I left it there. I wasn't counting love back into a fucking bag while everybody watched.

Rosa came down the stairs.

“And before all you niggas start singing about brotherhood, she's my friend.”

Nobody laughed. They knew her. Half the room stood up straighter when she came close.

“That means if you see her, you bring her. You don't stop to tell Red how hard you are. You don't start explaining a grudge from 2018. You bring her.”

The man with shaving foam behind his ear nodded.

“We got you, Rosa.”

“No, baby. You better have her.”

She turned to me.

I had held back part of the two million for her. I pushed it across the table.

She stared at it.

“What's this?”

“Yours.”

“For what?”

“Whatever you want.”

Her face went tight.

“You paying me to stay home?”

“I'm paying you because she loves you.”

Rosa looked up.

“Nigga, don't do that right now.”

“She gets out of that car tonight, I want somebody here she knew before every room had me in it.”

For the first time since she'd walked through the broken door, Rosa looked her age and her fear at once. Thirty-four years old, tired, one earring gone, holding the coat closed with a hand that had finally stopped shaking.

“You bring her,” she said.

I nodded.

She slapped my face.

Not hard enough to knock me down. Hard enough that the room went silent.

“With your mouth, Aiden.”

I swallowed.

“I'm bringing her.”

She kissed the same cheek.

“Then go, baby.”

I turned to the room.

“Any of you niggas here think Red owns Vegas?”

“Fuck Red,” somebody said.

“Anybody think that nigga owns my wife?”

Rosa made a sound behind me.

I turned halfway.

“What?”

“You ask her yet?”

“I'm going to.”

“Then quit inviting these niggas before me.”

The room broke open. Men laughed, slapped each other's shoulders, called out shit about weddings and suits and who wasn't allowed near an open bar. I let them. For a few seconds we had a future big enough to crowd a room.

Then I raised my hand.

“Niggas, listen to me.”

They quieted.

“I ain't asking you to die because I fell in love. I'm asking you to stand up with me because that nigga thinks he can take anything he sees. He took a man's wife. Took another man's diamond. Took Dante out to the desert and left him there. Tonight he took Shawna.”

I put my hand over the cross.

“He keeps telling everybody I'm wearing a dead nigga's jewelry. Fine. Let him look at it while I come get my girl.”

Tank stepped beside me.

“Ten toes,” he said.

The room answered.

“Down.”

He said it again, louder.

“Ten toes.”

“Down.”

Nigga, the windows shook. The broken front door moved in its frame. For one wild second I wanted the whole city to hear us, every penthouse and every parking lot and every woman waiting for a man to come back different.

I kissed the cross.

Then I went outside.

***

Tank drove the Mercedes.

I sat beside him because I still couldn't lean back without feeling T's bullet and because if anybody was going to meet Red first, it was going to be me.

Marcellus got into the back.

I looked over my shoulder.

“You sure about this?”

“No.”

“Nigga, you can wait with Rosa.”

“I have waited enough.”

He shut the door before I could offer him anything else.

The decoy sat in its box beside him. The letters and the papers were in his coat. My phone lay faceup on my knee. Rosa stood in the driveway with the money she hadn't bothered to pick up still inside the house.

Tank had put the bag with Shawna's million and his returned share in the back. Red had asked for three million. He was getting what was left after I'd paid the niggas coming to take his kingdom.

She came to my window.

“Aiden.”

I looked at her.

“She likes gardenias.”

“What?”

“For the wedding. She likes gardenias. And she will lie and tell you roses because men always buy roses.”

I gripped the door.

“Gardenias.”

“And don't let that old man give her away. I'll do it.”

Marcellus said, “I hadn't volunteered.”

Rosa pointed at him through the glass.

“Keep it that way.”

She stepped back.

The cars pulled out behind us until the street looked like the city had emptied its garages for a funeral and nobody had agreed whose.

Thirty engines. Maybe more by the time we reached the highway. Rex Crown came in a black coupe; Little Saint rode beside him. Mercedes and Porsche took the green Bentley. Bell had brought my police Lamborghini back, and Knox rode with her at the head of the convoy. Headlights filled both mirrors. My niggas had come wearing their money and their worst intentions, and I loved every last one of them for showing up.

Tank kept both hands on the wheel.

After a while he said, “You should let the doctor look at you after.”

“After.”

“I'm saying.”

“I heard you.”

He nodded.

The lights thinned outside the windows. Vegas went from towers to signs to little burning squares behind us. Ahead was black desert and the road laid through it.

“Tank.”

“Yeah.”

“When you came back for the money. Did he look like himself?”

He knew who I meant.

He drove another few seconds before he answered.

“No.”

I looked down at the cross.

“Good.”

Tank's hands tightened.

“You don't gotta say that.”

“I know.”

He didn't answer. I watched the side of his face and remembered him standing behind T in the parking lot, as big as a wall, waiting for somebody else to decide what he'd do.

“I'm glad you here.”

His jaw moved.

“Yeah.”

“Don't make me say it twice.”

“I heard you.”

In the back, Marcellus turned the decoy's box between his hands.

“She wore blue the last time I took her dancing,” he said.

Neither of us asked who.

“Celeste. I was late. She was furious. By the time I got there, she'd danced with three other men.”

“Three?” I said.

“She counted them for me.”

Tank glanced in the mirror.

“You do something to those niggas?”

“I asked for the fourth dance.”

I looked out at the dark.

“Could've been me.”

“It wasn't.”

He closed the box and rested his head against the seat.

We drove the rest of that stretch without talking.

At eleven fifty-four, Red called.

I put him on speaker.

“You coming?” he asked.

“You hear the cars?”

“I told you to come ready to apologize.”

“I am.”

Tank looked at me.

“I told her I'd never let you put your hands on her again. Got a lot to apologize for.”

Red breathed into the phone.

“You think all those niggas love you?”

“Enough to leave the house.”

“That's money.”

“Then you should've paid better.”

He went quiet.

I heard Shawna in the background. I couldn't make out the words, only her voice and the way he moved the phone away from her.

“Let me talk to her.”

“You'll see her soon.”

“Nigga, let me—”

He hung up.

I gripped the phone so hard Tank reached over and took it before I broke that too.

“We're here,” he said.

The casino rose out of the desert half finished, huge and white under lights that made the empty windows look blacker. Red had built columns tall enough for a king and stopped before anybody could decide what kingdom he thought he had. Plastic sheeting moved behind the glass. A fountain outside had never held water.

Cars waited across the entrance. Men stood between them. Above the front doors, a balcony ran along the second floor beneath an unfinished crown of stone.

There she was.

Shawna stood at the railing in Rosa's ruined dress. Her hair blew across her face. Even from the car I could see Dante's watch on her wrist.

Red stood beside her.

He lifted the hand with the ring and waved like he'd invited us for dinner.

Behind me, engine after engine went quiet. My niggas were here.

I opened my door.

My side hurt. My hand hurt. Everything in me that knew how to be scared was awake and screaming.

I put both feet on the ground anyway.

Shawna saw me.

She stepped toward the railing before Red caught her arm.

“Aiden!”

I looked straight up at her.

“I'm here, baby.”

The clock on my phone turned eleven fifty-nine.



The first roadblock waited beyond the last gas station.

Two trucks across the highway. Men beside them. No uniforms. No lights except the white glare of their headlights pointed into our faces. A line of barrels burned between the trucks, and behind the flames I could see the same kind of patience Red had worn across the breakfast table.

Tank slowed.

Behind us thirty engines changed their voices at once.

My phone rang. Knox.

"I see them," she said. "Stay in the convoy."

"Nigga, the convoy is me."

"Then don't make me explain to your wife why you turned into a road accident before you got there."

A shot hit the Mercedes hood.

Tank pulled left. Another struck the windshield and made a white star directly in front of him. Marcellus dropped in the back, his coat closed over the letters and the decoy like the old nigga had decided history could wait below the window line.

Knox's police Lamborghini came out beside us. Officer Bell was driving; the chief leaned forward in the passenger seat, looking at the roadblock like somebody had finally annoyed her enough to deserve the whole department.

The siren rose.

One of the men by the truck stepped backward.

Another raised his gun anyway.

"Hardheaded nigga," I said.

Tank put his foot down.

We left the road in a sheet of dust. The Mercedes bounced across the shoulder, hit a shallow ditch, and came up with its engine still screaming. My head struck the roof. I tasted blood. Behind us the convoy divided, cars sweeping wide through the desert while shots flashed between the trucks.

The men had expected a line.

They got a fucking horizon.

Rex's black coupe came past on our right. Little Saint rode beside it on a new motorcycle with no paint on the tank. He'd borrowed it from a man who apparently understood lending something to my nigga meant accepting an interesting return policy.

Mercedes and Porsche came through the dust in the green Bentley. Porsche had the roof down. Mercedes held her hair away from her face with one hand and a pistol in the other.

"Keep the old man down!" she shouted as they passed.

"Old man is down," Marcellus said from the back seat. "The old man is thoroughly fucking down."

I couldn't help it. I laughed.

Nigga, I laughed with a bullet hole in my windshield and the woman I loved waiting inside a nightmare, because that old man had come through eight years of prison and still knew when my friends needed correcting.

The first truck started moving.

Its driver turned toward the desert to cut off the cars passing on that side. Rex braked hard. Little Saint swerved clear. The truck's huge front wheel climbed the edge of a ditch, and for a second the whole thing leaned toward the coupe.

I saw Rex looking up through his windshield.

I saw Little Saint turn back.

"Tank."

"I see."

"Nigga, this time I believe you."

Tank drove the Mercedes straight into the truck's rear corner.

Metal struck metal. The car jumped sideways. My shoulder hit the door, and every stitch in my side tried to leave without me. The truck's rear swung away from Rex, its wheels clawing at loose dirt. It rolled far enough that the coupe could get clear.

Little Saint rode through the gap beside it and came out raising one fist.

"Aiden!"

"Tank!" I shouted back.

The big nigga glanced at me.

"What?"

"I'm giving you your fucking credit. Enjoy it."

He grinned despite the blood on his lip.

The truck stopped against a low rise. Its driver jumped out, took one look at the number of cars now surrounding him, and dropped the gun he'd brought down from the cab.

Bell and Knox reached him first.

The chief got out with her weapon raised.

"You blocked my captain's road."

The man stared at the gold on her uniform.

"Your captain?"

She pointed toward me through the dust.

"That one."

He looked. His face fell so completely I almost respected the honesty of it.

"They didn't say it was him."

"Nigga," I shouted from the window, "what part of thirty cars looked like a small mistake?"

Rex pulled beside us with his window down. His eyebrow was still bleeding where the gala guard had hit him. He looked at Tank, then at me.

"Three times."

"That one was Tank."

"Then I owe the family."

Tank lifted two fingers off the wheel. The nigga didn't even try to look modest. I'd have been angry if he had.

Behind us, Knox's officers took the men off the road. The second truck's crew had run before the first one stopped moving. I could see their flashlights bouncing through the distance, four little dots trying to become somebody else's fucking problem.

The convoy found the highway again.

Thirty engines. A few more scratched. A few more loud. Nobody missing.

The police Lamborghini took the front while Knox's remaining cruisers held the road behind us. Bell gave the siren one short burst, and the cars answered with their horns.

Marcellus sat up carefully in the back.

"Are we finished doing that?"

"For now."

"Good. My tie has given up."

I reached back and straightened it for him at the next slow bend.

"Nigga, you meeting forty million dollars. Look ready."

He looked at me, then down at the cross.

"Damn, boy," he said.

I smiled.

"Magnificent."

The old man nodded as if he'd completed the last repair the evening required.

At eleven fifty-nine, the unfinished casino rose out of the desert in front of us. Lights burned behind its empty windows. Our headlights spread across the parking lot until every naked wall had a shadow of my people on it.

I saw blue on a balcony.

Shawna.

My whole fucking body knew before my eyes finished the distance.

Tank stopped the Mercedes.

I opened the door.

## 15. The Last King of Vegas

Red had her standing beneath a chandelier that had never been turned on. Nigga hadn't even finished building the place where he wanted to die.

Everything around them was unfinished. Marble on one wall, naked concrete on the next. A staircase big enough for a king coming down into a floor covered with building dust. The place was supposed to be Red's next casino. He had brought my woman here to make me watch him take my whole life away before the fucking doors even opened.

I stepped out of the Mercedes.

Tank got out beside me. Behind us, the convoy stretched across the parking lot, headlights burning through the dust. Niggas I had known for years. Niggas who had started calling me boss eleven days ago. Blue on their wrists, blue at their throats, guns in their hands. Nobody was smiling. Nobody had come to make peace.

I looked up at Shawna.

Her dress was torn at one shoulder. Somebody had hurt her mouth. She held her chin high, but I could see her looking for me in the dark.

I raised my hand.

She saw it.

That was all I needed. That was the whole motherfucking world right there. Every fucking dollar I'd ever touch could burn before I'd leave her up there.

Red stepped into view beside her, wearing white from his shoes to the collar of his shirt. The blue stone on his right hand flashed when he put that hand on her shoulder.

Forty million dollars. Marcellus's life. Celeste's last letter. Dante's blood. All that shit sitting on a finger like it had always belonged to him.

"Aiden," he called down. "You brought everybody."

"I told them there was a dead nigga here."

Tank looked at me, and I could feel what he wanted to say. Don't let this nigga make you move before you think. Don't give him another piece of you because you're mad.

But I was past mad. I had gone through mad on the highway. Whatever was in me now had no place left to go except straight up those stairs.

"Come inside," Red said. "Just you and Tank."

I started walking.

Tank caught my sleeve.

"Nigga."

I stopped.

"We get her and we leave."

"We get her," I said.

He looked at me for another second. Then he let go.

Inside, Red's niggas stood between roulette tables covered in plastic. I could see guns beneath jackets. I could see the ones who weren't bothering to hide them. There must've been thirty motherfuckers waiting for us in that room, and I walked between them with my head up because Shawna was watching.

Thirty niggas. I counted them because I wanted to know how many men I'd tell her I walked through when we got home. My captain's badge showed inside the ruined white jacket. Some of those men looked at it longer than they looked at my gun. Outside, Knox and Bell held the road; Red could hear the sirens and knew there was no uniform left coming to save him. We were going home. I had already decided that shit in the car.

Red came down the staircase with Shawna beside him. He held her elbow. Every time his fingers tightened, I wanted to tear that arm out of his fucking jacket.

"Nigga, let her walk," I said.

"She is walking."

"Nigga, to me. Let my woman walk to me."

He stopped halfway down.

"You haven't paid for anything yet."

Tank stepped closer to me.

"We got your money."

Red laughed.

"My nigga, you think this is about the three million now?"

"That's what you been asking for."

"I asked for respect. The money was the easy part."

He looked at me.

"Tell me something, Aiden. How much did she tell you about that first night?"

Shawna closed her eyes.

I didn't look away from him.

"Enough."

"Did she tell you she was supposed to get in a car with whoever T sent? Could've been you. Could've been Tank. Could've been any nigga with a pulse and a place to hide the money."

"Don't," Shawna said.

Red leaned close to her.

"We're being honest. That's what lovers want, isn't it?"

I could hear Tank breathing beside me.

Red lifted Shawna's wrist. Dante's watch hung loose against her skin.

"Look at that. You got a palace, cars, an army. You got motherfuckers out here willing to die because they think you're the next big thing. And she still wears a dead man's watch."

Something opened up inside me.

It wasn't the wound.

I had looked at that watch every morning. At the breakfast table. In bed. When she put her hand on my face. I had pretended it didn't bother me because I thought a man with everything wasn't supposed to be jealous of somebody in the ground.

But I was. I was jealous enough to hate myself for it.

"Tell him," Red said to her. "Tell him whose chain made you go over there."

She looked at me.

"Dante's."

I felt Tank turn toward me.

I kept my eyes on her.

"First time I kissed you," she said, "I was looking at his cross. I wanted something of him back. I didn't know what I was doing."

Red smiled.

Nigga thought he had me. He was watching my hand, waiting for the gun to sag, waiting for me to look at her the way he wanted. He'd have paid to see me hate her.

"And now?" I asked.

Shawna swallowed. There was blood at the corner of her mouth.

"Now I'm looking at you."

Red's smile went away.

"Don't give that nigga that shit."

"I'm looking at you, Aiden."

I nodded once.

"Then keep looking, baby."

Red hit her. Nigga hit her right in front of me.

I moved before I thought about it.

Tank grabbed my arm, but I was already pulling free. Guns came up all around the room. I heard men shouting my name. I heard Red tell them not to fire yet.

Shawna caught the banister instead of falling. She lifted her head slowly, and the look she gave him was the same look she must've given Valentino in that car.

Red saw it too.

He put his pistol under her jaw.

Everything stopped.

"One more step," he said.

I stood at the foot of the stairs.

My heart was beating so hard it hurt the place where T had shot me.

"You win," I said.

Tank stared at me.

"Aiden."

"Let her come down. You want the west side, take it. You want the house, take it. My money. My name. Whatever the fuck you want."

Red watched my face.

I meant it. I had been telling everybody I was a king, but I would've walked out of that room with nothing but her hand in mine. We could sleep in the fucking car. Let the nigga have the house.

"You hear that?" he asked Shawna. "He'll give me everything."

"Then take it and let me go."

He shook his head.

"Dante offered me everything too."

The words hung between us.

Red looked down at the ring on his hand.

"Your husband thought having a brother made him untouchable. You think having these niggas outside makes you untouchable. Everybody thinks there's one nigga who won't sell them."

He looked at Tank.

"How much you take out of that pool again?"

Tank's face hardened.

"I gave it back."

"After I told him you had it."

"I gave it back."

Red laughed at him.

"Come stand over here, Tank. You don't gotta die for a nigga you met eleven days ago."

Tank looked at me.

I didn't say anything. I had already asked him for more than I had any right to ask. I wasn't going to beg him now with Red watching.

Tank put his hand on my shoulder.

Right over the place where Big T had put his hand on the first night.

"That's my brother," he said.

Red shot him.

Tank hit me as he went down. His weight knocked me sideways. The first burst of gunfire tore through the room before his body reached the floor.

I fired up the stairs.

Red pulled Shawna against him and went backward through the doorway at the top. I tried to follow him with the gun, but there was too much of her in front of him. Too much of my whole fucking life between me and the man I wanted dead.

Tank grabbed my ankle.

"Go," he said.

Blood was coming through his shirt below the shoulder.

"Nigga, go get her."

The men outside hit the doors.

Glass came down all over the entrance. I heard our people shouting. I saw blue rags moving between the tables. Somebody went down across a roulette wheel. Somebody else fell through the plastic over the bar. Guns flashed in the dark like the whole casino had caught fire from the inside.

I went up the stairs with Tank's voice still in my ears.

The first man came around the landing in a brown jacket. He fired before he saw how close I was. The shot broke the rail beside my hand. I hit him against the wall and kept moving while his gun struck the steps behind us.

Below, Rex Crown came through the doors with our people.

He didn't have a gun in his hand. He had a man in each hand, one by the jacket, one by the belt, and the look of a fighter who had finally found a room large enough to pay all his debts at once.

"Captain!" he shouted.

"Stairs!"

He threw one man into the other and came toward them.

I reached the first landing. Red was above me with Shawna. He looked down, saw I was still coming, and pulled her harder toward the unfinished corridor behind him.

She stumbled. Caught herself. Turned her face toward me for half a second.

Nigga, that half second got me up another flight.

A gunman stood between two empty light fixtures at the top. He was young enough to think standing high made him safe and old enough to regret learning otherwise. Twenty-seven, I found out afterward. Malik. Three people depending on the money Red paid him to stand in that spot and die if necessary.

He had his gun aimed at my chest.

I stopped one step below him.

"Move."

He looked at the badge showing through my torn jacket.

"Captain Aiden?"

"Nigga, this is a terrible place to introduce yourself. Move."

"Red said you weren't really—"

A shot came from behind him.

Malik ducked. The man deeper in the corridor was firing past his own employee to get at me.

I caught Malik by the collar and pulled him down the step beside me. The second shot struck the wall where his head had been. He stared at the white dust falling over his shoes.

"Your boss very generous," I told him.

His face changed.

I fired down the corridor. The man at the far end fell back behind a pillar. Malik turned his gun away from me and toward the pillar instead.

"Go," he said.

I looked at him.

"Nigga, decide properly."

He raised his voice.

"Go get her, Captain."

I went.

Behind me I heard him shouting at the others to put their guns down. Some did. Some didn't. The casino filled with choices being made at the loudest possible volume, and for once the niggas who chose me got to keep breathing long enough to appreciate the decision.

At the foot of the stairs, Porsche dragged a wounded man behind the roulette table where Tank lay. Mercedes stood over both of them, firing toward the dark bar whenever another shape moved there.

"Rosa's coming!" Porsche shouted up at me.

I didn't know how she knew. I didn't need to. My people had begun finding each other without waiting for me to hold all the names in my head.

Little Saint came through the side entrance with three more men. He pointed up at me.

"That's our nigga! Clear him a road!"

I was already on it.

The corridor split around an unfinished fountain. Red's white jacket disappeared through the far doors. I followed, one hand against the wall, blood warm beneath my bandages.

A man stepped out beside the fountain with a shotgun.

I dropped as he fired. The edge of the fountain burst. Water left in its bottom jumped into my face. He tried to bring the gun down toward me, but I was already against his legs.

We hit the floor together.

The shotgun slid away. He caught my wounded side with an elbow and the pain opened so wide I couldn't see. I heard Shawna shout my name from the room beyond us.

That brought me back.

I hit him until his hands came off me. Not because I stopped hurting. Nigga, I hurt everywhere. I hurt in years I hadn't even lived yet. But she had said my name like the whole world depended on whether I answered, and I wasn't going to make her ask a dead man again.

I got up.

The man reached for my ankle.

I looked down at him.

"Don't make this your whole life."

He let go.

I took the shotgun off the floor and fired toward the far wall when another man came through the doorway shooting. The man dropped behind a stack of marble tiles. I left the gun and kept my own pistol in my hand.

Ahead, the desert showed through a room without glass. Headlights burned below it. The balcony rail ran along the open edge, thin and dark against all that distance.

I heard Red breathing hard.

Then his voice.

"You don't get tired?"

I came through the door.

"Nigga, you keep giving me somewhere to be."


The room beyond was open to the desert. They hadn't put the glass in yet. A balcony ran along the edge, looking down over the lights of our cars.

Red had Shawna against the railing.

Her little silver pistol fell out of his jacket as he hauled her against the railing. It struck the floor beside his shoe.

"Nigga, that gun drops now," he told me.

I stopped in the doorway.

"Drop it or she goes over."

There was nothing beneath the balcony but concrete and steel.

Shawna looked at me. Her eyes were wide. She was scared now. Really scared. No black dress, no diamonds, no cold story about killing Valentino could hide that from me.

"Put her down," I said.

"Put the gun down."

I lowered it.

Set it on the floor.

Red watched me do it.

Then he smiled.

"That's how your husband died, Shawna. That's how Dante went down. Hands open. Begging. T couldn't even look at him."

"He wasn't begging for himself," she said.

Red's arm tightened.

"What?"

"You said he wanted somebody to take care of me."

"Shut the fuck up."

"He wasn't begging for himself."

She drove her head backward into his face.

He staggered. His gun went off into the empty sky. Shawna dropped to the floor, reached for her little silver pistol, and came up firing.

The first shot hit his leg.

The second hit him in the chest.

Red fell against the railing, one hand still reaching toward her.

"Dante," she said.

Just his name.

She tried to raise it again. Her hand was shaking so badly the barrel fell below his chest.

Red was still standing.

He lifted his pistol.

I had mine back in my hand by then.

I put him down.

I fired until his gun fell out of his hand. Until his knees hit the balcony. Until the nigga who had taken years from her life was on the ground looking up at a sky he wasn't ever going to own.

Then I went to her.

She was on her knees, still holding the silver gun.

"Baby."

She didn't look up.

"Shawna."

Her hand wouldn't open.

I put mine around it.

"It's done."

She shook her head.

I wanted her to say my name. Nigga, I wanted it so bad I could hardly breathe. She kept saying Dante's. I put my gun down beside hers and got both arms around her.

I held her on the floor while she cried for Dante.

And I held her tighter because I was the one who was there.

Downstairs, somebody shouted that Red was dead.

Then somebody shouted my name.

More voices picked it up. Through the hall. Across the casino. Out into the parking lot where all those headlights were still burning.

Aiden.

Aiden.

My nigga, I had blood in both shoes and her face against my neck, and they were calling me the king of Vegas.

I believed them.

Before we left, I took Blue Mercy off Red's hand. He'd stopped reaching for anything by then. Forty million dollars in my fist, and I closed it so hard the setting cut my palm.

***

Tank was alive when we got back downstairs.

Rosa had come after us with Dr. Vega. She told me later she'd sat in the house watching the clock until she couldn't fucking stand it, then gone to get the doctor and driven out behind the convoy. They came through the doors after the shooting stopped. Vega was bent over a wounded man near the entrance when I saw her.

Tank lay beside the roulette table with Rosa holding a folded tablecloth against him. Her dress was covered in blood. She looked at me like she was ready to fight God if he tried to take another person out of that room.

"Where the fuck you been?"

"With her."

She looked past me. Saw Shawna. Her face broke, and she had to press her mouth shut before she could talk again.

"Come here, baby."

Shawna went down beside her.

Tank opened his eyes when I knelt.

"My nigga. You got her?"

"Yeah."

"Red?"

"Dead."

He tried to smile. It hurt him.

"You better pay my fucking hospital bill."

I took his hand.

"Every penny."

"And the car."

"What car?"

"I want one."

"Nigga, a hundred. Your nigga will buy you a hundred fucking cars."

He shut his eyes again.

"Black ones."

I held on until the doctor came.

I kept my hand around his. The last nigga who called me family had put a bullet in me before the night was over. Tank had taken one instead. Every time a voice came through the door, I looked up expecting somebody to tell me what else I could pay to keep him breathing.

I wasn't letting him wake up alone.

***

Marcellus came into the casino after the shooting stopped.

He walked through the broken glass slowly. His shoes were old and polished. He looked at the walls, the marble, the great staircase Red had built with other people's lives.

Then he looked at me.

I put the ring in his hand.

Blue Mercy flashed under the work lights.

For a long time he didn't speak.

His thumb moved across the setting. Red had put her stone in his own ring. Marcellus turned it in his hand, held it beneath the light, and closed his eyes.

Then he took Celeste's letter out of his coat. He laid the ring against the paper and bent his head over both of them.

I let him take all the time he needed.

"What are you going to do?" I asked.

He closed his hand around the ring.

"Take my wife home."

I nodded.

Forty million dollars. I put forty million dollars in an old man's hand and watched him walk away because the woman I loved had just killed a man while saying another man's name, and for the first time that night I understood why some things couldn't be bought back.

Everything else in that casino was mine. Knox came through the entrance with Bell after the last guns were down. She looked at Shawna in my arms, the gold badge under the blood, and the men who had changed sides because a living captain had offered them more future than Red.

"You brought her home," she said.

"Told you my nigga doesn't forget."

She saluted. Bell followed. Then every officer in the doorway stood straight while the men inside the casino began saying my name again.

Captain. King. Aiden.

Shawna heard all three and held me tighter.

I made sure every nigga understood that too.

## 16. Ten Toes Down Forever

They put Tank in a private room with a view of the mountains.

I paid for the room next door for Rosa because she wouldn't leave him. She said she was there for Shawna. Tank said Rosa had called him handsome while she was keeping him alive, and he wanted witnesses.

She told him he was full of shit.

He smiled at her anyway. Nigga was hooked. I could've told him that from the doorway.

My nigga, I had seen that man face down in the dirt, seen him take punches that would've broken somebody else's neck, seen him stand beside T like nothing in the world could ever make him move. I hadn't ever seen him nervous before a woman walked into a room.

I bought him a black Cadillac.

Then I bought him another one because he called me from the hospital and said the first picture didn't do the color justice.

"Nigga, you buying me a car or showing me a car?" he asked.

"Look out your fucking window."

I heard Rosa open the blinds. Heard that big nigga start laughing. He had to stop because it hurt him. Then he started again.

Nigga had almost died for me. I would've painted the whole fucking city black if he'd asked.

I went back to the house with Shawna three days after Red died.

The lake was quiet. There were flowers at the gate, flowers on the stairs, flowers in the bedroom. Niggas I'd never met sent bottles and watches. Women sent silk, perfume, diamonds. Somebody sent a white horse with a blue ribbon tied into its mane.

I had the horse taken around to the back where she could see it from the balcony.

Shawna stood at the bedroom window and looked down at it.

"You buy that?"

"Somebody sent it."

"Why?"

"Because they know who you are."

She watched it walking beside the water.

"I don't know how to ride."

"Then we'll learn."

She turned toward me.

For a second, I thought she was going to cry again.

Then she laughed.

I had missed that sound so bad. I had been hearing gunfire in my sleep, hearing T say son, hearing Red tell me she'd have got in the car with anybody. I had started thinking that was all the world had left to say to me.

Then she laughed and came across the room and kissed me.

I picked her up. She wrapped her arms around my neck, and I carried her away from the window while the sun went down behind the mountains. My side hurt. I didn't put her down. Nigga, I'd carried worse for men who loved me less.

Later, we lay awake listening to the water.

Her watch rested on the nightstand.

I looked at it for a while.

She saw me looking.

"You want me to take it off?"

I didn't answer right away.

I wanted everything. Her mornings. Her nights. The way she turned her head when somebody said my name. I wanted to be the man she thought of when a song came on. I wanted to reach back three years and be the one carrying that cake into the club. I wanted to put myself in every photograph that had ever made her happy.

I couldn't.

And all the money in Vegas couldn't help me with that. I'd bought half a fucking city, and I couldn't buy one night three years ago.

"No," I said.

She rested her head on my chest.

"Sometimes I miss him when I'm happy."

I looked at the ceiling.

"With me?"

"Yeah."

That hurt. I'm not going to lie to you. That shit went straight through me.

She lifted her head.

"Because I wish he knew I wasn't hurting all the time anymore."

I looked at her then.

She touched the cross against my chest.

"I wish he knew somebody stayed."

I took her hand and held it there.

Neither of us said anything for a long time.

Then I asked her to marry me. Right there. No shirt, no ring, her dead husband's watch where both of us could see it.

She sat up.

"Aiden."

"I mean it."

"You just bought me a house."

"I'll buy you another one."

"That's not what I'm saying."

"Then tell me what you're saying."

She looked at me with tears in her eyes.

"You can't fix every bad thing that ever happened to me."

"I know."

"You gonna be mad when you find that out for real?"

I sat up beside her.

"I'm gonna be mad about a lot of shit, baby. I'm a fucked-up man. You know that."

She nodded.

"I'm asking you to marry me, baby. Bring the watch. Bring the pictures. Bring every fucking thing you can't leave behind. Just come with me."

She put her hand over my mouth.

Then she started laughing and crying at the same time.

"Yes," she said.

I kissed her palm.

"Say it again."

"Yes. I'll marry you."

I had fifty niggas outside that house ready to die for me and more money than I could count in one room, and I swear to you none of it had ever made me feel like that one word.

***

We got married beside the lake.

Three weeks after I walked into the Saint. The flowers cost more than every rent payment I'd ever made put together. Shawna came toward me in a white dress while a woman sang the song she used to sing in her mother's kitchen.

Blue roses and the gardenias I had promised her covered the aisle.

There were diamonds at her throat. Dante's watch on her wrist.

I wore the cross.

Tank stood beside me in a black suit with his arm still healing under the jacket. Rosa sat in the front row wearing a blue dress and trying not to look at him. He looked at her enough for both of them.

Every table had a bottle of Hennessy on it. Every nigga at the gate had a gun. Behind the flowers, my people watched the road while men from other cities came to shake my hand and find out whether the stories were true.

Nigga, they were true enough that none of them tried me.

I paid the singer more than she asked. Then I paid her band. Then I bought the place where she'd been playing because Shawna said the owner had treated her like shit once, years ago, when she was trying to get an audition.

I didn't bring him to the wedding.

I made that nigga listen to it from the parking lot.

Shawna reached me and put her hands in mine.

For a moment I forgot everybody else was there.

The preacher asked me if I would love her in sickness and in health.

I looked at the scar above her eyebrow. At the mark still fading on her mouth. At the wrist she had held against my bleeding side when all I had to give her was a promise about a house near the water.

"I will."

He asked her the same.

"I will."

That's how it happened. Her hand was shaking in mine. Tank kept wiping his face with the sleeve on his good arm. Rosa was crying into a napkin she'd stolen off his table. My girl said yes in front of the whole fucking city.

I kissed my wife while the band played and my people shouted my name.

The wedding presents arrived in a convoy longer than the one we'd taken into the desert.

Knox brought a gold-plated pair of handcuffs in a velvet box and told Shawna she trusted her to decide when they were necessary. Shawna held them up, looked at me, and smiled in a way that made Tank cover his eyes.

"Nigga, I'm trying to eat."

"Then look at your plate," Rosa told him.

Professor Halcyon came with Principal Mercer and six graduates who'd helped carry people out of the auditorium. They brought a framed photograph of my Lamborghini coming through the doors with fire behind it. Mercer had signed the bottom in gold.

*Our valedictorian.*

"Nigga, you signed this like you made me," I told him.

He began crying again.

Shawna took the frame before either of us dropped it.

"I know exactly where this goes."

"Over the bed?"

"Over the fireplace. You already think enough of yourself in bed."

Mercedes screamed laughing. Porsche nearly dropped her drink. Mercer didn't seem to understand the sentence, but he nodded like the academic quality of it was beyond dispute.

Rex Crown arrived with a white limousine full of fighters who all wanted to shake my hand. He introduced me to each one by telling them exactly how quickly I had put him down. Every time he told it, the time got shorter and his expression got prouder.

"One punch," he said to the last man. "Before I got comfortable."

"Rex, nigga, you weren't comfortable when you arrived."

"That's what I'm telling him. I never stood a chance."

The fighter looked at me, looked at Shawna, and bowed his head.

"Congratulations, Captain."

"See?" Rex said. "Nigga learns fast."

Little Saint brought a motorcycle painted dark blue with my initials on the tank. He told me it was for days when four wheels felt like too much company. Tank immediately told him no day in my life required fewer wheels.

"You jealous?" Little Saint asked.

"Nigga, I have watched this man drive. I am informed."

Leon brought a bicycle.

A real bicycle. Green. A little basket on the front. He wheeled it through the gate in a tuxedo and looked straight at Porsche.

"This one floats."

She kissed him on the cheek.

"Baby, so did the first car for a minute."

He shut his eyes while everybody laughed, then opened them on the house, the music, the lake full of lights.

"I wouldn't have missed any of it," he said.

Nigga, neither would I.

***

For our first dance, Shawna wanted a song she could hear without remembering a room somebody else had paid for.

So we made one.

She had written the melody in the week before the wedding. I'd found her at the piano after midnight, barefoot, chewing the end of a pencil while she tried to make the bridge stop sounding like she was saying goodbye.

I sat beside her and played the left hand while she sang.

"There," I said when her voice rose.

"Where?"

"Don't turn back. Keep going."

She tried it. The note opened. Her face changed.

"Baby."

"That's us."

We worked until the sun came up. No dead men in the song. No promises somebody had made with one hand on a door. Just a woman hearing a car in the driveway and knowing the person she wanted was finally coming in.

Now the band played it beside the lake while my wife put her hand in mine.

The first steps were easy. The next ones belonged to her. Shawna moved like music had been waiting all those years for somebody to give her enough room, and I followed until she laughed at how serious I looked.

"Nigga, you know how to dance."

"I know how to dance with you. Different subject. Higher degree."

She leaned back in my arm. I caught her, turned, brought her close again while the whole wedding cheered.

Rosa stood up first. Tank tried to follow and remembered his shoulder. She came to him instead, took his good hand, and led him onto the edge of the floor.

"I don't dance," he told her.

"You do tonight."

"Rosa—"

"Nigga, you got shot for these people. Survive four steps with me."

He survived them. Badly at first. Then better when he stopped looking at his feet and looked at her face.

I watched my brother discover that being large wasn't the only way to take up a woman's whole world.

He looked over at me once, embarrassed and helplessly happy.

I nodded.

Your nigga got it, I was telling him. Your nigga had finally fucking got it.

At the last chorus, the fireworks began over the water.

Blue and gold. Huge flowers opening in the sky above the house I'd bought before I knew where to put my own clothes. The guests turned to look. Shawna stayed looking at me.

I put my forehead against hers.

"You missing the expensive part."

"No, baby."

She touched the cross.

"I'm looking right at him."

Nigga, I didn't have a single smart thing left in my mouth. She kissed me before I could find one.


Then we went inside and got so drunk the sun came up before anybody remembered there had been a schedule.

There was cocaine in the upstairs bathroom, cash changing hands on the terrace, hookers dancing with men who had brought other women to the wedding. Somebody drove a convertible onto the lawn. Tank fell asleep with his good arm around Rosa, and she threatened to kill the first motherfucker who took a picture.

I bought every picture the next morning.

I kept one. Nigga looks at it now and swears he was awake. Rosa has the same picture by her bed.

***

People tell this story like everything ended when Red hit the ground.

It didn't.

The calls kept coming. The money kept coming. The west side still needed a boss on Monday. A man in another city still thought Red dying meant he could take what Red used to sell. Somebody still owed somebody, and somebody's brother still wanted blood.

I didn't become a good man because I put a ring on Shawna's finger.

I was still the nigga who walked into a hotel with blood on his collar and told another man's people the girl was coming with him. I still had a temper. Still had a gun. Still woke up some nights with my hand on the place T had shot me.

And I still wanted everything.

But now I knew who I was bringing it home to.

One night that week, I came back from handling business and found Shawna in the room we'd made for her music.

She had all the lights off except the little lamp beside the piano. There were papers on the floor. A half-finished drink on the windowsill. She was singing something I hadn't heard before.

I stood in the doorway and listened.

When she finished, she turned around.

"How long you been there?"

"Long enough."

"You like it?"

"Yeah."

"You always say that."

"I always mean it."

She held out her hand.

I went to her.

Outside, there were niggas guarding the gates and a city waiting for me to make the next decision. In that room, she pulled me down beside her and put my hand against her heart.

"Stay a minute," she said.

I stayed all night.

***

Aight, my nigga. Now you know which nigga you riding with.

You know about the money in the pool. You know about the blood in the car. You know why I wear a dead man's cross and why my wife still wears his watch. You know which nigga called me son and tried to kill me, and which nigga took a bullet before he'd let me stand alone.

Don't let anybody tell you I came out of that desert clean. I came out alive. I came out with Shawna's hand in mine and Tank bleeding in the back of an ambulance, and I made the whole fucking city learn our names.

My nigga, I gave away the most expensive diamond I ever held. Then I took everything the man wearing it thought he was going to leave behind. That's what happened. That's my money in the walls of that house. That's my name on the cars. That's my wife singing with the window open when the lake goes black at night.

And when she wakes up crying, I'm there. When Tank calls me at three in the morning, I answer. When some motherfucker thinks the years made me soft, I let him get close enough to see the scar.

You can call that love. You can call that crazy. Call it whatever the fuck you want. I was crazy before she loved me. I had blood on me before she touched me. She didn't make me dangerous. She gave all that danger somewhere to come home.

I remember Dante. I never met him, but I remember him every time that gold cross hits my chest. I remember T. I wish I could remember him without the gun. I remember Red. I remember what he looked like when he found out there was something in that room he couldn't buy.

And I remember her in the Mercedes. One hand on the wheel. One hand trying to keep my life inside me. She could've left me. She could've taken what she could carry and gone. But she stayed. My girl stayed.

So your nigga stayed too. What the fuck else was I going to do with a home?

Ten toes down, my nigga. In the club where twelve niggas tried me. In the desert where thirty engines answered. In that hospital hallway waiting for my nigga Tank to open his eyes and start requesting Cadillacs. A nigga can stand in a kingdom; a nigga can stand beside a bed. I stood in both. Ten toes down when the money came, and ten toes down when no nigga could buy the thing I was waiting to hear.

And if another man comes through that gate thinking he's going to make her cry like that again, he better bring every goddamn prayer he knows.

Because I'm home now.

Aiden.

Ten toes down. Forever.


***

The invitation arrived the morning we were packing for our honeymoon.

A blue envelope with a silver seal. Nobody had brought it through the gate. Nobody had rung the bell. It lay on the hood of my police Lamborghini when I came outside with Shawna's suitcase in one hand and my own smaller bag in the other.

Tank saw it first.

"If that's another college, I'm taking the test."

"Nigga, you can start by reading the envelope."

He picked it up.

"Sky High."

I looked at him.

"That a club?"

"School."

"Nigga, I just graduated."

"They seem excited about that."

Shawna came down the steps behind us. Rosa had one arm through hers. Mercedes and Porsche waited by the cars, arguing about how many suitcases one woman could take on somebody else's honeymoon before it became a group vacation.

Marcellus stood beside the white horse, feeding it something the trainer had told him was permitted. Blue Mercy was safe with him now, returned to a proper case. He had stopped carrying the case from room to room. That was how I knew he believed he had come home.

I opened the envelope.

Inside was a photograph of a campus above the clouds.

Not on a mountain. Above the fucking clouds. Buildings, lawns, a football field, towers shining in the sun, all of it standing on a huge piece of land that had apparently decided the ground wasn't good enough for its students.

There was a letter underneath.

Dean Seraphine Storm. Advanced adult hero program. Every member of the incoming class at least twenty-two. The dean had seen the graduation footage, the hospital rescue, the convoy, and enough other parts of my life to decide I had been taking the long route to the appropriate school.

She wanted me there after the honeymoon.

She wanted my people with me.

I read that part twice.

"Nigga," Tank said, looking over my shoulder, "the school is in the sky."

"I can see."

"Our school had steps. These niggas got weather."

Rosa took the photograph from him.

"They got rooms?"

"Whole residences," Shawna said, reading the second page.

"Piano?"

"Conservatory."

"Cars?" Porsche asked.

I looked down at the letter.

*Your automobile may accompany you, Captain. We would prefer that its first landing be supervised.*

I started smiling.

Shawna saw it happen and shook her head before I said a word.

"Baby. Honeymoon first."

"Absolutely."

"I mean a real honeymoon. With a bed. Somewhere the bed touches a floor that touches the fucking earth."

"Whatever my wife wants."

Tank looked at the photograph again.

"Nigga, you think you can be best in that school too?"

I folded the letter and put it inside my jacket beside the badge.

The gold cross settled against my chest.

"Tank."

"What?"

"Those niggas already invited me. They know."

Shawna laughed and took the Lamborghini's keys from my hand.

"Get in, valedictorian. I'm driving before somebody gives you a planet."

I got in.

Nigga, you have to understand. I had a wife, a badge, a kingdom, and a college waiting in the fucking sky.

And she still made me carry the bags.


# BOOK II: SKY HIGH, TEN TOES HIGHER

## 1. They Put My Parking Space in Heaven

The first time I drove my police Lamborghini into the clouds, the sky opened up and a woman told me I was already late for my own award.

I had not enrolled yet. Nigga, I hadn't found the parking lot. Some other nigga was already polishing a prize for me while I was trying to work out whether this cloud counted as a turn.

Tank called from the Mercedes behind us.

“This nigga said you late for an award?”

“Woman said it.”

“Aiden, nigga, don't get technical in heaven. What you win?”

“I don't know yet.”

“How this nigga win something he don't know?”

Shawna leaned toward the phone. “Tank, you've met him.”

That settled the question. I heard my nigga laugh, heard Rosa laugh beside him, heard the Mercedes engine rise through the white air. A nigga could get used to that sound: all his people following because the impossible road had finally decided to hold his weight.

Shawna sat beside me with her bare feet on the dashboard and a pair of white sunglasses bigger than the sins we had committed on our honeymoon. She had a new diamond on her wedding finger and Dante's old watch on her wrist. I had my badge in my pocket, his cross under my shirt, and a twelve-cylinder reason to believe the universe had finally gotten serious about respecting me.

The invitation said Sky High Advanced Hero Academy. A postgraduate program for heroes who had already graduated and somehow still wanted homework. It said my rescue in Vegas had demonstrated exceptional aptitude.

Exceptional aptitude was when you parallel parked without touching the curb.

I had driven through a burning auditorium and still delivered my valedictorian speech before the principal finished crying.

They should have put exceptional motherfucker.

“Aiden,” Shawna said. “Cloud.”

“Baby, I see it.”

“Inside the car.”

A little piece of weather rolled through the open window and rested on her lap. She pushed her sunglasses down and stared at it. The cloud drifted over her wedding ring, turned pink, and dissolved.

“Your diamonds doing shit to the climate now,” I said.

“Keep looking at the road.”

There was no road. That was the first issue.

There had been a road until thirty seconds ago. It had climbed a mountain, passed between two stone lions, and ended at a gate reading WELCOME, HEROES. Then a guard in silver armor had glanced at my gold badge, looked at my face, and saluted so hard his helmet fell off.

“Captain Aiden,” he'd said. “It's an honor.”

“Nigga, which way?”

“Up.”

I had appreciated his confidence.

Now the Lamborghini was climbing an invisible ramp through the clouds at a speed Shawna described as “why the fuck.” The wheel vibrated in my hands. Beneath us, the mountains shrank until they looked like somebody's pile of dirty clothes.

Behind us Tank's black Mercedes rose through the mist. Rosa sat beside him, singing into a hairbrush. Marcellus was in the back wearing a gray suit, carrying a small case, and looking as if he had already decided heaven charged too much for lunch. Dr. Vega had come for a three-day visit and was currently holding Tank's headrest like she intended to remove it.

Mercedes and Porsche followed in a red convertible I had bought them after they pointed out that I owned an island's worth of cars and kept asking them to share an Uber. The women were arguing over whose turn it was to meet a man who could fly.

All my people were ascending.

And at the top of the clouds waited a whole fucking city.

Not a building. A city.

White towers rose around a stadium shaped like a golden shield. A glass train moved between them without touching anything. Gardens hung off stone balconies. An enormous waterfall poured from one edge of the island and disappeared into blue air. Little vehicles streamed across bridges suspended between floating blocks of land. Farther out, a ring of separate islands carried hotels, stores, and a casino with a flashing sign visible from what appeared to be several religions.

SKY HIGH stood over the front gate in letters taller than my mansion.

I slowed down just enough for the Lamborghini to make its noise.

Shawna smiled.

“There he go.”

“Who?”

“My husband about to introduce himself to the atmosphere.”

“Baby, the atmosphere been waiting.”

The invisible ramp became a solid white drive. Students stopped where they were. A man with transparent wings folded them and turned. A woman carrying three refrigerators over her head looked at me and forgot she was carrying refrigerators. Somebody in a crimson cape walked straight into a fountain.

I parked in front of the main staircase.

There was a gold sign.

DEAN.

I read it carefully and remained parked.

A tall woman descended the steps wearing a white suit with silver lightning along the collar. Her hair fell black to her shoulders except for one white streak. She had the kind of face that made a man stand up straighter before he remembered he had a wife beside him. The air sharpened around her. Her eyes were gray, and behind the gray something bright moved.

“Captain Aiden,” she said.

I stepped out. “Dean.”

“Seraphine Storm.”

“That's a hell of a name.”

“I earned it.”

“So did I.”

We shook hands. A tiny spark jumped between us.

I did not let go.

Her eyebrow rose.

“Most visitors flinch.”

“Most visitors ain't me.”

Shawna came around the car. Storm's attention moved to her ring, then to her face.

“Mrs. Aiden.”

“Shawna.”

They shook hands without sparks. I respected the weather for knowing when to behave.

Tank parked behind me. “Nigga, you in her space.”

“I know where I'm at.”

“We can arrange another space,” Storm said.

Tank looked from her to me and slowly took off his sunglasses.

“We just got here.”

“I make a strong first impression.”

From the staircase a blond man in a blue uniform laughed once. He was broad through the shoulders, clean-shaven, with a silver emblem on his chest and a jaw he plainly expected other people to remember.

“That's the famous graduate?” he asked.

Storm didn't look away from me. “Victor Voltage. Twenty-seven. First in his division until this morning.”

Victor's smile stopped.

My smile began.

“Nigga, don't look at me. I ain't touched your division.”

“Your provisional placement puts you first overall,” Storm told me.

“Based on what?” Victor demanded.

She gestured toward the Lamborghini.

He looked at the car as if it had personally stolen his childhood.

“That's a vehicle.”

“The entrance ramp was closed,” Storm said.

Everybody got quiet.

I looked back at the sky.

Tank looked back at the sky.

Shawna took off her sunglasses very slowly.

“Aiden.”

“Now hold on.”

Storm's smile grew. “We were testing our emergency magnetic ascent field. You drove through its narrowest boundary at exactly the velocity required to remain inside it. Then three civilian cars followed your path.”

Dr. Vega got out of the Mercedes.

“I would like to go home.”

“You can use the open ramp,” Storm said.

“There was an open ramp?”

I put my arm around Shawna. “Baby, I brought us the scenic way.”

She pinched my side. The old wound still had opinions about people touching it.

“The scenic way to fucking death.”

“And look how beautiful we survived.”

Then the sky train exploded.

Not the whole train. The front coupling burst in orange flame as it came around the stadium. A sharp crack punched across the courtyard. Heads turned. A hundred windows flashed.

The train tilted.

Forty people screamed at once.

Victor was moving before the sound finished. Blue-white energy wrapped his fists. He launched himself upward, fast enough to knock spray out of the fountain. Storm raised both hands. Wind slammed through the courtyard.

The train's front carriage lurched back toward its rail.

The rear two kept falling.

I saw a woman pressed to the back window. Saw a man drag another man off the floor. Saw the distance between that train and the edge of the island closing.

Nigga, I was supposed to be receiving something.

Instead I had to go earn it again.

I jumped into the Lamborghini.

“Tank!”

He already had the Mercedes door open.

Shawna slid into my passenger seat.

“You staying here,” I said.

“Drive.”

“Baby—”

“Those people do not have time for you to win this argument.”

I hit the gas.

The car shot between the fountain and the steps. Somebody tried to tell me that was a pedestrian path. He said the first half to the windshield and the second half to the exhaust.

The rear carriages struck a maintenance platform beyond the stadium. Metal shrieked. The platform bent toward the open air. Victor hovered above it, both arms spread, electricity coursing into the damaged suspension rings. Sweat ran down his face. His boots flickered.

He was powerful.

He was also holding forty people over a drop nobody had bothered measuring for survivability.

I understood his problem immediately.

Too many niggas. Not enough ground.

I took a turn so hard Shawna's hair whipped across my mouth. The Lamborghini climbed a service stair, hit the landing, and flew over a strip of garden. We landed on the maintenance platform with a crash that made my teeth feel individually expensive.

The platform dipped.

“Get that car off!” Victor shouted.

I looked through the windshield at the hanging carriage.

“Shawna. Door.”

She unbuckled. “Which?”

“All of them.”

I shoved the Lamborghini nose beneath a sloping support beam. The hood buckled. A warning screamed from the dashboard. I kept going until the car wedged between the broken platform and the stone service wall.

The platform stopped dropping.

Victor stared at me.

“Nigga,” I shouted, “keep doing the light shit!”

Shawna was already at the carriage. She hit its emergency release, hauled the door open, and caught the first woman through it by both arms.

“Walk toward the wall,” she ordered. “Keep your hands on the rail. Don't look down.”

Somebody looked down and froze.

My wife slapped him.

“Look at me instead.”

He did. He moved.

Tank brought the Mercedes onto solid ground and jumped out. Rosa followed him. She took one look at the gap and began singing, loud and steady, a beat people could move to. Not a sad song. One of the nasty ones she performed in Vegas when men forgot how much cash they had brought.

Forty terrified adult heroes began crossing a ruined platform to a song about getting paid before breakfast.

I climbed onto my hood.
