It was an expensive hood. I would mourn it when niggas stopped falling out of the sky.

Inside the last carriage, a man had his leg trapped beneath a fallen seat. A silver-haired woman knelt beside him. One whole side of the carriage was opening over empty blue air.

I jumped through the door.

The woman looked at my badge.

“Are you rescue?”

“Today.”

I grabbed the seat. It didn't move.

The trapped man said, “My power's density. I can't turn it off when I'm scared.”

“How heavy?”

“A lot.”

“Nigga, that is a terrible number.”

The train shifted. Outside, Victor yelled. A burst of blue light turned the windows white.

I braced my shoes against the opposite seat and pulled. The metal bit my palms. Nothing. The man shook so hard the floor rattled.

I got close to his face.

“What's your name?”

“Elias.”

“Elias, listen to me. My wife standing outside this train.”

He blinked.

“That woman thinks I'm the greatest man alive. I happen to agree. Now you gonna make both of us look stupid?”

“No.”

“Then stop trying to weigh more than my reputation.”

He laughed. Just once. A frightened little cough of a laugh.

The floor lifted.

I tore the seat aside.

“There we fucking go.”

The woman helped me drag him. We reached the door as the back window broke away. Wind hit us. My cross slapped against my chest.

Below, the waterfall hung like a white ribbon all the way into the clouds.

Victor's left hand went dark.

The carriage dropped six inches.

I shoved Elias through the door into Tank's arms. The woman followed. I grabbed the rail.

Then the platform tore loose.

My Lamborghini went with it.

For one ugly second I saw my whole future reflected in that dark blue roof: car gone, wife watching, nigga floating down to Earth with a gold badge and an unpaid insurance argument.

Shawna caught my wrist.

Tank caught her waist.

Storm's wind caught the car.

Everything stopped.

Not gently. My shoulder made a noise. Shawna swore. Tank planted his feet and shouted, “I got all you motherfuckers!”

The dean stood at the end of the broken walkway with lightning in her hair. The entire Lamborghini hung sideways beneath us inside a spinning cradle of cloud.

“Captain,” she said through clenched teeth. “Would you please stop adding weight?”

I hauled myself up beside my wife.

“I'm trying to take some off.”

Victor brought the last carriage down into the grass. Storm lowered my car beside it. The engine ticked. The left headlight hung out like a tired eye.

Silence spread over the service yard.

Then Elias began clapping.

The silver-haired woman joined him.

By the time I stood up, everybody was doing it.

Shawna grabbed my face and kissed me hard enough to settle the disagreement we had not finished in the car. I held her against me. Around us forty rescued people cheered louder.

“That's my husband,” she said when she pulled back.

Nobody argued.

Victor landed beside the wrecked train. His uniform smoked at the wrists. He looked at the Lamborghini. Looked at my bleeding hands. Looked at Shawna holding me.

“You have no powers,” he said.

“I got several good qualities.”

“No. I mean you have no measurable power signature.”

“Nigga, measure the people who ain't dead.”

His mouth opened.

Then he looked at Elias sitting safely on the grass.

He closed it.

Storm came toward me. Her hair settled. Behind her, students poured around the corner, calling to the passengers, filming the wreckage, shouting my name even though I had introduced myself to approximately four people.

“Your award ceremony,” the dean said, “will now include an additional citation.”

I looked at my car.

“Will it include a body shop?”

“The best engineering faculty in the sky.”

“Good. That nigga need a doctor.”

Dr. Vega stepped around Tank carrying a medical bag.

“The car can wait. You are bleeding.”

“Little bit.”

“That is also a terrible number.”

She took my hand. Shawna stood against my other side. Tank looked at the shattered platform and shook his head with a smile he couldn't hide.

“You been here twelve minutes.”

“Thirteen,” Storm said.

“See?” I told him. “I gave the school an extra minute.”

At the edge of the crowd stood a thin man in a charcoal suit. He had silver hair combed straight back, a black cane, and eyes that did not seem interested in blinking. Two guards stood behind him in uniforms darker than the others.

Storm noticed him and straightened.

“Chancellor Voss.”

He approached the broken coupling first. Bent his head. Touched a scorched piece of metal with one gloved finger.

Then he turned to me.

“An extraordinary arrival.”

“We try.”

His smile showed no teeth.

“You saved a number of people whose gifts are important to this institution.”

I glanced at Elias. He was holding the silver-haired woman's hand. His whole body shook now that it was allowed to.

“Saved the rest too.”

“Naturally.”

Voss's eyes moved to my badge, then my cross, then Shawna. He lingered on none of them long enough for me to call it a problem.

But a nigga can feel a problem dressing itself.

“We will investigate the equipment failure,” he said.

“Do that.”

His guards collected the broken coupling before anybody else touched it.

Storm watched them go. Her face had changed for one second, then changed back.

She offered us the grand staircase, the open doors, the city of people waiting to meet me.

I put my good arm around Shawna. Tank lifted my overnight bag from the ruined car. Rosa took his other arm. Marcellus appeared carrying the case he had somehow never set down.

“First impression?” he asked.

“Strong,” I said.

He looked at the wrecked train, then at the whole school applauding.

“I should have brought a larger safe.”

We went up those steps together.

Above the entrance hung a banner they had apparently prepared before I arrived.

WELCOME, EXCEPTIONAL HEROES.

Somebody was already climbing a ladder to change it.

I didn't tell them to.

Nigga, excellence makes suggestions of its own.

Our rooms occupied the top floor of a tower overlooking the western edge. There were two balconies, a bath large enough to qualify for boat ownership, and a bedroom ceiling that showed the actual stars above the clouds. The bellman set down our bags and waited to be tipped.

I gave him enough money to change the direction of his afternoon.

He looked at it. Looked at me.

“Sir, I have worked here eleven years.”

“Then you was overdue.”

He left walking backward.

Shawna closed the door and leaned against it. Her smile had gone soft. That was the one that always made me feel more dangerous and less prepared at the same time.

“You scared me,” she said.

“I had it.”

“I know you had it. That's not the same thing.”

I crossed the room. She put her hands beneath my open jacket and rested them against my ribs, careful of the old hurt. Outside the balcony a woman flew past carrying a bouquet larger than herself. Somewhere below us people were still shouting about the train.

“You came with me,” I said.

“Always.”

“Even when I'm parking wrong.”

“Especially. Apparently that's when you become first in your class.”

I kissed her forehead. Then her mouth. She pulled me closer, and for a little while the biggest thing happening in the sky was our door staying shut.

Later, when we stood on the balcony wearing the school's expensive robes, I saw a second city beneath the first.

It wasn't really a city. More a collection of black buildings suspended under the island's lower rock. Bridges joined them. Red lights burned along their roofs. One tower descended farther than the rest and ended in a circular chamber that glowed through its windows like a covered furnace.

“What's that?” Shawna asked.

“Basement with ambition.”

A train moved along a track beneath it. The cars had no windows.

She stopped smiling.

The train entered the glowing chamber. For a moment the windows turned a strange yellow-white. Then every light went out together.

Above us, music began on the school lawn. People laughed. Somebody sent a ribbon of purple fire curling between two towers.

Shawna rested her head against my shoulder.

“Tomorrow,” she said, “I'm finding somebody who'll tell me what that is.”

I looked at the dark place under all our beautiful rooms.

“Tomorrow,” I said, “I'm getting my fucking car back.”

## 2. My Superpower Was Being That Nigga

The engineering professor cried when he returned my Lamborghini. This nigga had repaired half the greatest machines in the sky, and now he was holding a polishing cloth to his face because my car had made him believe again.

Actual tears. One fell on the hood, and he polished it away with his sleeve before he let himself have the next one.

His name was Professor Atlas Bell. He was forty-six, had four arms, and treated engines like other men treated their firstborn sons. He stood beside the car in the morning sunlight with two hands folded, one holding a clipboard, and the last stroking the repaired fender.

“It was beautiful before,” he told me. “But what you did with it—”

He had to stop.

Tank leaned toward me. “Nigga, you made a man cry with traffic.”

“It wasn't regular traffic.”

“Nigga was crying when we got here.”

“Maybe he started early.”

“No, nigga. Rosa asked that nigga what happened, and he said your suspension.”

I looked at Bell. The professor nodded gravely, like my suspension had died for his sins and risen on the third wheel.

“A magnificent structure,” he said.

Tank pointed at him. “See? Nigga grieving and praising at once.”

“Let that nigga feel his feelings,” I told him. “He brought my car back beautiful.”

Bell had restored the dark blue paint. The police lights were now hidden beneath the front edge, so the car looked like pure money until I decided somebody should be nervous. He had reinforced the suspension for campus roads and fitted the wheels with the academy's standard field receivers. That meant the Lamborghini could travel along the marked sky lanes like the other vehicles. It did not mean it could fly wherever I wanted.

He explained that last part three times.

I heard him all three times. I just refused to make my face less hopeful.

Shawna came down the steps in a white tracksuit with my name embroidered over her heart. Rosa wore red. Mercedes wore green leather. Porsche had found a silver jumpsuit and a pair of boots that made a nearby man forget how stairs worked.

“We going to your test,” Shawna said.

“What test?”

Victor emerged from the archway behind her.

“Power placement.”

He said it like an execution date.

“I already got a parking place,” I told him.

“Let's see how you perform without a car.”

“Nigga, ask my wife.”

Shawna slapped my chest and started laughing. Victor looked up at the sky as if requesting a different assignment from God.

The placement hall was bigger inside than outside. It had retractable walls, a floor divided into colored circles, and a spectator gallery rising around all four sides. Students filled the seats. Word of the train rescue had apparently traveled faster than the train was supposed to. Half the crowd wore little gold paper badges somebody had made overnight.

One woman held a sign reading ARREST ME, CAPTAIN.

Shawna saw it.

The woman slowly turned it around.

Storm stood in the center beside a stone pillar holding a blue crystal. The crystal wasn't the size of a jewel. It was the size of a man's head, cut into an uneven heart, and its light pulsed down through the pillar into the floor.

“The Heart of the Sky,” she said as we approached. “It anchors the academy's central field. Today you will be assessed around a fractional projection of its output.”

I looked at the thing.

“Whole school running off one diamond?”

“A power core. It amplifies gifts; it doesn't create them.”

Marcellus bent toward the crystal. He did not touch it. His expression narrowed.

“Interesting cut.”

Voss stood near the gallery stairs. “Please keep your distance, Mr. Vale.”

Marcellus straightened. “I was admiring it.”

“Of course.”

Storm clapped once. The first wall folded back, revealing a corridor full of swinging steel blocks. Beyond it stood three platforms and a bell suspended over a pool.

“Movement,” she said. “Judgment. Control. Rescue. We rank useful outcomes, not destruction.”

Tank looked at the steel blocks. “Good. Because some nigga absolutely about to destroy something.”

Victor went first.

I gave him that much: the man was magnificent when he stopped talking.

He turned into a streak of blue light, passed between the blocks, landed on the first platform, and sent a bolt into a target above the second. A bridge unfolded. He crossed it, caught a weighted rescue dummy as it fell, and reached the bell in twenty-three seconds.

The crowd roared.

He set the dummy down carefully. Looked straight at me. Rang the bell once more.

I nodded.

“Clean.”

He seemed annoyed I meant it.

A woman named Petra Stone went next. Twenty-nine, broad shoulders, calm eyes. She could turn her skin into white marble. She carried the rescue dummy through a steel block instead of around it. Her time was slower. The steel block's prospects were considerably worse.

Mercedes stood up clapping.

“Girl, yes!”

Petra looked up, spotted her, and nearly dropped the dummy.

Porsche leaned against the rail. “You already choosing?”

“I'm appreciating strength.”

“You appreciate everybody with shoulders.”

“Only if they use them right.”

Then Storm said my name.

The entire gallery stood.

Nigga, I had not done anything in this room yet.

I took off my jacket and gave it to Shawna. She smoothed my collar with both hands.

“Come back with all your teeth.”

“Baby, that's the minimum.”

At the starting line, a faculty member asked whether I required a special condition.

“Such as?”

“Reduced gravity. Protective barrier. A powered escort.”

“Some music.”

He blinked.

Rosa began tapping the railing.

Tank joined her. Then Porsche. Then half the room. A big rolling beat traveled through the hall. My people had turned a superhero examination into the entrance to my own heavyweight championship.

Storm lifted her hand.

The blocks began swinging.

I ran.

First block left. Second block right. A narrow opening appeared between them, and I went through sideways with my shoulder almost kissing steel. The third descended straight at my head. I dropped under it, slid across the floor, and came up laughing because a nigga knows when his body has decided to make him famous.

The first platform was farther than it looked.

I jumped anyway.

My fingers caught the edge. I pulled myself up, rolled under a sweeping bar, and saw the target Victor had struck with lightning.

I had no lightning.

I had shoes.

I took one off and threw it.

The shoe hit the center of the target.

The bridge unfolded.

Tank shouted so loud I heard him over everybody else.

“Nigga used a loafer!”

I crossed in one shoe, caught the falling dummy over my shoulder, and took the last platform in three strides. The bell hung above the pool. Victor had flown to it. Petra had jumped from the edge.

I threw the dummy onto the safe pad, caught its rebound with my knee, and used the spring in the pad to launch myself up the pillar beside the bell.

My hand struck gold.

The sound filled the room.

Twenty-two seconds.

I landed in the pool.

Nobody's masterpiece is dry all the way through.

When I surfaced, Storm was smiling. The faculty member stared at his clock. Victor stared at my shoe, which was slowly sliding off the target.

Shawna had both hands over her head.

“That's my fucking man!”

I climbed out dripping. Walked to Victor. Held out my hand.

He looked at it.

“You used the rescue dummy as a springboard.”

“I rescued it first.”

“That's not—”

Storm glanced at the safe pad. “The dummy remained entirely within the designated safety zone.”

Victor shook my hand.

Hard.

I shook it back.

Harder.

We both smiled like niggas deciding whether a friendship ought to begin with a fight.

The next test involved doors. Behind one stood a fire. Behind another, a trapped volunteer. Behind a third, a man pretending to be an attacker. You had to choose in six seconds using information flashed on a screen.

I looked at the screen.

Then I looked at the doors.

Then I walked up to the third door and knocked.

The volunteer attacker opened it out of surprise.

I took his padded weapon.

“You under arrest.”

The gallery exploded.

He said, “But the scenario—”

“Nigga, you armed behind a door while people dying in the next room. Come carry something.”

I put him to work. Together we carried the trapped volunteer through the safe corridor while Petra smothered the training fire with a wall of stone. The faculty member tried to say assistance wasn't part of the test.

Storm asked whether real disasters prohibited asking another adult for help.

He looked at his clipboard and discovered a deep interest in the lower half of it.

By lunch they had awarded me first place in movement, judgment, improvisation, and something called command presence.

Command presence was when other niggas did what you said because it sounded like the part of the day they should survive.

I had been practicing that since Vegas.

Then the real attacker came through the ceiling.

He wore a black flight harness and a mirrored mask. Three more followed him through the skylight. They fell in a line, landing around the crystal pillar with weapons already raised.

The first shot shattered a gallery lamp.

Screams replaced applause.

Victor moved toward the pillar. One of the attackers threw a dark metal hoop. It struck his chest and opened around him, pinning his arms to his sides. His lightning flared once, then guttered.

Storm lifted her hand.

The man in the mirrored mask held up a small device with a red light.

“Wind,” he said, “and the south gallery falls.”

Beneath the south seats, red lights blinked.

Shawna was in the south gallery.

So was everybody I loved.

I felt the whole room go narrow.

The man saw my badge.

“Sit down, officer.”

I looked at him.

Nigga had chosen the wrong profession to disrespect in front of my wife.

“What's your name?” I asked.

“Your last warning.”

“Your mama named you terribly.”

His weapon moved toward me.

My shoe hit his mask.

The same shoe. I had retrieved it between tests. A good object can have more than one destiny.

He stumbled. I crossed the space between us and hit him with every grievance I had about being wet in public. The red device flew from his hand. Porsche caught it over the gallery rail.

She stared at the blinking light.

“Do I press it?”

“Fuck no!” four of us shouted.

She tucked it into her purse. “Then nobody else getting it.”

The room erupted.

Petra stepped in front of the gallery stairs and turned to marble as gunfire struck her shoulders. Mercedes dragged two frozen students down behind the seats. Tank came over the railing like a refrigerator deciding it had wings. He landed on one attacker, picked him up by his harness, and introduced him to the training pool.

Rosa kept people moving. Shawna had my jacket. My gun was inside it.

She threw the jacket.

I caught it against my chest as the masked man recovered. He lunged. I swung the whole jacket into his face, pulled the gun free, and brought the fight to a clear disagreement he could understand.

“Down.”

He looked at the gun.

Looked at me.

Went down.

At the pillar, another attacker struck the crystal with a forked black instrument. Blue light cracked through the room. The floor tilted. Students slid against the gallery rail.

The crystal split down its center.

Instead of a blaze, it gave a thin, ugly flicker.

Marcellus saw it.

So did Storm.

Their faces told me different things about the same bad discovery.

The attacker cursed and tried again. Victor, trapped in the hoop, slammed himself sideways into the man's knees. Both fell. The forked instrument skidded toward the pool.

I kicked it away before anybody could reach it.

Tank emerged from the water holding his attacker by the collar. “This nigga allergic to drowning. Thought everybody should know.”

Storm's hands flashed.

With the red device safely inside Porsche's purse, the dean stopped being patient.

Wind tore the weapons out of the attackers' hands. A pressure wave lifted all four men and pinned them against the far wall. Their harnesses rattled. The mirrored mask broke in two.

Underneath was a lean man with a burned eyebrow and a grin too quick for the situation.

He looked at me.

“You're better than the picture.”

“And you worse than your introduction.”

Voss arrived through the side doors with six guards. He took in the smashed skylight, the fractured crystal, the attackers pinned to the wall. His jaw tightened before the rest of his face followed.

“Finn Cinder,” he said to the unmasked man.

Finn's grin faded.

“Chancellor.”

I caught that.

Storm caught it too.

“You know him?” she asked.

“A notorious sky-lane criminal.”

“Nigga,” I said, “he knew you back.”

Voss turned to me. “My position attracts enemies.”

“Apparently they know which door to use.”

His guards took the men from Storm's wind. Finn went quietly, but as he passed Victor he looked at the hoop around the man's arms and almost smiled again.

Almost.

I noticed almosts for a living.

Once they were gone, Bell hurried to the pillar with two assistants. The broken crystal had gone gray. Storm stood over it without speaking.

Marcellus touched my elbow.

“That isn't the core she described.”

“You sure?”

“Aiden, I have spent most of my life distinguishing beautiful things from expensive lies.”

Across the hall, Victor struggled with the hoop. Every time he summoned electricity, its dark surface drank the light. He was trying to make it look like he had chosen to stand there with his elbows glued to his ribs.

I went over.

“Hold still.”

“I have it.”

“You got it around you. Different accomplishment.”

He stopped moving. Bell took one look, muttered something furious about stolen equipment, and pressed the release concealed under its rim. The hoop opened.

Victor flexed his arms.

“Thank you.”

It came out like a little rock he had been forced to swallow backward.

“Anytime.”

“You still cheated on the course.”

“Nigga, you turned into lightning. I threw footwear.”

For the first time, he laughed.

Just briefly. But I saw the man hiding behind all that first-place anger, and the man seemed like somebody I could eventually drink with.

Shawna reached me. She ran her hands over my chest, checking what bullets had failed to do. Then she held my face and looked at me with those dark, bright eyes.

“You did all that with one shoe on.”

I looked down.

Still one shoe.

The other lay beside the shattered mask in a little patch of sunlight.

“Baby, imagine if I had dressed properly.”

She started laughing, and the laugh broke the last of the fear in my ribs.

The gallery began chanting my name.

Aiden. Aiden. Aiden.

Somebody added Captain. Somebody added King. Elias, the man from the train, stood at the front with both fists in the air as if we had been brothers since birth.

Storm raised her voice over them.

“Today's assessment is concluded.”

Victor looked at her. “The final rankings?”

She gestured at the room: forty safe students, four captured gunmen, one ruined crystal, my wife holding my face like I was the prize the academy should have been competing for.

“Do you require them read aloud?”

He considered that.

Then he stepped aside and let me pick up my shoe.

On our way out, Porsche handed me the red device from her purse.

“You owe me.”

“For saving the gallery?”

“For not pressing a button. You know how hard that is when it looks important?”

I took it. The light had stopped blinking.

On the back, beneath a scrape in the black paint, was a tiny silver crest.

A narrow tower. A downward-pointing wing.

The same crest Voss's guards wore on their shoulders.

I closed my hand around it before anybody else saw.

“Come on,” I said to my people. “Let's go find lunch.”

Tank studied my face.

“And after lunch?”

I looked toward the doors through which the chancellor had taken my prisoners.

“After lunch, nigga, I'm finding out who think this school belong to him.”

Lunch took place on a terrace where the tables floated six inches off the ground. I asked the waiter why. He said atmosphere. I told him we already had plenty. He laughed until he realized I meant the table should stop drifting while I tried to cut my steak.

Victor joined us uninvited, which I considered progress. He sat opposite Tank and ordered enough food for three men. Petra came with Mercedes. Porsche immediately asked whether Petra had any brothers, sisters, cousins, or enemies with similar shoulders.

Shawna took my hand beneath the table.

“You really don't feel any different?” she asked.

“From what?”

“The crystal. The test. All this.”

I turned my hand palm up. There were fresh bandages over yesterday's cuts. The fingers still belonged to a nigga who had to open his own jars.

“Same me.”

Victor leaned forward. “That makes what you did worse.”

“Worse?”

“More difficult to accept.”

Tank laughed into his drink.

“At least you honest now.”

A pair of uniformed campus officers approached our table. Both were older than me. One had a neatly trimmed gray beard; the other could apparently see through walls because she looked toward the kitchen and said our second round was coming.

The bearded officer saluted.

“Captain. Commander Orrin Pike. Campus patrol.”

“Sit down, Commander.”

“I'd be honored.”

He sat so fast Victor had to move his plate.

Pike explained that the chancellor maintained a separate security force for the lower facilities. Campus patrol could handle the sky lanes, the shops, and the residential towers. Anything below the island's foundation required Voss's approval.

“What lower facilities?” Shawna asked.

Pike looked at Storm's tower before answering.

“A detention and research annex. Established before the dean's appointment.”

“Detention for who?”

“People whose powers present unusual risks.”

“Charged with what?” I asked.

He shifted in his chair.

There it was.

Not proof. Not even half of proof. But enough for lunch to become something I ate while being angry.

The second officer put a folded slip beside my plate. She kept her voice low.

“The four men from your hall never reached our cells.”

Victor stopped cutting his steak.

I unfolded the slip. A patrol camera had captured Finn Cinder boarding a black car under his own power. No cuffs. Voss's guard held the door for him.

Pike looked ashamed enough to make me trust him a little.

“I thought you should know.”

I put the picture in my pocket.

“Commander, nigga, you just earned yourself a very interesting afternoon.”

## 3. You Can't Outrun a Nigga with a Siren

Commander Pike offered me a patrol car. A regular patrol car. Nigga had watched me turn a Lamborghini into a rescue platform and decided what I needed next was a sedan with enough trunk space for cones.

I looked out his window at my Lamborghini waiting below.

He looked too.

“That was a stupid offer,” he said.

“Not stupid. Hopeful.”

Tank looked at the patrol car through the window. “That nigga got cloth seats.”

Pike cleared his throat. “They're durable.”

“Nigga, so is my aunt's couch. I ain't chasing nobody in it.”

“Your aunt got a very aggressive couch,” I reminded him.

“That's different. That nigga been through things.”

Pike looked between us, trying to decide whether he had hired two idiots or discovered a form of policing his academy had failed to teach. Then he glanced at my gold badge and chose faith.

Campus patrol occupied a stone building between a bakery and a store selling capes. The bakery smelled better than any police station I had visited. The cape store had a line outside. People apparently bought new identities the way niggas in Vegas bought belts.

Pike spread a map over his desk. The academy occupied the largest island. Six smaller districts floated around it, joined by marked lanes sustained by the school's field. If you stayed on those lanes with the right receivers, your car could drive through open air. Leave the field and gravity remembered your ass immediately.

The largest satellite was called the Crown District. Hotels, restaurants, showrooms, a marina for airships, and the Cloud Nine casino. Finn Cinder's car had headed there after leaving the academy.

“Can your people follow him?” I asked.

“They can. He knows our cars.”

I turned my badge over in my hand.

“Then let's introduce him to mine.”

Tank drove with me. Victor asked to come, and I told him there was no third seat.

“I can fly.”

“Nigga, why you asking for a ride?”

He looked at Pike. Pike found a fascinating place on his map to point at until Victor left.

Shawna had plans of her own. The dean had invited her and Rosa to rehearse with the academy's evening orchestra. My wife had heard “orchestra” and “doors ordinarily locked to visitors” in the same sentence and decided music deserved her immediate attention.

Mercedes went with Petra to see the lower training gardens. Porsche announced she was going shopping. She said it with such innocence I gave her a second look.

“What?” she asked.

“Nothing.”

“Exactly. Mind your police business.”

That woman could sell rain to the clouds and make them apologize for being dry.

We left the patrol station under a bright afternoon sun. The Lamborghini rolled between white pillars and onto the first sky lane. Blue strips of light ran beneath the tires. Beyond either side was nothing but air.

Tank stared out his window.

“I miss curbs.”

“You used to hit every curb in Vegas.”

“That's how I knew they was there.”

Ahead of us the Crown District glittered. A red sports car passed on the other side of the lane, driven by a man with gold skin and a woman wearing a hat shaped like a small thunderstorm. Rain fell exclusively into her champagne glass.

Tank watched them go.

“Rosa gonna want that.”

“The hat?”

“The champagne weather.”

We spotted Finn outside a showroom called ASCENT. He stood between a black coupe and a salesman whose smile looked physically painful. Two guards waited near the door. None wore masks now. Finn had a strip of tape over the eyebrow I had helped him lose.

I parked across the road.

He saw the Lamborghini before he saw me.

That gave him half a second to enjoy life.

Then I stepped out.

“Finn.”

His face changed.

The salesman looked relieved someone else had become his problem.

“Captain,” Finn said. “We keep meeting.”

“That's because niggas keep letting you go.”

He looked up. Victor floated above the showroom roof, arms folded, electricity crawling over his shoulders.

Finn smiled at him.

“You get your bracelet off?”

Victor descended six feet.

I raised a hand.

“I got this.”

Finn's guards shifted.

Tank leaned against the Lamborghini and opened his jacket just enough for them to understand the local temperature.

“Y'all can keep standing,” he said. “Just stand peaceful.”

I approached Finn. “Who paid you to hit the hall?”

“You're assuming money.”

“Nigga, your shoes cost six thousand dollars and you look allergic to principles. I'm assuming correctly.”

The salesman made a little noise that might have been laughter and immediately pretended to cough.

Finn's eyes went flat.

“You don't know the city you're in.”

“Then show me.”

He did.

The black coupe leaped backward through the showroom window.

Glass burst into the street. Finn dove through the open passenger door as the car spun. One guard threw a smoke sphere. Tank caught it, looked offended, and threw it back.

The sphere burst under the man's feet.

His first cough sounded like regret.

The coupe shot onto the sky lane.

I was in the Lamborghini before the broken glass finished falling.

Tank landed beside me.

“Nigga, we arresting him or racing him?”

“He picking the format.”

I hit the siren.

Blue lights lit the clouds beneath us.

The Lamborghini lunged forward. Finn's car swerved around a delivery van and accelerated toward the Crown District's outer loop. I followed. The road curved around a hotel whose swimming pool hung over open air. People at the pool stood up when we passed. A woman waved. Her companion stared at the police lights and spilled an entire tray of drinks into his own lap.

Victor flew above us, keeping pace.

“He has two more vehicles joining,” he said through the patrol radio Pike had given me.

“Where?”

Two silver cars came out of a side lane.

“There.”

“Useful timing, nigga.”

The first silver car struck my rear quarter. The Lamborghini slid toward the lane's luminous edge. For one second Tank's window showed nothing below us at all.

He turned to me very calmly.

“Aiden.”

“I know.”

I steered into the slide, let the rear swing, and put us back between the blue strips. The silver car tried again. This time I braked. It shot past, clipped Finn's coupe, and bounced toward the outer barrier.

Victor caught it with a web of crackling light.

The driver stared through his windshield at the man holding his car over the clouds.

Victor smiled without warmth.

“Wait here.”

He set the car on a maintenance bay and welded its doors shut with a bright hiss. It wasn't going anywhere until somebody with tools and a better attitude arrived.

The second silver car pulled alongside us. A gun came through its window.

Tank leaned back as a shot shattered my mirror.

“Nigga shot the mirror.”

“I saw.”

“That's how we see other niggas.”

He returned fire. The attacking car veered off, sparks skipping from its door. I drove between it and a tourist coach full of adults in matching yellow jackets. The coach passengers flattened themselves against the opposite windows.

One of them gave me a thumbs-up.

I gave it back.

Customer service did not stop because somebody was trying to kill me.

Finn headed for a spiral lane climbing around a hotel tower. I followed him up. Faster. The engine climbed toward its beautiful, furious scream. Wind punched through the broken mirror housing. Tank laughed the way he always laughed when terror finally realized it had come to the wrong man.

We burst onto the hotel's roof.

A wedding reception was taking place there.

White chairs. Gold glasses. A fountain full of flowers. Two adult grooms stood beneath an arch, both in immaculate suits, both looking at Finn's car as it tore between their guests.

He knocked over the cake.

I will admit that made it personal in a new way.

“Hold tight.”

“Nigga, to what?”

I drove onto the narrow stone rim around the fountain. The Lamborghini rose sideways. Water flashed beneath Tank's door. We passed the fallen cake on two wheels, cleared a table, and landed in front of the arch.

Both grooms stared.

“Congratulations,” I shouted.

Then we were gone.

Behind us the wedding guests began cheering.

Ahead, Finn took the departure ramp toward the smaller northern island. The black coupe's rear lights flickered. Something unfolded from its sides: short angular wings, illegal enough that the patrol radio immediately began shouting about them.

“He's leaving the lane,” Pike warned.

Finn's car lifted.

My car did not have wings.

Bell had been very clear about that.

Tank turned his head slowly toward me.

“Remember what the four-arm nigga said.”

“I remember.”

“You got the remembering face and the doing-it-anyway face. Right now they fighting.”

I watched the coupe rise over the northern island's cliff. Beneath it a service lane curved through the rock, then emerged on the far side beside a loading platform.

I took the service lane.

Darkness swallowed us. The engine thundered against stone. Ahead, daylight shrank to a small white rectangle.

Tank braced both feet.

We came out under Finn's car.

Not flying. Driving up the last steep piece of lane at exactly the moment he drifted over it.

The Lamborghini's roof struck the underside of his wing.

The wing snapped backward.

The black coupe rolled, skidded across the loading platform, and hit a stack of empty crates with a crash that sent wood flying all the way to a restaurant balcony.

I stopped beside it.

The Lamborghini's hood smoked.

Tank stared at me.

“Nigga.”

“What?”

“You jumped a car without jumping your car.”

“Efficient.”

He began laughing so hard he had to lean against the door before he got out.

Finn crawled from the coupe. His coat was torn. His expensive shoes were covered in champagne-colored dust from somebody's broken shipment. He looked at my car with something dangerously close to reverence.

“You cannot be human.”

I showed him the badge.

“I'm employed.”

He reached toward his belt.

Tank drew.

Finn stopped reaching.

Then the loading platform's doors opened behind him.

Voss's guards stepped out.

Six of them. Weapons lowered but ready. At their center stood a woman with close-cropped red hair and a black uniform stitched with the downward wing. She looked about forty. Her voice could have broken a glass without raising its volume.

“This is restricted academy property.”

“Good,” I said. “Then you'll have cameras.”

“Hand over the prisoner.”

“Funny. That's how this morning started.”

Victor landed beside me. Blue light ran along his fingers. The guards looked at him and adjusted their expectations.

“Captain Aiden made this arrest,” Victor said.

The woman studied him.

“Mr. Voltage. Your scholarship review is next week.”

He went still.

I felt it: the invisible leash she had expected to tighten around his throat.

I stepped in front of him.

“Nigga, I didn't ask about his scholarship.”

She looked back at me.

“Do you understand where you are?”

“A loading platform with six guns and too much attitude.”

Pike's patrol cars arrived behind us. Eight officers got out. The gray-bearded commander walked to my side and held out a pair of cuffs.

I put them on Finn myself.

For the first time all afternoon, nobody had a clever thing to say.

We left with the prisoner.

The woman watched until the sky lane curved away.

Finn sat in the back of Pike's car. I followed in the battered Lamborghini with Victor overhead. Tank kept turning around to make sure no black uniforms had developed an urgent need to explain themselves with bullets.

My phone rang.

Shawna.

“Baby, I might have scratched the car,” I said.

“I know. Your wedding stunt already on six phones in this room.”

“They happy?”

“One groom wants you to sign his jacket.”

“Tell him yes.”

Her voice lowered.

“Aiden. We found something.”

I listened.

She and Rosa had been rehearsing in the old music hall. While the orchestra took a break, Rosa heard a voice coming through a brass ventilation grille beneath the stage. Not talking. Singing. The same four lines over and over, in a woman's tired but steady voice.

Shawna knelt beside the grille and sang the next line.

The voice stopped.

Then somebody said, very clearly, “Are you above us?”

My grip tightened on the wheel.

Shawna asked who was there.

The woman said her name was Lena March. Thirty-two. A singer who could carry her voice through solid matter if she knew where to aim it. She had been in the lower annex for five months. Her release date changed every time she reached it.

“She says there are people down there who aren't on any student list,” Shawna told me. “She says they take them through a round door, and some come back old. Some don't come back at all.”

Ahead of me Finn looked through the rear window of Pike's car.

Our eyes met.

The little grin was gone.

“What else?” I asked.

“She heard the name Winter Engine. And there's a doctor down there. Reiss. He told her if she ever found somebody outside, she had to say the real heart isn't in the hall.”

I looked up at the academy floating above the sunlit clouds.

“Baby, stay with Rosa. Tell Storm only. Nobody in black.”

“I'm not leaving that woman singing into a wall.”

“I know.”

“You know what that means?”

“Means we got plans tonight.”

Her breath softened in my ear.

“Come back first.”

“Always.”

When we reached the station, Finn asked to speak to me without Voss's people present. He sat in a cell with ordinary iron bars, which seemed almost embarrassingly old-fashioned after everything we had driven through.

I stood outside with Pike and Victor.

Finn rested his elbows on his knees.

“You think the bottom of this school is the bottom,” he said.

“Explain.”

He looked at the ceiling.

“There's a door under the prison. It doesn't open into another room.”

Victor's face tightened.

“Where does it open?”

Finn swallowed.

“Another year.”

The bakery next door rang its little bell. Somebody laughed out on the sidewalk. Through Pike's window I could see my car shining in the sun, every dent earned in front of witnesses.

For a moment those ordinary sounds felt far away.

Then I leaned toward the bars.

“Nigga,” I said, “you better start at the beginning.”

He began with a car, which was the first sensible thing the man had done all day.

Three months earlier, Voss's red-haired security commander had hired him to transport a sealed engine housing from the Crown District to the lower annex. Her name was Commander Sable. She paid well, asked no questions about his history, and made it clear she expected the same courtesy. Finn had driven the housing down the service ramp at midnight and waited while two technicians unloaded it beside a circular metal frame.

“The room smelled like cold iron,” he said. “There were rails going straight through the circle. Not our kind of rails. Old ones. And a clock over it with three hands.”

Victor folded his arms.

“A chronal aperture.”

Finn looked at him. “Whatever the fuck you call it, there was a field on the other side. Real grass. A little station building. Snow on the roof. I could feel cold coming through.”

“You went through?” I asked.

“No. A man came out.”

He rubbed his wrists where the cuffs had been.

The man had worn a long military coat and carried a leather case. Two others followed him, pushing a cart with a covered shape on it. Finn thought it was equipment until the covering moved. He heard a person beneath it ask for water. Sable told him to face the wall.

He faced it.

When he turned around, the strangers were gone. The cart remained. A dark stain spread across its blanket. Not blood, Finn insisted; something like blue ink that glowed on the edges.

“They'd taken somebody's power too far,” Victor said quietly.

Finn wouldn't meet his eyes.

I watched the man's face. The swagger kept trying to come back, finding no place to stand, and falling away again.

“And you went back to work for them.”

“I saw a thing I didn't understand. I've seen a lot of things I didn't understand.”

“You understood water.”

He went silent.

I let him sit in that silence. I didn't need a speech from him. I needed the part he hadn't yet decided to tell us.

Eventually he looked at Pike.

“There's a race tonight. The Sundown Circuit. Sable moves the lower-annex manifests during the race because half your patrol is managing the spectators. She carries them herself, in a silver case. If you want names, that case has names.”

Victor stared at him.

“The race was scheduled last month.”

“Yeah. And I'm telling you why your chancellor suddenly agreed to sponsor it.”

I looked at Pike. He had already reached for his phone.

“No,” I said. “We tell Storm in person.”

Pike stopped.

“And your next meal,” I told Finn, “comes after you give the commander every route you remember. Nobody asking you to be beautiful. Just useful.”

Outside, late afternoon had softened the towers to gold. Victor walked with me toward the Lamborghini without saying anything. He stopped by the repaired front fender and put his hand on it as if touching an animal he hadn't decided whether to trust.

“I'm entered in that race,” he said.

“You drive?”

“Very well.”

I waited.

He looked at me. “I know how that sounded.”

“Nigga, I'm letting you enjoy it.”

He almost smiled.

“There's another entry available. Bell prepared a demonstration car. It needs a driver.”

I glanced at my Lamborghini, then up at the circuit winding around the highest towers. The setting sun caught the lanes and turned them into long strips of fire.

Somewhere under us a woman was singing because it was the only way she could reach the world.

“Tell Bell I got a car,” I said. “Tell him what I need is a number.”

Victor nodded once.

“Which number?”

I looked at him until the answer arrived in his face.

“One,” he said.

“See, nigga? We learning together.”

## 4. First Place Was Wherever I Parked

Bell put the number one on my door in gold. Tank stood beside him with his arms folded, supervising a nigga with four hands like the fifth hand was going to be his if that number leaned.

He asked whether I preferred it centered.

“Nigga, I prefer it accurate.”

“It is your entry number,” Bell said.

Tank shook his head. “That's this nigga exit number too.”

“Placements remain to be determined.”

“Nigga, by who?”

Bell looked at me. I looked at the gold one. The professor sighed with the exhaustion of a man who knew engineering could explain a great many things and none of them would help him win this conversation.

He nodded as though I had just taught him something about art and measured the distance from both edges again.

The Sundown Circuit wrapped three times around the academy, crossed a canyon of empty air between two floating islands, passed through the Crown District, and ended on the stadium's upper terrace. Twelve drivers had entered. Every one of them had powers except me. Their cars glowed, floated, snarled, or did some combination that made the mechanics back away respectfully.

My Lamborghini looked like a police car had married a bank account and produced a very angry son.

That was enough.

Before the race, we met Storm in her private office. Shawna repeated what Lena had said. Pike showed Finn's release photograph. I put the red device from the hall on the dean's desk.

She turned it over and saw the downward wing.

The room grew colder.

“The lower annex predates my appointment,” she said. “Voss claims its most sensitive work is approved by the founding board. He has blocked my access three times.”

“Then let's make four different,” I said.

“If I strike at him without securing the school's field, he can put every person on this island in danger.”

“He already doing that.”

She met my eyes.

“Yes.”

One honest word. I liked her better for it than all the titles she had.

She knew the circular machine. Years earlier, before Voss became chancellor, a physicist had proposed using the Heart to open a passage into a single branch of the past. The faculty rejected the experiment after a test chamber lost power and came back coated in frost. The project was supposed to be dismantled. Dr. Ilya Reiss, its designer, retired soon afterward.

“Or got retired underneath us,” Tank said.

Storm's hands closed on the arms of her chair.

We agreed on two things. She would keep the academy's main field stable and quietly move her own trusted people into the control tower. We would get Sable's case during the race. Nobody would open a time door because some nigga with a cane had decided ordinary crime lacked imagination.

Shawna listened to every word. Then she put both palms on the desk.

“Lena stays in this conversation. Names on a page won't help her if we forget the woman who got them to us.”

Storm nodded.

“We won't.”

My wife held her gaze until she believed it.

That was why I loved her. I could fill a room. Shawna could make a room answer.

By sunset the stadium was packed. Spectators crowded balconies all along the circuit. Airships hovered outside the lanes, their passengers leaning over rails with drinks in their hands. A huge screen showed the drivers as we approached our cars.

Victor wore blue racing leathers. His vehicle was a low silver machine with three bright rings behind the cockpit. It looked fast standing still. He caught me admiring it and smiled.

“Built around my charge pattern.”

“Nice.”

“It can draw power directly from me.”

“Mine draws power from gas and disrespect.”

He laughed. A real laugh this time.

Then his face went serious.

“Don't leave the marked lane at the canyon.”

“You worried about me?”

“I'm worried I'll win and you'll have an excuse.”

“That's friendship trying to happen, nigga. You should stop fighting it.”

Across the grid, Shawna kissed me beside the car while every screen in the stadium showed us. I had one hand at her waist. Her fingers rested against my neck. The crowd made a sound so loud the starting official stopped talking.

She pulled back smiling.

“Win beautifully.”

“You know any other way?”

“Try coming back without spending another hood.”

Tank handed me my helmet. Rosa tied a red ribbon around his wrist for luck, then tied a blue one around mine because she said two idiots required separate colors.

Mercedes and Porsche were already gone.

Their part of the race did not involve driving.

Sable would watch from Voss's private terrace above the Crown District. She liked expensive company and disliked being bored. Porsche had spent the afternoon learning both facts from a bartender she tipped more generously than his employer. Mercedes had secured an invitation by introducing herself as the woman who knew Captain Aiden before the sky discovered him.

That was technically true, and technically was a beautiful country.

The lights above the grid turned red.

Twelve engines rose.

The stadium chanted Victor's name first. He was theirs. He had earned that.

Then my side began.

Aiden. Aiden. Aiden.

Both chants crashed together until the whole place sounded like it was arguing with thunder.

Green.

We launched.

Victor took the lead. A yellow coupe driven by a woman called Sunfire swept behind him. I went third, tight against the lane's inner edge. The first turn rose around the stadium, steep enough to put the sun under my left shoulder. The Lamborghini gripped. I felt every bit of it: wheel, road, engine, the gold number on my door announcing the future before we arrived there.

Sunfire's exhaust flashed bright orange. Heat shimmered over the lane. I couldn't see Victor.

“Nigga,” I said to nobody, “we doing weather already?”

I waited half a breath, found the darker line beneath the shimmer, and drove through it. Her car slid wide. I passed on the inside close enough to see her turn her head in disbelief.

She grinned.

Raised two fingers.

Then tried to take her place back.

I respected that.

The lane dropped toward the canyon. For a second the entire city rose above me. The car felt light. My stomach tried to resign. I held the wheel steady as the tires crossed onto the narrow field bridge spanning the gap.

Victor was a silver streak ahead.

A green car closed behind me, its driver making little jumps between patches of road. Each jump flashed the air purple. He appeared on my left, vanished, appeared on my right.

“Pick a side, nigga.”

He appeared ahead of me.

I accelerated into the space he had to leave to make the next jump. When he reappeared, he was behind my rear bumper.

The radio erupted with Bell shouting my name.

“You anticipated the recovery interval!”

“Nigga, I anticipated him being annoying!”

We swept into the Crown District at a speed that made windows reflect us after we were already gone.

High above the road, on Voss's terrace, Porsche dropped a champagne glass.

That was all I saw passing beneath her.

Later she told me the rest.

The glass broke near Sable's shoes. Mercedes caught Porsche by the elbow and apologized with the offended elegance of a woman whose evening had been spoiled by somebody else's clumsiness. Sable stood to avoid the spill. Her silver case remained under her chair.

Porsche bent to pick up the largest piece of glass.

Mercedes asked Sable whether Captain Aiden was really as impressive to the faculty as he had been in Vegas.

Sable answered before she remembered not to.

“More.”

That little word cost her the case.

Porsche slid a matching empty case beneath the chair and passed the real one behind a curtain into Petra's marble hand. Petra carried it down a service stair while pretending a twelve-pound locked box was a clutch purse.

By the time Sable sat again, Mercedes had persuaded her to explain why she enjoyed racing.

“Because it reveals weakness,” Sable said.

“Mm,” Mercedes replied. “Depends who driving.”

At the end of the first lap, Victor led me by three car lengths.

At the end of the second, one.

He was good. Nigga, he was better than good. He took the high turns with a precision that made the car look attached to his thoughts. Blue charge pulsed through the rings behind him. Whenever I closed, he found another little piece of speed.

I started laughing inside my helmet.

Not because he was losing.

Because finally somebody was making me work hard enough to enjoy how good I was.

Then his car screamed.

A bright bolt jumped between the rear rings. The silver body jerked sideways. Victor corrected, but the rings brightened again, feeding on him. I saw his shoulders stiffen through the cockpit glass.

“Victor?”

Static.

“Nigga, talk.”

His voice came thin through the radio.

“The draw won't stop.”

Bell shouted something to the race officials. The warning lights along the lane turned amber.

Victor's car accelerated.

Not because he wanted it to.

The rings pulled harder. Blue light wrapped his whole body. The silver machine shot toward the canyon at a speed it could not survive entering the next turn.

I followed.

Behind me Sunfire slowed. The green car vanished toward a safety bay. The spectators' cheers broke into a different sound.

“Cut your power,” I told Victor.

“It's taking it.”

I heard pain in the last word.

Storm's voice entered the radio. “Aiden, I am coming.”

“Can you reach him before the canyon?”

Silence for half a second.

Enough.

I pressed the Lamborghini harder.

Bell's beautiful engine gave me everything it had.

The distance closed.

Twenty feet.

Ten.

Victor's helmet turned toward me. His face behind the visor looked gray. The man who had wanted to beat me was disappearing inside his own gift.

“Don't hit the rings,” Bell warned. “They're overloaded.”

I brought my front bumper level with Victor's rear wheel.

“Wasn't planning to.”

There was a service split before the canyon, a short lane leading to an emergency terrace. Victor couldn't turn toward it. His car had locked itself into a straight hungry line.

I could turn him.

I struck the silver car low on its side.

The Lamborghini shuddered.

Victor's machine moved six inches.

Not enough.

“Again,” he whispered.

Nigga, I would remember that whisper longer than any trophy.

I hit him again.

Both cars crossed the split together. The terrace rushed toward us. My tires shrieked. Victor's rear rings tore bright scars through the air.

We struck the emergency barrier side by side.

Foam burst upward in a white wall.

My seat belt tried to cut me in half.

Then we stopped.

For one second all I heard was my own breathing.

Then Victor screamed.

I kicked my door open and ran to his car. The cockpit wouldn't release. Blue light poured through every seam. I caught the handle and felt heat bite through my glove.

“Aiden, don't touch the chassis,” Bell shouted.

I had already touched it.

Electricity snapped up my arm. My whole body locked. I fell backward onto the terrace, seeing white.

No new power came into me. No miracle. Just pain and the sharp understanding that a nigga could absolutely die here.

Victor hit the glass from inside.

Once.

Weaker the second time.

I got up.

My left hand shook. I made it hold the heavy emergency hammer mounted beside the terrace rail. Swung with the right.

The glass cracked.

I swung again.

A hole opened.

Victor's eyes found mine.

“Come on, nigga.”

I reached through, caught his shoulder strap, and pulled. He came halfway. The car held the rest of him in its light.

Then a white wind slammed across the terrace.

Storm landed beside me. Her hands spread over the rear rings. Lightning rose out of them and into her arms. She gasped but held it.

“Now.”

I pulled Victor free.

We fell together. The silver car burst behind us, its rings breaking upward in three bright arcs. Storm bent the explosion away from the terrace and sent it flowering over empty sky.

The sound rolled around the city.

Victor lay against me, breathing in hard little pieces.

I took off his helmet.

His eyes opened.

“Did you win?”

I looked back at my Lamborghini. One front corner was buried in foam. The engine was still running.

“Hold that thought.”

Storm stared at me.

“Captain.”

“He stable?”

She looked at Victor, then at the approaching medical team.

“Yes.”

I got back in the car.

Bell made a noise over the radio that might have been a prayer or a mechanical diagnosis. I put the Lamborghini in reverse. Foam peeled away from the hood. The wheel pulled left. I held it straight.

The officials were attempting to suspend the race. The other drivers were already entering the final circuit. Nobody had crossed the line. The track remained open until they could bring every car safely in.

I rejoined at the service split.

In ninth place.

Nigga, ninth was temporary.

I passed two cars before the canyon. Three more through the Crown District. Sunfire saw me in her mirror and laughed so hard I could see her shoulders move. She gave me no space at all.

I found some anyway.

At the last turn I was second.

The green car led.

He jumped forward in a flash of purple.

I drove into the space where he needed to finish.

He reappeared beside me.

We crossed the line together.

The stadium went silent for one impossible heartbeat.

Then the screen showed my front bumper.

Six inches ahead.

First.

I stopped beneath the finish arch. Got out. Took off my helmet.

Shawna reached me before anybody else and jumped into my arms so hard I nearly fell back into the car.

“You beautiful fucking lunatic.”

The whole stadium heard her.

The whole stadium agreed.

Tank stood on the hood with both fists up, yelling my name. Rosa danced beside the car. Porsche arrived carrying the silver case, and Mercedes kissed it like a baby she had stolen for a noble cause.

Victor came down the medical ramp leaning on a medic.

He stopped in front of me.

For a second I thought he might cry.

Instead he took my hand, lifted it over both our heads, and turned us toward the crowd.

“The best driver in the sky,” he shouted.

That was generous.

It was also geographically cautious.

I let him have it.

Above us, in his private box, Voss did not clap.

Beside him, Sable opened the empty case.

Even from the track, nigga, I could see the evening leave her face.

The trophy was four feet tall.

They tried handing it to me while Shawna was still in my arms. I looked at the trophy. Looked at my wife. The official looked at both and wisely gave the trophy to Tank.

“This nigga won a building,” Tank said.

“It's a sculpture,” the official told him.

“Nigga, it got windows.”

“Decorative panels.”

Tank turned the thing around. Somewhere inside it a little gold car circled a track of blue glass.

“Aiden, this nigga won a building with a nigga driving inside.”

I put Shawna down long enough to admire it. The tiny car crossed a tiny finish line. Tiny lights flashed.

“Make sure the little nigga get first too,” I said.

The official assured me it was designed that way.

“Good design.”

Sunfire reached us laughing. Up close she was a brown-skinned woman of thirty-one with orange curls and a small burn on her racing glove. She slapped my shoulder, looked at the Lamborghini, and shook her head.

“You left the race. Saved that man. Came back and beat all our asses.”

“Busy evening.”

“No. A busy evening is dinner and a movie. This nigga took a rescue break from winning.”

Victor stood beside me, pale but upright. “I was the break.”

“You were the reason,” I told him.

He stopped smiling.

Only for a second. But the words went somewhere in him that the trophy didn't reach in me.

“I'd have done the same,” he said.

“I know.”

I did know by then. He had been proud before he met me. Nothing wrong with that. A nigga with no pride would never have stayed in that broken train's sky long enough for me to get there. I wasn't interested in shrinking him so I could look tall. I was already tall enough to make people reconsider architecture.

Bell arrived with all four hands shaking.

“I need the car.”

“You just had the car.”

“I need to understand what you did to it.”

Tank pointed at me. “This nigga happened to it.”

Bell touched the hood. The Lamborghini ticked softly, as if agreeing it had been through an emotional experience.

Then the dean joined us. She embraced Victor first. He seemed surprised by how tightly she held him. When she let go, she took my unburned hand in both of hers.

“You brought him back.”

“He still owed me a fair race.”

“You brought him back,” she repeated.

I nodded. That time I let the joke wait.

Later, in our tower, Marcellus opened Sable's case while Tank stood guard at the door. It contained paper manifests, a black access seal, and three photographs held together with a blue ribbon.

The first photograph showed the lower prison.

The second showed the circular door.

The third showed a snow-covered station beneath a sky with no floating islands in it. Men in military coats stood beside a freight wagon. On the back, in neat black writing, somebody had put a date.

February 1944.

Shawna turned the photograph over again.

“Aiden.”

“I see it.”

Victor leaned closer. He had stopped being a rival so completely that I barely noticed when it happened. He was just one more man in the room whose face hardened because somebody else was being hurt.

Marcellus unfolded a manifest. Names. Ages. Powers where powers existed. Blank spaces where they didn't.

“They aren't only taking gifted people,” he said.

Outside our window, fireworks celebrated my victory over the clouds.

Inside, Shawna counted the names with her finger, carefully, as if refusing to let a single one of them disappear between lines.

## 5. The Party Was in My Honor, So the Gunfight Was Too

By eight the next night, three women had asked Shawna whether she shared.

By eight-oh-four, all three understood mathematics differently.

“One husband,” she told them. “One wife. Zero confusion.”

I stood beside her holding two drinks and trying not to smile too much. A nigga could be proud without making his own evening harder.

The tallest woman looked me up and down. She had silver eyes, a black evening dress, and the power to make all the candles near her lean in her direction. She was thirty-three and clearly used to rooms cooperating.

“I only asked,” she said.

Shawna smiled.

“And now you educated.”

Tank turned away before the laugh came out. Rosa hit his chest with her little purse, which only made him laugh harder.

We were at Cloud Nine for the race champion's banquet. The casino floated a short distance beyond the Crown District, joined by a broad blue lane and two narrow service bridges. Its windows curved around a central ballroom. Above the roof, an enormous glass moon rotated inside a ring of golden clouds.

Some rich nigga had looked at the real sky and decided it needed a ceiling ornament.

For once, it wasn't me.

The invitation came from Madame Afterglow. Her real name was Eveline Dusk, thirty-seven, and her gift made light linger in places after she left them. She wore gold like it had recently apologized. Every movement left a faint shining echo behind her, so when she crossed the ballroom you could admire her arrival three separate times.

“Captain Aiden,” she said, taking both my hands. “My casino has hosted princes, world champions, and men who swear they own the night.”

“Busy place.”

“None of them arrived with your reputation.”

Tank leaned toward Rosa. “This nigga reputation had to take the earlier car.”

“Needed more seats,” Rosa said.

Afterglow laughed without looking away from me. Shawna stepped beside my shoulder, and the golden woman turned her attention just as warmly.

“And you must be the reason he comes home.”

“He better,” Shawna said.

“I like her,” Afterglow told me.

“That's excellent judgment.”

The ballroom applauded when we entered. Not a polite little ripple. Chairs moved. People stood. The orchestra changed songs in the middle of a note because the conductor saw me and apparently believed timing was something lesser men worried about.

A huge picture of my Lamborghini hung behind the stage.

Under it, in gold, they had written THE MAN WHO CAUGHT LIGHTNING.

Victor stared at it.

“That would be me.”

“Nigga, you the lightning,” Tank told him. “Keep up.”

Victor considered the picture. Then he looked at me.

“Fair.”

He had recovered enough to attend, though Dr. Vega had forbidden him to use his powers until morning. He wore a dark suit and no emblem. Without the uniform, he looked younger and less determined to win an argument nobody else knew was happening.

Petra arrived with Mercedes. Both wore black. Porsche had a young man named Leon on her arm, twenty-six, whose power let him split into three versions of himself for about a minute.

Tank watched all three Leons help Porsche with her chair.

“Nigga cheating at manners.”

Porsche looked delighted. “Finally, enough man for my luggage.”

A waiter brought a silver bowl containing folded cards. Afterglow tapped her glass.

“Our little tradition,” she said. “A guest draws a name, and that guest receives a favor from the champion.”

Shawna's fork stopped.

“What kind of favor?”

“Usually a dance.”

“Then that tradition just got shorter.”

The waiter froze with the bowl halfway over our table. Nigga looked at my wife like she had just canceled the moon.

Afterglow laughed. “A song, then. Or a toast. Something innocent.”

Marcellus reached into the bowl.

“You ain't even competing,” Tank said.

“I am curious.”

He unfolded a card.

It said AIDEN.

He drew another.

AIDEN.

He looked into the bowl. Then he tipped the whole thing onto the table.

My name fell everywhere. Aiden in the breadbasket. Aiden beside the butter. One little Aiden landed directly in Victor's wine.

Victor lifted his glass and watched the card sink.

“Even the fucking refreshments.”

“Who wrote these?” Shawna asked.

The waiter swallowed.

“Several departments participated.”

“Nigga, the kitchen wanted a dance?” Tank asked.

“The kitchen wanted him to taste the soup.”

I picked up a card. A heart had been drawn around my name. Underneath it somebody had written PLEASE SAY IT NEEDS MORE SALT. HE WON'T LISTEN TO US.

That nigga was using my greatness to fix a soup dispute. I respected ambition when I found it.

“Bring the soup.”

The waiter almost dropped the bowl trying to bow.

“Captain, a great honor.”

“Bring enough for my wife.”

He bowed at Shawna too. Nearly put his forehead in the butter.

At the next table sat a enormous man in a white dinner jacket and a woman with a crown of actual living blue flowers. The man had been studying me with that particular face men make when the room has discovered a bigger reason to turn around. His name, according to the little plaque by his plate, was OREN TITAN. SKY HIGH CLASS OF THE YEAR BEFORE LAST. RECORD HOLDER.

Underneath, in smaller letters, it listed his records.

Nigga had so many they had given the plaque a second foot.

“I suppose,” he said, “we are all very impressed with driving.”

I turned in my chair.

“Depends who's driving.”

“Some of us performed our feats without an engine.”

Tank looked at the long plaque.

“This nigga brought his accomplishments to dinner.”

Oren's flower-crowned companion closed her eyes for a second. I recognized the look. A woman hearing her man choose the longest available route to embarrassment.

“Oren,” she said. “Eat.”

“I am speaking to the champion.”

“And the champion was happy eating.”

I liked her already.

Oren stood. His chair seemed grateful. He lifted one hand, and the massive marble pedestal beside his table rose into the air. A vase of blue roses rested on top. The pedestal turned slowly over his palm while guests applauded.

He could make things light. Or himself strong. I didn't know yet. Either way this nigga had interrupted my soup to argue with furniture.

“Six hundred pounds,” he said.

“Nice.”

“With one hand.”

“You want me to hold your plate?”

Porsche put her napkin over her mouth.

Oren smiled harder. The pedestal rose another foot.

“I can balance it indefinitely.”

His companion said, “Then do it outside. You're shedding plaster in my drink.”

He glanced down.

The pedestal tilted.

A very small thing. A shift. But its top was wider than its base, and the vase was wet underneath, and everybody at that table had finally received a reason to stop clapping.

The roses slid.

Oren tried to save the vase with his free hand. His shoulder turned. The pedestal rolled toward the woman in the blue flowers.

I was out of my chair before he knew he'd made two mistakes.

I caught her chair by the back and pulled it away. The pedestal struck the table. Wood cracked. Plates flew. Her glass turned over directly above her face.

I caught the glass too.

Nigga, I didn't want her evening ruined twice.

The table collapsed. The vase broke against the empty chair beside hers. Oren stood with one hand in the air and a rose stuck to his lapel.

I put her glass on our table.

“Shawna, we got company.”

Shawna moved her own chair over.

“Girl, sit.”

The woman looked from the wreckage to her drink in my hand.

“You didn't spill it.”

“It seemed expensive.”

“Nigga, it was,” she said, and started laughing so hard the little flowers in her crown shook.

Her name was Opaline. Forty, a sculptor, and very much tired of watching her dinner become an exhibition. Oren began explaining that the pedestal's balance had been altered by a defect in the floor.

Afterglow looked at the floor.

Then at him.

“My floor was here first.”

Tank pushed an empty chair toward Oren with his foot.

“Sit down, record holder.”

“I am not—”

“Nigga, you about to set one for standing beside a mess.”

He sat.

I expected him to stay furious. Instead he watched Opaline laughing with Shawna, looked down at the rose on his lapel, and started laughing too. Quiet at first. Then with his whole chest.

“I had a speech,” he admitted.

Opaline pointed at him without looking away from Shawna.

“He practiced it in the car.”

“What speech?” I asked.

“About grace under pressure.”

Tank slapped the table. Victor had to remove the card from his wine so he wouldn't inhale my name while he laughed.

“Nigga,” I told Oren, “you can still give it. Make the ending honest.”

He rubbed his face.

Then he stood again. This time both hands stayed where furniture couldn't misunderstand them.

“To the champion,” he said. “Who saved my wife's evening from her husband.”

Opaline lifted her glass.

“Best record you've set all year.”

We drank. Oren drank. The orchestra caught our table's laughter and decided it meant the room wanted a faster song.

Then the soup arrived.

Six cooks came with it.

Nigga, six. One carrying the bowl, five standing behind him with the deadly stillness of men whose whole afternoon had come down to a spoon.

I tasted it.

The cook in front gripped his hat.

“Well?”

I tasted again. Shawna watched me over her glass. She knew I was enjoying this. Aiden in the breadbasket, a record holder at my table, an entire kitchen waiting for judgment. A nigga didn't come to a school in the sky every day. Sometimes you had to let the sky show you what it had learned.

“Needs salt,” I said.

The shortest cook threw both hands up.

“I fucking told you.”

The head cook turned so slowly I thought somebody had stopped time just for his neck.

“You put the cards in the bowl.”

“I put the truth in the bowl.”

Afterglow covered her face. Her golden echo covered its face half a second later.

I held out my hand for the salt.

The head cook gave it to me. I added a little, tasted again, and nodded.

He tasted from his own spoon.

Stopped.

Tasted again.

Then that nigga took off his hat and held it against his chest like I had just returned it from a war.

“I will name it for you.”

“Don't name it before you feed my friends.”

“Every table,” he announced, turning to the kitchen doors. “Aiden's soup. Immediately.”

Oren watched the cooks hurry away.

“You defeated me and seasoned dinner in less than four minutes.”

“Three,” Victor said, checking his watch.

Shawna squeezed my knee under the table.

“Try being married to this nigga.”

“Lucky,” Opaline said.

My wife looked at me. Her smile got smaller and warmer.

“Yeah,” she said. “I know.”

We ate beneath chandeliers full of captured starlight. I don't mean the waiter said starlight and brought candles. Actual little points of fire drifted behind glass. The food was excellent. The wine cost enough to suggest the grapes had attended private school.

I enjoyed every fucking minute.

That mattered. We had bad things underneath us, but I was not about to let Voss steal a good evening before he had even paid for it. My people looked beautiful. Shawna's knee pressed against mine. Rosa talked with both hands while Tank watched her as if every story ended in treasure. Marcellus wore the Blue Mercy ring on a chain beneath his shirt and quietly assessed the chandeliers' settings for flaws.

Across the room, Voss sat with Sable.

The empty silver case was not present.

I raised my glass toward them.

Sable did not raise hers back.

Some niggas had no social skills at all.

Storm arrived late. Her white gown moved like a storm front behind her. She touched my shoulder as she passed and said quietly, “The records are secure.”

That meant our stolen case was now in her private safe, the names copied by people Voss couldn't order around. It meant the school finally possessed something firmer than my opinion that its chancellor looked like a funeral with shoes.

It did not mean we could storm the annex yet. The foundation field had been rerouted. Voss held the real Heart somewhere below, and the academy was balanced on a system he could threaten to interrupt. Storm's engineers were trying to give us another way to keep the island in the air.

In the meantime, she sat beside Victor and asked whether he was behaving.

“I haven't used my powers,” he said.

“Good.”

“I did threaten a champagne cork.”

“A warning is permitted.”

Shawna laughed. Victor looked pleased enough that I almost forgave him for being handsome near my wife.

Almost.

Then Afterglow announced that the champion would dance.

Nobody had asked the champion.

The champion stood anyway.

Shawna took my hand. Her dress was deep blue, soft through the waist, bright at the shoulders. When she turned toward the floor, half the room forgot they had come to look at me.

I understood. A nigga with eyes had to understand.

We moved beneath the glass moon's reflected light. I knew how to fight with music going. Dancing was mostly trusting the same feet to make a better decision. Shawna rested her hand behind my neck. I felt the old watch against my skin and the new ring against my shoulder.

“You like this?” I asked.

“Everybody worshipping you?”

“The view. The food. My extremely coordinated ass.”

“I like you trying to act like you didn't practice that turn in the bathroom.”

“Nigga, that bathroom had a lot of space.”

She laughed into my collar.

“You nervous?”

“About dancing?”

“About underneath us.”

I looked past her shoulder. Voss was watching. Sable whispered something to him, and his fingers tightened around the stem of his glass.

“I'm impatient.”

“That's not the same answer.”

“Baby, I know.”

She pulled back enough to see my face.

“I'm going to get Lena.”

“We going.”

“I said what I'm going to do. I know what you doing.”

I loved the little fire in her when she said that. Loved that she could stand inside a room built to make me feel enormous and still leave no confusion about the size of her own heart.

I turned her. The orchestra rose. Applause broke around us.

For a moment there was only her smile and the clean pleasure of being the man she had chosen in front of all these people who wanted something from me.

Then Voss stood and came onto the floor.

“May I?” he asked Shawna.

I looked at him.

“May you what?”

His smile didn't move.

“A dance.”

Shawna's hand stayed in mine.

“I'm dancing.”

“A private word, then.”

“You can have a public one,” she said.

The couples nearest us slowed.

Voss looked at me with the tired expression of a man accustomed to getting threats mistaken for wisdom.

“Your husband has made an extraordinary impression.”

“He does that,” Shawna said.

“Extraordinary impressions can tempt a person into believing every locked door is an invitation.”

I smiled.

“Nigga, if you wanted to talk about doors, why you ask my wife to dance?”

A man behind Voss made a choking sound into his drink.

The chancellor's face tightened.

“I hope you enjoy your evening.”

“Already am.”

He left the floor. Sable followed him out a side door.

Victor watched them go. Storm's eyes followed too.

Afterglow appeared beside us with a smile that had lost half its warmth.

“What did he want?”

“A personality,” I said. “We couldn't help.”

She laughed once, sharply. Then she leaned closer.

“His security people have been taking over my service floors. I permitted storage. I did not permit armed men to tell my staff where they could walk.”

“How many?”

“Tonight? Too many.”

Before I could answer, the orchestra stopped.

A man stood on the stage holding a gun.

Not Voss. One of Sable's guards, now wearing a dinner jacket over his black uniform. Three more appeared by the exits. Another locked the doors behind the bar.

The first guard spoke into the singer's microphone.

“Remain seated. This establishment is under temporary security control.”

Nigga, he said that at my party.

My party.

Tank looked at me across the dance floor. I looked back.

That was our whole conversation.

The guard onstage pointed at me.

“Captain Aiden. You will accompany us.”

I took Shawna's glass from her hand and set it on a passing tray.

“Baby, hold my applause.”

She rolled her eyes.

“Come back and get it.”

I walked toward the stage.

The guard watched me. He wanted me scared enough to move carefully. That was his first financial mistake. His second was standing under a chandelier while giving orders to a room containing multiple people who could break architecture with their feelings.

“Hands visible,” he said.

I lifted them.

“Like this?”

“Stop.”

“You wanted me to accompany you. Nigga, I'm accompanying.”

Behind him, Afterglow's light began to linger.

One gold reflection became two. Then four. The guards saw movement where no bodies stood. Their weapons shifted toward echoes.

I jumped onto the stage and hit the microphone stand sideways.

The stand struck the guard's wrist. His shot went into the ceiling. Starlight rained through broken glass.

Petra moved in front of Mercedes. Tank overturned a table and put three guests behind it before firing at the exit guards. Rosa dragged the orchestra down behind their instruments. The drummer refused to abandon his cymbals until she called him a beautiful idiot and promised to buy him louder ones.

Shawna went toward the locked bar door.

I saw her pick up a champagne bottle by the neck.

The guard turned.

My wife hit him so hard the expensive champagne became a weather event.

“That nigga interrupt my dance,” she said.

Porsche caught the man's keys before they hit the floor.

“Our dance floor now.”

Leon became three men. One opened the door, one helped people through, and one stood near Porsche trying to look useful enough to survive the evening romantically.

Victor started toward the gunfire.

Dr. Vega caught his sleeve.

“No powers.”

He looked at her.

Then picked up a chair.

“Fine.”

He hit a guard with the chair.
