Tank saw it and roared approval.

“There you go, lightning nigga! Analog!”

I fought the man onstage across the piano. He was bigger than me and well trained. He knew where to put his weight. Knew how to use the edge of the instrument. He drove an elbow into my ribs and tried to bring his gun around.

I caught his wrist. The old wound burned. The room narrowed around his face.

“You should've come quietly,” he said.

“Nigga, I didn't even arrive quietly.”

I drove him back into the piano. Keys crashed under his spine. His gun went sliding across the lid. I caught it before it fell, turned, and fired at a guard raising his weapon toward Shawna.

The man dropped behind the bar.

She looked at me.

I looked at her.

We went back to work.

Storm never threw a bolt through that crowded room. She moved the air around the guests instead, guiding them toward the open doors, knocking falling glass away from their faces. Afterglow filled the gunmen's vision with golden doubles. Between the two women, the ballroom became a place where innocent people could move and armed idiots could not agree on what was real.

The last guard ran for the service lift.

I followed.

He hit the button. The doors began closing.

I slid between them sideways and landed inside with him.

He stared.

“Nigga,” I said, “you forgot your host.”

The lift shot upward while we fought against its mirrored walls. He caught my lapel. I caught his throat. He slammed me into the rail. I drove my knee into him and tore free. The doors opened onto the roof beneath the enormous glass moon.

A black aircraft waited there with its engines turning.

Sable stood beside its open door.

She saw me come out holding her man's collar.

For the second night in a row, I ruined the end of her plan.

She drew.

I shoved the guard behind a stone planter and dropped as shots struck the lift doors. Glass sprayed. The aircraft's engines screamed louder.

Sable climbed aboard.

I ran after her.

The aircraft rose.

I jumped onto its low landing rail.

The city dropped beneath my shoes.

Nigga, I had briefly forgotten Bell's instructions because this wasn't technically my car.

Sable looked down at me through the doorway.

“Let go.”

“You first.”

She swung a boot at my hand. I pulled myself higher. Wind tore at my jacket. Below us the glass moon turned slowly above its golden ring.

I saw my opportunity and respected it immediately.

I caught Sable's wrist as she reached for her weapon. Twisted the gun away. It fell through the air, struck the moon, and disappeared inside with a bright crack.

She hit me across the face.

I smiled blood onto my own shirt.

“That was rude.”

Then I let go.

Not straight down.

Onto the moon's golden support ring.

My feet struck metal. I slid, caught a decorative cloud, and held on while the aircraft veered away. Sable stared back from the doorway, her weapon gone, her guard captured, her attempt to drag me away witnessed by half the casino.

I stood up on the ring.

The whole roof applauded.

They had followed me out. All these rich, gifted, half-drunk niggas had come upstairs to see whether I intended to fight an aircraft in formalwear.

Apparently I did.

Shawna stood at the front with both hands on her hips.

“Get off the fucking moon.”

“Baby, you gotta admit—”

“I admit everything. Get down.”

Storm brought me down on a ribbon of wind. The moment my shoes touched the roof, my wife grabbed me by both lapels and kissed me in front of every witness available.

When she let go, Afterglow stood behind her holding a gold key.

“Lifetime suite,” she said. “Anything you want. Any time.”

Tank looked at the key.

“Nigga got assaulted into property.”

I took it.

“Good evening after all.”

Then Storm's phone rang. She listened, and the smile left her face.

The lower annex had begun moving prisoners.

Lena's song had stopped.

## 6. The Basement Found Out Who Lived Upstairs

I returned to Sky High wearing a torn dinner jacket, carrying another man's gun, and smelling like champagne somebody had used as a weapon.

The night porter stood when he saw me.

“Good evening, Captain.”

“Debatable.”

He saw Shawna beside me, saw Tank behind her, saw Victor carrying a broken chair leg because he apparently had developed an attachment to doing things without powers.

The porter straightened even farther.

“Would you like your room prepared?”

“Nigga, prepare the basement.”

He had no idea what that meant.

Neither did the basement yet.

Storm met us in the music hall. Pike had brought six officers he trusted. Bell stood beside a hatch in the stage with all four hands occupied by tools. Dr. Vega had traded her evening bag for her medical one. Marcellus held the black access seal from Sable's case.

Rosa knelt at the brass grille.

She sang the four lines Lena had sung before.

Nothing answered.

She sang them again, softer.

The empty air below the stage remained empty.

Tank knelt beside her. Put his hand on her back.

“We going get her.”

Rosa nodded without looking up.

Then she stood, took off her earrings, and put them in his pocket.

That was the moment the evening changed for him. A nigga can hear a hundred plans. Then the woman he loves puts something small and precious in his hand, and suddenly the plan has a heartbeat.

Storm drew a line through the air. A pale image of the lower annex appeared above the piano. The prison hung beneath the island in three connected buildings. One housed the cells. One held the laboratories. The lowest contained the circular chamber we had seen from our balcony.

“Pike's people will secure the upper service lift,” she said. “Bell will keep the secondary support field alive. I have to remain near the foundation controls. If Voss cuts the main current, somebody must catch the load.”

“You catching a whole school?” Tank asked.

“For a little while.”

He looked at me.

“Nigga, your teachers serious.”

Victor would come with us, but with his power restricted until Vega cleared him. He looked ready to object. The doctor lifted one finger. He closed his mouth.

Shawna tucked her hair back and checked the little light Pike had given her. No grand speech. No asking permission. My wife had heard a woman singing through a prison wall and had been heading toward her ever since.

I touched her wrist.

“Beside me.”

She touched my badge.

“Keep up.”

Nigga, that woman.

Bell opened the hatch.

Cold air rose through the stage.

We went down.

The first ladder led into a maintenance room full of old theater machinery. Beneath that, stairs followed the inside of the island's rock. The walls sweated. The music above us faded until all I heard was shoes, breathing, and the distant beat of some enormous machine.

Halfway down, a narrow window opened onto the night.

We were outside the island now, walking through a bridge bolted to its underside. Above us hung black stone. Below us spread stars reflected in a sea of clouds.

Tank looked through the window.

“Nigga, the floor got sky.”

“Don't study it.”

“I'm trying not to major in falling.”

At the first locked door, Marcellus used Sable's seal. The panel flashed green. Beyond it stood a guard with a cup of coffee.

He saw me.

Saw the badge.

Saw the gun.

He carefully placed the cup on the floor.

I appreciated a man who could read a room before it became his last room.

“Hands,” I said.

He raised them.

Pike cuffed him to a rail and asked where the prisoners had been taken. The guard looked toward the lower stairs.

“Transfer chamber.”

“Who ordered it?”

The nigga looked genuinely confused by the possibility of more than one answer.

“The chancellor.”

We kept moving.

The corridor beyond his post narrowed around a little electric freight cart. Its driver had abandoned it sideways with a stack of clean blankets tied to the back. One blanket had fallen over the wheel. A mug sat in the little holder beside the seat.

Tank looked at the mug.

“Everybody downstairs got coffee except the niggas doing the work.”

I moved the blanket. Beneath it, on the lower shelf, lay a bundle of ordinary clothes: a blue blouse, a man's belt, a pair of red shoes with one broken heel.

Shawna touched the blouse. There was a little paper label tied through a buttonhole.

LENA MARCH.

She looked up at me.

“We close.”

A noise came from behind the service door beside the cart.

Not footsteps.

Scraping.

Tank opened it.

A man in green overalls stood on a stool inside a supply closet, his hands tied above him to a pipe. The stool wobbled every time he tried to turn around. A roll of packing tape lay at his feet. He had been trying to scrape a nail against the binding.

“Don't move,” Tank said.

The man looked at his gun and immediately began moving more.

“Nigga, I mean don't fall. I came to help.”

Tank held the stool while I freed him. He dropped onto his feet and grabbed the doorframe. Shawna gave him water from her little bottle.

“Your name?” she asked.

“Dennis.”

He drank, coughed, drank again.

“Dennis Vale. Laundry.”

He was forty-one, with a wedding ring hanging loose on a finger he'd been rubbing raw against the pipe. His left shoe was untied. That detail made me angrier than I expected. These niggas had tied a man up so carelessly he hadn't even had time to finish being dressed.

“You work here?” I asked.

“Upstairs. I came down because the collection wasn't arriving. Found the clothes. Found names on things. Asked where the people were.”

Tank looked back into the closet.

“That was their answer?”

Dennis nodded.

He saw the badge again. His eyes widened.

“You're the man from the race.”

“Yeah.”

“My wife said if you ever came to dinner she'd use the good dishes.”

“Tell her I'm hungry.”

Nigga started laughing and crying at the same time. He tried to stop both and managed neither. Shawna held his shoulder until his breathing settled.

Pike spoke to one of his officers, who took Dennis toward the stairs. Before he left, Dennis caught my sleeve.

“The bridge ahead is open from the control side. They rolled the walking section away. I heard them talking before they put me in there.”

I looked down the passage. A heavy door stood at the end. Light showed beneath it.

“How far?”

“Across? Maybe twelve feet. The cart rail still runs along the wall.”

Tank looked at the little freight cart.

Then at me.

“Nigga, no.”

“I ain't said nothing.”

“You looking at a vehicle. That's a sentence when you do it.”

Victor bent over the little cart. It had two seats and a flatbed. Its rubber wheels sat on the floor; beside it a narrow steel guide ran toward the door and vanished underneath. The laundry carts used it when the walkway moved away for maintenance. Dennis showed us the hinged little guide wheels tucked beneath the chassis.

“Empty loads only when the bridge is retracted,” he said. “Normally.”

Tank shut his eyes.

“He gave the nigga a normally.”

“Tank, take the rear.”

“Nigga, I can't take the rear. The rear a washcloth.”

He climbed on anyway. Victor stayed behind to help Pike bring the others through once we had the walkway back. Shawna got into the seat beside me.

“Where's my seat belt?” she asked.

I looked down.

There wasn't one.

She took a blanket from the stack and looped it around the front rail, holding the ends in her lap.

“Nigga, drive like you married.”

I pressed the little pedal.

The cart beeped.

It did not move.

Tank looked at me.

“Somebody finally said no.”

Dennis reached through the window and released the brake.

Then we moved.

Slowly.

Nigga, offensively slowly. I had driven through fire. I had outrun bullets in a Mercedes. This little bitch traveled at the speed of a man deciding whether he had forgotten something in the refrigerator.

Behind us Victor began walking.

Kept pace.

Passed us.

He reached the door first and held it open.

“Enjoy your journey.”

“Your doctor know you using sarcasm?”

“Brief use.”

The door opened onto the gap.

The whole middle of the passage was gone. Through it I saw the black underside of the island and a dizzy stretch of stars. A narrow guide rail ran along the outer wall to the other side, where two armed men stood beside the bridge controls.

They saw our little cart.

One laughed.

The other brought up his gun.

Tank stood on the flatbed with the blanket stack in front of his chest. Shawna fired at the hanging lamp above the guards. It burst. They ducked. I held the pedal down as if the little cart might discover a second personality if I believed in it hard enough.

Our front wheels left the ordinary floor.

The guide caught.

We hung against the wall, rolling above the empty air.

Tank stopped joking.

So did I.

For about two seconds.

Then the laundry cart played a little musical chime.

A cheerful four-note warning.

“Nigga,” Tank said, “is it singing us to death?”

“Low battery,” Shawna read from the dash.

We were halfway across.

Of course we were. A less ambitious nigga would've encountered this problem beside a charging socket.

The cart slowed. The guide wheels clicked over a join. On the far side the guards recovered, one reaching for his weapon while the other tried to close the heavy door in front of us.

I took my foot off the pedal.

“What you doing?” Tank said.

“Letting it think.”

Then I pressed down again.

The cart lurched forward on its last little act of loyalty. Shawna flung the blanket ahead of us. It caught the closing door's edge and bunched under it. The door stopped a hand's width short of its frame.

Our front bumper hit the blanket.

I stood and pushed.

Tank pushed behind me.

The door opened with all three of us still attached to the cart. We rolled through into the control room like the worst laundry delivery these niggas had ever received.

One guard swung at me. I pulled his dinner plate-sized control clipboard out of his hand and hit him with the blank side. The other tried to grab Shawna. She drove her elbow into his face and shoved him into Tank.

Tank set him down.

On the desk.

The desk stopped being one desk and became several smaller opportunities for carpentry.

The freight cart gave a final beep.

Died.

I patted its steering wheel.

“Good nigga.”

Shawna looked at the wrecked desk, the two groaning guards, and the little cart's blinking red light.

“You gonna name this one too?”

“Laundry Day.”

Tank started laughing before he could help it.

“Nigga, we almost died on Laundry Day.”

I found the bridge control. The walkway slid back across the gap with a long metallic groan. Victor and Pike came through first. Behind them Dennis stopped beside the cart and stared at the collapsed furniture.

“It only goes eleven miles an hour,” he said.

I handed him his mug.

“That's all I needed.”

He took it with both hands.

“My wife is getting out the fucking dishes.”

The next door opened into a long cell gallery. Some doors stood open. Others remained locked. Men and women watched us from behind thick glass. All adults. Some wore plain gray clothing. Some still wore pieces of whatever lives they had been taken out of: a mechanic's shirt, a dancer's leggings, a suit jacket with the lining torn.

A tall man pressed his palm to the glass.

“Are we being moved?”

I stopped outside his cell.

“You being let out.”

He looked at the badge again.

“They said—”

“Nigga, they said a lot. I'm speaking now.”

Shawna opened the first door with the seal. Rosa opened the second. Petra took one look at a jammed third door, turned her hands to marble, and removed its disagreement from the frame.

Mercedes guided the people toward Pike's officers.

“Up the stairs. Stay together. If you can help somebody walk, do it. If you can't, say so. Nobody gotta perform for us.”

A woman with silver burns along her forearms stared at Petra.

“You could break the whole wall.”

Petra glanced at Mercedes.

Mercedes smiled.

“Girl, don't encourage her unless we need it.”

We needed it about fifteen seconds later.

The far security door slammed shut. Red light washed the gallery. A voice ordered everybody to remain where they were.

Everybody kept moving.

That voice had plainly not met my people.

Two guards appeared on the upper walkway. Their weapons came down toward the escaping prisoners. I fired first. One dropped out of sight. The other ducked behind the rail.

Tank lifted a steel bench and held it over three people trying to cross the open floor. Bullets struck it with flat, ugly bangs. He kept walking.

“Nigga, this bench better appreciate its promotion.”

Victor ran beside him carrying the chair leg from the casino.

I looked at him.

He looked at the chair leg.

“It's been useful.”

“I ain't judging.”

He threw it at the second guard.

It hit square across the man's hands.

Victor smiled for the first time since we came underground.

“Very useful.”

Petra punched the security door off its hinges. The noise traveled down the gallery like a cannon shot. Beyond it lay a control room with three startled technicians and a supervisor already halfway toward another exit.

Shawna pointed her gun at him.

“Sit.”

He sat.

“Where's Lena March?”

He looked at the technicians.

“Nigga,” she said, “they ain't going to answer for you.”

The supervisor pointed toward the lower stairs.

“She resisted the transfer.”

Rosa moved before he finished.

Tank followed her.

I left Pike with the controls and went down after them with Shawna and Victor. The stairs opened onto a medical corridor. Doors stood ajar. Beds rolled against the walls. In one room, a woman lay on her side humming through clenched teeth while a guard tried to fasten a restraint around her wrist.

Tank caught the guard by the back of his uniform.

The nigga left the room horizontally.

Rosa went to the bed.

“Lena?”

The woman opened her eyes.

She was thin, brown-haired, with a bruise beneath one eye and a look so fierce it reached us before her voice did.

“You're the singer.”

“So are you.”

Rosa undid the restraint. Shawna helped Lena sit. Tank returned from placing the guard in a condition where he would remain available for later questions.

Lena took one step and nearly fell.

He caught her.

“I can walk,” she said.

“Then walk with assistance. Ain't no extra prize for hurting.”

She studied his enormous arm, then nodded.

“Reiss,” she said. “They took Dr. Reiss downstairs. He tried to stop them.”

I looked at Shawna.

She looked back.

There was always another downstairs.

We took Lena to Vega and the evacuation group. Twenty-seven prisoners had come out of the cells. Two needed stretchers. The rest insisted on helping carry them. A man whose hands shook with uncontrolled sparks wrapped them in his own coat so he could support someone without hurting them.

I watched him for one second longer than I needed.

Then the upper lift stopped.

The lights over its doors went red. Pike spoke into his radio, listened, and swore. Voss's men had cut access from the annex to the service bridge. The people we had taken out of cells were now crowded into a corridor with one locked route home.

I could feel fear trying to turn them backward. Shoulders drew in. Eyes went to the open cells. A woman began shaking her head as if the whole rescue had been a particularly cruel rehearsal.

Lena pushed herself away from Vega's arm.

“Let me hear it,” she said.

Pike held out his radio.

Sable's voice came over the security channel, ordering the upper guards to keep the bridge sealed. Lena listened with her eyes closed. Her lips moved once, shaping the other woman's cadence.

Rosa looked at her.

“You can do that?”

“I can sing through walls. Words aren't harder.”

She held out her hand. Pike gave her the radio.

When she spoke, Sable came out of her mouth.

“Open the upper bridge. We are conducting an inspection. Anyone who obstructs this order will answer directly to me.”

I stared at her.

Tank stared too.

“This woman stole a whole bitch,” he whispered.

Lena nearly laughed. Caught herself. Spoke again in Sable's clipped voice.

“Now.”

The red lights turned green.

The lift doors opened.

People began moving, faster now. Not pushed. Choosing. The woman who had shaken her head helped lift a stretcher. The sparking man took its other end. Lena stood by the doorway and kept Sable's voice talking long enough to buy them the corridor beyond.

Then the real Sable shouted over her.

“That is not my order.”

Lena's own voice returned.

“I know.”

She gave Pike the radio with a smile so sharp it could have cut its cord.

We heard boots approaching along the bridge.

Petra stepped into the lift with Mercedes. “We'll hold the top.”

Pike joined them with two officers. The rest stayed beside the stretchers. Nobody asked which people were powerful enough to deserve first place. The people who could walk made space for the ones who couldn't. The ones with strength used it. The ones without still had hands.

A man in a torn suit stopped beside me as the lift filled.

He was maybe fifty, with gray in his beard and one lens missing from his glasses. He studied my badge as if he had been waiting for it longer than I had been alive.

“Who sent you?”

I looked at Shawna.

She stood at the stairwell, watching the lower door, ready for the next thing that needed doing.

“My wife heard a song.”

The man followed my gaze.

Then he took off his broken glasses and wiped his eyes with his sleeve.

“Tell her thank you.”

“Tell her yourself upstairs.”

He nodded. Put his glasses back on. Went into the lift carrying somebody else's bag.

Lena waited until the last stretcher cleared before she let Vega guide her inside. Rosa went with her, still holding her hand. Tank watched until the doors closed.

“That nigga in the gray suit,” he said quietly. “He look like my uncle.”

“Yeah?”

“My uncle would've been asking who stole his shoes the whole time.”

I looked at the lift doors. At the boots and shoes people had left behind in their cells because nobody had expected to need them quickly.

“We buying shoes,” I said.

Tank nodded.

“A lot of fucking shoes.”

Then we went toward the machine.

The transfer chamber was round, high-ceilinged, and bright with a cold yellow light. Rails crossed its floor into the metal circle at the far end. Above the circle, a clock displayed a date that belonged to somebody else's lifetime.

1944.

Snow blew through the open frame.

Real snow. It settled on the floor and melted around our shoes.

Beyond the circle stood a dim station building under a night sky. A train waited beside it. Men moved with lanterns. One wore a military coat with an emblem I recognized even before my brain caught up with what my eyes had been handed.

A Nazi.

Not a costume at a party. Not some present-day idiot trying to be provocative. A man standing in a different year, carrying a gun, waiting for human beings to be delivered to him.

My stomach went cold in a way the snow couldn't explain.

At the control dais, Sable held a pistol beside the head of an older man in a rumpled shirt.

Dr. Reiss.

He looked at us over his glasses.

“Do not damage the ring,” he said immediately.

“Nigga, we just got here,” Tank said.

Sable tightened her grip on him.

“Back away.”

I stopped.

Shawna stopped beside me.

Victor's hands glimmered faintly. He closed them into fists before the charge could grow.

“Let him go,” I said.

Sable laughed once.

“You keep arriving at the end of things you don't understand.”

“And somehow niggas keep getting free.”

Behind her, a black carriage rolled toward the circle. Three adults inside it pressed their faces to a barred opening. On the other side, a soldier raised his hand to receive them.

I could not shoot without risking Reiss.

Shawna saw the same thing.

She looked at the carriage, then at the hanging work light above the control dais.

I knew her face when a decision arrived.

“Baby,” I said.

She shot the light.

Darkness hit half the room.

Reiss dropped.

Sable fired where his head had been and stumbled back as Tank charged. I ran for the carriage. Victor went toward the controls. Shawna covered both of us from behind the rail support.

The carriage reached the circle.

Cold air swallowed my arms as I grabbed its rear handle.

The soldier on the other side saw me.

His face changed at the sight of my clothes, my badge, my skin, and the fact that none of those things had asked his permission to be there.

He raised his gun.

I shot first.

He fell behind the platform edge.

I hauled the carriage back.

The wheels fought me. Three people pushed from inside, trying to help through the same floor that trapped them. My shoes slid in melting snow.

“Tank!”

He came out of the dark, grabbed beside me, and planted his feet.

“This nigga train going the wrong way.”

We pulled together.

The carriage rolled clear of the circle.

Behind us, Sable disappeared through a side passage. Victor caught Reiss before he could strike the floor. Shawna broke the carriage latch with the control lever somebody had left beside it.

The three prisoners came out holding each other.

One man kept saying, “Thank you,” in a language I didn't know, then found the same words in English and said them again.

I touched his shoulder.

“Go with her.”

On the other side of the ring, a whistle shrieked. More soldiers appeared beside the train.

Reiss struggled upright.

“Close it.”

Victor looked at the controls.

“Which—”

“The black handle. Slowly.”

Victor moved it.

The circle narrowed from the edges inward. Snow became a thin white line. Through the shrinking opening I saw a woman standing near the station wall, one hand pressed against her mouth, watching us take people away from the men who owned her night.

Our eyes met across eighty years of machinery and somebody's monstrous ambition.

Then the door closed.

The room was only a room again.

I stood with both hands on the empty carriage handle.

Shawna came beside me. Her shoulder touched mine.

“We saw her,” she said.

“Yeah.”

“She saw us.”

I looked at the blank metal circle.

Behind me Tank swore softly. Reiss began to cry without making a sound. Upstairs, people we had freed were walking toward the music they had heard through a wall.

I let go of the handle.

“Then she know somebody coming back.”

## 7. Forty Floors of Niggas Finding Out

At two in the morning, the first freed prisoner walked into Sky High's grand entrance wearing Tank's coat.

By two-fifteen, the entrance was full of blankets, food, doctors, and students who had come downstairs expecting an alarm drill and found a whole different school underneath the one they knew.

Nobody cheered at first.

They made room.

That was better.

Then the man in the gray suit saw Shawna and crossed the hall to take her hand. I couldn't hear what he said. I didn't need to. She held both his hands and listened until he finished. Behind them Rosa sat beside Lena with two steaming cups between them. Tank stood over the group like a roof that had learned to love people.

Elias, the density man from the train, brought chairs. He carried six at a time now that he wasn't frightened of becoming heavy. Petra helped the medical team. Mercedes found fresh clothes. Porsche somehow persuaded the night kitchen to produce steak for thirty people at once.

The chef objected that he had prepared a light supper.

“Nigga, prepare a heavier one,” she told him.

He did.

Storm took Dr. Reiss into a side room. I went with Shawna, Victor, Bell, and Marcellus. The doctor sat beneath a portrait of the academy's founder and stared at a glass of water for so long I thought he hadn't understood what it was.

Then he drank it all.

Bell refilled it without asking.

Reiss was fifty-seven, with thinning dark hair, a tired face, and hands that kept reaching toward his wrists where restraints had been. He had designed the time door before he understood what an ambitious man might do with a beautiful mistake.

“It doesn't lead to every past,” he told us. “It found one branch. One set of coordinates. A point in occupied France in 1944.”

Storm sat forward.

“You told the board it failed.”

“I told the board it should never be used.”

Voss had disagreed. First politely. Then financially. Then with Sable standing behind him. The chancellor discovered that a man on the other side of the door was willing to exchange prisoners, resources, and protection for technology he should never have seen.

“A colonel named Ernst Keller,” Reiss said. “He commands the Saint-Orage depot. It's a separate branch now. Changed from the moment our machine opened there. But the people inside it are real to themselves. Their pain is real. Their choices are real.”

He looked at me as if he expected an argument.

“Nigga, I saw a woman looking for a way out,” I said. “You don't need to explain her to me.”

He nodded and stared at his hands.

Keller used the depot to hold people the Nazis had imprisoned: Jewish adults, resistance prisoners, people taken because the regime had decided their existence or defiance was a reason to destroy them. Voss had added something newer and uglier to that machinery. He sent captive powered adults through the door and used Keller's guarded site for experiments he couldn't conceal forever under the academy.

“He wanted transferable power,” Reiss said. “A gift he could wear and remove. The Heart amplifies what's there. He wanted it to make him whatever he chose.”

“Can it?” Victor asked.

“Not safely. Not the way he imagines.”

I thought about Victor trapped in his own racing car while the rings drank him.

“The race.”

Reiss closed his eyes.

Bell's four hands went still.

Victor looked at the floor for a long moment. When he raised his head, whatever remained of his loyalty to the chancellor had burned away cleanly.

“Where's the real Heart?” he asked.

Reiss told us.

It had been in the lower laboratory until our raid. When the alarms began, Voss had ordered it moved to a secure vault at Cloud Nine. A portable housing kept the school's field drawing from it. Voss could hide among the casino's private lifts and armed guards while his core continued to hold the academy hostage from a distance.

My phone lit up.

Afterglow.

“He took my penthouse,” she said.

“I was just hearing about your hospitality problem.”

“Aiden. He has twelve people from my staff upstairs. He says if I object, he drops the building.”

I looked at Storm.

She had heard enough through the phone to stand.

“Tell your staff to stay away from the windows,” I said.

“What are you going to do?”

Nigga, people loved asking me that right before I did something expensive.

“Get your house back.”

Bell brought the Lamborghini to the front drive. It looked as if it had endured a disagreement with a train, a race, and somebody's military budget.

It had.

I put my hand on the hood.

“One more trip.”

Bell looked wounded.

“You said that yesterday.”

“Nigga, yesterday ended.”

Tank appeared in fresh black clothes. Rosa kissed him at the bottom of the steps and said something in his ear that made his whole face change.

He watched her go back inside.

“What she say?” I asked.

“Private.”

“You grinning publicly.”

“Nigga, let a man have a future.”

I did.

Shawna climbed into the Lamborghini. Tank took the Mercedes with Victor. Pike followed with patrol cars. Storm remained at the control tower, guiding us through the school's field and keeping the main island steady. Bell rode with her technicians toward the casino's lower service entrance.

We entered the Crown District under a sky beginning to pale.

No tourists waved this time. People watched from behind windows. The news of the prison had spread. So had the news that the academy's finest new graduate was driving toward its chancellor with police lights on and his wife beside him.

Outside Cloud Nine, Afterglow stood in a gold coat over her evening gown. Her light had grown sharp around the edges.

She handed me the private-lift key.

“Fortieth floor.”

“You coming?”

“It's my fucking building.”

I liked that answer.

We went through the side entrance because Voss had barricaded the front with a sculpture of two lovers embracing. It was enormous, naked, and made of polished bronze. A very serious artist had given the man wings, the woman a sword, and both of them asses so large Tank stopped for a second to consider the arrangement.

“Nigga, why her cheeks armed?”

“Keep walking,” Shawna said.

The side entrance opened onto a long shopping gallery. Closed jewelry stores. A fountain full of floating little golden fish. Beyond it, a staircase curled up to the lift lobby in two matching arms.

A security shutter began descending behind us.

Afterglow looked up.

“That is not mine.”

We ran. Pike's officers caught the shutter before it reached the floor, jamming it with the heavy ceremonial bench beside the door. Three of us made the stairs. A gunshot cracked from above, and the marble beside my shoe shattered.

I pulled Shawna behind the fountain.

Tank ducked beside a jewelry kiosk. The glass over him burst. He covered his head with one arm and came up furious.

“These niggas shooting at diamonds.”

“Focus.”

“I am focused. That's a second crime.”

Two men held the balcony. Another crouched beside the lifts. Voss had left a welcoming committee, and every member had apparently been instructed to make my morning worse.

Afterglow knelt beside us. Gold light gathered on her hands.

“The fountain,” she said. “It runs under both stairs.”

I looked down. Beneath the water, a clear maintenance tunnel connected the two sides of the gallery. Lights moved in it. The golden fish weren't ordinary fish. They were little mechanical things suspended above the water by the same kind of decorative field that made the whole rich-ass building impossible to explain to a normal plumber.

“You can open that?” I asked.

She pulled off her gold bracelet and pressed it against the fountain's rim. A little service panel slid aside.

“Staff passage.”

Tank glanced inside.

“Which staff? The staff ants?”

It was narrow. Too narrow for him. Wide enough for me if I didn't get sentimental about the shoulders of my jacket.

Shawna caught my sleeve.

“Come out where I can see you.”

I kissed her quickly.

“Nigga, I been doing that all week.”

Then I went into the fountain.

The passage smelled like water and warm wiring. I crawled beneath the shallow pool while shots struck the far wall above me. Through the clear ceiling I could see the golden fish and, past them, a distorted view of one gunman leaning over the rail.

A fish drifted directly above my face.

Looked down at me with its little jeweled eyes.

Nigga looked impressed.

I accepted that too.

Halfway through, a motor whined. The little fish began turning toward the center of the fountain. Lights flashed blue, then gold. Music started from somewhere under my elbow.

The fountain was doing its sunrise show.

With me inside it.

A jet of water rose above the glass. Then another. The pool churned. Outside, Tank began laughing so loudly I could hear him through the tunnel.

“That nigga got aquatic accompaniment!”

“Tank!” Shawna shouted.

“He said make it loud!”

The music swelled. Some rich bastard's idea of dawn, all trumpets and tiny spinning fish, hid the sound of me pushing open the maintenance hatch on the other side.

I came out behind the left staircase.

A guard had his back to me. He was trying to understand why the fountain had become more dramatic than his ambush.

I caught the back of his jacket and dragged him into the service recess. He swung. His fist hit the wall beside my face. I drove him against the marble, took the gun, and pushed him down behind the cleaning trolley.

The balcony guard saw us.

He turned his weapon.

Victor sent one blue flash into the metal lamp above him. The lamp burst. The guard stumbled back, and Shawna's shot struck the railing where his hand had been. He dropped his gun.

Tank charged up the other staircase.

The last man tried to retreat toward the lifts. Tank reached the top before he did. Nigga had crossed an entire decorative staircase like the stairs owed Rosa money.

He caught the gunman's wrist, spun him, and sat him in the velvet chair beside the lift buttons.

The gunman tried to stand.

Tank put one hand on his shoulder.

“Seated experience.”

The man remained seated.

I came up the left side with my prisoner. Pike's officers followed and took all three. Afterglow reached the top, looked down at the fountain, and let out a breath that seemed to contain the whole building.

“You came through the water.”

“Under it.”

“You were beneath the fish.”

“They seemed cool.”

She looked at me like she was deciding where to put a plaque.

Shawna pulled a piece of gold ribbon off my shoulder. It must have been caught in the service passage. She tucked it into her pocket.

“Souvenir?” I asked.

“Evidence for when you tell this story wrong.”

“Nigga, I ain't told a wrong story in my life.”

She looked back at the bronze lovers visible through the gallery doors.

“Your wedding speech said you invented commitment.”

“Improved it.”

“See?”

Afterglow laughed. Then a voice called from inside the closed perfume shop beside us.

“Eveline?”

She stopped.

“Claudine?”

A woman stood behind the glass holding a little dog in one arm and a store stool in the other. She had barricaded the shop door from inside. A young man in a clerk's waistcoat stood behind her with an enormous bottle of perfume raised like a weapon.

“Are they gone?” she asked.

“From this floor,” Afterglow said. “Open the door.”

The clerk moved the stool. Claudine came out in a pink dressing gown and slippers with feathers on them. She was sixty-three, a guest who had come down early because her dog needed walking. The gunmen had chased her into the shop. She had spent the whole time trying to persuade the little animal not to bark at people carrying rifles.

The dog saw Tank.

Barked once.

Thought about it.

Sat down.

“Good nigga,” Tank said.

Claudine stared at me.

“You're Aiden.”

“Yes, ma'am.”

“I saw you on the moon.”

“Busy night.”

She handed her dog to Tank before he could object, caught both my hands, and kissed my cheek.

“You get younger every time you do something impossible.”

“I started early.”

The perfume clerk looked at the weapon in his hand. Put it down. Picked up a smaller bottle from the display and offered it to me.

“For your wife.”

Shawna took it.

Claudine opened the handbag hanging from her wrist and took out a huge ruby ring. She pressed it against my palm.

I shook my head.

“Keep your ring.”

“My third husband gave it to me.”

“You might want the memory.”

“I kept the second husband's yacht. That is enough memory.”

Tank looked up from the dog.

“This lady understands separation.”

She laughed and closed my fingers around the ruby.

“Then give it to somebody you love.”

I handed it straight to Shawna.

My wife looked at it, then at Claudine.

“Girl.”

“Exactly,” Claudine said.

Afterglow sent a patrol officer down with the woman, the clerk, and the little dog. Tank watched the dog go with surprising reluctance.

“Don't,” I told him.

“I ain't said nothing.”

“You looking at a responsibility. That's a sentence when you do it.”

Shawna laughed first. Then Tank. Even Victor smiled.

The private-lift key was warm in my hand. Above us, twelve staff members were still waiting for the same chance to laugh. I turned toward the stairs, and my people turned with me.

The main lift was disabled above the thirty-sixth. Voss's men held the top stairs. The service lift could reach a glass observation lounge beside the penthouse, but it was watched from inside.

Afterglow smiled without warmth.

“They can watch light.”

She filled the lounge's windows with reflections of us approaching from the main stairs. Guards moved toward the wrong door. We rose in the service lift while our golden doubles arrived somewhere else.

Tank stared at his own bright reflection through the distant glass.

“Nigga, I look incredible.”

Victor looked at him.

“That's what you're focusing on?”

“You telling me the light nigga ain't handsome?”

Shawna elbowed me before I could join in.

The doors opened.

We moved into the lounge.

For six seconds it worked perfectly.

Then a guard looked behind him and saw two versions of Tank, one gold and one holding a gun.

He made the correct choice about which one to fear.

Too late.

Tank hit him with the stock and caught him before he fell through a table. Victor disarmed the second man with a short, controlled burst of charge. Vega had allowed brief use. He seemed to enjoy making that brief use count.

I crossed into the penthouse behind Shawna.

Twelve staff members knelt near the windows. A chef still wore his hat. Two cleaners held hands. The cocktail pianist sat on the floor with a bloodied lip and fury in his eyes.

Sable stood beside them.

Voss stood behind a glass desk.

On the desk, inside a black frame, floated the real Heart of the Sky.

It was smaller than the fake. Darker blue. Alive in a way the false crystal had never been. Its light moved through the room like a slow, enormous pulse.

Marcellus had called beautiful things different from expensive lies.

I understood now.

Voss looked at me with genuine astonishment.

“Again.”

“Nigga, you keep leaving doors.”

Sable raised her weapon toward the hostages.

Shawna had hers aimed at Sable before the movement finished.

“Try me,” my wife said.

Nobody in that room doubted she meant it.

Voss rested his hand on the Heart's frame.

The floor tilted.

One of the cleaners screamed. Outside the windows, the horizon moved.

“The housing controls the support link,” he said. “Do you imagine strength is only what a man can do with his own hands?”

I looked at the hostages.

Looked at Shawna.

Looked back at him.

“No. I imagine weakness is needing twelve people on their knees to finish a sentence.”

The pianist smiled through his split lip.

Voss saw it. His face hardened.

“You have been admired for two days. I built my authority over twenty years.”

“Nigga, that's embarrassing. I caught up on a weekend.”

Tank made a noise behind me.

I knew that noise. A nigga trying very hard not to laugh while keeping a gun level.

Voss pressed something on the frame.

The windows cracked.

Storm's voice came through my earpiece, strained but steady.

“I have the building. Briefly.”

I moved.

So did everybody else.

Afterglow threw light across Sable's eyes. Shawna drove toward the hostages, putting her body between them and the gun. Victor's charge struck the metal rail beside Sable, jolting her arm upward. Her shot went through the ceiling.

Tank took her down.

Not gently.

I went over the desk at Voss.

He struck me with his cane. Pain burst along my shoulder. I landed hard, caught the desk edge, and pulled myself forward. The old man was faster than he looked. Not old-old. Fifty and mean enough to spend the next fifty complaining that the world hadn't knelt properly.

His cane flashed again.

I caught it.

“Nigga, stop conducting.”

I tore it out of his hands and broke it across the desk.

His eyes widened.

For one lovely second the chancellor had no symbol left to hide behind.

Then he hit a switch beneath the glass.

The floor under me opened.

I fell into an observation shaft.

The city rushed past on all sides.

I caught a crossbar with both hands. My shoulders screamed. Below me, thirty-nine floors of glass dropped toward the clouds.

Above, Voss grabbed the Heart's housing.

Shawna saw him move.

She fired at the mechanism over the private escape door.

The door jammed halfway open.

He ducked through anyway, dragging the housing behind him. The black frame struck the narrow gap and stuck.

That was all the invitation I needed.

I pulled myself up, braced a foot against the shaft wall, and climbed back into the penthouse like a nigga returning from a disappointing basement.

Voss looked over his shoulder.

“Impossible.”

“You been saying that with your face all night.”

I caught the housing.

He pulled from the other side.

For a second we held the Heart between us: him in the escape passage, me standing over the open shaft, blue light covering both our hands.

It did not enter me. It did not choose me. It sat inside its frame and made everything around it feel more dangerous.

Voss let go.

I staggered backward with the weight.

The escape door slammed.

Somewhere beyond it an engine started.

I had the Heart.

He had a route out.

For once, nigga, I accepted the better prize.

“Bell,” I said into the radio. “Got it.”

The professor's voice broke.

“Bring it to the service station. Carefully.”

“I know what carefully mean.”

Tank looked around at the broken desk, open shaft, cracked windows, and Sable unconscious under his knee.

“Definition been growing.”

We took the Heart downstairs with the hostages around us. The chef insisted on carrying one side of the frame. The pianist carried my broken half of Voss's cane like a trophy. Sable went down in cuffs between Pike's officers, awake now and too furious to speak.

Afterglow walked through her lobby.

The staff applauded her.

She pointed at us.

The applause changed direction.

A cleaner ran forward and hugged Shawna. The chef hugged Tank, which briefly made him disappear. The pianist shook my hand and told me he would write something worthy of what he had seen.

“Make it loud,” I said.

“It will require brass.”

“Nigga, get all the brass.”

Outside, Bell connected the housing to a secured transport platform. Storm's wind settled the casino gently back onto its proper plane. The sunrise spilled across the Crown District.

My phone rang.

Chief Knox.

“Captain,” she said. “Why am I watching footage of you falling through a casino forty stories above a fucking cloud?”

“Training.”

“Outstanding.”

She paused.

“Bring me a souvenir.”

I looked at the half cane in the pianist's hands.

“Might have something.”

Then I looked up at the academy, where a closed metal ring waited beneath the foundation and a woman in another year still had reason to watch the door.

I had won the Heart.

Now I had to keep a promise bigger than the sky.

## 8. A Nigga Can't Be Late to Yesterday

They tried to give me a medal before breakfast.

Nigga, I had blood on my cuff, no sleep in my eyes, and a wife leaning against my shoulder who had helped liberate a prison before most of the faculty remembered to put their slippers on. The medal could have waited until somebody brought eggs.

The faculty disagreed.

They assembled in the main hall with a blue ribbon, a gold star, and enough respectful silence to make Tank suspicious.

“What these niggas want?” he whispered.

“Apparently me.”

“Everybody want you. I'm asking what format.”

Storm stepped forward. She looked exhausted. Faint silver lines trembled around her wrists where she had held the casino upright through the Heart's unstable link. She had changed into a plain white shirt and dark trousers, but somehow still looked like the person a storm asked before making landfall.

“For exceptional courage in the rescue of the lower-annex prisoners,” she said, “and for returning the Heart of the Sky to this academy—”

I lifted a hand.

She stopped.

“My people,” I said.

I pointed at Shawna. At Tank and Rosa. At Mercedes, Porsche, Petra, Victor, Pike, Bell, Vega, Marcellus. At Lena sitting in a chair nearby with a blanket around her shoulders.

“Whatever that sentence is about to give me, make enough.”

Storm looked down at the medal.

Then she smiled.

“We will.”

Tank leaned toward Rosa.

“Nigga got us jewelry through collective bargaining.”

“You don't know what that means.”

“I know I'm collectively about to shine.”

The room laughed. The freed prisoners laughed too, some cautiously, some like they were surprised their bodies still remembered where laughter lived. I let Storm put the ribbon around my neck. Then I put the medal around Shawna's.

She looked at me.

“You earned this.”

“Baby, I got you.”

That was corny as fuck.

It was also true enough to make her eyes go bright.

Breakfast finally arrived. We ate in the main hall because nobody wanted to leave the people still being examined by the medical team. Tables filled with food, borrowed clothes, shoes in every size, and phones people could use to call somebody who had not known where they were.

Tank personally distributed the shoes.

He knelt in front of the gray-suited man, who introduced himself as Mr. Harlan Moss, fifty-two, a landscape architect whose gift let him persuade roots to grow through stone. He had been taken after refusing to work on one of Voss's private properties.

Tank offered him two pairs.

Moss looked at them.

“Both?”

“Nigga, you got two kinds of occasions.”

Moss laughed and chose the polished brown pair for now. He set the boots beside his chair with the careful pleasure of a man arranging evidence that tomorrow might exist.

His phone call came through while Tank was lacing the boots for him.

A woman filled the screen. Gray curls, a blue bathrobe, eyes so wide she looked almost angry with him.

“Harlan?”

He set the phone against a water glass. Missed. Caught it before it fell.

“Anne.”

She covered her mouth.

He covered his.

For a few seconds the niggas couldn't say anything at all.

Tank stopped touching the boots. I put my coffee down. Around us breakfast kept happening, but slowly, as if everybody near that table had understood there was a voice trying to find its way home.

Anne dropped her hand first.

“Where the fuck have you been?”

Harlan started laughing.

Then crying.

Then trying to answer both questions with the same breath.

“I've had a bad few months.”

“I can see that. Your hair looks terrible.”

He touched it. She began crying too.

Nigga, there are people who need a whole orchestra to tell somebody they love them. That woman had done it with a complaint about his hair, and Harlan heard every note.

He turned the phone to show her the room. Blankets. Breakfast. Shoes. My badge, which she studied with the ferocity of a woman deciding whether to trust the next thing a man in a uniform told her.

“Did you find him?” she asked me.

“My wife did.”

“Then put her on.”

I waved Shawna over. She took the phone, sat beside Harlan, and listened to Anne thank her so many times she finally had to say, “Girl, breathe. We got him.”

Harlan looked at his boots.

“She bought me shoes before our wedding,” he told Tank. “I'd spent everything on the ring.”

Tank nodded gravely.

“Respectable allocation.”

“They were brown. Like these. I wanted black because I thought black looked distinguished.”

“What happened?”

Harlan looked at Anne on the screen.

“What do you think happened?”

Tank looked at Rosa across the room.

“Brown shoes.”

“Brown shoes,” Harlan agreed.

He told us about their wedding while Anne corrected him from the phone. It had rained. The roof had leaked over the little rented chapel's piano. His brother had put a cooking pot under the leak and called it percussion. Anne's mother had objected to the music. Anne had walked down the aisle anyway, carrying her own umbrella, and closed it over her mother's face just long enough to finish saying yes.

“That isn't how it happened,” Anne said.

Harlan smiled at the screen.

“You told your sister you wished it had.”

“My sister talks too much.”

“She sent me the letter.”

Anne stopped.

Then she laughed so hard the picture shook.

That was their whole marriage coming through a little glowing rectangle: the rain, the ridiculous shoes, a letter somebody had kept, an argument that had survived thirty years because neither of them wanted to win it enough to stop having it together.

I looked at Shawna. She looked back.

Thirty years sounded like something a nigga ought to earn one morning at a time.

Anne's face steadied on the screen.

“I'm coming,” she said.

Harlan looked around the floating school. “It's a little complicated to get here.”

“Nigga, I spent five months trying to get you back. Don't tell me about parking.”

Tank bowed his head so she wouldn't see him laughing.

Pike arranged a ground escort to the academy's landing station. Storm offered a shuttle. By the time Anne ended the call, Harlan had said her name so often it had become the easiest word in the room.

He put the phone down gently.

Then he looked at me.

“I don't know what to give you.”

“Take her dancing.”

He looked at the brown shoes.

I pointed.

“Nigga, you already equipped.”

He laughed again. This time it came easily.

Tank finished the last knot, stood, and inspected his work.

“Wedding shoes,” he said.

“Thirty years late,” Harlan answered.

“Thirty years still going.”

Harlan pressed his lips together and nodded.

Then he picked up his fork and ate like a man with somewhere to be.

Shawna sat with Lena. Rosa poured coffee. The three women spoke low enough that I heard only pieces: songs, five months, a sister in Denver, a room with a window. None of it needed me in the middle.

I ate my eggs.

A nigga can save a room and still let other people have conversations inside it.

Afterward Reiss took us back beneath the school.

The transfer chamber looked smaller with the lights fully on. Without Voss's guards and the snow blowing through it, the place showed its seams: cables enclosed in heavy channels, rails bolted to the floor, a control platform crowded with dials Reiss touched as if apologizing to them.

The Heart stood in a secured housing behind reinforced glass. Bell had connected it to the academy's restored support system. It remained the school's core; we were not putting it in my trunk and hoping the clouds would understand.

Storm stood at the controls.

Reiss showed her the three rings governing the door's alignment. She listened, asked two questions, and repeated the sequence back without touching anything.

“Only you can hold the boundary stable without drawing too much from the school,” he said. “Once I set the coordinates, you open it. I can't guarantee a second attempt if we close it fully.”

“Then we make one passage out and one passage back,” Storm said.

He nodded.

“A single operation. After that, the frame comes apart.”

I looked at the empty circle.

“And we don't come back with everybody suddenly unborn or some shit?”

Reiss shook his head.

“This isn't a road to your own childhood. Voss connected us to a branch and changed it. The history we came from still happened. We can't erase the Holocaust by driving through this machine.”

The room stayed quiet.

“We can help people trapped on its other side,” he said. “People who exist there now. That is the choice in front of us.”

Shawna looked at me.

“That's enough.”

“Yeah,” I said. “It is.”

Tank ran his hand along the closed carriage's empty rail.

“How many?”

Reiss spread the depot papers across a workbench. Keller's site held eighty-three adult prisoners at the last count. Thirty-one were people Voss had sent from the present. The rest belonged to that altered year: Jewish prisoners, resistance members, other adults seized by the Nazi occupation. Some were forced to maintain the depot. Some were used in the power experiments. Some were awaiting transport to places whose names did not need to be written down for the fear to make sense.

“We don't know if the count has changed,” Reiss said.

“Then we count when we get there,” Shawna answered.

He showed us the station layout. Not a plan for conquering history. One depot, one connecting yard, one machine chamber Keller had built around the other end of Voss's door. A holding building stood beyond the tracks. A repair shed faced the station. A road led into the town of Saint-Orage, whose name Reiss said had not appeared in the records of the world he had grown up in.

I studied the repair shed.

“People in there work on engines?”

“Some do.”

“Good. People who know a machine can usually tell you which nigga keeps breaking it.”

Pike wanted to send a full patrol squad. Storm shook her head. Voss was still free somewhere in the surrounding sky, and the academy had thousands of people to protect. We could take a small team through. The rest had to hold the way home.

I chose Tank, Shawna, Victor, and Petra.

Rosa stood up immediately.

“No.”

Tank looked at her.

“Baby—”

“You not disappearing into another century while I wait upstairs wondering if some dead motherfucker got lucky.”

He opened his mouth.

She put a finger against his chest.

“I know what I'm saying.”

Mercedes stood beside Petra.

“Same.”

Porsche looked around the room.

“Nigga, y'all not leaving me to explain all this to the luggage.”

I looked at Storm.

She looked at the ring, then the vehicles waiting beyond the chamber doors.

“The limit is power draw and transport space,” she said. “Not whether someone seems impressive on a roster.”

“Good,” Shawna said. “Because the roster didn't open the cells.”

We settled it the way my people settled things: by deciding what each of us could do and trusting each other to do it. Rosa would help move prisoners and keep people together. Mercedes had worked enough crowded rooms to read a frightened group before it turned into a crush. Porsche spoke French well enough to make Marcellus raise both eyebrows when she finally admitted it.

“My first serious boyfriend was from Marseille,” she said.

“You never mentioned that,” Tank told her.

“Nigga, you never asked me a question that wasn't about where I parked.”

Vega would come as the doctor. Reiss would remain with Storm to hold the return point. Marcellus stayed at Sky High with Lena and the freed prisoners; he said somebody needed to keep track of people while all the beautiful idiots went charging through a clock.

“You calling me beautiful?” Tank asked.

Marcellus looked at him over his glasses.

“I included you in a group. Don't get greedy.”

Bell prepared three vehicles. My dark blue police Lamborghini. Tank's black Mercedes. A broad academy rescue van with room for supplies and people who could not walk. They would run on ordinary ground once through the door. Their sky-lane receivers would have nothing to hold onto in the other year.

“No roads made of light,” Bell said.

Tank looked almost moved.

“Nigga, finally some pavement with manners.”

We were not taking a convoy large enough to empty the whole depot in one trip. The papers showed trucks and rail carriages already there. Getting the prisoners to the door would depend partly on what they knew and what we could secure when we arrived.

I didn't love uncertainty.

I loved pretending it scared me even less.

While Bell worked, my phone rang again. Knox had seen the prison footage. This time she didn't begin with a joke.

“You have what you need?”

I looked around the chamber at my people. Shawna speaking with Vega. Tank listening to Rosa. Victor beside Petra, testing one small spark between his fingers. Porsche arguing with Bell about whether the rescue van had a proper heater.

“Mostly.”

“I asked about equipment, Captain.”

“So did I.”

She was quiet for a second.

Then she said, “Bring them back.”

“That's the plan.”

“And Aiden?”

“Yeah?”

“If anybody asks which department sent you, say mine.”

I smiled.

“Chief, you sure you want that paperwork?”

“Nigga, I want the picture.”

At noon, Voss tried to take his machine back.

The first sign was a low metallic boom above us. Dust sifted from the ceiling. Storm looked up sharply. The control lights flickered.

Pike's voice burst over the radio.

“Three armed skiffs approaching the lower service bridge.”

Tank closed the Mercedes door.

“This nigga don't know when the party over.”

I went toward the bridge with him and Victor. Shawna followed, because apparently I still needed reminding that marriage was a formation.

The skiffs hovered outside the maintenance windows. Black hulls. Men crouched behind their rails. A loudspeaker crackled.

“Surrender the core and release Commander Sable.”

I looked at the speaker.

“Nigga, he asking for refunds.”

Victor's hands lit.

Vega's voice came over his radio immediately.

“Brief use.”

He stared at the radio.

“How does she always know?”

“Because she a doctor and you a patient. That relationship follows a nigga.”

The first skiff fired into the bridge. Glass shattered over us. We dropped behind the stone wall. Tank pulled a maintenance worker down beside him and held him there while the man tried to explain that he had only come to change a light.

“Nigga, the whole light changing. Stay down.”

I returned fire through the broken window. The skiff veered. Victor sent a short bolt into its steering ring, and the craft spun away toward an empty service platform. The men aboard scrambled to hold on.

The second skiff came lower, aiming for the transfer chamber's outer doors.

Shawna saw it before I did.

“They're going underneath.”

We ran back down the passage. The chamber doors shook under the first impact. Bell stood behind the Heart's reinforced housing with two tools in each hand and the expression of a man prepared to defend his profession physically.

“Move the van,” I told him.

“Where?”

“Away from the part I'm about to use.”

I got into the Lamborghini.

Shawna got in beside me.

The outer doors buckled inward.

Beyond them the second skiff hung level with the floor, its nose pressed against the damaged frame. Two gunmen prepared to jump across.

I turned on the police lights.

They paused.

Nigga, even in the sky, a man with a gun could still have an unresolved feeling about a traffic stop.

I drove straight at them.

Not out into the air. Into the heavy rolling barrier parked beside the entrance. The Lamborghini shoved it across the floor and into the skiff's nose. The craft rocked backward. Its gunmen fell against each other. Bell hit the emergency shutters, and a steel screen came down between us and the sky.

The skiff crashed against the outside.

The third fled before Storm's wind reached it.

When I got out, Bell stared at the Lamborghini's newest dent.

I held up one finger.

“That was barely a trip.”

He covered his face with two hands and pointed at the van with the other two.

“Please just go save people in another year.”

We finished preparing under guard.

That evening, Shawna and I went back to our room for twenty minutes. We washed. Changed. Stood at the balcony looking out over a sky that had somehow become familiar in four days.

She wore dark trousers, boots, and a blue sweater beneath her jacket. The medal lay on the dresser. Her ring remained on her hand. Dante's watch ticked against her wrist.

My cross rested outside my shirt.

She touched its engraved back.

“Damn, boy,” she said softly.

“Magnificent.”

She smiled.

“You really believe that.”

“Baby, you engraved supporting evidence.”

She pulled me toward her. We kissed slowly, without an audience, without somebody announcing that the sky had developed another emergency. I held the back of her head and felt how much I wanted all the future waiting after this one difficult tomorrow.

“You scared?” she asked.

“Yeah.”

She nodded.

No disappointment. No surprise.

Just her hand tightening in mine.

“Me too.”

We stood there another minute. Then she picked up her jacket.

“Come on. That woman been waiting.”

When we returned to the chamber, everybody was ready.

Lena had come down with Marcellus to see us off. She took Rosa's hands and sang one clear note. Rosa answered it. No secret code. Just two singers promising to recognize each other when the door opened again.

Storm stood at the controls.

The Heart glowed behind its glass.

“One branch,” she said. “One outward passage. One return. I hold this side. Reiss holds the alignment. You bring everyone you can back through the same point.”

I nodded.

She turned the first ring.

Blue light crawled around the frame.

The second ring moved.

Cold entered the room before the view did.

Then the metal circle filled with a snow-covered rail yard beneath an evening sky. A low station. A repair shed. The dark shape of a train. Beyond them, a building with barred windows and a light burning in one upper room.

The place where somebody had seen us leave.

I started the Lamborghini.

Tank started the Mercedes behind me. The rescue van's engine joined ours.

Shawna reached across and touched my arm.

“Ready?”

I looked at her. At my wife, who could have stayed in a room above the clouds and had instead chosen this impossible road beside me.

“Nigga,” I said softly, “I been ready for you my whole life.”

She laughed once and wiped her eye with the heel of her hand.

Then I put the car in gear.

The snow beyond the door began turning blue beneath my police lights.

## 9. The Wrong Men Saw the Blue Lights

Snow hit my windshield.

Real snow. Heavy, wet, dirty at the edges of the rail yard. The Lamborghini's tires crunched onto ground that had never heard an engine like mine, and every man carrying a gun turned toward the sound.

I gave them the siren too.

Nigga, if we were introducing ourselves to a century, we were going to enunciate.

Shawna sat very still beside me. Behind us Tank's Mercedes crossed the shining circle, followed by the rescue van. For a second I could see Sky High's clean floor in my mirror, Storm standing at the controls, blue light reflected in her white shirt.

Then Reiss narrowed the opening to a dim seam. He would keep the return boundary alive without leaving a bright invitation for Keller's soldiers. We would signal when we needed it widened. The machinery remained connected; the way home had become small, not gone.

Ahead of us stood the station.

A man in a gray coat shouted something.

Porsche's voice came through the van radio.

“He wants us to stop.”

“Nigga, I gathered the mood.”

The soldier raised his gun.

I drove past him before he could decide where the noise ended and the car began. His shot cracked behind us. Tank swerved the Mercedes between the soldier and the van. Victor sent one bright bolt through the man's weapon, knocking it from his hands.

The soldier fell into the snow holding his wrist.

Nobody stopped to explain electricity to him.

We crossed the yard toward the repair shed. Its doors stood open. A woman in a dark work coat watched us from inside, a heavy wrench in one hand. For one second her face was all astonishment.

Then she saw the guards running behind us.

She swung the shed door wider.

That was all the permission I needed.

The Lamborghini shot inside. The Mercedes followed. Petra drove the van through last, and the woman with the wrench pulled the door shut behind it.

Tank got out laughing once, hard.

“Nigga, pavement. I missed your ugly ass.”

The woman looked at him. Looked at the cars. Looked at Shawna stepping out beside me with her gun held low.

She spoke French.

Porsche answered.

I heard my name, heard something that sounded like police, heard the woman make a disbelieving noise at the sight of my badge.

Porsche turned to me.

“She's asking if we're the people from the blue door.”

“Tell her yes.”

The woman's eyes filled before her face allowed anything else to change.

“Miriam Levin,” she said in careful English. “I work here.”

She tapped the wrench against her palm.

“Not by choice.”

“Aiden.”

She looked at the Lamborghini.

“I have many questions.”

“We going to earn you time for them.”

Outside, boots approached. Miriam pulled a canvas cover over the nearest window. She knew the shed's blind corners, the little door behind a stack of wheels, the place where a loose floor panel could hide six people or one awkwardly positioned Tank.

She didn't hide us there.

She went to the main door and shouted in German.

A guard shouted back.

Her voice became angry in a way that sounded practiced and dangerous. She pointed toward the roof. The guard looked up.

Victor moved behind him.

The man came inside unconscious before his eyes finished coming down.

Miriam shut the door again.

Porsche stared at her.

“What did you say?”

“That his bullets would damage the fuel pipes, and Keller would have him shot for ruining the work.”

Tank looked at the roof.

“Fuel pipes up there?”

“No.”

He smiled at her with open admiration.

“Ma'am, I like how you think.”

More guards were coming. We could hear them gathering outside, trying to understand the three impossible cars now concealed in a building full of tools they did understand.

Miriam led us through the small rear door into a passage beside the holding building. A man waited there with a bundle of cloth under one arm. He was lean, bearded, and tired enough that his eyes looked older than the rest of his face.

“David,” Miriam said.

David Adler. Thirty-four. A physician. Jewish, like Miriam. He had been forced to work in Keller's infirmary and had spent every day since trying to keep people alive with too little medicine and too many orders.

Vega stepped forward.

“Dr. Marisol Vega.”

He looked at her medical bag.

For the first time since we crossed the door, I saw a man look at something other than my car as if it might be a miracle.

“You have supplies?”

“Show me who needs them.”

He did not waste a second on amazement. He took her toward the infirmary. Rosa and Mercedes followed, carrying bags from the van.

Miriam stayed with us.

“There are fewer guards at the rear building now,” she said. “Most are watching your door. They think your machines are an attack.”

I looked toward the sound of men shouting in the yard.

“Finally, some accurate thinking.”

She gave me a sharp little smile.

Then she took us to the woman who had seen me leave.

Her name was Léonie Arnaud. Twenty-nine. She had carried messages for a resistance group before her arrest. She stood behind the holding building's service window with a cut on her lower lip and a folded strip of fabric tied around one hand.

When she saw me, she didn't cry.

She gripped the window bars.

“You came back.”

“Told myself I would.”

“I told them you would too.”

Behind her, faces appeared in the dim room. Men and women. Young adults and older adults. People standing because sitting would have hidden the window. People too tired to stand who looked up from benches when the others made room.

I felt Shawna's hand at my back.

Léonie looked at her.

Something passed between them before either spoke.

“We're getting this open,” Shawna said.

Miriam showed Petra the door.

Petra turned her hands to stone.

Léonie stepped back and told the others to move away from the frame.

The door came inward with one heavy crack.

Nobody cheered.

They listened for the guards.

That hurt more than cheering would have helped.

Shawna went inside first.

“We have a way out. We need you together. We need you listening to the people who know this place. If someone can't walk, tell us now.”

Léonie translated where she needed to. Porsche helped. Miriam moved through the room calling names, asking about injuries, touching shoulders with the quick certainty of a woman who knew exactly who had been missing from breakfast.

I watched her count.

Not numbers first.

People.

Then the rear yard filled with shouting.

The guards had found the empty side of the repair shed.

Tank stepped into the passage beside me.

“How many?”

“Enough to be rude.”

He looked at my badge.

“You arresting these niggas?”

I looked at the uniforms coming around the corner. At the weapons raised toward a door full of people they had locked away.

“Depends how cooperative the evening gets.”

The first shots tore into the brick above us.

The evening was not cooperative.

We answered from the corner while Victor moved across the roof. He used his charge in short bursts, dropping weapons, darkening lamps, giving people space to move. He was not an endless lightning storm. After the third burst, he braced one hand on the chimney and breathed hard.

Tank pulled a metal cart into the passage as cover. I fired around it. Shawna moved the prisoners toward the repair shed while Petra stood between them and the open yard, bullets striking marble shoulders.

A man on the far side of the yard stared at Petra and lowered his gun in pure disbelief.

Miriam threw her wrench.

It hit him square in the face.

“Stop staring,” she said.

Tank looked at her.

“Ma'am.”

“He was blocking the path.”

“Yes, ma'am.”

The prisoners moved. Some supported each other. One older woman, Rivka, sixty, refused to leave until a man named Jakob had his violin case. Not because the case mattered more than life. Because he had been using its strap to help an injured friend walk, and she had noticed when everyone else missed it.

Jakob reached us with the case across his back and his friend's arm over his shoulders.

I caught the other side.

“I got him.”

Jakob looked at me, then at the police lights still flashing through the shed's covered window.

“What country are you from?”

“Long story.”

“Are you winning?”

I tightened my hold on his friend.

“Nigga, look who walking out.”

He didn't know all my words.

He understood that one.

Inside the repair shed, Vega and David worked together over two stretchers. Rosa kept a little clear space around them by the force of her voice alone. Mercedes brought water. Porsche translated a frightened man's questions until his breathing slowed enough for him to answer one of hers.

“Thirty-eight here,” Miriam told me. “Twenty-one in the infirmary and east rooms. The rest at the machine building.”

“Eighty-three still?”

She shook her head.

“Eighty-six. Three arrived yesterday.”

I nodded.

Three more names for the world to keep.

A loudspeaker crackled over the yard.

Keller's voice arrived smooth and amplified.

Porsche listened. Her face hardened.

“He says return the prisoners and he'll permit us to leave.”

I looked around the shed. At the people beginning to believe the door in front of them might open outward. At my wife carrying a cup to a man whose hands shook too badly to hold it alone.

“Tell him I ain't taking requests.”

“He can't hear me from here.”

I glanced at the Lamborghini.

Its police loudspeaker waited behind the siren switch.

Tank saw where I was looking and grinned.

“This nigga brought amplification.”

I got into the car and lifted the microphone.

“Colonel Keller.”

My voice rolled across the yard.

The guards stopped shouting.

“I'm Captain Aiden. You got eighty-six people that belong to themselves. I'm collecting every fucking one.”

Porsche translated beside me into French, then Miriam shouted the essential demand in German from the doorway.

Keller answered immediately.

His voice was angry now.

Good. Some men sounded worse when they were pretending to be reasonable.

Miriam listened, then looked at me.

“He says you have no authority here.”

I looked at the medal ribbon peeking from Shawna's jacket. At Tank loading people into the van's warm interior. At the broken prison door lying where Petra had put it.

“Nigga,” I said into the microphone, “the door disagrees.”

I lowered it and got out.

Léonie stood beside the rear exit, watching the road beyond the yard.

“He will bring men from the barracks,” she said. “We cannot hold this shed all night.”

“Then we don't.”

“The return door is between us and them.”

Miriam joined us. She pointed toward the old service track running behind the shed.

“There is another engine in the machine building. A locomotive. Keller uses it to move the experimental carriages. If we can bring the people there, we can bring the train to your door.”

I looked at the tracks disappearing into the dark.

A train. Of course a nigga's first trip through time needed a train.

Shawna came beside me.

“What you thinking?”

I looked back at the Lamborghini, sitting in the shed like the future had parked wrong on purpose.

“Thinking we gonna make transportation very fucking confusing.”

## 10. My Wife Was Already Inside

Miriam drew the depot in soot on the repair shed's concrete floor.

No ruler. No hesitation. She marked the holding rooms, the infirmary, the machine building, the barracks, and the command house on the little rise beyond the tracks. Then she drew a narrow line beneath the largest building.

“Drainage passage,” she said. “It floods in spring. It is clear now.”

Tank crouched beside her.

“How clear?”

She looked at his shoulders.

“You will hate it.”

“Nigga, I can hate things while fitting through them.”

“Not this one.”

Rosa laughed softly from beside the stretchers. Tank looked at her.

“You supposed to support my dimensions.”

“Baby, I do. That's why I know you ain't fitting.”

For a second, the people nearest us smiled. Then the sound of boots outside brought their faces back to the room they were in.

We didn't have much time. Keller's men held the route to the return door. The prisoners in the machine building would be moved before dawn if the colonel decided the yard could not be secured. Some modern captives wore the same power-draining restraints Finn had used on Victor. Others had no gifts at all and were there because Keller had a use for their hands or Voss wanted people who could not fight back with lightning.

Shawna knelt beside Miriam's drawing.

“This passage comes up where?”

“Under the boiler room.”

“Can you take us?”

Miriam nodded.

“Then take us.”

I looked at my wife.

She looked back before I said anything.

“You making the loud part, aren't you?”

I looked at Tank.

The nigga was already smiling.

“We have some experience.”

Our loud part would be a meeting.

Keller had offered to talk. He clearly believed a man could arrive in an impossible car, rescue thirty-eight prisoners, and still be persuaded by an expensive desk. I had met niggas like that in every year I'd personally occupied.

He wanted the vehicles, the return mechanism, and the people we had taken out of his rooms. He especially wanted Victor and Petra, whose gifts had made his soldiers frightened enough to forget their training. Reiss had warned us Keller thought power was something he could own by putting the right body behind the right lock.

I intended to waste his time beautifully.

Shawna, Miriam, Petra, Mercedes, and Porsche would go through the drainage passage. Victor would stay with the shed group to protect them and conserve his strength. Vega and David would prepare the injured to move. Rosa and Léonie would guide the first group toward the machine building once the way opened.

Tank and I would take the Lamborghini to the command house.

“He will search you,” Miriam warned.

“He can look.”

“He will take your weapons.”

Tank flexed both hands.

“Nigga gonna need a bigger pocket.”

Miriam studied him, then me, and shook her head in something halfway between disbelief and reluctant affection.

“You are either the luckiest men I have ever met, or the most dangerous.”

“Both can fit in one car,” I said.

Before we separated, Shawna pulled me into the narrow space beside the van. She adjusted my collar. There was soot on her cheek. A small tear at the cuff of her sweater. Her eyes were steady.

“Don't get so busy impressing that bastard you forget what we're doing.”

“Baby, I can multitask.”

“Aiden.”

I put my forehead against hers.

“I know.”

We stayed like that for a breath. Then she kissed me once, hard, and went back to Miriam.

I watched her walk away with the women.

That was the part nobody applauded. The part where my greatest strength became a person going somewhere I couldn't stand between her and every gun. I had to trust her skill, her nerve, her right to be more than somebody I protected.

Nigga, trusting that woman had already made my life bigger than Vegas.

I kept doing it.

Outside the shed, a white cloth hung from the Lamborghini's antenna. Keller's men watched us emerge. I drove slowly, police lights turning the snow blue, engine making a low promise beneath the hood.

Tank sat beside me looking out at the guards.

“These niggas dressed like they own the night.”

“Then somebody better tell these niggas morning coming.”
