Tank took the driver's seat. I moved into the passenger side. Shawna climbed onto the rear platform of a nearby rescue cart with Victor, and Petra joined them from the stairs. Knox's officers kept the evacuation lanes clear. Rook and the men who had abandoned Voss put their weapons down in a visible line and helped the last spectators leave the lower seats.

Voss saw them.

“Traitors.”

Rook looked up at the platform.

“You dropped our bridge.”

“I gave you purpose.”

“You gave us a long fall.”

Tank started the Lamborghini.

“Nigga, even his employees reviewing him badly.”

We drove down the stadium access road toward the field. The tires rolled over grass as green and perfect as if nobody had spent the morning trying to turn it into wreckage. I looked at the finish arch from the race. It stood above the far entrance, bent but intact.

Two days ago I had arrived beneath it in first place.

Today I intended to leave the same way, even if I had to let my brother drive.

Voss lifted his armored hand.

Tank swerved before the blast struck. Blue force tore a long groove through the turf behind us. The Lamborghini slid sideways and came around facing the platform.

“Nigga got no respect for landscaping,” Tank said.

“Harlan gonna be furious.”

Voss struck again.

Petra stepped in front of the rescue cart and took the edge of the blast across her marble shoulders. It drove her back three feet. Mercedes caught the cart before it rolled into the stairs. Victor sent a brief answering bolt at the coupling, making Voss turn away from them.

I got out of the Lamborghini.

Voss smiled.

“At last.”

“Nigga, you been looking at me all week.”

“Without the car.”

I glanced at Tank.

He revved the engine.

“Car still here,” I said.

Voss lunged.

He crossed the platform in one enormous step and struck down with the broken staff. I moved sideways, slower than I wanted, fast enough to live. The blow smashed the edge of the trophy pedestal.

Gold-painted stone burst across the grass.

I picked up a broken piece and hit him in the face with it.

His head snapped back.

Tank shouted through the open window.

“Nigga used the award!”

“It's educational.”

Voss hit me across the shoulder. I fell onto the platform steps, caught the rail, and dragged myself up before he could strike again. Pain flashed through my ribs. I had no fresh body waiting under the damaged one. Blue Thunder had not given me a replacement.

He saw the weakness and came closer.

That was useful.

Shawna moved behind him.

Lena's voice suddenly rang across the stadium, clear as a bell.

“Voss.”

He turned toward the sound, searching the seats.

Her gift carried the word from one speaker to the next, moving his attention away from the woman approaching his blind side. Rosa stood beside her in the upper gallery, one hand on her back. Two singers, no longer reaching through prison walls, using the whole open sky.

Shawna reached the coupling.

She struck its exposed latch with the broken staff head she had recovered from the support chamber.

The black casing shifted.

Voss spun toward her.

I caught his arm.

Current tore through my hand.

Blue woke beneath my skin.

This time I knew it was limited. Knew the pain that came after. Knew I was choosing a few seconds, not becoming a god with the whole afternoon available.

I spent them on his hand.

The charge moved through me and into the ground, a hard bright arc that made my teeth ache. Voss's grip loosened. Shawna pulled the coupling free of its chest bracket.

The armor went dark.

I went down on one knee.

Shawna ran the coupling toward Victor and Bell's waiting transport case.

Voss followed her with a gun drawn from inside his coat.

Nigga, after all that machinery, he still came back to the same ugly decision every other coward had made in front of my wife.

I drew first.

“Drop it.”

He froze.

For a moment the stadium held its breath.

The gun remained in his hand.

He looked at me kneeling on the grass, shaking, bruised, tired enough that staying upright had become work.

He thought he had found the part of greatness that could be outwaited.

Then he looked at Shawna.

His weapon moved.

I fired.

Voss fell backward against the broken pedestal.

The gun dropped from his hand.

He tried to rise once.

Failed.

I kept my weapon steady until Knox reached him with two officers and Vega came behind them. The doctor knelt, checked, and looked up at me.

One small shake of her head.

Finished.

The chancellor was dead.

The Heart's last old lock opened under Bell's control. The stadium settled with a long, deep sound that ran through the ground beneath my knee. Above us, the towers stopped leaning. The clouds resumed their proper position below the windows.

For a second nobody cheered.

We listened to the school stay in the air.

Then the sound began.

From the upper gallery. From the evacuation stairs. From the helicopter crews hovering beyond the rail. From the people who had been hidden beneath the academy and the people who had arrived through a door that would never open again.

Aiden.

Shawna reached me before the chant could become too large to hear her voice inside it.

“Look at me.”

I did.

“You done?”

I looked at Voss. At the steady towers. At Tank climbing out of my car with tears in his eyes and a grin too big to hide them.

“Yeah.”

My wife put both hands on my face.

“Then come back to me.”

I tried to stand.

My legs said no.

Tank caught me under one arm. Victor caught the other. Between them they hauled me upright while the stadium roared louder at the sight of us together.

“This nigga finally heavy,” Tank said.

Victor laughed, breathless.

“He has always been heavy.”

“Nigga, emotionally ain't a lifting category.”

Shawna walked in front of us, making room, keeping her eyes on mine every few steps. I could not produce one more spark. Could barely lift my hand to wave. Every joint hurt. Every old injury had returned to remind me it had paid rent before the new power moved in.

But the sky stayed up.

My people stayed alive.

And when we passed the broken race arch, Tank stopped and looked at the sign still hanging above it.

FIRST PLACE.

He nodded toward me.

“Nigga, even when we carrying him.”

I laughed so hard my ribs nearly ended the celebration.

They carried me through anyway.

## 19. Valedictorian Again, Because Niggas Keep Graduating Me

I woke up with Shawna asleep against my chest and Tank arguing with a nurse about fruit.

Nigga, I knew immediately I had survived.

Death might have had trumpets. It did not have my brother explaining that a pear was now an emotional subject.

“He can have one when he wakes,” the nurse said.

“This nigga saved a school.”

“And his stomach needs rest.”

“His greatness don't.”

“His greatness can wait until breakfast.”

I opened one eye.

“Nigga, let the woman work.”

Tank turned so fast his chair scraped across the floor. His face opened into a grin that told me how frightened he had been while I wasn't awake to make it easier.

“There he is.”

Shawna lifted her head.

For one second she looked lost between sleep and the last thing she remembered fearing. Then she saw my eyes open and put her hand against my cheek.

“Hey.”

“Hey, baby.”

She kissed me carefully.

That scared me more than a hard kiss would have.

“How bad I look?”

“Like somebody hit a very expensive statue with a truck.”

“Statue still handsome?”

“Obnoxiously.”

I relaxed.

Vega appeared at the door with Storm behind her. The doctor checked me before she let anybody explain the outside world. My ribs were bruised, my shoulder strained, my hands burned, and my body thoroughly offended by being used as the temporary pathway for the Heart's charge. Nothing about the new ability had healed the old wounds. Nothing about the title people were shouting in the corridors changed the fact that I needed sleep.

“No powers today,” Vega said.

“Nigga, I just got them.”

“Then you can enjoy knowing where they are.”

Storm laughed softly.

The dean looked better. Tired, but no longer holding the sky up through force of will and a series of increasingly personal disagreements. She sat beside the bed and told me the school was stable. Bell and Miriam had severed the old tower's controls. The real Heart remained inside the restored central housing. Voss's armor and the stolen coupling were secured. His surviving guards had surrendered. Sable and Finn remained in custody, separately, so neither could improve the other's story before Pike finished asking questions.

The time door had been dismantled completely.

Reiss had watched the final ring come off its mount.

Then he had gone upstairs and slept in a room with an unlocked door.

I listened with Shawna's hand in mine.

When Storm finished, I asked about the people.

All sixty-two returnees were safe. The thirty rescued before the historical mission were safe too. Dennis from the laundry had gone home with his own keys and had already returned to work long enough to tell his supervisor which locked storage rooms he would never enter again. Nobody had required gratitude as a condition of staying. People were calling families, arranging rooms, asking questions, refusing questions, resting.

The ones who had come from 1944 were taking the new world at the pace they could bear.

That seemed right to me.

Some surprises deserved more than an afternoon.

Storm took my unbandaged wrist gently.

“You changed this place.”

I looked at the window. Beyond it the academy floated in bright morning air, scarred in places, beautiful in others, still very much a school.

“It needed a little parking correction.”

She smiled.

“Yes. Apparently it did.”

For two days I was forbidden to leave the medical tower without somebody sensible beside me.

Tank volunteered.

Vega looked at him for so long he withdrew the application himself.

Shawna took me walking instead. Slowly at first. Across the balcony. Down one corridor. Eventually into the garden where Harlan Moss was repairing the damaged paths with roots coaxed carefully through the stone.

He wore the polished brown shoes Tank had bought him.

That afternoon his wife arrived.

Anne came up the garden steps carrying a small overnight bag and stopped when she saw him. She was a little shorter than Shawna, with graying curls and a face that seemed to lose five months of exhaustion in one breath.

Harlan dropped the pruning shears.

Neither of them ran at first.

They walked toward each other, slowly enough to believe each step.

Then she reached him and hit his chest with both hands before folding herself against it.

“You still have those shoes,” she said through tears.

He looked down at the brown leather.

“New pair.”

“Same fool wearing them.”

“Your fool.”

She cried harder.

Tank stood beside me with his mouth pressed into a line. Rosa slipped her hand into his. He squeezed it without looking away from the couple.

“Good shoes,” he said quietly.

I nodded.

“Excellent fucking shoes.”

A week later Bell let me sit in the Lamborghini again.

He had repaired every dent except one small mark near the rear fender, which he said he would preserve if I wanted a reminder of the train. Gold badge emblems now shone on the doors, and a discreet second strip of police lights sat above the windshield. Bell said a graduate deserved appropriate trim. Nigga, the car had received formalwear.

I looked at it.

“Leave that.”

Miriam stood beside him in a clean blue work coat. She had spent the week learning the academy's engines one careful question at a time. The floating roads still astonished her. The mechanical problems did not.

“You drive as if roads are suggestions,” she told me.

“They been flexible.”

“The car has not always appreciated your confidence.”

Bell nodded so vigorously all four hands moved.

“Thank you.”

She looked at him.

“But it is a remarkable car.”

He nearly cried again.

Nigga, I was going to start carrying tissues for that man.

My new ability came with lessons, which I considered rude but useful. Storm and Victor helped me learn the difference between feeling charge and having enough to spend. Bell watched what happened when I passed it through the car. Vega watched what happened to me afterward and ended every session before my pride could become an injury.

One short burst could sharpen my reactions and send blue current through my hands. A car could carry that charge into a brief surge of acceleration. Afterward I shook, sweated, and tired quickly. Trying to hold it longer made everything worse. I could not fly. I could not call up an endless storm. I could not fix a wound by admiring it. The body beneath the light still needed food, rest, and a wife willing to say, “Nigga, enough,” with final authority.

I had that wife.

The power had no chance of making me completely unmanageable.

Only impressively difficult.

Two weeks after Voss fell, the academy held its graduation.

They put my name first on the program.

Then they put it in larger print than the title.

Tank unfolded the paper and stared at it.

“Nigga, this school's graduating from you.”

“They learned a lot.”

“You attended one class.”

“Intensively.”

The ceremony took place in the restored stadium. Every seat was full. Helicopters and airships hovered beyond the upper rail, carrying guests who had decided a normal chair lacked ambition. The orchestra sat beneath a blue canopy. Rosa sang the opening number. Lena joined her for the second verse, and their voices rose through the open air without a wall between them.

Shawna sat in the front row wearing the ruby Claudine had given us, set now in a simple pendant Marcellus made to keep the stone close to her skin. The red flashed against her blue dress. She caught me looking and smiled as if the whole stadium existed mainly to give us more room for that smile.

I wore a dark suit, my gold badge, the cross, and an honors robe so heavy Tank said they had stitched my ego into the lining.

Victor stood beside me in blue.

He had his own honors. He had earned them. When the dean called his name, I stood before anybody else and cheered loud enough to make him laugh on the way to the platform.

That nigga had tried to beat me.

Then he had helped me save people who would never have known his name otherwise.

I wanted the whole sky to know it now.

Petra graduated with distinction in rescue strength. She accepted her award, turned toward Mercedes, and kissed her in front of the entire faculty. Mercedes looked startled for one beautiful second, then put both arms around her and made the applause last longer.

Porsche stood up cheering.

Leon became three men beside her and cheered three times as loudly.

Knox leaned toward Pike.

“Do all three need separate identification?”

Pike closed his eyes.

“Please let me have one peaceful afternoon.”

Before Storm called my name, the great screen replayed our arrival: the broken train, my car beneath the platform, Shawna pulling people through the carriage door. Tank watched himself catch three people at once and nodded with satisfaction.

“Nigga, that man strong.”

“That's you,” Rosa said.

“Exactly. Camera telling the truth.”

Then Storm said my name.

The stadium stood.

All of it.

Nigga, even some people who had been sitting comfortably on air came down so they could stand properly.

I walked onto the platform beneath the repaired finish arch. The dean held a diploma in one hand and a gold captain's insignia in the other.

“Aiden,” she said, “Top Graduate Captain of Sky High.”

The roar rolled across the clouds.

She waited for it to quiet, failed, and continued over it.

“For extraordinary command, ingenuity, courage, and devotion to those placed in his care.”

Tank shouted, “And the driving!”

“And the driving,” Storm agreed.

The engineering faculty stood and applauded as one wounded profession.

She gave me the diploma.

Then another.

I looked at it.

“What's this one?”

“An honorary distinction for your vehicle.”

Nigga.

My car had graduated.

I turned toward Tank.

He had both hands on his head.

“This nigga ride more educated than my cousins!”

I held up both diplomas.

The stadium lost its fucking mind.

Storm stepped aside for my speech.

I looked down at the paper somebody had offered me backstage.

Then folded it and put it in my pocket.

“Aight,” I said.

The room settled into the kind of quiet a man felt in his chest.

“First, I want everybody to appreciate that I arrived here late, parked wrong, destroyed a platform, missed most of my classes, and still graduated first.”

Laughter broke across the stands.

“That's not advice. Most niggas try that and wind up walking home with a bill.”

More laughter.

I looked at Shawna.

“I came because somebody saw something I did in Vegas and figured I ought to try it higher up. I brought my people because everywhere I go gets better when they there. Then I met more people. Some tried to beat me. Some fed me. Some fixed the car after I made their profession nervous. Some were singing where nobody could hear them.”

Lena looked up from beside Rosa.

“I hear you now,” I said.

She pressed her lips together and nodded.

I raised the diploma.

“This got my name on it. Fine. Nigga, I like my name. But every person who held a door, carried a stretcher, told the truth, brought a shoe, flew back for a friend, or stood beside somebody who couldn't stand alone—you're in it.”

I let the silence hold that.

Then I smiled.

“My wife's still getting the good parking space.”

The stadium roared again.

Shawna stood, laughing, and lifted both hands toward me.

I came down from the platform before anybody could announce another honor.

Went straight to her.

Put my arms around her waist.

“How I do?”

She looked at the diplomas, the badge, the cheering school, the car waiting beside the field with a blue ribbon tied around its mirror.

Then she looked at me.

“Damn, boy.”

I kissed her before she finished.

Nigga, I knew the rest by heart.

## 20. A Nigga This Great Needed an Ocean

After graduation, Madame Afterglow opened every table in Cloud Nine and announced that my first hand at each one would be played on the house.

Nigga, she should have specified which house.

By midnight I had won enough money for the casino's finance manager to come downstairs personally. He stood behind the blackjack table in a beautiful gray suit, watching me turn over another winning card while Tank laughed into his drink.

“This nigga been counting the future,” Tank said.

“Can't do that,” I told him.

“Then why you keep winning?”

I looked at my cards.

Looked at my wife standing beside me in blue silk and the ruby pendant.

Looked back at my brother.

“Nigga, patterns.”

Shawna laughed and kissed the top of my head.

The finance manager looked at Afterglow.

She waved him away.

“Let the captain play.”

“Madame, the probability—”

“Has met him.”

He withdrew with the injured dignity of a man whose entire education had failed to prepare him for the evening's central problem.

Cloud Nine had repaired its shattered windows and replaced the glass moon. The new moon was slightly larger. Afterglow said the old one had looked timid in photographs of me standing on it.

I respected an owner who could learn from an event.

The ballroom glittered. Music climbed through its open doors onto the roof terrace. Adult heroes danced beside cops, singers, gamblers, mechanics, and the friends from Vegas who had arrived because Rosa told them there was a party in the sky and they refused to believe her without checking.

Some wore gowns. Some wore capes. One man wore a cape over a gown and looked so pleased with himself I shook his hand on principle. A table near the far wall had enough champagne, pills, and white powder on it to explain why two wealthy guests believed they had personally invented dancing. Their friends moved the table farther from the orchestra before the drummer began accepting scientific suggestions.

My people were beautiful in every corner.

Rosa sang with Lena, then stepped offstage and let her take a song alone. Tank stood beneath the lights watching both women, but his face changed whenever Rosa looked his way. The nigga's whole expression went soft and proud, and I loved seeing him unable to hide it.

Mercedes danced with Petra. Porsche danced with one Leon while another fetched drinks and the third stood near the terrace door recovering from being asked to do too much with the same legs.

“He's only got a minute,” Mercedes warned her.

“Then he better use it beautifully.”

Petra laughed so hard the floor beneath her shoes briefly turned white with marble dust.

I won another hand.

The dealer looked at me with open admiration.

“Sir, I have dealt cards for twenty years.”

“You doing good.”

“I have never seen this.”

Tank slapped the table.

“Nigga, that's what the school said!”

Shawna took the chips from in front of me and put them into a little velvet bag.

“You're finished.”

I looked up at her.

“Baby, the universe talking.”

“It can call tomorrow. You're dancing with me.”

I stood so fast the finance manager nearly cried with relief.

“Excellent decision,” he said.

I pointed at him.

“Nigga, don't get comfortable. We walking past roulette.”

Shawna pulled me away laughing.

We danced beneath the new moon with no chancellor waiting to interrupt us. Nobody asked her for a private word. Nobody threatened a locked door. The only thing coming toward us was a waiter carrying drinks and looking mildly frightened that I might somehow win those too.

She rested her cheek against mine.

“You like being a superhero?”

“I like the parking.”

“Aiden.”

I thought about the blue charge in my hands. The fatigue afterward. Victor sitting beside my car and telling me to listen when my body said enough. Storm standing in the air to hold an entire school. Lena making one word travel where bullets couldn't reach.

“I like knowing another thing I can do,” I said.

Shawna nodded.

“That's a better answer.”

“I had it behind the parking.”

She smiled against my cheek.

For a while we let the song do the talking. I could feel the room looking at us, but it stayed outside the small space between her hand and my shoulder. My fame had gotten louder in the sky. My love for her had gotten quieter in certain places, stronger where it didn't need anybody listening.

Then she spun away from me, came back with both hands on my chest, and said, “Show these people what all that greatness does on a dance floor.”

Nigga, a direct request from my wife was a sacred assignment.

I did the turn I had practiced in the bathroom.

Perfectly.

The orchestra saw us and changed its rhythm. Rosa laughed into the microphone. Tank climbed onto a chair to announce that the captain was now operating across multiple disciplines. I turned Shawna again, caught her at the waist, and dipped her low enough for the ruby at her throat to catch the moonlight.

She looked up at me, smiling.

The ballroom applauded.

This time I didn't even pretend to dislike it.

Oren Titan approached afterward with Opaline on his arm. The big man had apparently recovered from the indignity of watching me rescue his wife while keeping a drink upright. He carried a trophy he had bought himself: a small silver pedestal with two champagne glasses fixed to its top.

“For the man with the steadiest hands in the sky,” he said.

Tank looked at the trophy.

“Nigga, another building?”

“A sculpture,” Oren said.

“These niggas keep doing architecture to us.”

Opaline hugged Shawna, then thanked me again. Oren did not look smaller beside her gratitude. He looked relieved he had found a way to join it without making the whole thing about the moment he had failed to catch her.

That was progress.

I shook his hand.

“Next time we lift the furniture together.”

He laughed and agreed immediately.

Across the room, Claudine raised her glass toward us. The older casino guest wore enough emeralds to make Marcellus turn his head despite himself. She saw Shawna's ruby pendant and smiled with the satisfaction of a woman who had given the right thing to the right person.

Shawna went to her.

They talked for a long time.

I didn't follow. Some gifts kept becoming conversations after the man who carried them had left the room.

Near the terrace, Marcellus sat at a small table with Miriam and Bell. A blue cloth lay between them. On it rested the Blue Mercy ring, a tiny clock mechanism Miriam had brought from the depot, and one of Bell's unfamiliar engine parts.

Three beautiful things. Three people who knew how much care could fit inside something a careless man might call an object.

Marcellus looked up when I approached.

“Come admire something you aren't allowed to drive.”

“Nigga, that sentence leaves me very little.”

He showed Miriam the ring. Told her its name. Told her about Celeste, briefly, in the voice he used when the person mattered more than the story surrounding the jewel.

Miriam listened without trying to make his grief resemble hers.

Then she showed him the clock piece. It had belonged to a workshop where she worked before she was taken. She had kept it hidden because it was proof she had once fixed things for people who said thank you.

Marcellus held it carefully.

“We could make it run again.”

She looked at him.

“I would like that.”

Bell quietly cleared space on the table.

The party went on around them while they bent over a small machine and gave it the possibility of another morning.

I left them to it.

On the terrace, Tank stood alone looking out at the clouds. He had taken off his jacket. The red ribbon remained on his wrist. Rosa's singing drifted through the open doors behind us, warm enough to make the night feel less high.

I stood beside him.

“You good?”

He nodded.

Then shook his head.

Then laughed at himself.

“Nigga, I don't know what this is.”

“Clouds.”

“Fuck you.”

I smiled.

He looked toward the ballroom. Rosa was laughing with Lena between songs, one hand at her waist, head tilted back. My brother watched her the way a man watched a door he had finally realized he was allowed to walk through.

“I keep thinking about houses,” he said.

“You got a house.”

“A different kind.”

I let him find the words.

“A place where her coat already there. Where I don't got to ask if she staying. Where I come in and she mad I forgot some little shit, and I get to go back out and buy it because that's the problem we having that day.”

He looked embarrassed by how much he had said.

I looked at my brother until the embarrassment had nowhere useful to stand.

“Nigga, that sound like something worth buying the little shit for.”

He laughed quietly.

“You got that.”

I looked through the doors and saw Shawna searching the room for me.

“Yeah.”

“Don't get stupid with it.”

“Nigga, you met me.”

“I said with it. You can keep being stupid everywhere else.”

We stood there another minute. Then Rosa came out and slipped her arm through his. He kissed the top of her head without checking whether anybody was watching.

I went back inside to my wife.

The next morning, the school attempted to hold a quiet farewell breakfast.

That lasted until somebody unveiled a statue of me on the lawn.

Nigga, the statue was taller than the dining hall.

It showed me standing on the hood of a Lamborghini with lightning in one hand and a diploma in the other. The sculptor had given my chest an extra six inches of confidence. My coat blew backward in a wind that seemed to exist solely because I deserved dramatic weather.

Tank walked around the base in silence.

Then he looked at me.

“This nigga got a permanent entrance.”

Shawna put both hands over her face.

I stood very still.

Because I respected art.

Storm came beside me with a smile she was not trying hard enough to hide.

“The students insisted.”

“All of them?”

“Enough of them to carry the stone.”

Bell cleared his throat.

“There was disagreement about whether the car should receive a separate statue.”

I looked at him.

He looked at the Lamborghini parked nearby.

“I remain in favor.”

Shawna started laughing so hard she had to hold my arm.

The statue's lightning rod chose that moment to catch a harmless little spark from the passing weather. Blue light ran down the stone arm and into the carved car.

The students applauded.

Tank pointed at it.

“Nigga, even the statue got powers.”

I looked up at my enormous stone face.

The sculptor had gotten one thing exactly right.

That nigga looked pleased to be there.

Breakfast became a parade before anybody could stop it. Students lined the main drive with banners. The orchestra marched between the towers. Faculty walked beside our cars, shaking hands through the windows, offering invitations we would never have enough ordinary days to accept.

Miriam brought Bell's final inspection sheet for the Lamborghini and made me promise to listen if the engine sounded unhappy. I promised. She looked at Shawna until my wife promised too.

“Now I believe it,” Miriam said.

Jakob played his violin beside the fountain. Not a song I knew. A song he had chosen for a morning with open air around him. Rivka sat nearby with her bag at her feet and a cup of coffee in both hands. She watched the absurd parade, then caught my eye and raised the cup.

I bowed my head to her.

No speech needed.

Harlan and Anne stood beneath a newly repaired arch of flowering branches. He wore the brown shoes. She had one hand tucked into his arm like she intended to keep it there for the rest of the day and perhaps several years afterward. He showed me a small flower growing out of a crack in the stone.

“This one wanted to be first,” he said.

Tank nodded approvingly.

“Nigga got good influences.”

We said goodbye to people whose lives would continue after our engines faded. That mattered to me more than I expected. Sky High wasn't becoming a place we had saved and could now forget. Victor would remain to train the next advanced class. Petra had accepted a rescue-instructor post and made Mercedes promise to visit before either of them tried pretending distance was a personality trait. Mercedes kissed her and said she had never been shy about booking a flight.

Porsche said goodbye to Leon three times because he insisted on making the most of his gift.

“Don't get arrogant,” she told him after the third kiss.

“You kissed all three.”

“Nigga, I was checking consistency.”

Lena and Rosa promised to sing together again. Amaya had accepted a place at the academy's aquatic center, with a pool whose doors opened from the inside and a teaching schedule she had helped choose. Reiss was staying long enough to dismantle every remaining part of Voss's experiment. After that, he said, he wanted to see an ordinary beach with no physics involved beyond the waves.

I told him that sounded excellent.

Storm waited by the front staircase where I had first parked in her space.

The gold sign was still there.

It now read CAPTAIN AIDEN — WHENEVER HE IS HERE.

I looked at it.

Then at her.

“Dean.”

“Captain.”

We shook hands. No accidental spark this time. I knew enough to keep the little blue current inside me quiet.

“Come back,” she said.

“You sure? I made repairs expensive.”

“You made the place worth repairing.”

She embraced Shawna. Then Tank. Rosa. The whole crew, one by one, without making it ceremonial enough to hide that she meant it.

Victor stood beside my car.

He put a hand on the roof.

“One more race when you return.”

“You sure, nigga?”

“A fair one. No collapsing trains. No overloaded rings. No rescuing anybody halfway through.”

I looked at the sky.

“You asking a lot from the environment.”

He laughed.

Then he hugged me, hard.

“Thank you,” he said quietly.

I held him a second longer.

“Stay magnificent.”

He stepped back and smiled.

“You make it difficult to do anything else.”

The invitation arrived before I could get into the car.

A black airship descended beyond the front gate. Its side carried a gold crown above a checkered flag. A woman in a white driving suit came down the steps holding a long envelope on a silver tray.

Tank watched her approach.

“Nigga, another school?”

“I can't keep graduating. We running out of wall.”

She stopped before me and bowed her head.

“Captain Aiden. On behalf of Duke Aurelio Cruel, you are invited to the Grand Prix of Kings.”

The crowd around us quieted.

Victor's smile faded slightly.

“Cruel,” he said.

Storm looked at the crown on the airship.

“An ambitious host.”

I opened the envelope.

Inside lay a heavy card showing a coastline, a harbor full of yachts, and a race circuit curling between pale buildings beneath a blue Mediterranean sky. The winner would receive a prize fleet and the deed to a private island called Isla Gloria. The invitation promised a month of racing, music, luxury, and competition among people who considered losing a personal insult.

Nigga, they had written me a holiday.

There was a second card for Shawna.

An invitation to headline one of the evening performances.

And one for Rosa.

She read it over Tank's shoulder and stopped breathing for half a second.

“Aiden.”

“I see it.”

Shawna studied the picture of the ocean.

Not the yachts.

The water.

I watched her face change at the thought of it: sun, salt, a shore that stayed beneath your feet, a room where the loudest thing outside might be waves if I behaved for ten consecutive minutes.

“You want to go?” I asked.

She looked at me.

“I want the ocean.”

“Then we getting the ocean.”

Tank leaned over the invitation.

“Nigga, it says island too.”

“Baby asked for water. I like to include accessories.”

Storm laughed despite herself.

Victor shook his head with a grin that had returned in full.

The messenger looked from me to the Lamborghini, to the statue behind us, to the school full of people still waiting to wave goodbye.

For the first time, she seemed less certain about the competition she had come to invite me into.

“Shall I tell the duke you accept?”

I put the card inside my jacket, beside my badge.

“Tell that nigga to make room.”

Then I got into the Lamborghini.

Shawna sat beside me. Tank and Rosa climbed into the Mercedes. Mercedes and Porsche took their red convertible. Marcellus and Vega would travel with us as far as the city below before the whole crew arranged the next flight together.

The Heart remained above us, holding Sky High where it belonged.

The time door remained gone.

My new power rested quietly in my hands, a little blue promise with very clear limits.

The engine needed none of it to sound magnificent.

I started the car.

The whole school cheered.

We rolled down the open ramp this time. The proper one. The road shone beneath the tires and curved gently through the clouds. Behind us the academy rose into sunlight, scarred, repaired, loud with people who had earned the right to enjoy their own morning.

Shawna took my hand off the gearshift and held it against her knee.

“You happy?” she asked.

I looked at my wife. At the ruby. At the watch. At the road opening beyond the windshield.

Then I looked in the mirror and saw my people following.

“Nigga,” I said, “look how much world we still got.”

She smiled.

I put my foot down.

The clouds opened, and we went toward the sea.


# BOOK III: THE FASTEST KING ALIVE

## 1. The Ocean Was Waiting on Me

The first thing I saw in Monaco was a man falling off a yacht with my name on it.

Not his name. Mine. AIDEN, in gold letters so big the helicopter had to swing around to get all of them in the window. Under that, somebody had written THE FASTEST KING ALIVE.

I hadn't even raced these niggas yet.

Shawna leaned across me. Her hair brushed my mouth, she smelled like the expensive part of a flower, and below us this grown man in a white dinner jacket was descending through the Mediterranean afternoon with a bottle of champagne still in his hand.

“Is that part of the welcome?” she said.

“Better not be the captain.”

Tank pressed his face against the opposite window. “Nigga, the captain got his own boat.”

“He better get back on it.”

The falling man caught a striped awning. It tore. He dropped another six feet, landed on a lower deck, bounced against a table and stood up holding the bottle over his head. A hundred people cheered. He bowed with the deeply relaxed expression of a man who had never paid a hospital bill himself.

Rosa put her sunglasses back on. “I'm singing for these people at nine. If they're dead by eight, I'm keeping the deposit.”

We had come down from Sky High two days earlier. Nigga, I had saved an entire school out of the sky and graduated so hard they played my arrival at the graduation before they played the graduation. I was supposed to take a vacation. Dean Storm had told me to rest, Chief Knox had told me to represent the department, and my wife had asked for an ocean.

An ocean sounded easy.

The duke’s invitation, delivered before we left the floating campus, said the winner of his monthlong Grand Prix of Kings would receive a fleet of cars, a fleet of yachts and an island called Isla Gloria. The island had a palace, an opera house, a private harbor and twelve beaches. Twelve, nigga. I figured Shawna could have one for each month, and I'd keep the water between them.

So we came to race.

My police Lamborghini arrived before I did. Dark blue, gold badge on the doors, blue lights tucked above the windshield. I could see it sitting on the yacht's upper platform now, strapped beside a swimming pool full of women in shining swimsuits and men too rich to admit they couldn't swim. Beside the car stood Mercedes in white and Porsche in yellow, both arguing with a man whose hat had a feather three feet long.

They had flown ahead with Marcellus to make sure the rooms were right. Apparently the rooms had started a fight.

Our helicopter settled onto the rear deck. A valet hurried toward it with a little numbered ticket.

"For the aircraft, sir."

Tank looked at the ticket.

"Nigga, you parking the helicopter?"

"I supervise arrivals."

"This nigga supervised gravity and called it a job," I said.

The valet looked from Tank to me, then at the pool full of people watching us.

"You're Captain Aiden."

"Now you supervising recognition."

He laughed before he could stop himself. Then he put the ticket away and opened both arms toward the yacht like he had personally built it during our flight.

"Anything you need, Captain."

"Nigga, start with my people. Everybody eats, everybody gets a room, nobody got to explain who they came with twice."

He nodded hard and went to work.

Before the blades stopped, the man in the feathered hat marched toward us carrying a silver tray. He had a mustache thin enough to have been signed by a jeweler.

“Captain Aiden,” he announced. “By special instruction of His Grace, Duke Aurelio Cruel—”

“Nigga, somebody really put Cruel on the birth certificate?”

“An ancient name.”

“That don't improve it.”

Shawna squeezed my arm. The man tried again.

“I am Bellario, master of ceremonies and chief marshal of the Grand Prix. His Grace regrets that he cannot personally greet every invited contestant.”

He gestured toward the harbor. At the far end stood a black yacht with four decks and a gold statue of a horse kicking another gold horse in the face. A man in a pale green suit stood on its balcony beneath a huge umbrella. Even from three hundred yards away I could tell he was looking directly at me.

“He's right there,” I said.

“His Grace is at luncheon.”

“Tell him chew faster.”

Bellario's mustache moved without the rest of his face. Mercedes came over carrying the hat's missing feather.

“This nigga said we can't be on the drivers' floor,” she said.

Porsche followed with a room key between two fingers. “Then he offered to upgrade us if we had dinner with him.”

Bellario straightened. “A misunderstanding.”

“Then misunderstand this.” Porsche dropped the key onto his tray. “We already bought the floor.”

I looked at her.

“With your money,” she added.

“Good.”

“Both floors.”

“Better.”

Bellario took a breath. On his tray lay a blue velvet box. He opened it, revealing a little bronze steering wheel on a chain.

“Each contestant must earn the gold wheel before participating in the Grand Prix. The qualification exhibition begins in one hour. An unfortunate late arrival may find the entry list already closed.”

“Nigga, I'm on time.”

“For your arrival, certainly.”

He turned the tray slightly, like that was going to make his sentence less stupid.

Tank stepped out of the helicopter behind me. The rear of the helicopter lifted when his weight came off it. Bellario saw him and briefly reconsidered everything his family had done to bring him into the world.

“The course,” Bellario continued, “is a ceremonial run from the harbor to the Royal Meridian Hotel. Contestants depart from the eastern quay. We are, regrettably, moored at the western quay.”

“How far?”

“Eleven minutes by tender. Forty by road.”

“And when do they close the list?”

“In seven.”

Shawna turned toward the duke's yacht. The man in green raised a glass.

Oh, this nigga wanted to play before I unpacked.

I took the little bronze wheel and hung it around Bellario's neck.

“You wear that, my nigga. It'll remind you of what almost happened.”

Then I walked toward my car.

There are people who think because you own a helicopter you have to use the helicopter. These are the same people who look at a Lamborghini on a yacht and see a transportation problem. I saw my car. My car saw me. Its doors came up before I touched them, and one of the women in the pool screamed like the machine had proposed marriage.

Shawna got in beside me.

“Baby,” she said, “tell me this yacht has a road.”

“It got a front.”

“Aiden.”

“Trust the front.”

Tank climbed onto a nearby launch with Rosa. Mercedes and Porsche followed him, still carrying the feather. Marcellus emerged from the cabin holding a little cup of coffee, saw me putting the car in motion, and sat back down very carefully.

“I'll meet you at the hotel,” he said.

Smart nigga.

Ahead, a service ramp reached from our yacht to a broad floating stage. The stage held a piano, six flower towers and a singer who had started warming up. Beyond it, a smaller yacht rocked gently at its moorings. Beyond that, the eastern quay glittered in the sun.

A reasonable person would have stopped at the word beyond.

I kissed my wife.

“You ready to see the ocean?”

“I was hoping from a chair.”

The engine rose under us. People turned. The singer held one note so long it became fear. I took us down the service ramp, across the stage and past the piano with maybe an inch on each side. The pianist kept playing. That nigga respected his craft.

We hit the edge of the stage with enough speed to make the sea disappear below the windshield.

For a second, all I could see was sky.

Shawna grabbed my arm and laughed one huge terrified laugh directly into my ear.

“Aiden, you stupid beautiful motherfucker!”

Then the tires landed on the smaller yacht's sun deck.

A table collapsed behind us. A man in a silk robe threw both hands up, either praying or awarding me points. I kept the wheel straight. The front of his yacht dipped under our weight; its bow lifted into a ramp. Nigga, the boat helped me. Some things understand greatness immediately.

We launched again.

The car hit the quay sideways, tires shouting, and I pulled it into a turn so clean a line of photographers all stepped backward at the same time. My blue lights flashed across their faces. Behind us, the smaller yacht's owner stood on his deck cheering with the broken table leg over his head.

We had six minutes left.

At the entry gate a woman in a silver racing suit looked from my badge to my car to the two yachts we had just crossed.

“You were on the wrong side,” she said.

“I corrected it.”

She held out a clipboard.

“Name?”

“Nigga, look at the yacht.”

She did. Then she wrote AIDEN in letters large enough to be seen from the yacht.

The starting area was already full of cars. A red machine with white stripes sat low as a threat beside a silver coupe. Behind them waited a black car wearing the number one, its nose shaped like a shark that had married money. The driver leaned on its door in a chrome jacket, thirty-one years old, handsome and aware of it.

He watched the torn flowers falling out of my grille.

“Interesting route,” he said.

“You should see the parking.”

“Cassius Chrome.”

“Aiden.”

“I know.”

He said it without smiling. I liked that. A nigga who knew my name and still wanted to beat me was at least taking his life seriously.

The driver of the red car came over pulling off her gloves. Inez Inferno, the woman whose face appeared on half the racing posters between the airport and the harbor. She had dark hair braided tight, a narrow scar on her chin and eyes that assessed me like she was deciding which part of my car to pass first.

“You brought a passenger,” she said.

“My wife.”

“This isn't a scenic tour.”

“It is for her.”

Shawna leaned out. “I'm Shawna.”

“Inez.”

They shook hands through the window.

“If he scares you,” Inez told her, “you can ride with me.”

Shawna glanced at the sea behind us. “I think we passed scared at the piano.”

Inez laughed. Not polite, either. A real laugh that changed her whole face. Then she looked at me again.

“Keep up, Captain.”

Bellario's voice crackled over the speakers. Somehow the nigga had reached his microphone before his dignity. He announced that the exhibition would follow the Royal Corniche, climb through the old town and finish at the hotel. The first three would receive gold wheels. Everybody else could enjoy the parties and explain to their children why they had become spectators.

I didn't need a gold wheel. I had four black ones and a wife wearing diamonds. But sometimes you let the occasion catch up to your standards.

Cassius leaned across his window one last time.

"Nigga, was that really your first time crossing those boats?"

"That nigga's asking about practice," I told Shawna. "He thinks I practiced disrespecting the marina."

"Did you?" she asked.

"Nigga, you were there."

"I'm checking whether you had a smaller marina at home."

Cassius laughed. "This nigga got a wife who investigates him."

"Nigga needs one," Inez said from the other side.

"Niggas," I said, "the investigation can follow my taillights."

The light changed.

Cassius left like the devil had called him personally. Inez went beside him, red car snapping through the first bend. I let them get out together. Then I put my foot down.

The Lamborghini roared between two white cars whose drivers both looked over at once. I could see one man's mouth shape the word police. Nigga, yes. Put your seat belt on emotionally.

We swept beside the harbor. Yachts leaned in their ropes. On the balconies, people waved flags. At the first sharp turn, Cassius slipped inside Inez, and she answered by driving so close to his rear bumper their reflections touched. They were good. I could see it immediately. Neither wasted a movement. Neither needed to look back to know the other was there.

I liked them even more.

Then a green car came out of a side street where no race car should have been.

It had no number.

Its driver wore a pale mask.

He aimed straight at Cassius.

“Nigga, what—”

Cassius swerved. The green car struck the wall and spun across the road. Inez shot through the gap. Cassius's front wheel caught the stone curb. His black car lifted, struck a low barrier and hung there with the right side over a hundred feet of open air.

The crowd stopped sounding like a crowd.

Shawna's hand closed on my wrist.

“Aiden.”

“I see him.”

The road was still full of racing cars. I pulled across it, blocked the next two and jumped out before mine finished rocking. Cassius was fighting his belt inside the black car. Every movement lowered its nose farther over the drop.

“Stay still!” I shouted.

“Get me out!”

“Nigga, that is the plan. Help the plan by not rolling into the sea.”

I climbed onto the barrier. The metal under my hands was hot. Below me the harbor flashed between buildings, and I could hear a woman's voice screaming Cassius's name over and over.

He looked up at me through the open side window.

“You can't hold the car.”

“I can hold you.”

The wheel slipped.

Blue light cracked across my fingers.

It came fast, the way it had at Sky High, a sharp electric pressure that seemed to start behind my teeth and run down my bones. I could use it. I could not ask it to last forever. The first time I had tried that, my knees had explained the limits to the rest of me.

So I spent it on one thing.

I caught Cassius by the front of his jacket, pulled him through the window and threw both of us backward onto the road just as the car went over.

The black machine dropped out of sight.

A beat later something huge struck the water below.

Cassius lay across me, breathing like he had stolen the air.

“Nigga,” I said, “you got to get off my chain.”

He looked down. Dante's gold cross was caught beneath his sleeve. He freed it with shaking fingers.

I sat up. The road tilted once. Shawna was already beside me, her hands on my face, checking my eyes.

“How much?” she asked quietly.

“One burst.”

“Tell me the truth.”

“One burst, baby.”

She nodded. Then she kissed me hard enough to make the whole street remember there were other reasons to lose your breath.

By the time she pulled away, the crowd had found its voice.

They were screaming my name.

People on the balconies screamed it. Drivers standing beside their stopped cars screamed it. The silver-suited woman from the entry gate had apparently run half the course and now stood on a staircase shouting, “That's the yacht man!” like it was a title passed through generations.

Cassius got to his feet slowly. He stared at the broken barrier, then at me.

“You stopped your race.”

“You was in it.”

He shook his head.

“Nobody stops here.”

I stood. My legs were steady again, mostly. I dusted off my jacket, straightened the cross and looked toward the hill.

“Nigga, I didn't say I quit.”

We put Cassius in the back of a marshal's car. I got behind my wheel. Shawna tightened her belt and gave me the look she used when she wanted to call me an idiot but was too proud of me to make it sound convincing.

“Three minutes behind,” she said.

“Then we should go.”

The Lamborghini climbed.

I didn't use the blue thunder again. I used my eyes, my hands and the fact that I had not come all this way to lose a little wheel to men who wore driving gloves at breakfast. We passed four cars through the old town. We passed two more beneath a railway bridge. At a bend lined with white flowers, I saw Inez ahead and a yellow car beside her, fighting for first.

Shawna started laughing.

“What?” I said.

“You really think you're going to do it.”

“Nigga, I know I'm going to do it.”

The hotel rose at the top of the hill, all marble balconies and flags. The final straight narrowed between fountains. Inez moved left. The yellow car moved right. Neither had left room for me.

So I drove through the fountain.

Water hit the windshield like applause with weight. Shawna shrieked. Stone dolphins vanished on either side. We came out in a shining wall of spray, hit the finish line half a hood ahead of Inez and stopped beneath the hotel's canopy with a live ornamental fish on the windshield.

For two seconds nobody moved.

Then the doorman took off his hat.

“Welcome, Your Majesty.”

I looked at Shawna.

She was soaked, gorgeous and laughing so hard she couldn't answer.

Inez rolled up beside us. She looked at the fish. She looked at me. Finally she slapped both hands against her steering wheel and laughed too.

“You ridiculous motherfucker.”

I picked the fish off the glass and handed it to the doorman.

“Put my nigga back in his house.”

Above us, on the grand balcony, Duke Aurelio Cruel stood beside a table laid for lunch. His green suit shone. His glass had stopped halfway to his mouth.

Bellario arrived carrying a gold wheel.

This time he didn't make a speech.

He put it around my neck with both hands.

Shawna stepped out of the car. The crowd moved toward us in a wave, shouting, filming, holding out hats and champagne and one man's marriage certificate for reasons he was going to have to explain to his wife. I pulled Shawna against me before they could separate us.

“Got your ocean,” I said.

She brushed a drop of fountain water off my cheek.

“Now get me a towel, fastest man alive.”

I looked up at the duke.

He set his glass down.

The month had begun.

## 2. The Woman Who Drove Through Fire

The Royal Meridian gave me a bedroom with a ceiling painted like heaven and a bathtub big enough to baptize a basketball team. Two porters argued over which bags belonged to me.

"The black ones are the captain's."

"Nigga, all of them are the captain's," Tank said.

"Even the white—"

"Especially the white ones. That's his wife."

"And the trunks?"

"That's the nigga preparing to stay great in different weather."

I let them finish before pointing to Shawna's little blue case.

"That one comes with me."

A porter reached for it anyway.

"Nigga, I said with me. My wife asked me to carry it. I ain't promoting you into my marriage."

Shawna leaned against the door laughing. The porter apologized, grinning now, and Tank took the two largest trunks himself because the conversation had apparently made him impatient with luggage.

I put Shawna in the bathtub before anybody had a chance to ask me another question.

She sat among the bubbles with her hair pinned up, holding the gold wheel I had won and turning it between her fingers. Through the open balcony doors we could see the harbor, the yacht with my name, and the smaller yacht whose owner had already renamed it AIDEN LANDED HERE.

“Nigga got a gift shop open,” I said.

Shawna looked over my shoulder. On the smaller boat, somebody was carrying boxes of shirts onto the deck.

“You owe that man a table.”

“I gave him a business.”

“You gave him tire tracks.”

“Limited edition.”

She tried to stay serious. Failed. I took that as permission to kiss her again.

For a while the whole Grand Prix could do whatever the fuck it wanted outside. I had warm water, my wife and a door that locked. When we finally got dressed, her lipstick was on my shoulder and a bell was ringing somewhere in the suite with the desperate persistence of a man who didn't know how close he was to getting fired.

Tank stood at the door holding the room-service bell between two fingers.

“Why didn't you knock?” I asked.

“I did. The door didn't answer.”

Behind him, Rosa had a plate of fruit. Mercedes wore a silk robe over her clothes because, according to her, the robe was included and she was getting her money's worth. Porsche had three phones laid out on a tray and was talking into the fourth.

“No,” she told somebody. “He saved your favorite driver and beat your other favorite driver. The price changed twice.”

I pointed at her.

“What's that?”

“Appearances.”

“I ain't said yes to appearances.”

“That's why they cost extra.”

She covered the phone with her hand. “You want six hundred thousand to eat dinner near a watch?”

“Does the watch eat?”

“No.”

“Make it eight.”

She nodded and went back to the call like this was exactly the kind of business judgment she had expected.

Marcellus sat beside the balcony with a little screwdriver and my gold wheel. He had taken the chain off because the clasp was cheap.

“Gold plate,” he said.

“Nigga.”

“Very thick plate.”

“That ain't the point.”

“No,” he agreed. “It rarely is.”

He fitted a better clasp, one of his own, then held the wheel to the light.

“Beautiful work on the face. Someone talented made the original design. Someone cheap ordered the copies.”

Rosa stopped eating her grapes.

“The musicians say nobody's been paid in three weeks.”

Porsche lowered her phone.

“They told the dancers tomorrow.”

Mercedes leaned against the doorway. “They told the drivers' hosts next week. One girl asked to leave, and the hotel said her passport was at the island office.”

The room changed. Not dramatically. Nobody stood up with a speech. But Tank put the bell down, and Shawna stopped turning the wheel.

“How many?” I asked.

“Don't know yet,” Mercedes said. “Enough that they're scared to count in front of anybody.”

There are lies rich niggas tell because they want more money, and lies they tell because they think other people belong to them. The second kind always pisses me off faster. I had bought enough things to know the difference between owning a building and owning the woman standing in it.

Porsche's phone started ringing again. She silenced it.

“There's a mechanic downstairs who wants to see you. She says you picked up something in your grille.”

“The fish?”

“No. A piece of the green car.”

We went downstairs together.

The hotel's underground garage looked like somebody had threatened a museum until it learned to accelerate. Red Ferraris, silver machines with doors like wings, a white car sitting under its own chandelier. My Lamborghini stood in the middle with half the harbor still drying on it.

A woman with close-cut hair and grease on one cheek waited beside the front wheel. She wore blue overalls tied at the waist and a pair of gold hoops so large I respected her confidence around machinery.

“Lark,” she said. “Thirty-two, chief mechanic for the Silver Arrow team until somebody sold the team without telling the people inside it.”

She gave me a handshake strong enough to be honest.

“Aiden.”

“I watched.”

She held up a bent piece of green metal.

“This was lodged below your light. The car that hit Chrome wasn't part of the field.”

“I noticed the mask.”

“I mean it belongs to the harbor service. It should have been carrying luggage.”

Tank took the fragment and turned it over.

“That's some violent luggage.”

Lark didn't smile.

“My partner drove one of those cars. Mateo. He's been missing nine days.”

Shawna stepped closer. “Your partner on the team?”

“My partner in my house.”

She said it firmly, like she was tired of people trying to make the missing part smaller.

“He's thirty-four. Laughs with his whole mouth. Puts salt on pineapple. Buys me flowers even though I keep telling him a plant would survive longer. His last message said they wanted extra crew for the island. Then nothing.”

Mercedes folded her arms.

“They keep sending people there.”

Lark looked at her. “You heard it too?”

“I hear things men think women ain't listening to.”

I took the green fragment from Tank.

“What do you need?” I asked.

“To know whether you really stopped for Cassius. Or whether it was a show.”

“Nigga was hanging off a cliff. That's an expensive show.”

She studied me. Then she nodded once.

“I need somebody who can get through a door they won't open for me.”

“Show me the door.”

Before she could answer, an engine shouted from the garage entrance.

Inez's red car came down the ramp and stopped close enough for its heat to reach my shoes. She climbed out in black jeans and a red sleeveless shirt, braid down her back, the gold wheel she had won hanging against her chest.

“I've been looking for you,” she said.

“Everybody has.”

“I found you first.”

She looked at Shawna. “You hungry?”

“Yes.”

“Good. My father cooks. He lives on the mountain. I brought two cars.”

I looked past her. A second red car waited at the top of the ramp.

“Nigga, that sounds like a race wearing a dinner jacket.”

“It can be both.”

Her eyes dropped to the green metal in my hand. For the first time since I'd met her, her smile went away completely.

“Where did you get that?”

“Out of my fish tank.”

“Aiden,” Shawna said.

“Out of the car.”

Inez reached for the fragment, then stopped before touching it.

“Bring Lark,” she said. “And don't let a hotel car follow you.”

The mountain road started above the city and climbed into terraces of olive trees, old stone walls and houses whose balconies seemed to be standing on faith. Inez led in her red machine. Shawna sat beside me, Lark in the back of a car Porsche had obtained by pointing at it and saying, “That one belongs with us now.” Tank followed in a black SUV so large it made the little stone villages look recently built around it.

At the first overlook, Inez stopped and got out.

“There's a restaurant at the top,” she said. “Nine turns. Two narrow bridges. No traffic this afternoon; they close it for race practice.”

“Your father live at the restaurant?”

“No. We eat there first, so he's got time to stop pretending he isn't excited.”

Shawna laughed.

Inez rested her arms on my open window.

“The exhibition was one thing. You went through a fountain.”

“It was in the way.”

“You're fast. But this road is mine.”

I looked at the road curling up behind her. Beautiful road. Lots of opportunity to be wrong in public.

“What we racing for?”

“An honest answer.”

“To what?”

“Why you're here.”

“Shawna wanted the ocean.”

Inez waited.

“Nigga, that is the honest answer.”

She looked at my wife. Shawna shrugged.

“I did.”

For a moment Inez seemed almost disappointed. She had probably expected a secret revenge, a lost fortune, a hidden father. People see a man driving a police Lamborghini across yachts and assume his life requires explanation. Sometimes a nigga just loves his wife.

“Then race for dinner,” she said.

I glanced at Shawna.

“Baby?”

She tightened her belt.

“Win me something with potatoes.”

Inez went first.

She knew every inch of that mountain. I could tell by the way she entered a turn before the turn seemed to exist, the way her red car moved from sunlight to shadow without any hesitation. She wasn't performing for me. She was speaking a language she'd learned before anybody told her it was difficult.

I answered with my right foot.

We climbed past a chapel and two empty market squares. At the first bridge she gained half a car. At the second I took it back. Shawna watched the road with one hand on the dashboard and the other on my thigh, not holding me down, just staying connected to the nigga who had decided dinner should happen at a hundred impossible miles an hour.

Inez's car flicked left around a stone fountain.

I stayed on the road this time. Growth.

Then we hit the smoke.

It rolled across the upper bend, black and thick, carrying the bitter smell of burning rubber. Inez braked. I pulled beside her. Through the smoke, a delivery truck sat sideways against the wall, its cab burning. Beyond it, a little open-top car had stopped with its driver trapped between the truck and the drop.

A man in a chef's jacket stood on the far side waving both arms.

“Papa,” Inez said.

She was out of her car before the word finished.

I caught her wrist as she passed.

“Together.”

“That's my father.”

“I heard you.”

Her eyes hit mine, hot with the kind of fear that wants to turn itself into violence. Then she nodded, and we ran into the smoke.

The heat slapped us. Inez pulled her shirt over her mouth and reached the small car. Her father was outside it, trying to free the truck's driver from the burning cab. Another man lay on the road, dazed, one arm over his face.

Inez went to the man on the road. I went to her father.

“Move back,” I said.

“He's caught.”

“I see him.”

The truck driver was conscious, terrified, his belt jammed beneath a twisted piece of door. I didn't need a lesson in trucks to know we had very little time. I grabbed what was in the way and pulled.

It moved an inch.

Fire climbed the dashboard.

“Nigga,” I told the truck, “don't make this complicated.”

I pulled again.

This time the metal gave enough. Inez's father reached in beside me, and between us we dragged the driver out. His shoes hit the road. He tried to stand. Couldn't. I threw his arm over my shoulder and carried him away while Inez helped the other man toward our cars.

Shawna was already there with water and a cloth from the back seat. She took the driver's face gently between her hands.

“Look at me. You're out. Stay with me.”

Behind us the truck's front tire burst with a sound like a shot.

Tank's SUV came around the bend. He stopped, took in the fire, the men, Inez and her father, then looked at me.

“Nigga, we left you alone for six minutes.”

“Dinner got delayed.”

He lifted the second injured man into the SUV like the man weighed the same as a suit jacket. Lark got in beside him. Porsche called ahead to the mountain clinic. Mercedes flagged the practice marshals arriving from below, and within a minute everybody had a job except the fire, which continued being a disrespectful motherfucker until a crew put it out.

Inez stood beside her father. He had gray at his temples, a burn on one sleeve and hands that wouldn't stop shaking. She held both of them.

“Why were you up here?” she asked.

“The restaurant called. They said you wanted—”

He stopped.

I saw her face change.

“I didn't call the restaurant.”

Nobody spoke for a moment.

Then her father looked at me.

“You are Aiden.”

“Yes, sir.”

“My daughter said you were very annoying.”

“Papa.”

He held out his shaking hand.

“She was smiling when she said it.”

I shook it carefully.

“Esteban Inferno,” he said. “You saved my life, and my daughter's pride will never recover.”

“Nigga, her pride looked healthy in them turns.”

Inez let out a breath that almost became a laugh. She brushed soot off her father's cheek, then turned toward the burned truck.

Its rear doors had fallen open. Inside were cases of fruit, a few crates of flowers and a green service-car panel stacked behind them.

The same green as the fragment in my pocket.

Lark saw it too.

“They didn't want you at his house,” she said.

Esteban closed his eyes.

For the first time, he looked old.

Tank watched the emergency crew load the last injured man into a vehicle.

"Nigga, we was racing for potatoes."

"We still eating potatoes," I said.

"Nigga, the potatoes got witnesses now."

Esteban looked between us. "Does he always talk like this?"

"Which nigga?" Shawna asked.

He pointed at me.

"That nigga makes it everybody's evening," Tank said.

"You came," I told him.

"Nigga, you had the address."

Inez took her father's arm. "Come on. Let the niggas argue where the food is."

We ate at his house anyway.

It stood above the road, white walls, blue shutters, a courtyard full of lemon trees. The dining table was long enough for all of us. Esteban insisted on cooking, even with the burn on his sleeve, and Inez argued with him until Shawna quietly handed her a knife and a bowl of vegetables.

“Help him do it,” she said.

So Inez helped.

I stood at the courtyard wall watching the sea below. Cassius arrived in a borrowed silver car with one arm in a sling and a bottle of wine under the other.

“Nigga, you drive that yourself?” I asked.

“With one good arm I'm still quicker than most people with two.”

“Most people ain't me.”

“No,” he said. “They aren't.”

He put the bottle on the table and held out his good hand. This handshake felt different from the one we had never actually had at the starting line. His fingers closed hard around mine.

“I watched the harbor footage,” he said. “You jumped a Lamborghini across two yachts, pulled me out of my car and still won.”

“Three things.”

“What?”

“You forgot the fish.”

He stared at me. Then he started laughing. It hurt his shoulder, so he held it and kept laughing anyway.

At dinner Esteban served lamb, potatoes crisp at the edges, bread warm enough to steam when Tank tore it. Shawna held up her fork toward me.

“You won the potatoes.”

Inez shook her head. “We didn't finish.”

“My wife eating them, ain't she?”

Everybody laughed except Esteban, who was looking at the green fragment beside my plate.

Finally he picked it up.

“Seven years ago,” he said, “a car this color followed my wife to the last race she ever attended.”

Inez put her fork down.

“Papa.”

“You brought him here.”

“Because he saved Cassius.”

“And now he has saved me.” Esteban turned the piece of metal in his hand. “Perhaps I have been waiting for a man who would stop.”

The courtyard grew quiet. Beyond the wall, the sun touched the sea.

Esteban reached into his shirt and drew out a little folded photograph. He placed it beside the green metal. A woman stood in front of a racing car, smiling into the camera with one hand lifted to block the sun. She wore a plain blue dress. On the car behind her, someone had painted a white bird.

“My wife was Amalia,” he said. “She loved this race before the duke turned it into a kingdom.”

I looked at the photograph. Then at the mountains, the road and the impossible amount of money glittering below us.

“What happened?” I asked.

Esteban watched his daughter's face for a long moment.

“I believed the wrong man,” he said.

And underneath the table, Shawna took my hand.

## 3. Dinner with a Man Named Cruel

Esteban said the wrong man's name, and Cassius stood up so fast his chair fell over.

“Nero Chrome,” Esteban said.

“That was my father.”

“I know whose father he was.”

“Nigga,” I said, “everybody leave the potatoes out of this.”

Cassius wasn't looking at me. He had one hand flat on the table and the other held against his injured shoulder. Esteban sat very straight, his wife's picture beneath his palm. Inez stood between them before either man moved again.

“Papa, you don't know everything.”

“I know who was beside the car.”

“You know what Bellario told you.”

Cassius laughed once. No amusement in it.

“Of course. Bellario.”

He turned toward the courtyard gate.

I caught him there.

“Where you going?”

“Somewhere my father isn't being tried by a man who let the duke buy his mouth.”

Esteban's chair scraped behind us.

Tank put one hand on its back.

“Sit down, my nigga.”

“I will not—”

“Then stand still. Pick one.”

I kept my eyes on Cassius.

“You can hear him and still hate what he says.”

“I've heard it for seven years.”

“Then hear it once with me here.”

His jaw moved. He looked at Shawna, who had come to stand beside the table, holding Amalia's photograph carefully by the edges.

“Your father drove this car?” she asked.

Cassius looked back despite himself.

“The White Heron,” he said. “He built it with Esteban.”

“Then sit down and tell us something nobody else gets right.”

That reached him.

He picked his chair up. He didn't apologize, and Esteban didn't ask him to. Sometimes, nigga, the best you can get from two men is both their asses back at the table.

Esteban began again.

Seven years earlier, the Grand Prix had been smaller. There were rich men in it, but money wasn't the only invitation. Mechanics entered cars they had built behind their houses. Boat captains raced old engines down the coast. The drivers ate at the same tables as the people who changed their tires, and at the end of the month the winner sailed to Isla Gloria with everybody who had helped him get there.

“Amalia loved the last night,” Esteban said. “She would dance until the musicians begged her to stop.”

Rosa smiled faintly. “I know that kind of woman.”

“She collected people. If a waiter looked lonely, suddenly he was sitting with us. If a driver lost, she found something he had done well and made him talk about that. When Aurelio bought the race, she told him the prize was already here. He only needed to leave it alone.”

“What'd he say?” I asked.

“That a woman who enjoyed giving things away should marry a poorer man.”

“Nigga.”

Esteban nodded.

“He said it smiling.”

That year Esteban and Nero had entered the White Heron together. One drove the mountain stages, the other the coastal ones. Amalia kept their books, knew every worker by name and had discovered that the prize fleet included vessels the duke had never actually paid for. Their owners had been promised shares in the Grand Prix. Instead, crews stopped receiving wages, captains disappeared from the entry list and the harbor gates began closing at night.

“She went to the island,” Esteban said. “A captain named Celadon took her. She came back with a packet of papers and told me we had to finish the race. Win it in front of everybody. Then we could make him give back what he had taken.”

“Why didn't she show you the papers?” Shawna asked.

“She did. I looked at the first page, kissed her forehead and said I trusted her.”

His voice roughened.

“I thought that was the same as listening.”

I felt Shawna's thumb move against my hand.

Esteban told us about the final mountain stage. The White Heron led by eleven seconds. Nero had driven the morning. Esteban was due to take over at the ridge. Amalia traveled ahead in a little blue support car carrying the papers and the team's food, because even when a man was about to expose a duke she thought he ought to have lunch.

At the ridge, Nero never arrived.

Instead, Bellario brought news that the support car had gone over the road. Amalia was dead. Nero had vanished. A green harbor car had been seen leaving the scene.

“The duke showed me a signed withdrawal,” Esteban said. “Nero's name. Money paid. A place on a ship leaving that night. Bellario said he watched Nero get into the green car.”

Cassius leaned forward.

“My father couldn't write with his right hand that week. He'd broken two fingers.”

Esteban blinked.

“The signature was steady as a schoolmaster's,” Cassius said. “I told them. I was twenty-four, and I told every man in that room. They said grief was making me irrational.”

“Why didn't you tell me?”

“You wouldn't open your gate.”

The words landed harder than shouting would have.

Esteban stared at him. Inez looked away, and I understood this was a conversation they had been walking around for seven years, keeping it alive by never allowing it to finish.

Cassius took something out of his jacket. A little metal bird, white paint worn off one wing.

“My father gave me this the morning of the race. Said if he won, I'd drive the first lap next year.”

He set it beside Amalia's photograph.

“He never came home.”

Outside the courtyard a car horn sounded.

Nobody moved.

It sounded again, and Tank stood up with the expression of a man grateful for a fresh target. He opened the gate. Bellario stood beyond it beside a cream-colored limousine, dressed for dinner, feather restored.

“His Grace requests Captain Aiden's presence at the opening banquet.”

I looked at the nigga for a long time.

“Does he?”

“Attendance is traditional.”

“So is knocking.”

Bellario glanced past Tank and saw the table. Saw Cassius, Esteban, Inez. His face didn't change, but his eyes counted us twice.

“An intimate gathering,” he said.

“Getting less intimate.”

Shawna squeezed my hand and stood.

“We'll be there.”

Bellario bowed to her with the precise depth of a man who practiced alone.

“His Grace particularly hopes you will sing.”

“Then he should particularly hope he's paid my musicians.”

The bow ended early.

After he left, Esteban went inside and returned with a small lacquer box. He opened it to reveal a folded letter, a yellow ribbon and a photograph of Amalia laughing beside a white boat.

“This came three days after she died,” he said. “A woman delivered it. She wouldn't give her name. I read the first line so many times I almost wore through it.”

“What's it say?” I asked.

He unfolded the top edge.

“Esteban, if you are reading this without me, do not let a man who never loved either of us explain my last day.”

Cassius closed his eyes.

Esteban held the letter toward Inez.

“I wasn't brave enough to obey her.”

She took it without a word.

We left the table standing. Plates, bread, photograph, the little white bird. Nobody tried to make it look like a dinner that had ended normally.

At the hotel, Shawna changed into a blue dress that moved around her legs like water had learned her name. She wore Dante's watch on her wrist and earrings I had given her after Sky High. She stood before the mirror fastening one, and I came up behind her.

“You want to skip this?” I asked.

“No.”

“We can eat somewhere nobody named Cruel owns the forks.”

She met my eyes in the mirror.

“I want to sing. I want Rosa to get paid. I want that nigga to look at us across his own table while we find out what he's hiding.”

“That's my wife.”

She turned around.

“And you want to race him.”

“I want to beat him.”

“Then do it with your eyes open.”

I kissed her forehead.

She pushed my chest lightly.

“Don't Esteban me.”

Nigga, I laughed so hard she smiled before she could help it. Then I took her face in both hands.

“I hear you. You want to sing, Rosa gets paid, we watch the duke. I don't go running off because somebody waves a faster car.”

“And?”

“And if it's a really fast car, I bring you.”

She hit me with the earring box.

The banquet occupied a terrace above the sea. Three hundred people sat beneath chandeliers hanging from living trees. At the entrance, a young doorman looked at my invitation, then at my badge, then back at the invitation.

"It says king."

"It also says captain," I told him.

"Which should I announce?"

Tank leaned over his shoulder.

"Nigga, use your diaphragm and say both."

"Is there a preferred order?"

"The nigga arrived first at everything today. Any order works."

The doorman laughed, took a breath and announced me so loudly the nearest chandelier trembled.

I slipped a folded bill into his palm.

"That's for respecting punctuation."

He looked at the amount, looked at me and announced my wife with even more feeling. Nigga had found a second diaphragm. A string orchestra played on a platform over the swimming pool. Along the terrace stood twelve cars under silk covers, each with its own guard and a woman holding a silver card naming the race it belonged to.

I walked in with Shawna on my arm, my badge against my chest and Tank behind me in a white suit that made him look like he had personally purchased summer.

Conversations stopped in waves.

The first wave was people recognizing me. The second was people asking the first wave who I was. The third was everybody looking at Shawna and deciding the answer must be more impressive than they had heard.

The duke rose from a long table at the center.

Aurelio Cruel was forty-eight, tall, broad through the shoulders, handsome in the way a sword can be handsome before somebody pulls it out. His hair was black with two white streaks. He wore a green diamond on one hand and a watch whose face seemed larger than the gold wheel I'd won.

“Captain,” he said. “Your entrance this afternoon was costly.”

“For who?”

The people close enough to hear laughed before they looked at him. He let them finish.

“For the harbor's dignity.”

“Nigga, the harbor selling shirts.”

This time the laughter reached the next table.

He smiled. “Come. Sit beside me.”

There were two chairs waiting. One for me, one for Shawna. Farther down the terrace, Mercedes and Porsche had been directed toward a little table behind a pillar.

I stopped.

“Where's my people?”

“We've arranged seating by distinction.”

“Then you arranged it wrong.”

The duke rested his fingertips on the back of my chair.

“A captain. A celebrated singer. Naturally, some guests have qualifications others do not.”

Mercedes had heard him. She walked over before I could answer, yellow silk catching the light.

“Mine got you to call my agency three times last year,” she said. “Porsche's got your minister to pay double for dinner and still ask if she had a sister.”

Porsche appeared beside her.

“I told him no. He looked financially devastated.”

A man at the duke's table suddenly became fascinated by his soup.

The duke's smile thinned.

“There is no need for vulgarity.”

“Nigga, you invited me,” I said.

I took the chair beside him, lifted it and carried it to Mercedes's table. Tank picked up the table itself. Rosa brought the flowers.
