Just a man who had come home and a nigga helping him remember dinner.

When we returned, Shawna waited outside the hotel with Inez and Cassius.

Nero handed his son the keys.

“Keep them tonight.”

Cassius looked at him.

“I'll see you in the morning?”

The question came out smaller than he meant it to.

Nero put a hand on his shoulder.

“In the morning.”

Cassius nodded.

Inez took his hand, and they walked into the hotel together.

Shawna came to me.

“You add any years?”

“Fed him instead.”

“Good.”

I pulled her close.

Upstairs, on our bed, lay the invitation to the fifth race. Black paper. Silver letters. The Night Baptism, a coastal run after sunset, with a storm expected before the finish.

The duke had added one handwritten sentence.

*Perhaps the weather will do what your friends prevent.*

I showed it to Shawna.

She read it, looked at the clear night outside and handed it back.

“Nigga,” she said, “he still thinks you're going alone.”

## 16. The Storm Asked Who Was Driving

“Nigga, that's a hurricane.”

Tank stood under the hotel canopy looking at the sky. The sky looked back like it had come to collect money.

“It's a storm,” Lark said.

“That storm got a management position.”

Mateo laughed beside her. He had been out of captivity three days and already learned that Tank's weather reports came with threats.

The Night Baptism was scheduled to begin at sunset. Sunset had arrived behind a black wall of cloud, so the duke's officials simply announced that it had happened somewhere and continued laying out the flags.

Rain swept across the harbor in long silver sheets. Boats strained against their ropes. The race road ran along the coast, through old tunnels and over a causeway to a lighthouse before turning back toward the city. It should have been postponed.

Aurelio offered every driver the chance to withdraw.

He did it while standing beside a camera.

Nigga had finally found a way to make weather smug.

I chose an Aston Martin from the loan fleet for the race. Dark green, broad-shouldered, built to carry a man through a bad evening with his suit still attached. The police Lamborghini needed a rest, and Lark had informed me that machines could not file complaints but she could speak for them.

“You'll bring this one back,” she said, standing beside the Aston.

“Nigga, you said that about the last one.”

“And look how necessary it was.”

She and Mateo had prepared the car together. They moved around each other without colliding, handing over tools before the other asked, arguing about small things with the joy of people who had missed having small things to argue about.

I watched them for a second.

Then Lark caught me.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“Nigga, you smiling.”

“Car looks good.”

She looked at Mateo.

He smiled too.

Shawna wore a dark coat over her team jacket. Rain shone in her hair as she came toward me, carrying my helmet in both hands.

“You don't have to prove the storm wrong,” she said.

“I ain't mad at the storm.”

“Good.”

“Storm ain't met me.”

She closed her eyes briefly.

Then she handed over the helmet.

“Come back and tell me about it.”

I kissed her forehead.

“Every turn.”

Nero stood beside Cassius's silver car at the grid, speaking quietly to his son. Inez waited nearby in red, watching the rain strike the road. Rafe had withdrawn. Adrian had entered. So had six other drivers whose pride, ambition or bank accounts had made a complicated decision on their behalf.

The duke stood beneath a huge green umbrella.

The stranger in the dark uniform stood behind him without one.

Rain ran off his shoulders.

Nigga didn't blink.

I walked past both of them toward the car.

Aurelio spoke.

“Perhaps tonight we discover whether you are fortunate or talented.”

“Nigga, you discovered talent at the fountain. Now you're investigating denial.”

The mechanics nearby burst out laughing.

He let the sound pass over him.

“The sea gives nothing back for admiration.”

“Then stop watching me so hard.”

I got in.

The light changed.

We left into the rain.

The Aston moved differently from the Lamborghini, heavier through the first turn, planted when the road opened. I kept it steady while water blurred the windshield and headlights tore long tunnels through the darkness ahead. Adrian took an early lead. Inez followed him. Cassius stayed just behind me, patient, listening to the road instead of the audience.

The city vanished behind us.

On the coast road, the wind struck sideways hard enough to move the whole car. I corrected and felt the tires answer. Rain drummed against the roof. The engine held its deep note beneath everything, a sound I could trust when the world outside had become water and occasional stone.

“Nigga,” I told the car, “we doing fine.”

It did not answer in words.

Cars know when to be professional.

We reached the first tunnel in fourth. Inside, the sudden absence of rain felt almost violent. The road shone under the lamps. I passed Adrian's teammate at the exit, came out into the storm in third and saw Inez's red taillights ahead.

She moved left before the next bend.

I stayed right.

We ran side by side through a wall of spray.

Then her voice came over the channel.

“You enjoying the ocean now?”

“Nigga, my wife wanted all of it.”

She laughed, and we took the curve together.

At the lighthouse causeway, the marshals waved yellow flags. Water washed over the low wall in bursts, not deep enough to stop the cars but enough to make every movement matter. Adrian slowed. Inez held back. I came alongside the white car at the first long straight and saw his face through the window, jaw tight, eyes fixed ahead.

He was frightened.

Good drivers get frightened. They just don't always let the fear choose their hands.

I passed him cleanly.

The lighthouse rose ahead, its beam sweeping the rain. We circled beneath it and turned back toward the mainland. The sea hit the wall with a force that made the road shake.

Then the lights went out again.

Not the harbor this time. The lighthouse.

The beam stopped.

For one second the whole causeway disappeared.

A truck came out of the darkness at the far end, headlights high, moving toward the race against the traffic.

“Nigga.”

I saw the shape. The distance. The narrow space between its wheels and the wall.

I didn't have time to be angry.

I took the Aston toward the low sea barrier.

The right wheels climbed the stone edge. The car tilted. Rain struck the side window. For a breath we ran on two wheels, the truck filling the space where my hood should have been.

Its mirror struck mine.

Glass vanished.

Then I was past.

The Aston came down hard, rear tire bursting as it hit the road. I fought the wheel, kept the nose straight and heard the truck brake behind me as Inez and Adrian scattered around it.

“Truck on the causeway!” I shouted into the channel.

Cassius answered.

“I see it.”

A crash sounded behind me.

Then his voice again.

“Clear. We're clear.”

I breathed.

The tire was gone. The car dragged to the right. Sparks ran beneath the rear corner, bright against the rain. Ahead lay five miles to the city and the finish.

Lark's voice came through.

“Aiden, stop.”

“The wheel still on.”

“Nigga, that isn't the whole requirement.”

“I can feel it.”

“Then feel where you can pull over.”

I slowed enough to bring the car under control. Other drivers passed. Inez first, then Adrian, then Cassius, who stayed beside me for a moment.

“You need me?” he called.

“Nigga, go win something.”

He hesitated.

“Go!”

He went.

I found a marshal's shelter near the mainland end of the causeway. Two officials stood beneath it, white-faced. One had a radio that wasn't working. The other stared at my ruined wheel.

“Do you have a service car?” I asked.

He nodded toward an old blue coupe parked beneath a tree.

It was not a racing car.

It looked like a schoolteacher had lent it to his cousin and expected it back with a full tank.

The rules allowed a replacement vehicle in the event of race interference, provided the driver completed the course from the point of the stop.

Nero had made me read that part before the start.

Nigga believed in knowing where a duke might try to lie.

I pointed at the coupe.

“That one.”

The official shook his head.

“It's mine.”

“You got insurance?”

“Yes, but—”

“I got money. We both protected.”

He looked at my face.

Then at the race disappearing into the rain.

Then he handed me the keys.

“My wife named it Clementine.”

“Nigga, Clementine about to become famous.”

The marshal looked at his keys in my hand.

"Nigga, you really taking Clementine?"

"Nigga, she ready."

"She's never been in a race."

"Neither had that nigga's boat yesterday. Look what happened."

He stared toward the storm. "My wife going to kill me."

"Tell her the nigga with the badge borrowed it."

"She'll say which nigga."

"Then show her the race."

He laughed, frightened and delighted at once. "Nigga, bring my eggs."

"I heard you the first time, breakfast captain."

I got in.

The seat smelled faintly of peppermint. A little knitted bird hung from the mirror. There was a bag of groceries in the back and a classical music station playing softly beneath the storm.

I moved the eggs onto the floor.

Greatness respects breakfast.

Then I drove.

Clementine did not leap forward.

Clementine considered.

Then she went.

I took the first bend clean, let the little car gather speed on the descent and felt its narrow body slip through the wind more easily than the heavier Aston had. It had no business being in the race. Neither had I, according to most of the people whose names were now beneath mine on the standings.

We understood each other.

At the old tunnel I caught the last racing car.

The driver looked over.

Looked again.

“Nigga,” I said through the open window, “you getting passed by groceries.”

I went around him.

The radio crackled with disbelief from the commentary booth. They had found me on a camera and were trying to decide whether the picture had been mislabeled.

“Captain Aiden appears to be driving—”

“A car,” Tank shouted somewhere behind the open team channel. “Nigga, finish the sentence.”

Lark was laughing now. She didn't want to. I could hear her fighting it.

“Keep it together,” she told me.

“Me or Clementine?”

“Both of you fools.”

We climbed toward the city.

One car. Then another. The little blue coupe ran beneath the lamps with its knitted bird swinging wildly and the eggs safe on the floor. I drove every turn as if I had known the machine my whole life. No blue thunder. No borrowed power. Just hands, road and a stubborn little engine discovering it had more in it than its owner had ever asked.

By the harbor I was fourth.

The crowd saw me.

Nigga, I will never forget that sound.

It started with laughter. Not mockery. Astonishment too large to come out politely. Then it became shouting. People pointed at the blue coupe, at my badge held against the windshield, at the grocery bag visible through the rear window.

“That's him!”

“Nigga, that's Aiden!”

“He in a regular car!”

“The nigga made it irregular!”

Inez saw me in her mirror and started laughing over the radio.

“No.”

“Yes.”

“Aiden.”

“Nigga, move. I got milk.”

She fought me through the next bend anyway. Nearly held me. I passed her at the exit with the knitted bird swinging like it was cheering for its own family.

Cassius was second.

Adrian first.

The final straight opened before us, wet and bright beneath the city lights. Adrian's boat-race pride had become a car-race lead, and he meant to keep it. Cassius pressed him on the inside.

I came through the gap between their spray.

Clementine's engine screamed.

The little bird hit the windshield.

We crossed first by half a bumper.

I stopped beneath the finish arch with steam rising from the hood and the classical station still playing.

For three seconds nobody moved.

Then the official whose car I had borrowed arrived on the back of a service motorcycle and fell to his knees in front of Clementine.

“My wife is never going to believe this.”

I got out and handed him the eggs.

“Nigga, breakfast intact.”

Shawna ran toward me laughing so hard she could barely breathe. She hit my chest with both hands, then kissed me, rain on her face, joy everywhere.

“You won in that?”

I looked back at the little blue coupe.

“Baby, that's Clementine.”

The crowd took up the name.

Clementine. Clementine. Clementine.

The duke presented the fifth key while a thousand people chanted for a schoolteacher's grocery car.

Nigga, I had never seen a rich man lose to produce before.

It looked excellent on him.

## 17. They Gave Me a Crown I Didn't Enter For

The Rose and Thunder Ball was supposed to honor the most glamorous people of the Grand Prix.

I did not enter.

I want that understood before anybody starts lying about my humility. I entered a car race. I entered another car race. I entered a boat race because a nigga challenged my relationship with water. I had not entered a contest requiring a sash.

Then Mercedes came into our suite carrying a crown.

“Nigga, stand still.”

“Why?”

“Head measurements.”

“For who?”

She looked at me.

“Nigga, whose head are we discussing?”

Porsche followed with a white suit laid across both arms. The jacket had blue silk inside and gold buttons stamped with a little steering wheel.

Shawna looked up from her music.

“Oh, that's good.”

“You knew?” I asked.

“I suspected the world would notice you were handsome eventually.”

“Nigga, it noticed early.”

“Then put on the suit.”

The ball had started as one of the duke's side events, another evening where rich men paid to be seen beside beautiful women and everybody pretended the seating hadn't been negotiated. Mercedes and Porsche had taken over its hosting after the original organizers tried to underpay the performers.

Now the performers were choosing the prizes.

Rocco said it was a bold direction.

Porsche told him bold directions were expensive and he should sign the check before developing an opinion.

The event took place in the old winter garden, a glass palace above the harbor filled with palms and white flowers. Rain from the storm still glittered on the roof. The city outside smelled clean, as if even the streets had washed up for me.

When we arrived, the band stopped halfway through a song.

The singer pointed.

“That nigga brought the whole moon in a suit.”

The drummer hit a roll so long the saxophonist laughed into his instrument.

I looked at Shawna.

“See? Early.”

She took my arm tighter.

“Try to survive the compliment.”

Mercedes greeted us at the stage. She wore white feathers and diamonds, hair swept up, looking like a woman who could ruin a rich man's sleep by forgetting his name. Porsche wore blue satin with a slit that made three men at the nearest table sit straighter and one woman turn her chair for a better view.

Alina stood beside them in green, holding the microphone with a confidence I hadn't seen on the yacht. She had chosen to host part of the evening. Chosen it herself. That mattered enough that I noticed it before I noticed how beautifully she wore the dress.

“You ready?” Mercedes asked me.

“For what?”

“Nigga, stop pretending the lights ain't on you.”

The lights moved onto me.

The crowd cheered.

Porsche announced the first award: the Golden Heart, chosen by the rescued workers for the person whose name they had heard before they knew his face.

I stopped smiling for a second.

Julian came onstage. The mechanic whose mother had called him from the bakery. He held a little gold heart on a blue ribbon.

“My mother told me to make sure you knew,” he said, voice shaking slightly, “she's keeping bread ready.”

I bent so he could put the ribbon around my neck.

“Nigga, tell her I don't miss dinner.”

He laughed. The room stood.

Then Porsche announced the next award.

Best Dressed.

I looked down at the suit she had literally brought me that afternoon.

“Nigga, you rigged this.”

“We dressed the winner,” she said. “That's different.”

Mercedes put a blue sash across my chest.

The crowd lost its mind again.

Then Alina announced Most Wanted.

I raised an eyebrow.

“By which department?”

“All of them,” Tank shouted from our table.

Rosa nearly fell against him laughing.

Shawna came onto the stage and stood beside me.

“I accept this one on behalf of the household.”

The women in the front row cheered her. One held up a hand-painted sign reading WE RESPECT THE WIFE BUT THE MAN IS BEAUTIFUL.

Shawna read it.

Nodded gravely.

“Accurate.”

Nigga, I loved this room.

Alina tried to ask me to move to the center of the stage.

"Which center?" Tank shouted. "That nigga makes every spot the center."

"Nigga, let her host," I said.

"Then let the nigga be centered."

Mercedes took my elbow and moved me two feet. "There. Nigga centered."

Porsche adjusted the light. "This nigga reflects expensive."

Shawna looked up at me. "He reflects loud too."

"Niggas," I told the room, "I appreciate the technical crew."

Alina was laughing too hard to read the next line, and Mercedes put an arm around her until she could find her place again.

The crown came last.

Not the Grand Prix crown. Not the island. A smaller gold thing with blue stones, chosen by the performers, drivers and hospitality crews as their king of the month. Mercedes held it above my head while Porsche adjusted the sash to make room for the new disaster my appearance was about to cause.

“You got a speech?” Mercedes asked.

I looked over the crowd. My people. New friends. Men I'd beaten. Women whose names I had learned because they had more to say than a rich nigga had bothered to hear.

Then I looked at Shawna.

“Nigga,” I said, “I came for a beach.”

The room exploded.

I didn't get to say anything else for almost a minute.

When the noise settled, I lifted my glass.

“To my wife. To my people. To every nigga who thought he could make this month belong to him before we got here.”

I smiled.

“We appreciate your preparation.”

They drank to that so hard the waiters had to move faster.

The dancing began immediately afterward.

Shawna took me onto the floor. She had changed into silver, and under the glass roof she looked like the storm had left its best light on her shoulders. We moved together while the band played something slow enough for the room to watch and fast enough for her to make me work.

“You enjoying your crown?” she asked.

“Nigga, it fits.”

“That's because Mercedes measured your head.”

“She should measure my future.”

Shawna laughed and spun away, then came back against me with one hand at the back of my neck.

“Your future's dancing.”

I kissed her before the turn finished.

The band hit the next note like it approved.

At the edge of the floor, Cassius danced with Inez. He wasn't as smooth as she was. She knew it. She let him find the rhythm without making him feel examined, and when he finally relaxed, she rested her forehead briefly against his.

Nero watched from the table.

Esteban sat beside him.

“Your son steps heavy,” Esteban said.

“Your daughter drives angry.”

“They'll manage.”

“Yes,” Nero said. “They will.”

Celadon and Renee barely moved at all. They stood together in the middle of the floor, holding one another, letting the music pass around them. After seven years, nigga, a man can dance by staying exactly where he wants to be.

Then the glass roof broke.

A black car came through the winter garden's upper service entrance, smashing the doors inward and sending a wave of broken glass across the empty reception area. Two motorcycles followed. Men in dark masks jumped off them with guns in their hands.

The music stopped.

I pulled Shawna down behind a stone planter.

“Nigga,” Tank roared from the other side of the room, “at the dance?”

Apparently at the dance.

The first gunman fired into the ceiling. People screamed and dropped. Alina took the microphone, crouched behind the stage and told the crowd where to move, voice clear enough to cut through the panic. Mercedes and Porsche opened the side doors. Rosa led the people nearest her toward them. Bruno put himself between the gunmen and the dancers like somebody had moved a wall into the room on purpose.

I looked at Shawna.

“You got the side?”

“I got it.”

I went.

The crown stayed on my head.

Nigga, it had a good fit.

I crossed behind the planters while the gunmen looked toward the exits. Tank met the first one at the edge of the dance floor and put him into a table that had done nothing to deserve its evening. Bruno caught another man before he could raise his weapon and lifted him off the ground with a patience that frightened me more than shouting would have.

The third ran toward me.

I hit him with the Most Wanted trophy.

It was heavier than it looked.

He went down.

Somewhere behind me, Porsche shouted, “Nigga, that's engraved!”

“I'll read it later!”

The driver of the black car tried to reverse out through the broken doors. I climbed onto the hood, caught the edge of the roof and swung myself through the open side window before the car moved ten feet.

He stared at me.

I still wore the crown and the sash.

“Nigga,” I said, “you interrupted the king.”

He reached for a gun beside his seat.

I caught his wrist, drove it against the wheel and brought the car to a stop with one foot across the console. The horn sounded beneath his elbow. He tried to hit me. I hit him first.

Then I dragged him out through his own door.

Odette's officers came through the side entrance moments later. They had been stationed nearby because the duke had stopped pretending he respected parties. She took one look at me, the crown, the ruined trophy and the man at my feet.

“Captain.”

“Commandant.”

“Congratulations.”

“On which part?”

She looked around the room.

“All of it, apparently.”

The attackers were taken away alive. One had a broken arm, another would need stitches, and the driver had discovered that a sash did not reduce a man's ability to throw him onto marble.

Nobody in our crowd was shot.

A few cuts. A sprained wrist. Fear that would last longer than the cleanup. But people stood again. Found their friends. Asked where their shoes had gone. Started helping one another gather the pieces of the evening.

Shawna came to me and straightened the crown.

“Crooked.”

“Fight was crooked.”

She kissed me.

Then she looked toward the band.

“Can you still play?”

The pianist checked his hands.

The drummer lifted his sticks.

The singer looked at the broken glass, the overturned tables, the people holding one another in the middle of the floor.

Then he looked at me.

“Nigga, what you want to hear?”

I took Shawna's hand.

“The rest of the song.”

They played it.

The room began dancing again.

Not because nobody was scared. Because the gunmen were gone and we were still there, and my wife had chosen a silver dress she was not going home in after half a song.

The duke sent no flowers this time.

He had left the mainland for his island palace, taking his guards and the stranger in the dark uniform with him. Odette could hold the men we caught. She could protect witnesses. But Aurelio's palace had its own armed gates, and he had decided to make the final days of his race a war from behind them.

Nigga should have stayed at the dance.

At least there I had been dressed for mercy.

## 18. The Duke Finally Drove His Own Bullshit

Aurelio Cruel entered the sixth race himself.

The announcement came from Isla Gloria at breakfast. His Grace would personally defend the honor of the Grand Prix in the Bridge of Kings, a crossing of the floating road between the island's eastern harbor and the old naval fort.

Tank looked at the photograph of the course.

“Nigga, that's water with opinions.”

The road had been assembled from broad linked platforms, each wide enough for two cars, stretching across a sheltered bay. Boats held the outer sections steady. At the far end, a steep ramp climbed onto the fort's quay. The drivers would cross twice, circle the island's coastal road and finish at the palace gate.

Nero studied the picture.

“It used to be a ceremonial crossing. Slow. Flags. Music.”

“Nigga made everything a threat,” I said.

“Yes.”

Celadon stood beside him, arms folded.

“The platforms can carry the cars. The danger is what he asks the drivers to do on them.”

I looked toward the harbor, where the Sovereign Sun now flew its old white bird above the bridge. Celadon had reclaimed the ship in every way that mattered to the people who worked aboard it. The duke still claimed to own it. He also claimed I had ruined the winter garden, which was technically true in enough places to make arguing tedious.

Tank stood at the dock counting the cars going aboard.

"Nigga, why we bringing a boat to a car race?"

"Because the road in the water," I said.

"And why the road in the water?"

"Because that nigga owns an island."

"So when you own it, we fixing that?"

Shawna looked over her shoulder. "Nigga, he'll put another road higher up and race both."

"See?" Tank said to Bruno. "That nigga ain't a solution. That nigga's more geography."

Bruno laughed and ducked beneath the gangway frame.

We took the flagship to the race.

Nigga, if somebody steals a man's boat and that man gets it back, you ride with the man.

The whole crew came aboard in the morning. Lark and Mateo loaded the Lamborghini. Tank brought the replacement black coupe. Porsche brought her Ferrari. Cassius drove the White Heron onto the lower deck with Nero beside him. Inez arrived in red and kissed Cassius before handing him his gloves, a gesture so ordinary now that both their fathers looked away to give it room.

Shawna carried her music in a blue case.

“Rehearsal after?” I asked.

“Victory after. Then rehearsal.”

“Nigga, order matters.”

“It does.”

We sailed into Isla Gloria's harbor with the ship's bell ringing. People crowded the quay. They saw Celadon on the bridge, saw Nero standing beside him and began cheering before they even found me on the deck.

I liked that.

Then they found me.

Nigga, I liked that too.

The duke waited at the starting area in a green racing suit. His car was black and gold, long, low and ugly with money. He wore no mask of courtesy now. The white streaks in his hair stood out sharply against the dark suit, and his eyes followed me with a kind of hunger that had forgotten how to look charming.

“You brought stolen property to my island,” he said.

Celadon stepped forward.

“I brought my ship home.”

Aurelio looked at him.

For a moment I saw the old habit in his face: speak sharply, summon a guard, return the man to a room. Then he saw Nero. Cassius. Odette's officers on the quay. The cameras. The crowd pressing close enough to hear every word.

He swallowed the command.

Nigga, it looked painful.

“The race,” he said, “will proceed.”

I stood beside my Lamborghini.

“Good. You been talking for three weeks.”

His jaw tightened.

“You think these people love you.”

I looked around.

A woman held up a loaf of bread from the bakery. Julian stood beside her, waving both arms. Alina stood with Mercedes and Porsche on the viewing platform. Rocco wore a blue shirt with my face on it and looked delighted to have found a profitable form of courage.

“Nigga,” I said, “ask them.”

He didn't.

We lined up at the floating road. Six cars entered. Inez and Cassius had chosen to race. Adrian joined too, along with a veteran driver named Sabine Cross, forty-one, who had told a reporter she considered Aiden impossible but wanted to confirm it at close range.

I respected scientific curiosity.

The first horn sounded.

The platforms moved gently beneath our wheels. Water shone on both sides. The road ahead rose and fell in long shallow motions, never quite still, making distance a thing you had to feel as much as see.

The second horn sounded.

The duke looked across at me.

I smiled.

The third horn sent us forward.

His black car surged first. Mine came beside it. We reached the first joint together, wheels striking the metal seam with a hard ringing sound. The platform dipped beneath us, rose again, and the sea came up level with the lower edge of my window.

Nigga, that got my attention.

Aurelio knew the course. He had practiced. His car moved with ugly confidence, taking the center of each platform and forcing me toward the edge. I let him have the first bend. Stayed close. Watched the way the floating road lifted before the next joint.

Behind us, Inez and Cassius ran side by side in red and white, their cars bright against the blue water. Sabine held fifth. Adrian stayed back, patient after discovering twice that my existence complicated his wagers.

At the halfway point, the duke struck my rear quarter.

Lightly.

Deliberately.

The Lamborghini moved toward the edge.

I caught it.

“Nigga,” I said, “you want to make this personal in public?”

He hit me again.

This time I let the car move farther, gave him the space he expected to take and watched him overcommit into it. His front wheels crossed the seam at the wrong angle. The black car bounced, lost its clean line and fell half a length behind.

I took the center.

The crowd on the fort's quay began screaming.

We hit the final ramp together, blue and black climbing out of the sea. I landed first on the stone road, turned beneath the fort wall and headed back toward the second crossing.

The duke followed.

Close.

He was furious now, but still good. That mattered. A bad driver could have excused himself. Aurelio knew exactly how well I was beating him.

On the return crossing, a platform ahead of us shifted sharply.

One of its holding boats had moved away.

The floating road opened into a narrow gap.

Not huge. Huge would have made the trap obvious enough for everybody to stop. This was the kind of gap meant to catch one car wrong and turn the rest of the race into a tragic discussion about conditions.

I saw the duke look toward it.

Then toward me.

Nigga, there it was.

I didn't call the thunder.

I called his bluff.

I stayed beside him.

Closer.

So close he could not change his line without hitting me hard enough for every camera to see the choice. The gap came toward us. His hands tightened on the wheel.

He braked.

I didn't.

The Lamborghini left the edge, cleared the broken space and landed on the next platform with a crack that went through my teeth. The car stayed straight. Behind me, Aurelio's black machine hit the gap slower, nose dipping, rear wheels lifting before the front caught the far side.

It landed badly.

Its front bumper tore away.

I kept going.

The other drivers slowed and took the gap under the marshals' direction. The race wasn't over. The trap hadn't swallowed anybody. The duke had simply damaged his own car trying to arrange the shape of my fear.

Nigga, expensive lesson.

We came off the floating road onto the island circuit. The coast flashed past my windows. Villages, gardens, the opera house, the bakery where Julian's mother stood waving a blue cloth as I passed.

Inez caught the duke before the palace hill.

Cassius caught him after.

Aurelio tried to hold them off. Couldn't. The black car's damaged front scraped at every dip, throwing sparks beneath the gold paint. He had enough speed to remain dangerous and not enough control to look graceful doing it.

I crossed the finish first.

Inez second.

Cassius third.

The duke came fourth, his car smoking, his face so still it looked painted.

Sabine climbed out behind him and walked straight to me.

“I can confirm it,” she said.

“What?”

“You're impossible.”

“Nigga, peer review.”

She laughed and shook my hand with both of hers.

The sixth key was brought forward by Lord Orlan, who now looked like he had begun rehearsing a life in which he worked for somebody else. He held the cushion out at arm's length.

I took the key.

Behind him, the duke stepped out of his ruined car.

The crowd booed.

Not everybody. Enough.

He looked up at the palace, then back at me.

“You haven't won the island.”

“One more race.”

“One more road.”

“Nigga, I like roads.”

He came closer.

For the first time there were no cameras between us, only at our sides. His voice dropped.

“I can make the island empty before you claim it.”

My smile went away.

He saw it and thought he had found something useful.

“I can burn every car, sink every ship, silence every stage. You can arrive first to ashes.”

I looked at him for a long moment.

Then I took the key off its ribbon and held it between two fingers.

“Nigga, you keep mistaking your last chance to walk away for suspense.”

His eyes hardened.

I didn't raise my voice.

“You touch my people, your last race happens on foot.”

He stepped back.

His guards closed around him. The crowd parted as he walked toward the palace gates. At the top of the steps stood the stranger in the dark uniform.

This time the stranger smiled at me openly.

Like he had enjoyed every second.

Shawna came beside me.

“What'd he say?”

I told her.

All of it.

She looked toward the palace, then down at the six keys in the case Porsche held open beside us.

“Then we don't leave everybody here alone tonight.”

“No.”

“Nigga, good.”

We took over the opera house before sunset.

Not by force. Valentina opened the doors and told us which rooms had beds, which corridors reached the street and which windows stuck when the sea wind turned. The company stayed. Workers brought food. Rocco sent supplies. Celadon kept the Sovereign Sun ready in the harbor, its lights bright, its crew finally working for a captain they trusted.

Tank and Bruno stood at the main doors while people came and went.

Mercedes and Porsche organized rooms with the efficiency of women who had spent their adult lives judging whether a strange building wanted anything good for them.

Nero and Esteban sat with the old island mechanics, drawing the final race course from memory. No secret instructions. Just the shape of roads they loved and the places the duke had changed.

Shawna rehearsed with Rosa and the full company.

I stood in the back of the hall listening.

Outside, the island waited for the night.

Inside, my wife filled the room with a voice the duke had promised to silence.

Nigga, he was going to have to come through me first.

## 19. The Opera Had Security

Chief Gloria Knox arrived on Isla Gloria wearing a blue suit, sunglasses and the expression of a woman whose captain had made her vacation an international event.

She came through the opera house doors while Tank and Bruno were arguing about which one of them occupied more of the entrance.

“Move,” she said.

They moved.

Bruno looked down at Knox. "Ma'am, are you his commander?"

"When he remembers."

"Nigga remembers," Tank said. "Nigga just remembers at speed."

Knox looked toward me. "Captain, did you send my car over an ocean?"

"Which ocean?"

"That answer concerns me."

"Nigga's being precise," Tank said.

"Nigga's being evasive," Shawna corrected.

Knox put her sunglasses in her pocket. "At least everybody here knows him."

"We know that nigga," Rosa said warmly. "We packed accordingly."

“Nigga,” Tank whispered to Bruno, “that's where he got it.”

Knox took off her sunglasses and looked down the aisle at me.

“Captain.”

“Chief.”

“Nice theater.”

“My wife likes it.”

“So I've heard. The entire department has heard. One officer has started taking singing lessons in case you promote the orchestra.”

Shawna laughed from the stage.

Knox looked up at her.

“Mrs. Aiden.”

“Chief.”

“Keep him breathing.”

“Working full time.”

Nigga, women meet and immediately form a government around your stupid decisions.

Knox had come with six officers who were technically on leave and practically dressed like they expected trouble to recognize them. Odette met her near the front doors. The two women shook hands, exchanged a few words and began making the building safer without asking either of us how strongly we felt about furniture placement.

I appreciated expertise.

Especially when it arrived with my department's name on the jackets.

The night before the final race, the opera house held more life than it had seen in years. Singers rehearsed onstage. Workers ate in the side rooms. Drivers talked with mechanics in the courtyard. Somebody had found a television, and Clementine's victory played on it every twenty minutes, provoking the same delighted shouting each time the eggs appeared.

The marshal who owned Clementine had brought his wife to the island. Her name was Elise. She was fifty, cheerful, and had informed her husband that they were never selling the car because it now had a better story than either of them.

I gave them a new luxury sedan anyway.

She looked at the keys.

“Nigga,” she said, then covered her mouth. “I'm sorry. My husband keeps playing the video.”

I laughed and hugged her.

“Your car earned the accent.”

By nine, the square outside the opera house glowed with lanterns. Julian's mother sent bread. Rocco sent wine. Mercedes and Porsche arranged tables so the workers and performers could eat together. No separate room behind a pillar. No invitation stamped important enough to excuse a man being rude.

Tank sat with Rosa on the steps.

I passed them carrying a plate.

He looked up at me.

“Nigga, can you stop saving countries during dinner?”

“Only an island.”

“That's how you start.”

Rosa leaned against his shoulder.

“He saved my rehearsal.”

“He drove a car through it.”

“And brought the singers back.”

Tank considered that.

“Nigga's thorough.”

Across the square, Cassius and Inez stood beside the White Heron. She had one foot on the low curb, red dress moving in the evening breeze. He leaned against the car, listening while she spoke. Not planning his answer. Listening.

Nero watched them from a table with Esteban.

“I would have been terrible at this age,” Nero said.

“You were terrible at this age,” Esteban replied.

“Yes. But beautifully.”

They clinked glasses.

I went upstairs to find Shawna.

She stood in the blue room she'd chosen from the ferry, looking out over the harbor. It was exactly what she had imagined: pale walls, blue curtains, a little balcony facing the sea. Her music lay open on a desk. Dante's watch sat beside it while she adjusted the strap.

“You were right,” I said.

She turned.

“About the room?”

“About everything. But start there.”

She smiled and came to me.

Down below, the square hummed. The island had a night before it had a king, and we stood above it holding each other like the future was close enough to touch but not yet safe enough to trust completely.

“Tomorrow,” she said.

“Yeah.”

“You win. We sing. Everybody gets to sleep.”

“Nigga, that's a beautiful schedule.”

“Follow it.”

I kissed her.

Then the first explosion shook the harbor.

The windows rattled. A blue flare rose above the shipyard ridge. Down in the square, voices changed pitch. Music stopped.

Shawna closed her eyes for one second.

“Nigga.”

“I know.”

We ran downstairs together.

Black vehicles came down the royal road toward the opera square. Six of them. Armed men stood in the rear of two open trucks. Behind them, motorcycles spread through the narrow streets, engines rising over the sound of people moving toward the doors.

The duke had sent the rest of his evening.

Knox met me at the bottom of the stairs.

“People inside. Hold the square.”

Odette was already moving her officers toward the side streets. Tank and Bruno stood at the main doors, directing the crowd inward. Mercedes took the women nearest the tables toward the rear corridor. Porsche helped Elise and her husband through the courtyard gate. Rosa stayed with the singers, keeping them together while Valentina led the oldest musicians down the side steps.

Shawna looked at me.

“I'll get them through.”

“I know.”

She kissed me once, quick and fierce.

Then she went to work.

I walked down the opera steps.

Nigga, the square looked different when everybody you loved was behind you.

The first black car stopped near the fountain. A man climbed out wearing a gray coat and carrying a long gun. He was older, thick through the neck, his face calm with the certainty of somebody who had survived by making other men afraid first.

“Captain Aiden,” he called.

“Nigga, you know my name. Save us time.”

“Walk away from the building.”

I looked back at the opera house.

Then at him.

“That's my wife's rehearsal.”

He lifted the gun.

The world became noise.

Stone chipped beside me. I went behind the fountain as Knox's officers answered from the steps. The gray-coated man ducked behind his car. Two motorcycles cut across the square, riders trying to reach the side entrance.

Tank met the first one with a table.

He lifted it, turned and put it directly into the motorcycle's future.

The rider hit the wood, flew sideways and landed in the flower bed.

“Nigga,” Tank shouted, “closed section!”

Bruno caught the second rider when he tried to get past the doorway. The bike skidded away. Bruno put the man down, took his weapon and kicked it out of reach with the irritated efficiency of a champion clearing a gym floor.

I moved between the fountain and the parked cars.

A gunman came around the hood of a silver sedan. I struck his arm, drove him backward and fired when his partner raised a weapon from the opposite side. The second man fell. The first stumbled away with his hands up, his courage suddenly interested in retirement.

“Nigga, stay there.”

He stayed.

Across the square, Cassius and Inez had brought the White Heron out of the courtyard. Not into the gunfire. Between the side street and the people still crossing to shelter. Its white body blocked the opening long enough for Nero and Esteban to guide the last group inside.

A truck accelerated toward the gap.

Inez saw it.

She got behind the wheel, turned the White Heron sharply and moved the car out of the way just as the truck struck the stone bollards hidden beside the curb.

Its front rose.

Stopped.

The driver hit the windshield and slumped, alive but no longer participating.

Cassius looked at Inez through the open window.

“Nigga, marry—”

He stopped himself.

She stared.

Then she grinned.

“Finish the fight first.”

I heard it from ten feet away and almost laughed in the middle of a gun battle.

Love, nigga. Terrible timing. Excellent taste.

The gray-coated man had reached the steps.

Knox confronted him halfway up. He fired, forcing her behind a pillar, then turned toward the main doors where Shawna was helping Valentina move a wounded musician.

I crossed the square at a run.

Blue thunder flashed through my body.

One burst.

The distance seemed to tighten. My hands moved faster than the thought finishing in my head. I hit the gray-coated man before he reached the door, drove him off the steps and landed with him on the stone below.

His gun went one way.

My breath went another.

We rolled. He struck me in the jaw. I answered. He reached for a knife. I caught his wrist and held it against the pavement while the thunder burned out of me, leaving every muscle suddenly aware of its own weight.

“Nigga,” I told him through my teeth, “you picked the wrong building.”

He tried to headbutt me.

I put him down.

When I stood, the square tilted.

Knox caught my arm.

“Captain.”

“I'm here.”

“I can see that. Stay useful by sitting.”

She pushed me onto the lower step, took the man's weapon and went back into the fight.

Nigga, my chief had promoted bossing me around into an international discipline.

I sat for thirty seconds. Long enough to get my breath. Long enough to see the fight turn.

Odette's officers came through the side street behind the trucks. The attackers' line broke. Some ran. Some dropped their weapons. One tried to drive away and found Bruno standing beside his open door, holding it in place with one hand.

“Nigga,” Bruno said, “engine off.”

The engine went off.

The square fell quiet in pieces.

Sirens. Groans. People calling names. The little crackle of a damaged car cooling beneath the fountain's spray.

We had wounded. Cuts, bruises, one officer hit in the shoulder, a violinist with glass in his arm. Two attackers were dead. The others who hadn't fled lay under guard or sat with their hands visible, discovering how ordinary a bad decision looked after the shooting stopped.

Shawna came down the steps and knelt in front of me.

“How much thunder?”

“One burst.”

She checked my eyes.

Then she pressed her forehead against mine.

“Okay.”

Behind her, Rosa began singing.

Softly at first, from somewhere inside the doors. A note to find the people who were shaking. Another to tell them the room was still there. The singers joined her one by one, no orchestra, just voices moving through the broken quiet.

Shawna looked back.

Then she stood, helped me up and sang with them.

The sound filled the square.

People came to the windows. To the doors. The workers who had hidden under the stage came upstairs and stood shoulder to shoulder in the aisle. Celadon rang the Sovereign Sun's bell from the harbor, and its deep answer crossed the water into the music.

I stood between my wife and my brother, bruised, exhausted, wearing a badge over a gold cross and six keys waiting inside the building behind me.

The duke had sent guns to end her song.

Nigga, he had made the audience bigger.

## 20. Breakfast Before Paradise

The morning of the final race, Tank burned the toast.

After everything we had survived, nigga, that felt personal.

He stood in the opera house kitchen holding two black slices between his fingers while Rosa watched with the expression of a woman reconsidering the limits of a man's usefulness.

“You can lift a car,” she said.

“Car don't burn this fast.”

“You left it in there.”

“I was checking the doors.”

“Nigga, the toast wasn't attacking the doors.”

I came in and took one look at the plate.

“Duke send that?”

Tank threw a towel at me.

Everybody laughed.

It was a good sound to hear in a building that still had bullet marks beside the entrance.

The injured had been taken to the clinic. The wounded officer was stable. The violinist had insisted he could still play and then been told by Valentina that optimism was not a substitute for an uninjured arm. Nobody from our company had died in the attack. Two of the duke's men had. Their bodies were taken away before breakfast, and the square had been washed clean without pretending the night had never happened.

Knox sat at the kitchen table with Odette, coffee between them. They had the calm, tired faces of women who had spent the night keeping other people from becoming tomorrow's bad news.

“Captain,” Knox said when she saw me.

“Chief.”

“Race. Win. Come home.”

“Nigga, concise leadership.”

“I'm practicing for when you start interrupting.”

Shawna came in carrying a plate of eggs.

Clementine's eggs.

The marshal's wife had insisted on cooking them for us before the final race. Apparently groceries could become ceremonial if a nigga drove them fast enough.

We ate at long tables pushed together beneath the kitchen windows. Drivers, musicians, mechanics, police, sex workers, boat captains, jewelers. Marcellus had come from the mainland with a case of tools and the real Blue Mercy ring on his hand. He had spent the early morning repairing the clasp on my key case because, he said, one should not win an island and lose its entrance into a drain.

I sat beside him.

“You been quiet.”

“I've been watching you damage things.”

“Nigga, that's almost a career now.”

“For both of us, apparently.”

He lifted the case. Six jeweled keys lay inside, each different, each bright. The gold wheel, the little steering crown, the sea-blue stone. He had cleaned them all.

“Original work,” he said. “The old race commissioned a different maker for each. Your last one is the largest.”

“How you know?”

“I know the man who made it.”

“Of course you do.”

“He was very vain.”

“Nigga, was it you?”

Marcellus smiled into his coffee.

Tank nearly choked.

“You made the big key?”

“Forty years in a trade leads to the occasional relevant object.”

I looked at him.

“Nigga, you could have mentioned it.”

“You were busy driving through the doors the smaller ones opened.”

Fair.

Tank leaned over Marcellus's shoulder.

"Nigga made the biggest key before Aiden even got here."

"Years before," Marcellus said.

"So that nigga was preparing."

"I was working."

"Preparing while working," Tank insisted.

I shook my head. "Nigga, let the man have a past without making it my appointment."

Shawna looked at me in surprise. "That was almost modest."

"Nigga, almost. The key still ends up in my hand."

Marcellus laughed softly and opened the case wider. "You young niggas exhaust a very old object."

He showed me a little photograph from the case. A much younger Marcellus stood beside an older jeweler, both holding the unfinished ceremonial key. The date was more than twenty years earlier. No secret prophecy. No destiny waiting in a workshop. Just an old man whose life had been larger than the corner of it I'd met.

“I wanted the teeth shaped like waves,” he said. “My teacher told me a key must first open something.”

“And?”

“It does both.”

I shook his hand.

“Then I'll bring it back for inspection.”

He nodded.

“Please bring the hand holding it too.”

Across the table, Mercedes and Porsche argued about the names of the clubs they planned to open on Isla Gloria.

“Blue Hour stays,” Mercedes said.

“For the yacht,” Porsche replied. “The island room needs its own name.”

“Nigga, it's the same ocean.”

“Different door.”

Alina leaned between them.

“What about No Second Door?”

They both looked at her.

She shrugged.

“Nobody gets sent around the back.”

Mercedes smiled slowly.

“That I like.”

Porsche wrote it down.

I pointed at them with my fork.

“You got the building by the eastern quay.”

“You haven't won it yet,” Porsche said.

“Nigga, put it on hold.”

She grinned.

“Already did.”

Lark and Mateo planned a garage. Not a palace workshop where drivers swept in, shouted and vanished. A place with windows, decent food and enough room for mechanics to sit down without somebody accusing them of laziness. Mateo wanted a little garden behind it. Lark told him if he managed to keep the plant at home alive for a month, she would consider expanding his responsibilities.

He kissed her cheek.

“Nigga, I watered it before they took me.”

“Then it survived better than your communication.”

He laughed. She did too.

Nero and Esteban wanted the White Heron on the final road, but Cassius refused to race it that day.

“She's done enough,” he said. “I'll drive my own.”

Nero nodded.

No argument.

The old car would wait at the finish with them inside it.

Inez sat beside Cassius, watching him across the rim of her cup.

“What?” he asked.

“You started a sentence last night.”

Tank looked up immediately.

“Nigga.”

Cassius put his cup down.

“I remember.”

“You planning to finish it?”

“After the race.”

She considered him.

Then she smiled.

“Drive well.”

Nigga, that man had acquired a finish line inside the finish line.

After breakfast I went to the courtyard.

The police Lamborghini waited in the sun. Dark blue, gold badge, repaired body, familiar shape. Lark stood beside it with Mateo, both of them wearing clean team shirts for the first time all month. She held out the keys.

“She'll bring you through.”

“I know.”

“Don't ask her to be a boat.”

“Nigga, that was another car.”

“Don't ask her to be a plane.”

“Context matters.”

Mateo laughed and stepped back as Shawna came through the doors.

She wore white.

Not a wedding dress. White trousers, a fitted jacket, blue silk at the throat. Dante's watch on her wrist. My earrings. Her own beautiful face, looking at me like she had found the one place in the courtyard she meant to stand.

“You riding?” I asked.

“Final race is single driver.”

“I can argue.”

“Nigga, I know.”

She put her hand against my chest, over the cross.

“I'll be at the finish. I want you to see me before you stop.”

I held her close.

The noise of the courtyard moved around us. Tools. Footsteps. Tank asking somebody whether the toast had been thrown out or merely relocated. Life, nigga. All these people making plans because they expected a tomorrow big enough to hold them.

“I love you,” I said.

Shawna looked up.

“I know. I love you too.”

“Even when I do too much?”

“Especially when you come back and tell me.”

I kissed her.

Then a messenger arrived from the palace.

No feather this time. No velvet tray. Just a young man in a gray jacket holding an envelope with both hands. He looked frightened enough that I thanked him before opening it.

Inside was an offer.

The duke would surrender the prize fleet, withdraw his objections to the rescued workers leaving and pay me fifty million if I left Isla Gloria before noon.

He would retain the island.

The opera house was not mentioned.

Nigga really thought he had found a number larger than my wife.

I handed the letter to Porsche.

“Keep that.”

She read it and whistled.

“You want me to answer?”

“Yeah.”

“What should I say?”

Shawna looked at the blue curtains visible through the upstairs window.

“Tell him I already chose the room.”

Porsche smiled and began writing.

We left for the starting line with the whole square cheering.

The final race would begin at the eastern harbor, climb through the old vineyards, pass the naval fort, cross the island's interior and descend through the palace gates into the great courtyard. The seventh key waited there. So did the duke.

He had withdrawn from the driving field.

After the floating road, perhaps the nigga had learned that a steering wheel was not improved by ownership papers.

Five drivers remained: Inez, Cassius, Adrian, Sabine and me.

At the grid, we stood together beside our cars.

No speeches about noble competition. No promises to slow down for one another. We wanted to win. That was why we had come. But every one of us had seen enough of the duke to know the last road would ask for more than speed.

Sabine held out her hand.

“See you at the palace.”

Inez put hers over it.

Cassius added his.

Adrian looked at me.

“I'd like to beat you once.”

“Nigga, ambition keeps a man young.”

He laughed and put his hand in.

I covered theirs with mine.

Then we went to our cars.

From the Sovereign Sun in the harbor, Celadon rang the ship's bell.

Nero and Esteban stood beside the White Heron at the far end of the quay, ready to take the ordinary road to the finish.

Shawna waited in the open car with Rosa, Mercedes and Porsche. Tank drove. Chief Knox sat in the car behind them with Odette, and Bruno occupied most of its remaining hope.

My wife lifted one hand.

I lifted mine.

The lights began counting down.

Nigga, the whole month had brought me to this one beautiful stretch of road.

I intended to own the end of it.

## 21. The Finish Line Was a Fucking Palace

Inez took the lead at the first turn.

Cassius took it from her at the second.

I took it from both of them at the third, because a nigga can appreciate romance without letting it control the standings.

The Lamborghini climbed out of the harbor with the sea flashing behind us. Flags snapped above the road. People crowded the balconies, shouting our names as we passed. Mine came loudest, but I could hear Inez's too, and Cassius's, and once Nero's from a man who saw the silver car and forgot which generation had come back to race.

The engine settled beneath my hands.

No passenger this time.

Shawna's seat held only the blue handkerchief she had given me before the boat race. I had folded it carefully and tucked one corner beneath the belt so it wouldn't fly away.

Nigga, a man can drive alone without leaving everybody behind.

The first miles ran through vineyards. Low stone walls. Green hills. Sun on the hood. Sabine pressed hard on my left, her yellow car taking the turns with clean, patient precision. Adrian came up behind her. Inez stayed close to Cassius, then split away on the long bend and passed him with a laugh over the race channel.

“Try to finish that sentence before next year,” she told him.

“Nigga, I'm busy.”

“So am I.”

I smiled and took the next turn faster.

At the old fort, the road narrowed beneath an archway. I went through first. Sabine followed. Behind her, a black car came out of a side entrance wearing no number and no interest in the rules.

Here we fucking go.

It struck Adrian's rear corner. His car slid toward the wall. He caught it, swore and kept moving. Two more black cars emerged behind the first, engines roaring, windows dark.

The duke's final team.

“Unmarked cars at the fort,” I said into the channel.

Odette answered immediately.

“We see them.”

Knox's voice followed.

“Keep your road, Captain.”

Nigga, I planned to.

The first black car pushed between Sabine and me. Its driver wore a helmet with a gold stripe. He looked over as he came alongside, and I could see the smile behind his visor.

That nigga had been hired to be a problem. I could see him rehearsing the moment in his own head: the famous captain frightened, the crowd quiet, the duke nodding like he'd bought himself the correct nigga.

"You see him?" Inez asked over the channel.

"I see the nigga."

"He's looking at you."

"Nigga should look where he's going."

Cassius laughed. "You about to change where that nigga's going, aren't you?"

"Depends how hard he asks."

Sabine's voice joined us. "These niggas do this every race?"

"Every beautiful race," Inez said.

I hoped he had been paid in advance.

He moved toward me.

I let him come.

Then I braked just enough to let his front cross mine and turned behind him before he could correct. He struck the wall with his rear quarter, bounced back onto the road and found Sabine already gone past him on the other side.

“Nigga,” she said over the channel, “that was rude.”

“You talking to me?”

“No. I'm learning your punctuation.”

I laughed and accelerated.

The black car recovered. Came again. Behind us, Inez and Cassius boxed the second attacker away from Adrian, keeping him from being forced toward the drop. They didn't touch the black car. They gave its driver no clean space to become violent without losing his own road.

He lost it anyway.

The car struck a low wall, spun and stopped across a gravel turnout. Its driver climbed out with both hands raised when Odette's pursuit car reached him.

One down.

Two still coming.

The interior road ran through a pine forest. Sunlight broke in strips across the windshield. My speed climbed. The gold-striped driver stayed with me, closer now, his car powerful enough to make arrogance feel supported.

He showed me a gun through the side window.

Nigga, that was his introduction.

I answered with my siren.

The blue lights flashed through the trees.

He fired.

The shot struck the road ahead of my front wheel. I moved, felt the car slide, brought it back and saw the narrow service lane opening on my right.

I took it.

The black car followed.

The lane led through an old stone winery courtyard and rejoined the race road above the next bend. Barrels lined one wall. A tractor stood beneath a canopy. Two workers jumped aside as I came through, my siren giving them the only explanation they needed.

The black car entered too fast.

Its side struck the tractor's rear wheel.

The machine spun across the courtyard in a long ugly scrape and stopped against a stack of empty barrels. The driver tried to reverse. Couldn't. His gun hand came up again as I turned through the far gate.

I fired once from my window.

His windshield cracked in front of him. He ducked and dropped the gun.

I kept going.

“Nigga, stay parked.”

At the rejoining road, Sabine flashed past.

Then Adrian.

I came in behind them, still third, with Inez and Cassius close enough to make the race feel like a promise instead of a procession.

The last unmarked car waited at the gorge.

Not on the road.

Across it.

Beyond the car, the old stone bridge had been blocked by two service trucks. Men stood beside them with weapons visible. The race officials on the near side waved frantically, trying to stop us before the road narrowed.

Sabine braked.

Adrian pulled beside her.

I stopped behind them.

The other drivers arrived and got out.

For the first time all day, the engines sounded small against the space around us.

Across the gorge, the palace road climbed toward the finish. We could see its flags above the trees.

The duke had put a wall between the race and the result.

A man in a green coat stepped onto the bridge with a loudspeaker.

“By order of His Grace, the Grand Prix is suspended.”

“Nigga,” I said, “he losing so hard he canceled geography.”

Inez came beside me.

“There's an old bridge below.”

I looked down.

A narrow stone crossing lay farther along the gorge, reached by a steep track cut into the hillside. It had been built for carts, not modern race cars. Ivy covered one side. A fallen branch lay across its far end.

Cassius followed my eyes.

“No.”

“Yes,” I said.

“Aiden.”

“Nigga, you keep saying my name like it means stop.”

Sabine looked at the track.

Then at my car.

“You're serious.”

“Very attractive too. We got a list going.”

Adrian laughed once, sharp and disbelieving.

The man on the bridge lifted the loudspeaker again.

“All drivers will remain where they are.”

I held up my badge.

“Captain Aiden. All niggas with borrowed guns can put them down.”

He stared.

I got back in my car.

The others followed.

We took the old track together.

Slow at first. The slope was rough, the edge close. I kept the Lamborghini steady while stones cracked beneath the tires and dust rose around the hood. Above us, the duke's men shouted. One fired into the air. Odette's officers reached the main bridge behind them and answered with commands that sounded much more practiced than mine.

We kept descending.

At the old crossing, I stopped.

The stone bridge was narrower than it had looked from above. My mirrors had inches on either side. The branch at the far end was larger too, a whole fallen limb across the exit.

I got out.

Tank's voice came through the channel.

“Nigga, why you out of the car?”

“Moving a tree.”

“Of course you are.”

I climbed onto the bridge and crossed on foot. The gorge opened beneath me, water bright far below. The old stones felt solid under my shoes. At the far end I caught the branch in both hands and pulled.

It moved a little.

Sabine got out behind me.

Then Adrian.

Then Cassius and Inez.

We lifted it together and rolled it off the road.

No speech. No photograph arranged afterward. Five drivers who wanted to beat one another cleared the same bridge because none of us had come to let Aurelio choose where we stopped.

I looked at them.

“Niggas ready?”

Inez grinned.

“Move your beautiful car.”

I did.

The Lamborghini crossed first. Slowly enough that every stone had time to judge us. Then Sabine. Adrian. Inez. Cassius last.

As his silver car reached the far end, the duke's men appeared on the upper path.

Gunfire struck the slope above us.

We drove.

The track climbed toward the palace road in a series of tight turns. Dirt flew. Engines roared. I hit the paved road first and let the Lamborghini stretch beneath me, all the careful restraint of the gorge releasing at once.

Ahead stood the final hill.

Beyond it, the finish.

The duke had one more idea.

A helicopter rose from the palace grounds and hovered above the road, low enough for its wind to tear leaves from the trees. A man leaned out with a weapon aimed toward the cars.

Nigga had upgraded the weather.

I saw the first flashes and drove beneath the line of trees. Branches struck the roof. The helicopter followed, its shadow racing beside me. Behind, the others spread out, making themselves harder to trap in one straight line.

I called the thunder.

One short burst.

Blue light ran through the wheel, into the dash, beneath the hood. The Lamborghini surged. The road came toward me faster, the car answering like a living thing that had waited for the last demand.

I passed beneath the helicopter before the gunman could follow my movement.

Ahead, a low stone ramp rose beside the road, part of an old loading terrace.

I took it.

The car lifted.

For a second the palace gates filled the windshield.

Then the Lamborghini landed beyond the line of concrete barriers the duke had placed across the entrance, tires striking the courtyard road with a sound that made every guard turn.

Blue lights flashed over white marble.

My siren filled the palace.

Nigga, the finish line had been trying to hide in a fortress.

I brought the whole police department to its door.

The official race arch still stood in the courtyard, ribbons moving in the helicopter's wind. Lord Orlan waited beneath it with the seventh key in a velvet case, pale and sweating. The duke stood on the palace steps beside the stranger in the dark uniform.

Shawna was at the far side of the courtyard with my people.

I saw her before I stopped.

Just like she asked.

I crossed the line first.

The bells began ringing.

The crowd outside the gates heard them and roared. Inez came through the opening the guards had finally cleared. Cassius followed. Sabine. Adrian. All five of us reached the courtyard alive.

I sat in the car for one breath while the thunder's cost rolled through my shoulders.

One breath.

Then I opened the door and stood.

Shawna ran to me.

I caught her with both arms, lifted her and kissed her in front of the palace, the drivers, the guards, the duke and every camera that had followed me across a month of his bad decisions.

“Nigga,” she whispered against my mouth, “you did it.”

I looked over her shoulder at Aurelio.

His face had gone empty.

No smile. No threat. Nothing left to arrange between himself and what everybody had seen.

I put Shawna gently on her feet.

Then I walked toward the seventh key.

Lord Orlan held it out.

The duke drew a gun.

“Nobody moves,” he said.

Nigga, the race was over.

Now he wanted to meet me.

## 22. I Was the Last Thing He Owned

Aurelio pointed the gun at the key.

That told me everything.

Not at the driver who had beaten him. Not at the police coming through his gates. At the little gold object that would make it impossible for him to keep pretending his promises were only decorations.

“Nobody touches it,” he said.

Lord Orlan froze with the case in his hands.

I stood three steps away.

Behind me, Shawna moved toward Rosa and the others. Not running. Making room. Keeping the people she loved out of the line the duke was trying to draw through the courtyard.

I could feel the thunder's cost in my legs.

I had no more to spend.

Nigga, I still had me.

“You lost,” I said.

Aurelio laughed.

It sounded painful.

“I built this.”

“Nigga, half the men you stole it from standing behind me.”

He glanced toward Nero and Celadon.

Looked away quickly.

“You think they made it beautiful? They made boats. Cars. Little races for men who wanted trophies cheap enough to carry home. I made kings come here.”

“And one came.”

His eyes hit mine.

The stranger in the dark uniform stood beside the palace door, watching us with his hands clasped behind his back. He had moved out of the gun's line without seeming to move at all. His attention bothered me more than the weapon.

But Aurelio had the weapon.

One nigga at a time.

“You walked into my harbor,” the duke said. “You wrecked my boats. You humiliated my men. You took my guests, my drivers, my staff—”

“Nigga, listen to how much of your sentence is people.”

“They were mine.”

“No.”

He shook the gun toward me.

“They came because I paid.”

“They stayed because I came back.”

The courtyard went quiet.

Aurelio looked past me at the crowd beyond the gates. Workers. Drivers. Musicians. Islanders who had followed the final race into the palace square and now stood watching the man whose name had been over every door they entered.

Some of them had spent years lowering their eyes when he passed.

They weren't lowering them now.

“You think they love you?” he asked again.

I smiled faintly.

“Nigga, you already asked that. Answer got louder.”

A hand touched his shoulder.

The stranger in the dark uniform.

“Put it down, Aurelio.”

The duke jerked away.

“Don't tell me what to do in my own house.”

The stranger removed his hand.

“Then finish your lesson.”

He stepped back.

Nigga, I did not like him at all.

Aurelio turned toward Lord Orlan.

“Give me the case.”

Orlan's hands shook.

He looked at the gun.

Then at me.

Then, very carefully, he placed the case on the ground between us and stepped away from it.

The duke's face changed.

Another man had chosen.

He fired.

The shot struck the stone beside Orlan's foot. Orlan fell backward. The crowd screamed. Knox shouted. I moved.

Not thunder.

Me.

I crossed the last steps and struck Aurelio's gun arm upward as he fired again. The bullet shattered a palace window. I drove him against the stair rail, his shoulder hitting stone, and we went down together with the gun trapped between our bodies.

He was stronger than he looked.

Anger can lend a nigga strength too. It just charges interest in judgment.

He hit my ribs. The old wound flared. I answered with an elbow and felt him gasp. His gun came free for half a second. I caught his wrist and slammed it against the rail until the weapon fell between the steps.

He kicked me hard enough to break my balance.

I went onto one knee.

Aurelio ran.

Up the palace stairs. Through the open doors. Past the stranger, who moved aside and let him go with an expression almost like disappointment.

I followed.

Shawna called my name behind me.

I looked back once.

She stood beside Knox, gun lowered, eyes on mine.

“Come back,” she said.

“Nigga, always.”

Then I went into the palace.

Aurelio had built the interior to make a man feel small. High ceilings. Marble floors. Portraits twice the size of the people they described. Gold everywhere, even on things nobody needed to look at. He ran through it like a man fleeing his own advertisement.

I chased him past a fountain full of blue stones and into a gallery lined with cars.

His private collection.

Ferraris. Bentleys. A gold roadster. A black racing machine on a raised platform beneath a portrait of him holding a falcon. Nigga had made the bird look impressed too.

He reached the black car and pulled open its door.

I caught the edge before he closed it.

He struck my hand with the frame.

Pain shot up my arm.

I let go.

The engine started.

Aurelio looked at me through the windshield.

For a second he smiled again.

Then he drove straight at me.

I jumped onto the raised platform beside the gold roadster. His car tore past, struck a display stand and smashed through the gallery's glass doors into the inner courtyard.

Nigga had finally joined me in respecting architecture creatively.

I went after him.

Outside, the black car spun around the courtyard fountain. A narrow ramp climbed toward the palace's upper terrace, wide enough for one vehicle. Aurelio took it, tires shrieking, heading for the private road beyond the northern wall.

He had a way out.

I had a gold roadster with its keys still hanging from a little ceremonial hook.

Some rich niggas mistake display for security right up to the end.

I started it and drove through the broken doors.

The roadster roared beneath me, engine huge, hood long and bright as sunrise. I hit the ramp behind Aurelio and climbed through a storm of dust and broken stone. The palace courtyard fell away below. Ahead, his black car reached the terrace and turned toward the outer gate.

I came alongside at the top.

There was barely room.

He looked over, and I saw the exact moment he realized I was driving one of his favorite cars.

“Nigga,” I said through the open side, “you got good taste in defeat.”

He rammed me.

The roadster struck the terrace wall. Stone broke away. Beyond it lay the lower gardens, a long drop broken by cypress trees and statues of men who had never had to fight me.

I held the wheel.

He hit me again.

The gold car's front wheel climbed the low wall. For a breath I looked down at the gardens beneath my door. Then I turned into him, hard enough to catch his front corner and force his black car sideways across the narrow terrace.

Both engines screamed.

The cars locked together.

We slid toward the fountain at the terrace's center and struck it in a crash that threw water over both windshields.

The engines died.

Nigga, we had reached the end of the road in a very expensive manner.

I got out slowly.

My legs shook. My hand burned. Blood ran from a cut at my hairline into one eye. I wiped it away and saw Aurelio climbing from the black car, a pistol in his hand.

Another one.

The nigga owned backups for everything except character.

He aimed.

I went behind the roadster as the shot tore through its open door. Gold paint flew. I drew my own gun, came up on the other side and held him in my sights.

For the first time we stood still together.

The sea spread behind him.

The island lay below.

He looked around as if hoping the palace, the cars, the whole brilliant thing he had built around himself might speak on his behalf.

Nothing did.

“You could have taken the money,” he said.

“Nigga, I got money.”

“The ships.”

“Got a captain for them.”

“The women.”

I stared at him.

“My wife chose me. That's why you don't understand any of this.”

His face twisted.

“You are nothing but noise.”

I thought of the harbor crowd. Of the band changing its song when I stepped off the ferry. Of Rosa singing after the attack. Of Shawna filling an empty opera house with a voice big enough to make it hers before I owned a single stone.

I smiled.

“Nigga, you heard me coming.”

Aurelio fired.

I fired back.

His shot struck the fountain beside me.

Mine struck him in the chest.

He took one step backward.

Then another.

The gun fell from his hand. He sat down heavily against the broken edge of the fountain, green racing suit darkening, eyes fixed on the palace doors.

I kept my weapon trained on him until he stopped moving.

Aurelio Cruel died looking toward a house that no longer answered him.

No speech at the end.

No secret son. No last contract. No letter explaining that he had loved somebody too much to stop being cruel.

Just a man who had finally run out of people between himself and the consequences.

I lowered my gun.

My hand shook.

Footsteps came from the terrace stairs.

Shawna reached me first.

She looked at the duke, then at my face, then put both arms around me so hard I let the weight of my body settle against hers.

“You came back,” she whispered.

“Nigga, I took the scenic route.”

She laughed once through the tears in her eyes.

Then she kissed me.

Tank came up behind her with Knox and Odette. He looked at the two wrecked cars, the broken fountain, the duke and me.

“Nigga,” he said slowly, “you cannot be trusted with a tour.”

I laughed.

It hurt.

I laughed anyway.

Odette checked Aurelio. Stood. Nodded once to Knox.

The duke was dead.

Below us, the palace gates opened fully.

His remaining guards had laid down their weapons. Some because they were frightened. Some because they had been waiting for a reason. Some because the man who had paid them was dead and the man who had beaten him stood above them with his wife in his arms, looking like a future they wanted to survive into.

I didn't pretend all those reasons were the same.

I accepted the guns off the road.

Lord Orlan waited at the foot of the stairs with the seventh key.

This time his hands didn't shake.

He held it out to me.

Tank looked at the case, then at me.

"Nigga, count them."

"Seven," I said.

"Count the niggas who tried to stop you."

"Nigga, I need dinner first."

Porsche laughed. "That nigga's list needs a table."

Mercedes opened the key case wider. "Give the man room. Nigga just won a country-shaped honeymoon."

Shawna took my uninjured hand. "He won a bed before he wins anything else tonight."

"That nigga deserves a bed," Tank said solemnly.

"Several," Bruno added.

I looked at my wife. "One. Correct company."

She kissed me, and the niggas stopped counting.

“The final key,” he said. “To Captain Aiden. Winner of the Grand Prix of Kings.”

The courtyard began cheering before he finished.

I took the key.

Marcellus came forward through the crowd, examined it for one second and nodded.

“Still opens,” he said.

“Nigga, you proud?”

“Of the workmanship? Certainly.”

I laughed and hugged him with one arm.

The stranger in the dark uniform stood near the palace doors.

He watched me holding the seventh key.

Then he inclined his head, turned and walked away through a side entrance with two men following him.

I remembered his face.

But the crowd was calling my name.

My wife was holding my hand.

The island had opened its gates.

Nigga, I had won.

## 23. My Wife Sang on My Island

They wanted to put me on a horse for the handover.

“Nigga, I just won fifty-two cars.”

Lord Orlan looked at the white horse waiting outside the palace gate. The horse looked back with the calm confidence of an animal unaware it had entered a discussion about value.

“Tradition,” Orlan said.

“Does tradition have a transmission?”

Tank bent over laughing.

Shawna stroked the horse's neck.

“I like him.”

I looked at her.

Then at the horse.

“Nigga, welcome to the family.”

So I rode the horse down to the harbor with my wife beside me in an open carriage, because apparently winning an island meant discovering new ways to be handsome at low speed.

The road was lined with people.

Every balcony. Every doorway. Workers who had come out of the shipyard that morning when the gates opened. Musicians carrying instruments. Drivers holding their helmets. Women from Blue Hour waving blue scarves. Men who had spent the month trying to beat me now shouting my name like they wanted the horse to understand its responsibility.

“Nigga,” Tank called from the carriage behind us, “sit kinglier.”

“How?”

“I don't know. You the king.”

The horse shook its head.

“Even he tired of you,” I said.

Shawna laughed so hard she had to hold the carriage rail.

The shipyard was open. All the remaining workers on Luc's list had been found alive, along with others whose names hadn't reached us. Some had already left the island. Some stayed to collect wages from the seized race funds. Some simply sat in the sun with food and a phone, doing nothing a rich man could turn into an obligation.

Lark and Mateo went there together before the ceremony. They came back with grease on their hands and a list of people who wanted work at their new garage.

“Good mechanics?” I asked.

“Better than good,” Lark said.

“Nigga, hire them before somebody gets intelligent.”

Mercedes and Porsche had taken over the former guesthouse at the eastern quay for No Second Door. The first thing they removed was the little side entrance marked STAFF ONLY. They didn't tear out the wall. They changed where people were greeted and made the main doors wide enough for everybody's pride.

Alina would help run it.

Rocco invested after Porsche made him say the number without smiling like he expected applause for paying a fair share.

Nero and Cassius claimed the old racing shed. Esteban brought his tools. Inez brought three cars and an opinion about every shelf. Within an hour, the place sounded so alive with argument that I could hear it from the road.

Nigga, some buildings need a family fighting over where the wrench goes before they become home.

At the harbor, the Sovereign Sun waited beneath a forest of flags.

Celadon stood on the bridge in his old captain's coat. Renee stood beside him, one hand on his arm. The crew lined the decks, clean uniforms, shoulders straight. The white bird flew above them all.
