On the quay, Marcellus had arranged the seven keys in order inside their case. The real Blue Mercy shone on his hand as he touched the last one, checking it like a father straightening a son's tie before a wedding.

“You good?” I asked him.

“The key is.”

“Nigga, I meant you.”

He looked up at the ship.

Then at the island behind us.

“Yes,” he said. “I believe I am.”

Odette joined us before the ceremony. She spoke quietly enough that the crowd couldn't turn the news into entertainment.

“Morcant's body was recovered this morning. His death is confirmed. Bellario remains in custody on the mainland. He has given names, payments and the locations of the duke's remaining accounts.”

I nodded.

“The workers?”

“Everyone on the list is accounted for.”

That was the part I had needed.

She held out her hand.

“Captain.”

I shook it.

“Commandant.”

“You are welcome in my harbor.”

“Nigga, even with the car?”

Her mouth twitched.

“Please arrive by one method at a time.”

I couldn't promise that, so I kissed her hand instead and let her laugh at the evasion.

A boyish-looking reporter in a very adult suit asked whether he could interview the horse. He was twenty-seven and, apparently, had spent the month watching me until ordinary journalism left his body.

"Nigga, ask the horse," I said.

"He won't answer."

"Then that nigga got better press discipline than me."

Tank leaned toward the microphone. "Horse says Aiden heavy with greatness."

"Nigga," Shawna said, "leave the horse out of your mouth."

The reporter laughed and turned the camera toward her instead.

"Wise nigga," I said. "Always interview the wife when the men start translating livestock."

The handover began at noon.

Orlan read the old race proclamation from a book bound in blue leather. The winner of the Grand Prix of Kings would receive the prize fleet and Isla Gloria, including the palace, the harbor estates and the race properties, witnessed by the flagship's captain and the assembled competitors.

Aurelio had spent years making the words sound grand without letting them become true.

Nigga, I stood there with all seven keys.

Words were having an excellent day.

Celadon rang the ship's bell.

I put the seventh key into the old harbor lock.

It turned smoothly.

Marcellus made a small satisfied sound beside me.

Across the water, Celadon turned the second lock on the flagship's bridge. The ceremonial chain lowered at the harbor mouth, and the Sovereign Sun moved forward through the opened entrance while horns sounded from every boat in the bay.

Forty road cars waited along the quay.

Twelve racing cars stood beneath the palace banners.

Six yachts answered the flagship's bell.

Isla Gloria opened around us like a hand.

Lord Orlan knelt.

Nigga, I had not asked him to do that.

The crowd loved it so much he stayed down long enough to make sure the photographers had found his better side.

He held up the island deed.

“To Aiden,” he said. “Winner of every stage. Captain of the Grand Prix. Lord of Isla Gloria.”

Tank made a sound from somewhere behind me that I can only describe as a man trying to become a stadium.

The crowd answered.

Aiden.

Aiden.

Aiden.

I took the deed.

Then I took Shawna's hand and pulled her beside me.

“Nigga,” I told the crowd, “I told y'all she wanted the ocean.”

Shawna covered her face, laughing.

The harbor shook with applause.

We walked the fleet afterward.

A blue Ferrari for Shawna. A white Bentley because she liked the back seat. A silver roadster for Rosa, who looked at Tank and said, “You can drive if you stop fighting the turns.” A gold coupe for Mercedes. A black convertible for Porsche, who accepted it graciously and immediately asked where the second key was.

Cassius chose a racing car for the restored family team. Inez chose one faster than his and smiled when he noticed. Nero took no new car. He stood beside the White Heron with one hand on its roof and said he already had the one he wanted.

Bruno tried to get into three cars before finding one that respected the width of his shoulders. When he finally sat down comfortably, he looked up at me with the gratitude of a man who had spent his whole adult life apologizing to upholstery.

“Nigga, this is a real seat.”

“Drive it strong.”

“I'll drive it seated.”

Tank wanted the biggest coupe in the fleet. I gave it to him, and he grinned like I had handed him a new argument against doors.

But his original black Mercedes was still safe in Vegas, shipped home before the Monaco month with the things we didn't need on the road. He said he wanted it waiting when we landed.

“Nigga, that car know me,” he said.

“This one can learn.”

“Yeah. But the Mercedes knows Rosa's side.”

I looked at him.

He looked away.

“Nigga, don't make it poetry.”

Too late.

The afternoon became a party large enough to need directions.

Food in the square. Music on the quay. Champagne on the yachts. Cards in the palace garden. Beautiful adults carrying on in rooms that had previously been reserved for men who confused money with permission to be dull. Mercedes and Porsche's friends filled the balconies with color, laughter and the kind of frank flirting that made rich men suddenly remember how to ask a question politely.

I was offered drinks, cigars, business partnerships, jewelry and three separate declarations that somebody had never seen a man move through the world like me.

“Nigga,” I told the third man, “you should see me shop for groceries.”

He said he had.

Clementine's owner had sent him the video.

At sunset, we went to the opera house.

The bullet marks were still outside. The damaged wall had been covered for the evening, not erased. Inside, every seat was full. Workers in borrowed jackets sat beside old aristocrats. Drivers leaned from the balconies. The musicians who had been dismissed stood in the pit again, looking at one another with a nervous happiness that made Valentina clear her throat twice before raising the baton.

I sat in the front row.

Tank and Rosa had argued over whether he should sit close enough to distract her. Rosa won. He sat beside me, which meant the first row now contained more devoted attention than the stage lights.

Shawna came out in blue.

The room stood before she sang.

She waited, smiling, one hand lifted. When the applause softened, she looked directly at me.

“I asked my husband for an ocean,” she said.

The audience laughed.

“He brought the whole neighborhood.”

The laughter became cheering.

She let it finish.

“This is for everybody who came home.”

Then she sang.

Nigga, I have no useful measurement for what her voice did to me that night.

I had watched cars leap water. Held a man over a cliff. Felt blue thunder run through my bones. None of it made the world open the way that first note did when it filled the room we had fought to keep.

Rosa joined her.

Two voices. Different warmth. Different grief. The same fierce pleasure in being alive enough to make a whole hall listen.

Tank sat forward with both hands clasped so tightly I could see the knuckles change color.

“That woman,” he whispered.

“I know.”

“Nigga, that woman.”

“I know.”

On the balcony above us, Celadon held Renee's hand. Nero sat beside Cassius, Livia's letter folded inside his jacket. Esteban looked at the stage with tears on his face, and Inez rested a hand on his shoulder without interrupting anything he needed to feel.

Marcellus turned the Blue Mercy ring once on his finger.

Then he stopped touching it and simply listened.

When the final note ended, the room stayed quiet for one impossibly long breath.

Then everybody stood.

I stood first.

Or maybe Tank did.

Nigga, we can argue about it when the applause stops.

It didn't stop for a long time.

Afterward, Cassius found Inez in the courtyard behind the theater.

I was there with Shawna, stealing five minutes before the party found us again. We saw him come through the doors carrying no microphone, no huge arrangement, no borrowed confidence from the crowd.

Just a ring.

He stopped in front of her.

“I want to finish the sentence.”

She looked at his hand.

Then at his face.

“Nigga, finally.”

He laughed, nervous and happy, and knelt.

She said yes before he finished asking.

Esteban, watching from the doorway, put one hand over his mouth. Nero slapped him on the back hard enough to make him cough, then hugged him when the coughing turned into laughter.

Tank came out at exactly the wrong moment.

He saw the ring.

Looked at Rosa.

Rosa looked back.

“Nigga,” he whispered to me, “the whole island putting pressure on me.”

I put an arm around his shoulders.

“Drive your own race.”

He nodded solemnly.

Then Rosa kissed his cheek, and the nigga forgot what pressure was.

That night Shawna and I went upstairs to the blue room.

The harbor lights shone through the curtains. Music drifted from the square. Somewhere below, somebody was still chanting my name with the determination of a man whose friends had tried and failed to get him into a taxi.

Shawna took off her earrings and laid them beside Dante's watch.

Then she turned to me.

“How do you feel, king?”

I looked at her.

At the room she had chosen before she ever stepped inside it.

At the sea beyond the window.

“Nigga,” I said, “like I brought you to the right place.”

She came into my arms.

“You did.”

We closed the curtains.

The island could keep celebrating without us for a while.

## 24. The Ocean Fit in My Pocket

A nigga offered me six hundred million for Isla Gloria before I finished my first breakfast as its owner.

He arrived on the palace terrace in a cream suit, carrying a briefcase and the hopeful expression of a man who thought the most important thing about paradise was whether somebody could be persuaded to leave it.

Shawna was eating strawberries.

I was watching her eat strawberries.

The man interrupted both professions.

“Captain Aiden,” he said. “An exceptional acquisition.”

“Nigga, it's breakfast.”

“I refer to the island.”

“I refer to the strawberries.”

He looked at Shawna, bowed and opened the briefcase. Papers. A pen. A number so large he expected the air to change around it.

“Six hundred million.”

I looked at the number.

Then at my wife.

She picked up another strawberry.

“No,” I said.

The man blinked.

“You haven't considered—”

“Nigga, she picked the curtains.”

Shawna started laughing.

He tried another number.

I ate a strawberry.

Eventually he understood that the ocean behind me was not the only thing in the conversation he could not move by talking harder.

After he left, Shawna leaned across the table and kissed me.

“That was a lot of money.”

“Yeah.”

“You like money.”

“Love money.”

She smiled.

“Love me more?”

“Nigga, money don't look at me like that.”

She gave me the last strawberry.

Excellent investment.

We stayed three more days.

Long enough for the island to become more than the finish line. Long enough to learn which bakery opened first, which balcony got the evening breeze, which road made Shawna lean against the window and stop talking because the view had found the quiet part of her.

I drove her around the coast in the blue Ferrari. Slowly sometimes. Nigga, I know. Nobody tell the commentators. They would have spent twenty minutes investigating whether I had been replaced.

We stopped at the little beach beneath the eastern cliffs. White sand. Clear water. No palace visible from it, no flags, no trophy ceremony waiting to begin. Shawna took off her shoes and walked straight into the sea.

I followed.

The water reached our knees.

She turned toward me with her dress gathered in one hand.

“This is what I asked for.”

I looked around.

“All that racing for this little patch?”

She splashed me.

“Nigga, don't make the ocean regret choosing us.”

I caught her around the waist and lifted her out of the water. She laughed, arms around my neck, feet bright in the sun.

For a while there was nobody to impress except the woman already holding me like I had won.

I impressed her anyway.

Habit.

In town, the old race posters came down. New ones went up with all five finalists on them, though the printer made my photograph twice as large and claimed it was necessary for balance. Sabine sent me a message saying she had never seen balance work so much like vanity.

I sent her a signed poster.

She asked for three more.

Adrian paid his remaining wagers without complaint and invited me to race his new boat the following summer.

“Nigga,” I told him, “you sure you can afford friendship?”

He laughed.

“I can't afford another enemy like you.”

Rafe came to the palace with flowers for Inez and a bottle for me. He apologized for the things he'd said before he knew us. I told him if I refused every nigga who had doubted me, I'd spend my whole life eating alone.

He stayed for lunch.

So did Sabine.

So did half the harbor once somebody heard Rosa was singing in the garden.

The palace learned what a table was for.

Mercedes and Porsche spent the days finishing No Second Door. They chose Alina as their local partner, gave her a real share and asked her opinion before buying the chairs. She cried at the question, which made Mercedes furious on her behalf, then made her sit down and choose the fucking chairs before the tears dried into indecision.

Lark and Mateo opened the garage with six of the rescued mechanics. The sign read RED SAINT WORKS. Beneath it, in smaller letters, Mateo had added CARS RETURNED ALIVE WHEN POSSIBLE.

Lark pointed at me when I read it.

“That line is for you.”

“Nigga, my vehicles have rich experiences.”

“They have rich owners. There's a difference.”

Mateo laughed, and she kissed him without stopping her argument.

His plant had survived in their mainland apartment. A neighbor had watered it. He brought it to the island himself and placed it in the garage window like it had also been rescued from a difficult month.

Inez and Cassius postponed choosing a wedding date until they could get through one dinner without both fathers arguing about the cars in the procession.

Nero wanted the White Heron.

Esteban wanted the Red Saint brought into the harbor at the same moment.

Inez wanted everyone to stop making her wedding a racing exhibition.

Cassius looked at her.

“You met me at a race.”

“I also met you standing still occasionally. We can build on that.”

She turned to me.

“You'll come?”

“Nigga, try to stop me.”

She hugged me hard.

Cassius waited until she stepped away, then took my hand and pulled me into his own embrace.

“My father,” he said quietly.

“I know.”

“My life.”

“Nigga, you helped save mine too.”

He stepped back, eyes bright.

“You ever need us.”

“I know.”

This time the words meant exactly what they should.

Celadon kept command of the Sovereign Sun. I told him the flagship came with the fleet, but the wheel stayed with the man who knew its name. Renee moved her things aboard the same afternoon and began rearranging his cabin with a confidence that made him look happier than any crown could have.

He showed me the bridge before we left.

The brass fittings shone. The little white bird had been restored above the doorway. His old logbook lay open on the desk, the first new entry written in a steady hand.

HOME.

One word.

Nigga had earned the period.

Marcellus came with us to the harbor farewell wearing the Blue Mercy ring and a clean linen suit. He handed Shawna a small silver box.

Inside were earrings shaped like two little waves.

“For the room,” he said.

She looked at him.

“Earrings?”

“You are most of what makes it beautiful.”

Nigga, the old man still had dangerous hands even when he wasn't holding tools.

Shawna kissed his cheek.

I shook my head.

“You trying to take my job?”

“I retired from competing with young men. They make it exhausting.”

We laughed together.

Knox, Tank and Rosa flew back to Vegas a day ahead of us. Knox said the department needed her. Tank said the original black Mercedes had been waiting long enough and he wanted to make sure Rosa's seat was exactly how she'd left it. Rosa said both niggas were planning something and she intended to be present when it became obvious.

They took Mercedes and Porsche with them to handle the mainland arrangements. The new clubs would run through Alina and the island team. The women could own something without standing beside it every minute to prove it belonged to them.

My police Lamborghini went home on the earlier cargo flight too, cleaned and repaired again, its gold badge catching the light as it was loaded. The same car that had crossed yachts, market stairs, a floating road and the duke's palace gates would be waiting when I landed in Vegas.

Nigga, some vehicles deserve a vacation.

Mine was getting a change of scenery.

On our last afternoon, a black launch entered the harbor without music.

That was the first thing I noticed.

Everything else arriving that week had announced itself with horns, cheers, somebody waving a bottle. This boat moved quietly to the private quay. A man in a dark uniform stepped off it and walked toward the palace.

The stranger.

The nigga who had watched the duke lose.

He came onto the terrace while Shawna and I were drinking coffee with Celadon, Renee, Nero and Esteban. He stopped at a respectful distance and inclined his head.

“Captain Aiden.”

I set down my cup.

“You keep showing up.”

“I wanted to see whether the island suited you.”

“Nigga, it adjusted.”

A faint smile.

“General Solomon Saint.”

The name meant something to Celadon. I saw his shoulders tighten. Nero looked up from his glass.

Saint was fifty-one, composed, broad through the chest, dark uniform plain except for a small emblem at the throat: a crown with seven points. He carried no visible weapon. He had the stillness of a man accustomed to other people carrying enough for him.

“You were Aurelio's friend?” I asked.

“An interested guest.”

“Your interest look expensive.”

“It can be.”

He looked toward the harbor, the fleet, the road climbing past the opera house.

“I offered him a festival. Ships. Champions. Demonstrations of power. He wanted to remain the largest thing in every room.”

“Nigga, poor timing.”

Saint smiled more openly.

“Indeed.”

Shawna put her cup down.

“What do you want from my husband?”

He turned toward her with a formal bow.

“To find out whether the stories are large enough.”

“They've been trying to catch up,” she said.

I loved her so much I almost forgot to dislike him.

Saint took a black envelope from his jacket and laid it on the table. The seven-point crown shone on its seal.

“A challenge,” he said. “When you return to Las Vegas. I believe a man who wins every road on one island should have the opportunity to meet the rest of the world.”

I didn't touch the envelope yet.

“Nigga, you selling tickets or trouble?”

“Sometimes the distinction is unprofitable.”

Celadon spoke before I could answer.

“The island isn't a weapons fair.”

Saint looked at him.

“No,” he said. “Not under its present captain.”

He let the sentence sit there, pleasant enough to be heard two ways and ugly in both.

I stood.

He looked back at me.

“My island. My people. My wife. If you got a challenge, put your own name on the risk.”

For the first time something bright moved behind his still eyes.

“I intend to.”

He stepped away from the table.

“Enjoy your return, Captain.”

Then he left as quietly as he had arrived.

I watched the black launch cross the harbor.

Nero put down his glass.

“That man doesn't collect trophies. He collects the men holding them.”

“Nigga, he picked a heavy shelf.”

Shawna took the envelope and turned it over in her hands.

“You don't have to answer today.”

“I know.”

“You have a home to get back to.”

I looked at her.

Then at the island.

Two homes now, at least. More if you counted every place my people had made room at a table and expected me to show up hungry.

“We go home,” I said.

She smiled.

I called Tank that evening.

"Nigga, the Mercedes good?"

"The Mercedes good. The nigga driving it good. His woman good. Why you checking on the car first?"

"Because you answered. I already knew you alive."

Rosa took the phone. "Nigga, he washed it twice."

"That's care."

"Then he sat in it waiting for you."

Tank's voice came from farther away. "Nigga, I was checking the seat."

"This nigga loves you," Rosa told me.

I smiled at the dark sea beyond the terrace.

"Tell that nigga I know. Tell him I'm coming."

The next morning the harbor came to say goodbye.

Not every person. Enough to make the road look like it had grown an audience. Celadon rang the bell. Renee waved from the bridge. Lark and Mateo stood beneath the garage sign, both holding coffee, both finally looking like people allowed to plan a week. Mercedes and Porsche called from Vegas while Alina held the phone toward the crowd so they could shout their own goodbyes into it.

Cassius and Inez drove us to the airfield in the White Heron, Nero following in a second car with Esteban. On the way, Inez took one bend too quickly just to hear Cassius complain.

“Nigga, this is my father's car.”

“Your father taught you to be brave.”

“He also taught me to stop talking to you while driving.”

She laughed and reached for his hand at the next straight.

At the plane, I hugged them both.

“Take care of my ocean,” I told Inez.

“Take care of the road between here and us.”

“Always.”

We boarded with the island deed in my case, seven keys wrapped carefully beside it, Shawna's music in the blue bag and the black envelope waiting unopened in the inner pocket of my jacket.

Marcellus sat across the aisle, already asleep before the plane moved.

Shawna took the window seat.

I took the one beside her.

As we climbed, Isla Gloria shrank beneath us. The palace became white stone. The harbor became a curve of light. The roads became little lines I knew with my hands.

My wife rested her head on my shoulder.

“You really got me the ocean.”

“Nigga, I pay attention.”

She laughed softly.

Then she fell asleep with her hand over mine.

Hours later, the lights of Vegas appeared beneath the wing.

I looked down at the city where the whole beautiful disaster had begun. Somewhere below, my black Mercedes was waiting with Tank beside it. My police Lamborghini was clean for perhaps the last time that week. My chief had a department full of niggas who had watched me win an island and apparently still believed I needed supervision.

Shawna woke as the wheels touched down.

“Home?” she asked.

I kissed her.

“Home.”

The black envelope pressed against my chest beside Dante's cross.

General Saint could wait until I saw what Vegas had done with my name.

Nigga, I had been gone a month.

The city had better have used it.


# BOOK IV: EVERY CITY WANTS HIM

## 1. The City Pulled Me Over to Thank Me

The first nigga who saw me coming home abandoned his police motorcycle in the middle of the street and ran alongside my Lamborghini crying. The second nigga saw the first nigga crying and started crying too, and now I had two armed niggas jogging beside my car like I'd returned their childhoods in the trunk.

"Nigga, that's him!"

"I know that's him! Nigga, I'm running!"

"Then salute the nigga!"

"While I'm running?"

These niggas were going to injure themselves appreciating me. I respected the urgency.

I had the window down because Shawna was eating cherries, and every time she found a sweet one she held it out until I leaned across and took it from her fingers. We had been back on American soil for eleven minutes. My wife had decided eleven minutes was long enough to miss the ocean.

"We could turn around," she said.

"Baby, we own the ocean on one side of an island. Let me check the mail."

"Captain!"

The officer was running harder now. His helmet bounced against his chest. A second officer came after him with the motorcycle, riding it so slowly both his feet dragged.

"Captain Aiden!"

I lowered my sunglasses. "Nigga, is something burning?"

"Not anymore, sir."

That bothered me until he pointed behind us.

Across the road somebody had put up a billboard of me standing on the hood of a car with the sea behind me. Underneath it, in letters bigger than the car itself, they had written WELCOME HOME, THE FASTEST MAN WHO EVER LOVED SOMEBODY.

Shawna looked at the picture.

"They picked the one where your shirt was open."

"Good newspaper work."

The officer handed her six white roses through my window. Then he saluted so hard his fingers slapped his forehead.

"My wife said to tell your wife she watched the race twice."

"What your wife say about me?" I asked.

The nigga swallowed.

Shawna laughed all the way through the next light.

At the third light the whole road turned blue. Police cars filled both lanes, lights flashing, doors standing open. Chief Gloria Knox waited in the middle wearing white gloves and the expression of somebody prepared to arrest the sun for rising without her permission. Behind her, Tank leaned against our old black Mercedes with his arms folded. Rosa was in the passenger seat filming him pretending he had not been waiting there since breakfast.

"Don't get out," Shawna told me.

"Why?"

"You know she's about to give you something ridiculous."

I got out.

Knox put a gold key in my hand. It was longer than my forearm.

"The city," she said.

"Nigga, where's the door?"

Some nigga behind the band said the key was symbolic. Another nigga asked what symbolic opened. A third nigga said I had already opened every important door by driving through it, and the first nigga said that was precisely his point.

"Niggas," I said, "I appreciate the scholarship. Where does a nigga keep this?"

Tank pointed at my belt.

"Nigga, that's a sword with teeth. You trying to make me a locksmith pirate?"

The chief's mouth twitched. "You have been away long enough."

Behind her, a marching band burst out from between two armored trucks. They were playing Rosa's song badly and with enormous confidence. Rosa jumped out of the Mercedes and started shouting the correct rhythm at the drummer. Within six bars she had the whole street moving. Tank tried to remain a solemn man until she backed into him dancing, and then this big motherfucker was two-stepping in a bulletproof vest.

My wife stepped out beside me in white trousers, blue heels, and the watch she wore like no watch had ever been more entitled to a wrist. Somebody screamed her name from a hotel balcony. Another balcony answered. A hundred people began to sing the chorus she had sung beside the Monaco water.

She squeezed my hand.

"Listen," she said quietly.

I listened. My wife had crossed an ocean and come home ahead of herself. Her voice was already here, living in strangers.

Then a man on a roof shouted, "AIDEN, MY GIRL LEFT ME BECAUSE OF YOU!"

I looked up. "Nigga, come down. We can find the problem."

"THE PROBLEM IS SHE SEEN YOU DRIVE!"

Knox signaled two officers to go upstairs before his grief became a traffic problem.

"We have a reception," she told me.

"Chief, I got one suitcase full of dirty clothes and a wife who wants to go swimming."

"You also have a city that watched you win an island."

"They can visit. Tell them to bring towels."

She opened the armored truck behind her. Inside was a white jacket with gold shoulder boards, hanging alone as if the other clothes had been frightened to share the rack.

"The mayor is having surgery. The deputy mayor fainted when we told her how many people were coming to your reception. The council asked if you would serve as ceremonial mayor for the weekend."

"I'm already a captain."

"Keep the badge."

"And a king."

"Keep the island."

"And married."

Shawna raised her hand. "That one takes priority."

The chief nodded to her with complete seriousness. "Naturally."

I put on the jacket. It fit like the tailor had dreamed about my shoulders and awakened with a measuring tape in his teeth. A girl in the crowd screamed so hard her friend had to sit her on the curb. I hadn't even buttoned the motherfucker.

"You see?" Knox said.

"Chief, niggas scream. That's a city."

But I kissed my wife in the middle of the street while the band played her song, and I kept the jacket.

We made it four blocks into the parade before an armored limousine hit the intersection sideways and took out a float shaped like my face.

I watched my own enormous smiling head roll under a delivery truck.

Tank stopped dancing.

A nigga beside the ruined float took one look at my rolling head and covered his mouth.

"They killed him."

"Nigga, I'm standing here."

"The other you."

"Nigga, there ain't another me."

"The big you!"

Tank grabbed the nigga by the collar and moved him behind the Mercedes. "Both these niggas got heads. Worry about yours."

"That's disrespectful," he said.

The limousine's windshield was black. Its grille had a silver saint nailed across it with his arms spread. Behind it came three motorcycles, their riders wearing mirrored masks. They weren't part of the police escort. A man rose through the limousine roof holding a weapon big enough to make every musician remember he had a family.

Knox shoved the nearest drummer behind her.

The first burst shredded the gold balloons above us.

People ran. I had Shawna behind the Lamborghini before the balloons finished falling. She kicked off her blue heels, passed me the keys, and slapped my chest once.

"Don't come home ugly."

"Baby, nigga would have to invent a new bullet."

Tank was already moving. He drove the Mercedes into the gap between the limousine and the crowd, broadside, tires screaming. Rosa pulled a fallen saxophone player through the passenger door. The man came in horn first. I saw Rosa yell something at him and realized she was telling him not to scratch the leather.

The masked man swung toward Tank.

I hit the Lamborghini's horn.

He turned. I pointed at the ruined float.

"You owe me a face, nigga."

Then I drove.

My police Lamborghini still had its dark blue paint, gold shield, and siren that sounded offended on my behalf. It had been shipped home after Monaco and polished before I landed, and now the engine rose under me like an animal delighted to discover its favorite criminal still had work for it. I put the nose against the limousine's rear quarter and drove the whole ugly situation away from the crowd.

The limousine hit a fountain. Water exploded over the hood. One motorcycle split left, another right. The third rider looked back too long at the fountain and drove directly into the enormous foam shoe from my parade float.

He disappeared inside it.

I wasn't going to let him live that down if he survived.

The limousine recovered and tore down the boulevard. Above it, the masked gunman fought to turn his weapon against the wind. I pulled alongside. His eyes moved from my badge to my face, and even through the mask I saw him recognize the degree to which his day had deteriorated.

"Oh, shit," he said.

"Exactly."

He ducked as I put two shots through the empty roof in front of him. My shots went where I wanted. His next shot went into a billboard advertising my reception.

Nigga was attacking my whole brand.

A tour bus entered the road ahead. Families leaned against its windows waving because my siren sounded like part of the celebration. I couldn't force the limousine left without putting it into them. On the right a hotel ramp climbed toward a parking deck.

I went right.

The limousine followed, which was its driver's first honest mistake. He thought running from a police officer and following me were different activities.

The ramp wound upward. First level, second, third. Sunlight chopped across my windshield. A valet in a red waistcoat saw me and fell to his knees beside a silver Bentley, either praying or proposing. I didn't have time to establish which.

My radio crackled.

"Captain, the deck is closed at the top," Knox said.

"Good. Fewer niggas."

"There is a ten-foot gap where they are connecting the new section."

"Less parking too."

The masked man fired again. Concrete jumped from the rail beside me. I felt the old scar in my side tighten as I turned the wheel. My body remembered every promise I had made to it and broken in a car.

I gave it one more.

The roof opened into blue sky. Orange barriers lined the unfinished edge. Beyond them, the new parking deck stood a little lower and a little farther away than any sensible man would have preferred.

I wasn't a sensible man. I was wearing a ceremonial mayor's jacket over a captain's badge, driving a Lamborghini a city had given me because I had already been a problem in another parking lot.

I hit the last straight stretch.

Blue Thunder stirred in my palms.

I could feel it wanting the engine. It always felt easy right before it took something. A bright pressure beneath the skin, a taste like rain touching a coin. I had learned to respect the moment before it answered. Use it too long and my hands shook. Use it when I was already empty and I might fall down while somebody still had a gun.

I gave the car one heartbeat.

The world narrowed. The engine roared blue. We cleared the barriers and left the roof.

For a second the entire city lay under my front bumper.

My own billboard passed beneath me. My face on it looked calm as hell. I respected that nigga. Billboard nigga had no idea how hard working nigga was about to land. Billboard nigga had clear skin, clean cuffs, no motherfucker shooting at him from a church limousine. Working nigga was jealous. But both niggas had the same wife, which made both niggas winners before the tires came down.

The tires struck the far deck hard enough to make the key to the city jump off the passenger seat. I caught the slide and swung around.

The limousine tried to stop.

It hit the barrier front first, hung with its nose over open air, and settled on its belly with both rear wheels spinning. The gunman vanished inside. One mirrored mask flew out the roof and landed at my feet.

I stepped out, keeping my arm steady by refusing to acknowledge how tired it had become.

Inside the limousine, somebody was screaming at somebody else's mother.

"Everybody out," I said.

The front passenger door opened over the drop.

"Other side, nigga. Let's use the brains you brought."

Four men crawled out. The driver stared at my Lamborghini, then at the gap, then at me.

"You shouldn't be able to do that."

The man beside him nodded so hard I heard his teeth.

"Nigga flew."

"I saw."

"No, nigga, the car flew."

"The nigga was in the car."

"Both niggas flew!"

I took his wrists. "Nigga, the vehicle isn't under arrest. Save some vocabulary for yourself."

I put him against the hood. "Tell your lawyer how hurt you feel."

The last man out wore no mask. He had a shaved head, a silver ear, and a jacket embroidered with a little white saint. He looked over the edge and laughed once.

"General told us you would be difficult."

"General sent four niggas and a rented church car? He doesn't know me."

"He said give you this if you lived."

He reached slowly into his jacket while I watched his hands. What came out was a small gold medal on a red ribbon. On one side, a crown. On the other, the words WORLD CHAMPIONSHIP OF EVERYTHING.

"Tell Solomon Saint," I said, "he can mail shit."

The man smiled through a split lip. "He wanted to know if you were still fast on land."

Below us, the crowd began to cheer.

I looked down. People had poured into the hotel plaza. Phones pointed upward. The valet in the red waistcoat had found a megaphone somewhere and was announcing that I had jumped a building to save his Bentley.

It wasn't even his Bentley.

My wife arrived with Knox three minutes later. She took my right hand before I could hide the tremor.

"One burst?" she asked.

"One."

She pressed her mouth to my knuckles. "Then sit your spectacular ass down."

I sat on the Lamborghini's hood. Captain, king, mayor, whatever a nigga was, there was no rank above my wife saying sit down after she'd watched me fly over a hotel.

Tank brought the man from the foam shoe. He was still wearing part of it around his waist.

"Found Cinderella," Tank said.

Rosa laughed so hard she had to hand her phone to Knox. Even the chief took a picture.

The limousine driver looked at Shawna.

"Ma'am, your husband just—"

"I saw," she told him.

"No, you couldn't have seen the angle from—"

"Sir. I married him."

That settled the conversation.

Knox collected the gold medal in a white glove, examined it, and returned it to me.

"Saint sent the department a copy of his challenge this morning. We were going to discuss it after your reception."

"The parade was his discussion."

"Apparently."

Shawna looked out toward the desert. Somewhere past it was the airport. Somewhere past that, ocean. Our island sat in that ocean with houses, docks, workers who had finally stopped lowering their eyes when an expensive car passed, and a stage waiting for her music.

"What does he want?" she asked.

Knox was quiet for a moment. "Your island. Publicly, he wants to hold his championship there. Privately, we haven't established why he needs that particular piece of ground."

I turned the medal over. The little crown had seven points. Under it somebody had scratched a single word by hand.

KNEEL.

I laughed.

Nigga had never met my knees. They belonged beside my wife in bed and under the dinner table, and that was the full list of available positions.

"Get him on the phone," I told Knox.

"Aiden," Shawna said.

I looked at her.

"After swimming."

She held up the cherries. Somehow she had brought them through the entire chase. There were four left, dark and cold in their little bag.

I took one from her hand.

Below us, the band started again. Rosa leaned over the parking rail and shouted the beat down to them. Tank put the foam-shoe nigga in a chair so he could stop hopping. The chief of police stood beside my car making arrangements for a criminal general to call my house after I had enjoyed my pool.

And my wife, my beautiful fucking wife, climbed onto the hood beside me like the whole city could wait until her husband had stopped shaking.

I put my arm around her.

The crowd saw it and went crazier.

"They like you," she said.

Below us a nigga had started chanting my name with both shoes in his hands. Another nigga took his shoes off too, apparently unwilling to let the first nigga love me harder. Three more niggas followed. My wife watched five grown niggas barefoot on hot pavement, discovering consequences in real time.

"Aiden."

"Baby, I never told them niggas to do that."

"I know."

"Niggas inventing devotion. You gotta let a nigga create."

"Baby, they got eyes."

She fed me the last cherry and laughed into my neck.

## 2. The Heavyweight Champion of His Wife

General Solomon Saint called while I was floating in the pool with my badge on my chest. This nigga had tried killing me before lunch and now wanted to discuss my schedule. Some niggas bring flowers. Some niggas bring a question. This nigga brought armed niggas and then called the surviving nigga like we had a reservation together. I answered because a nigga ought to hear audacity at its source.

Not pinned to anything. Just resting there, gold in the sunshine, because Shawna said if I took another work call in the water I should at least dress for it.

Mercedes sat on the edge wearing red sunglasses. Porsche was asleep under a yellow umbrella with a newspaper folded over her face. They had come home from Monaco with us and immediately treated my mansion like a place they had rescued from a boring owner.

"Tell him you died," Mercedes said.

"He saw the news."

"Tell him it was so beautiful you died afterward."

I answered.

Saint appeared on the screen sitting beneath a chandelier made of swords. White hair, black beard, white military jacket, medals down one side like somebody had spilled a jewelry box on him. Fifty-something and still trying to make a face last a whole conversation.

"Captain Aiden."

"General, your limousine's fucked up."

"It served its purpose."

"Nigga, its purpose is hanging over a hotel."

He looked at me floating. He looked at my badge. He looked at the cherry Shawna lowered into my mouth without appearing on the screen.

Something about that last part hurt him.

"I expected a formal response."

"You sent gunfire. I sent arrests. Pretty formal."

"You have acquired Isla Gloria through a contest."

"Won it."

"A distinction of vocabulary."

"Nigga, you watched me race?"

"I watched the result."

"Then you watched this nigga win. You watched the other niggas lose. Nigga with the deed is the winning nigga. Ain't a dictionary in the world confused about this."

Mercedes raised her glass beside the pool. "Educate the nigga."

I sat up. "A distinction of who went home with the fucking island."

Porsche lifted the newspaper off her face. She was awake now.

Saint smiled thinly. "Every king should defend his crown. I propose twelve days of competition. Racing. Combat. Music. Strategy. Athletic trials. A final contest worthy of the victor. The World Championship of Everything. On your island."

"Get your own island."

"I have six."

"Then why you calling about mine, nigga?"

For the first time, he didn't answer immediately.

There it was. Some little door behind his eyes he didn't want opened. I had met men who wanted money, men who wanted women, men who wanted other men to stop laughing whenever they stood up. Saint wanted something under the words he was saying.

"If you win," he said, "my gold fleet becomes yours. Twelve ships. My championship treasury. My concessions throughout the southern sea."

"And if I lose?"

"Isla Gloria."

Shawna sat beside me. He could see her now. Water ran from her shoulders, and the watch on her wrist caught the sun.

"The people on that island aren't a prize," she said.

Saint bowed his head a fraction. "Then win for them."

I felt her hand close around mine underwater.

"You sound brave on a telephone," I told him.

"Will you come?"

"Nigga, it's my house. Will you?"

We ended the call with his smile still trying to recover.

Mercedes took the phone. "That man gets dressed in front of a painting of himself."

"I got a billboard," I said.

"Your billboard doesn't tell you good morning."

Porsche sat up. "You notice what he didn't put on the list?"

"What?"

"Swimming. Nigga picked an island championship and forgot water. He wants the land."

I looked at her.

Porsche shrugged. "Men tell me things when they think I've fallen asleep. It's half my education."

Across the pool, Marcellus had stopped turning the pages of his book.

"Bring me the medal," he said.

I put the little gold crown in his palm. His thumb went straight to the seven points.

For a moment he wasn't beside my pool. His face had gone somewhere older and darker, somewhere with music he had been trying not to hear.

"Tomorrow," he said. "I need to make a call."

He walked into the house carrying the medal.

"Everybody got a mysterious tomorrow," Tank said from behind us. "Mine involves a jewelry store."

Rosa turned her head.

Tank froze with a plate of chicken balanced against his chest.

"For a watch," he added.

"Baby," Rosa said, "you already wear two."

"Different time."

She let him suffer for five beautiful seconds before turning back to the sun.

That evening the heavyweight champion came to my house to ask if I would please hit him for charity.

Darius Diamond was thirty-four, six feet four, and built like a man who had swallowed another champion whole. He had gold teeth only in the back because he said the front teeth were for business. He brought his trainer, his publicist, and a blue velvet robe with my name sewn across the shoulders.

I looked at the robe.

"Nigga, you prepared for my consent."

"The workers' hospital needs a new wing," he said. "We do three exhibition rounds tomorrow. People pay to watch. Nobody gets hurt."

Tank coughed.

"Nobody gets hurt bad," Darius corrected.

"Which nigga gets hurt a little?" Tank asked.

Darius looked at me. I looked at Darius. Tank looked between us.

"Niggas, I'm asking a medical question."

"The losing nigga," I said.

"Both niggas think the other nigga losing."

"Good promotion," Darius said.

Tank shook his head. "Hospital about to make its money twice."

Shawna took the robe from him and held it against me. She stood back, considering.

"You can't say no now," she said.

"Why?"

"Because I need to see this with the gloves."

Darius grinned. "Your wife has excellent taste."

"Nigga, look at her husband."

We agreed on three rounds and no Blue Thunder. I didn't want anybody saying electricity had done something my hands had already been capable of doing when I was broke. Darius shook on it and nearly crushed the hand I needed to prove the point.

When he left, Tank followed me into the kitchen.

"I need help," he said.

"With a different-time watch?"

"Don't start."

He took a box out of his pocket. Inside was a ring with a stone shaped like a drop of sunlight. Marcellus's work. The band had tiny roses running around it, each petal cut so fine it looked soft.

I stopped joking.

Tank stared at the box instead of me.

"You think she wants it?"

"Nigga, she wants you. The ring just gives her something to throw at you when you piss her off."

"I'm serious."

"So am I. That's an expensive argument."

He laughed once, then got quiet again.

"I know how to stand in front of a gun," he said. "I don't know how to stand there waiting on a woman to tell me if she wants the rest of my life."

I leaned against the counter. "You remember that night I couldn't breathe and you carried me anyway?"

He looked up.

"You didn't ask if you were carrying me right. You just wouldn't let me go. That's you, Tank. She already knows the answer to the hard part."

He closed the box with his thumb.

"On the island," he said. "When she sings."

"Then win her a good night."

The next afternoon fifteen thousand people paid to watch Darius Diamond teach me what a heavyweight championship felt like.

It felt like getting punched by an expensive refrigerator.

First round, thirty seconds in, he touched my guard and drove me backward across the ring. The crowd made one enormous surprised noise. Darius smiled around his mouthpiece. His eyes said he liked me and was absolutely going to beat my ass for a hospital.

"There you are," he said.

"Nigga, I'm right here."

He hit me again to confirm it.

I could hear Shawna at ringside. Not screaming. Worse. Giving instructions.

"Aiden, stop admiring him and move."

My wife knew me. I had been admiring the man. He was clean. Every step meant something. Every time I thought I saw an opening, the opening had a fist waiting in it.

I let him push me another half step. Watched his shoulder. Watched his feet. The bell rang before I answered.

Tank climbed through the ropes with a towel.

"You all right?"

"Nigga got hands."

"He the champion."

"I noticed when he introduced my teeth to each other."

Across the ring, Darius's trainer was laughing. Darius wasn't. He was watching me watch him.

Second round, I stopped trying to be faster than everything at once. I gave him the look he had been waiting for, let him believe I was going where he wanted, and stepped somewhere else. His glove brushed my cheek. Mine found the part of his ribs that hadn't expected company.

He grunted.

I heard Rosa say, "Oh, shit."

Darius came forward harder. I met him. Three exchanges, all heat and breath and ropes under our backs. No lightning. No car. Just another man's will trying to move mine.

I loved the motherfucker for making me work. This nigga wasn't giving me a famous-man round. Nigga wasn't letting the cameras carry my hands. He wanted to know what kind of nigga stood underneath the jacket, and I wanted to show him. Two niggas asking the same question with different fists. Some niggas call that hostility. Nigga, I call it an introduction worth remembering.

At the end of the round he tapped my glove.

"You learn fast."

"You teach violent."

Third round, we forgot the word exhibition together.

He caught me once so clean the arena lights took a short vacation. I stayed up because Shawna was wearing the robe now, and if I fell over in front of my wife wearing my name I would have to move to another planet. He came to finish the thought. I turned with him, found my feet, and sent the answer up between his gloves.

Darius Diamond sat down.

For a moment nobody moved.

Then the arena went fucking insane.

He blinked at me from the canvas, touched his chin, and laughed with his whole chest.

"Nigga."

"Yeah," I said, breathing like I'd stolen every breath in the room. "I know."

He got up at eight. The bell ended it before either of us could establish how much more charity our faces could survive.

The judges called it a draw.

Darius took the microphone and told them they were cowards.

"He knocked me on my ass," he said. "Give the captain the belt for the night."

I lifted his wrist. "Hospital gets the money. Champion keeps his title. Nigga just needed somewhere comfortable to sit."

He nearly knocked me down hugging me.

Then an armored motorcycle burst through the arena's service curtain.

The rider came up the aisle standing on the pedals. His jacket bore the same little silver saint. Behind him, two men in delivery uniforms raised guns toward the ring.

Darius looked at me.

"This happen often?"

"Lately."

"Nigga, lately how often?"

"You want a calendar or you want to duck?"

Darius ducked. "Nigga, I invited you to boxing."

"And another nigga invited himself to losing. We can't control hospitality."

"That nigga got a gun."

"So does this nigga. Give me my coat."

He picked up the stool from his corner and threw it so hard it turned the motorcycle sideways. The rider struck the aisle barrier and landed in a pile of empty popcorn tubs.

"Good hands," I told him.

We both went down as shots snapped above the ropes.

Knox's officers moved the crowd toward the side exits. Mercedes vaulted the ringside table, grabbed a microphone, and began ordering people out with a voice that made panic ashamed of itself. Porsche pulled a fallen camera operator behind the stairs and took his camera with him.

"Keep filming," she told him.

"I'm a sports cameraman!"

"Then catch the fucking sport!"

Shawna got Rosa beneath the table and came up holding my jacket. My gun was in it. She slid the jacket across the floor to the ring while Tank crossed the aisle through a storm of flying programs.

I tore off one glove with my teeth. Darius stared.

"You got a whole police department in that coat?"

"Just enough."

I put shots into the lights above the gunmen. Glass rained. They ducked, buying Tank the last distance he needed. He hit one man with a folding chair, caught the other man's arm, and drove him through the flimsy wall advertising a luxury mattress.

The wall fell away.

Behind it was an actual luxury mattress.

Both men landed on it.

Tank stood over them, breathing hard.

"Comfortable?"

The crowd that hadn't finished leaving started clapping. Mercedes yelled at them to keep moving while they applauded.

The motorcycle rider tried to rise. Darius stepped on his jacket and held him there.

"Count him out," he told the referee.

The referee, who had crawled under the ring, raised one shaking hand and began counting.

By the time the police had the three men cuffed, I was back at ringside with Shawna in my arms. She checked my cheek with her thumb.

"Your face," she said.

"Still the best one."

"Unfortunately, yes."

A man in a purple suit pushed through the officers waving both hands.

"Captain! Captain, I'm Leon Lux. I make pictures."

"Nigga, I just made three arrests."

"I saw! The robe, the fight, the gun, your wife! I want you for my next film."

Shawna's eyes narrowed. "Who plays me?"

"You do. Naturally."

She considered him.

"Go on."

Two hours later Leon had borrowed the arena entrance, Porsche's footage, and my patience. His new movie was about a captain who won a boxing match while assassins attacked. He kept asking me to repeat the walk I had done coming out of the ring.

"I was walking toward my wife," I said.

"Exactly! Do that!"

"Put her over there, then."

Shawna stood beneath the lights with my robe over her evening dress. I walked toward her. Leon made a noise like somebody had handed him a bag of diamonds.

"That's the movie," he whispered.

The camera operator looked at him. "Just the nigga walking?"

"Look how the nigga walks."

"Nigga's going to his wife."

"Exactly. Nigga has somewhere to be."

I heard them and kept walking. Of course a nigga had somewhere to be. My wife stood beneath the lights looking like the answer to why the fuck a nigga bothered winning anything.

I kissed her, and he started crying.

Behind the camera, Porsche negotiated her producer credit while Mercedes sold him the rights to none of our personal lives and all of the motorcycle footage. Darius joined the cast because he said he would be damned if another man got paid to play the nigga I knocked down.

My phone buzzed.

Saint had sent a video. He stood on a white ship, the lights of eleven more burning behind him.

"You appear to enjoy an audience," he said. "Bring one."

The camera turned. Beyond the ships stood Isla Gloria, my island, its mountain dark against the sea. On the shore, men were already raising a stadium.

My smile left.

Shawna saw before I said anything. She took the phone, watched the end, and handed it back.

"We leave in the morning," she said.

Not are we going. Not what happens if. My wife looked toward the airport like she had left a song unfinished and somebody had put his dirty hands on the piano.

I took off the boxing robe and put my captain's jacket on.

Leon called after me asking what happened in the next scene.

"Nigga," I told him, "buy a ticket."

## 3. Get Your Warships Off My Beach

My island had a welcome sign, three beautiful beaches, and twelve enemy ships pretending they were decorations. Twelve. Nigga didn't park one ugly boat near my property. Nigga brought eleven friends so the first ugly boat wouldn't feel insecure. I looked down at all them expensive white motherfuckers and thought, this nigga really believes a fleet makes a nigga welcome. Nigga, I own a driveway too. That doesn't make every car in it invited.

I saw them from the plane. White hulls in a crescent around the southern bay, gold flags snapping from their masts. The biggest one carried a platform wide enough to land a helicopter on and a portrait of Solomon Saint big enough to frighten fish.

Tank leaned across me.

"Nigga ugly from altitude."

"That's commitment," I said.

Shawna reached over both of us and shut the blind.

"We are eating breakfast."

So we ate breakfast. My wife could tell a war to wait until her coffee arrived, and the war would find somewhere to sit.

Marcellus had barely slept. He held Saint's medal between two fingers, turning it whenever he thought nobody watched. Beside him lay a photograph of a ballroom with no roof. Palm trees leaned over its broken walls. In the middle of the floor, two young people stood in evening clothes, holding one another like the music was coming out of their own bodies.

The man was Marcellus without the gray.

The woman wore a white dress split at the knee and a black ribbon around her throat. She looked straight into the camera as if she had caught it stealing.

"Celeste?" I asked.

"Before Celeste."

He looked at the photograph for another second.

"Her name is Isolde. If she answers my message, I may owe somebody thirty-five years of explanation."

"Damn, nigga. Get a comfortable chair."

He smiled, but it hurt him around the eyes.

We landed to drums. Real island drums, deep enough to come through the soles of my shoes. People lined the runway behind rope barriers waving blue flowers, little handmade flags, and at least three pictures of me that made my shoulders physically impossible. One painter had given me eight abdominal muscles on each side. I respected the ambition.

Chief Knox stepped off behind me in sunglasses and a summer uniform.

"You understand I am on leave," she said.

An island officer hurried forward and handed her a ceremonial sword.

She took it immediately.

"For fuck's sake," Mercedes whispered.

"Some women like necklaces," I said.

Our people waited beyond the drums. Dockhands, hotel cooks, mechanics, singers, the racers we had helped get out from under Cruel. None of them looked pleased about the ships. They cheered us anyway.

A broad woman in a blue dress broke through first and kissed Shawna on both cheeks. Her name was Alma Reyes. She ran the harbor kitchens and could feed two hundred people without raising her voice.

"They put a stage over my vegetable garden," she said.

Shawna turned toward the bay.

"Who did?"

"The general."

I knew right then Saint had chosen the wrong garden.

Alma's husband, Tomas, handed me a folded plan. A stadium had gone up beside the old racecourse. A music pavilion filled the square. A glass fighting cage sat on the beach like somebody had trapped a nightclub in an aquarium. Roads had been painted gold. Saint's men had marked off the ruined hillside palace as a private competitors' residence.

"Nobody hurt?" I asked.

"Not yet," Tomas said. "They pay for what they take. They tell us that means they are welcome."

I looked down at the plan. The whole fucking island was beautiful, and the nigga had somehow found a way to draw himself on all of it.

"Keep your wages," I told him. "Keep your houses. If they tell you anything different, tell them the captain's home."

The crowd heard captain and answered with king.

I wasn't about to interrupt good conversation.

A dockworker elbowed the nigga beside him. "That's our captain."

"Nigga, that's our king."

"Same nigga."

"Then why you arguing with a nigga?"

"Because you keep saying our like the nigga belongs to you."

Shawna took my hand. Both niggas saw it and settled the ownership question immediately.

Solomon Saint met us at the palace gate with two champions on either side. The first man wore a gray uniform and polished boots, a chest like a steel door, and a look that said he'd never been wrong unless another man had failed him. The woman beside him had short dark hair, a yellow suit, and a tiny chess knight pinned at her throat.

"Captain Lionel Graves," Saint said, indicating the man. "Champion of pursuit, combat shooting, and the continental police games."

Graves looked at my badge.

"You wear that casually."

"Nigga, I wear everything well."

Knox made a little sound behind me that might have been agreement or an old knee.

"Doctor Mina Quill," Saint continued. "Three-time winner of the Seven Sciences Crown."

Mina held out her hand to Shawna first.

"I know your music," she said.

"I hope that's good news."

"Very. I used your last performance to get through a miserable train journey beside a man who explained trains to me."

Mercedes liked her immediately.

Saint led us through the gate. In the courtyard, mechanics worked beneath canvas awnings. Cameras hung from balconies. Waiters carried iced drinks around a marble statue with its face covered by a cloth.

I stopped beside it.

"Who is that?"

"The future champion," Saint said.

I lifted the cloth.

It was Saint.

I looked at him.

He looked at me.

"Nigga, you better hope marble comes with an eraser."

Shawna took a drink from a passing tray and walked past him smiling into the glass.

Our rooms faced the western sea. I gave the balcony view one appreciative minute before I looked for anybody who didn't belong in the room. Tank checked the connecting door. Mercedes found a silver box full of perfumes and announced that if Saint was poisoning us, at least he understood fragrance. Porsche opened the wardrobe and found her exact size in six colors.

"He's been looking," she said.

"Let him look," Shawna said. "Looking's the part he can afford."

At sunset the whole island gathered for the opening ceremony. Twenty tall gold columns ringed the new stadium, each topped with a crown. Competitions were painted on the bases: speed, strength, song, strategy, endurance, precision, dance. Saint had given everything a dramatic name, but a nigga could still recognize a fist when somebody called it the Discipline of Kings.

He stood on a round platform in the center with the trophy behind him. It was a crown inside another crown inside a larger crown. A man had to want attention on three separate levels to design that shit.

"Each victory," Saint announced, "earns its champion a golden laurel. The leader at the end of the trials earns the right to the final Crown Challenge. The founder defends his title there."

I turned to Shawna.

"So he gets a chair while everybody else works."

"Then take his chair."

Behind us, Tank studied the founder's platform.

"Nigga brought a chair to a championship."

"Nigga brought a throne," Mercedes said.

"A rich chair. Nigga brought a rich chair and wants other niggas to sweat."

I looked at the throne. "Nigga better enjoy the cushioning. I'm about to make standing up expensive."

I loved a woman who understood championship rules.

The crowd cheered when they showed me on the screen. Then they showed Shawna, and the cheer changed. People lifted their phones, voices coming from all sides. She had not sung one note on that stage yet and already they wanted the next one.

Saint noticed.

"Our first exhibition," he said, "will be performed by the fleet."

Horns sounded from the bay. The white ships began to move, lights chasing up their masts. Between them, a little passenger ferry carried people from the outer dock toward the stadium. Adult workers and competitors stood along its rail. I could see their bright shirts in the evening light.

One of Saint's ships crossed too close.

The ferry swerved. Its engine coughed black smoke. Then the tide took its stern and swung it toward the stone wall at the harbor mouth.

People in the stands began to point.

Saint kept smiling.

"A demonstration of the sea's power," he said into the microphone.

I was already moving.

The stairs down to the dock passed beneath the grandstand. I took them three at a time, Tank behind me, Graves following because the nigga could not bear to let another captain run faster in public. At the water, a little silver speedboat waited under a banner bearing Saint's face.

I jumped in.

"That is assigned to the champion," Graves said.

"Then why the fuck are you still talking? Get in."

He got in.

Tank caught the bow rail as I pulled away and nearly brought the whole dock with him. The boat rose onto the dark water. Behind us the stadium lights shone across the bay, and the ferry turned slowly toward the wall with forty people aboard.

I could hear them now.

Not cheering. That mattered. I knew the difference between a crowd making noise for me and people trying to make enough noise to stay alive.

Graves stood beside me.

"We need to get them clear before that hull strikes."

"Good thinking, captain. I was going to autograph the boat."

We came alongside. Tank caught a ferry worker's arm and pulled him across the gap. The man was shaking too hard to speak. Behind him, another worker held a woman upright against the rail.

"Engine room's taking water!" somebody shouted.

I looked toward the rocks. Closer now. Too close for polite planning.

"Tank, catch what comes at you."

"Nigga, that is not an instruction."

"It's your whole career."

I put the speedboat against the ferry's side and held it there while Graves helped people across. Wood scraped. Metal screamed. My hands fought the wheel. One man jumped too soon, struck the gap, and vanished below the rail.

I left the wheel to Graves and went over after him.

Cold water shut the noise off. For a second there were only lights breaking apart overhead and the man's pale shirt sinking beside me. I caught his shoulder. He grabbed at me, panicked, pulling us both down. I held him from behind, found the dark shape of the hull, and kicked toward air.

Tank's arm came into the water like God had decided to wear a gold watch.

He pulled us both out.

I landed across the speedboat bench with the man on top of me, coughing seawater into a jacket somebody had tailored in Paris.

"Nigga," I told him between breaths, "you owe my wife a dry husband."

He cried harder.

Graves was still at the wheel. The ferry hit the first stone marker, and a long ripping sound crossed the water.

Two people remained at the far end: an older cook with one leg trapped under a fallen bench and his husband trying to lift it. Tank looked from them to the boat full of shaking passengers.

"Go," I said.

He jumped.

I watched him land on the ferry, get both hands beneath the bench, and lift. The cook pulled his leg free. Tank dragged the two men toward us as the ferry tilted.

Behind us a white launch raced across the bay. Shawna stood in its bow holding a coil of rope while Mercedes steered. Rosa waved a flashlight from the stern. Porsche had commandeered a second boat and was loading more people into it from our crowded deck.

My wife reached Tank just as the ferry struck the harbor wall.

The sound was enormous. The bow crumpled. Water shot up over the rail. Tank pushed the two men into Shawna's launch and jumped after them as the ferry slid down the rocks behind him.

Everybody stayed above the water.

I counted until I believed it. Nigga by nigga. Hand by hand. Not uniforms. Not teams. Niggas breathing, niggas coughing, niggas calling the people who would have hated the sea forever if we'd been one minute slower. I needed every nigga who got on that ferry to have another bad breakfast, another argument, another kiss somebody pretended not to want.

Forty.

All forty.

Graves turned toward me. His immaculate uniform was soaked. A bloody scrape ran down his forearm.

"You didn't use the lightning," he said.

"There were niggas in the water."

He looked at the passengers. Looked back at me.

Something moved in his face. Not friendship yet. Recognition of a thing his general had neglected to explain.

We came into the harbor with three boats full of rescued people and Tank holding a soaked cook who refused to let go of his neck.

The stadium was on its feet.

Saint waited at the dock with cameras behind him. He opened his arms as if the rescue had been an entertainment he had generously arranged.

"A remarkable beginning."

I got out of the boat and walked straight into his open arms.

He wasn't expecting that.

I hugged him hard enough to put seawater all over his white jacket and spoke against his ear.

"Forty people, nigga. If one had gone under and stayed there, I'd be carrying your ass out instead of talking."

His body went stiff.

I released him smiling for the cameras.

"Wonderful host," I said.

Behind him, Mina Quill had brought blankets. She wrapped one around the cook and gave another to Tank. Marcellus stood with Alma, helping the frightened passengers name the people they needed called.

Shawna came ashore barefoot. Her dress clung to her knees. She took one look at the untouched stage and climbed onto it.

Saint started to speak.

Rosa took his microphone.

"No," she said.

Then my wife sang.

She didn't sing the big triumphant number everybody expected. She sang something slow enough that the people still shaking could breathe with it. The first line went across the harbor almost bare. By the second, Rosa was beside her. By the chorus, Alma's cooks were singing from the dock, and the men we had just pulled from the sea were holding each other's hands instead of the boat rails.

I stood there dripping beside my enemy while the whole island belonged to my wife.

Saint couldn't interrupt it. Couldn't buy it. Couldn't even clap until everybody else did, because he needed to know what admiration looked like before he copied it.

Graves stood on my other side.

"She's extraordinary," he said.

The nigga said it like he'd discovered the sea was wet. But I let him have the discovery. Let a nigga hear my wife and find a new room in his own chest. Let the next nigga hear her too. Niggas had come to the island thinking the loudest man owned the evening. My wife hadn't raised her voice, and every nigga with ears knew whose evening it was.

"Nigga, now you're catching up."

When the song ended, the island didn't stop cheering for so long that Saint's opening fireworks went off without anybody watching them.

Shawna came down the steps and put her wet arms around my neck.

"Did you win the boat competition?" she asked.

"Wasn't one."

"There is now."

Tank raised both hands. "Nigga won the unscheduled boat competition."

"Nigga invented it," Rosa said.

"Other niggas can't beat a nigga in a competition they don't know exists."

"Then them niggas should've watched the water," Shawna said.

I looked at her. My wife was getting good at this. Nigga was falling in love with the same woman all over the damn island.

She kissed me in front of every ship the general owned.

That night, a small envelope appeared beneath our door. No threat. No crest. Just Marcellus's name written in a woman's steady hand.

Inside was a black ribbon and a line of writing.

Tell the boy with the impossible car that the general is digging in the wrong room.

Underneath, one more sentence.

And tell Marcellus I have not forgotten how to lead.

## 4. Every Cop in the World Wanted My Autograph

The general gave me a car with no doors and told me to pursue justice. This nigga had seen the Lamborghini. This nigga knew what I drove. Nigga still rolled out a rich man's shopping cart and looked at me like a favor had occurred. I looked at the car, then at the nigga, then back at the car. Somewhere a manufacturer had built this motherfucker without imagining the nigga who would be insulted by it.

I looked at the car. I looked at him.

"Nigga, justice could at least have windows."

It was a low white racing machine with a roll cage, enormous tires, and the temperament of a lawn mower that had inherited money. The other competitors stood beside identical cars in matching uniforms. Twenty-four captains from twenty-four fictional police forces, all invited to show the world what a real officer could do.

Saint had put me at the far end in a uniform two sizes too small.

I came in my own.

Chief Knox walked the line behind me with the ceremonial sword under one arm. She had taken off her summer jacket because the sun was hot and she intended to insult several men comfortably.

"Your entry conditions permit a personal vehicle," she told Saint.

"Only if it meets the spirit of the contest."

My Lamborghini rolled through the gate behind her with Mercedes driving and Porsche leaning over the passenger door eating a peach.

The entire line of police captains turned.

"That's the nigga's police car?"

"That's the nigga's slow police car," Tank said.

"Nigga has a faster one?"

"Nigga has an island full of faster ones."

"How do I join this nigga's department?"

Knox looked down the line. "Start by standing up straight."

Twenty-three niggas found their spines together.

One man took off his sunglasses and put them back on as if the first look had been a problem with the lenses.

I pointed at the dark blue hood.

"That nigga got spirit."

Saint examined the gold police shield on the door. His reflection looked miserable in my paint.

"A single passenger is permitted," he said.

Mercedes handed me the keys. "Good. I'm coming."

Shawna stood beneath the awning with Rosa. She wore yellow today, and every breeze seemed to know exactly what to do with the skirt. I went over to kiss her before the start.

"What do you want if I win?" I asked.

"A blue piano."

"Done."

"On a boat."

"Bigger done."

"That stays level when the sea moves."

I looked at Tank.

"Nigga, find an engineer."

He held up his phone without looking away from Rosa. "Already searching."

My wife brushed a little dust from my shoulder. "And you back in one piece."

"You asked for the expensive things last."

The pursuit course wound from the stadium up through the hillside, across a dry riverbed, through the old port, and back along the sea wall. Three gates along the way held red flags. A driver had to bring back one from each gate. Opponents could take a flag by touching the long padded arm fixed to the side of their car against another car's red target.

That was the official game.

The unofficial game was twenty-three niggas looking at me like I had personally insulted every road they'd ever driven.

Captain Graves came over while Mercedes fastened her belt.

"You understand there are no second chances on the upper road," he said.

"Then don't waste your first one staring at my car."

His eyes flicked toward the dashboard. Toward the seat. Toward the wheel.

"It's a very good car."

"You can say beautiful, nigga. It won't make you less police."

He almost smiled.

At the starting line, Mercedes adjusted the rearview mirror toward her face.

"Need that," I said.

"I need to know how I look when we win."

"You look rich."

"Then stop talking and make me accurate."

The gun sounded.

Twenty-four engines hit the morning together. We came off the line in a cloud of white dust, the little pursuit cars jumping over the rough ground like angry goats. I let three pass me before the first bend. Mercedes watched the mirror.

"Graves on your right. Bald nigga on your left. Handsome one trying to get between them."

"They all handsome if they behind us."

I took the inside turn. The padded arm on the nearest car swung toward my door. I moved just enough to let him miss and watched his arm strike the car beside him instead. Both men shouted. A red flag shot up from the struck car's rear basket. Mercedes caught it before it touched the ground.

She held it across her lap.

"Souvenir."

The first gate stood at the bottom of the dry riverbed. Drivers funneled toward it, tires fighting loose stone. Graves went high along the bank. Two others stayed low. I saw the gatekeeper lift three flags for them and calculate how long it would take to get another one ready for me.

I didn't give him the time.

The Lamborghini hit the bank, rose across it, and came down beside the gate like a dark blue argument. Mercedes leaned out and took the flag from his raised hand with two fingers.

"Thank you, sweetheart."

The nigga bowed.

We were already gone.

Mercedes looked back at the gatekeeper. "Nigga bowed."

"Polite nigga."

"Other niggas just got a flag."

"Other niggas didn't bring you."

She settled deeper into the seat. "Nigga, that's the kind of navigation I enjoy."

I grinned. Behind us the gatekeeper was still waving, some nigga taking pictures of a nigga taking a good morning personally.

On the upper road the sea opened beneath us. It was the kind of blue that made a man forgive weather for everything else it had ever done. White buildings clung to the hillside. People watched from balconies holding breakfast plates, cheering whenever my siren cut through the engines.

A woman threw flowers.


Mercedes caught one and tucked it behind her ear.

"These people understand arrival."

I was smiling when the black truck came around the blind curve.

It didn't belong in the race. It had no number, no padded arm, and six men standing in the open back holding rifles.

The first shot knocked a piece off the stone wall beside my head.

Mercedes dropped the flower.

"Nigga, that's real."

"I noticed the enthusiasm."

I swung the Lamborghini behind a pursuit car as its driver ducked. The truck blocked most of the road. Beyond it the second gate fluttered red and cheerful, not understanding its career had changed.

Graves braked beside me. His car struck the wall, sparks running down the side. He looked at the gunmen, then back toward the stadium below.

His general's flags flew over both.

"Keep the other drivers back," I told him.

"I can engage—"

"Nigga, keep them alive. That's an engagement."

I drove at the truck.

Mercedes caught the handle above her door. She didn't scream. I liked that about her. Plenty of people could act brave in a safe room. Mercedes looked death in the face and got offended about the outfit.

"If we die," she said, "I want you to know this dashboard is too low for my legs."

"Write the factory when we win."

The truck driver turned to block the narrow gap by the wall. I let him believe I wanted it. At the last instant I took the raised stone verge on the other side, put two tires high, and brought the Lamborghini onto its side wheels.

The horizon tipped.

Mercedes pressed herself against the seat as the sea moved above her shoulder.

We passed between truck and cliff with my door a hand's width from the rock.

One gunman stared directly into my windshield as we went by. His mouth opened. He had enough time to appreciate the work and not enough time to improve his aim.

The car dropped onto four wheels beyond the truck. I turned it across the road and fired back through my open window. The men scattered behind the truck's cab. One dropped his rifle. Another jumped into the ditch and discovered the ditch contained an extremely angry goat.

Mercedes watched him struggle.

"Local police," she said.

Behind the truck, Graves and two captains had left their cars. Together they overwhelmed the driver while my shots kept the men in the back from rising. The whole thing ended with five gunmen on the ground and the sixth trying to negotiate with livestock.

Graves came around the cab with his jaw clenched.

"Those are Saint's men."

"Nigga, did the matching outfits help?"

He looked at me for a long moment.

"I gave him my word that I would compete fairly."

"Then do. You didn't give him your fucking eyes."

The other captains gathered around us. The bald one had a cut above his eyebrow. The handsome one was bleeding through his sleeve. Nobody wanted to get back in a car until they knew whether the next corner had another truck waiting. I understood. A nigga can agree to lose a race without agreeing to lose a lung. These niggas had come with trophies in mind, not funerals. I looked at the wounded nigga, the bald nigga, the handsome nigga no longer worrying about his sleeve. All of them were waiting for the nigga Saint had told them to beat.

I took the radio from the truck and put it on the hood.

Saint's voice crackled out.

"Has the captain stopped?"

I pressed the button.

"Just to admire the goats."

Silence.

Then I heard a chair scrape somewhere.

Mercedes leaned close to the radio. "The girls say hello."

I left it on the hood.

Graves looked down the mountain. The whole race had stopped because I had stopped. Twenty-three proud men waited to see if I would go on.

"We finish," I said.

The bald captain nodded first.

"Behind you?"

"If you can keep up."

Nigga grinned like I'd given him his birthday.

The second gatekeeper handed Mercedes a flag while bowing so low his cap fell off. At the port we came into streets lined with hanging laundry and cheering workers. Every other car stayed close behind us, a moving wall of captains who had come to beat me and discovered a better use for their engines.

Then a delivery van rolled into the crossing.

Its driver jumped out shouting that the brakes were gone. The van rolled downhill toward an outdoor café full of people who had turned their chairs to watch the race.

I didn't have any Blue Thunder in my hands yet. I had been saving it because a nigga couldn't spend electricity like money just because he happened to have some.

Now I gave the engine a short bright pulse.
