"Quiet," I told him.

He looked at the drummer.

The drummer waved both sticks.

"Nigga, define quiet."

"Nobody's shooting."

Tank considered that.

"Fair."

The first hour went beautifully.

We played pool. We drank. Cassius told a story about a Monaco hotel that had tried to charge him for damaging a fountain he insisted had damaged him first. Victor described the faculty meeting where my portrait had been approved and did impressions of three professors so accurate Seraphine would have expelled him from dinner if she heard.

Roland listened for a while before laughing.

When he finally did, Tank pointed at him.

"There. Nigga's becoming a person."

"I was a person before."

"You wore a white suit to shoot at my brother. That's a job description."

Roland raised his glass.

"A former job description."

We drank to that.

Downstairs, the women's party grew louder. Adult dancers came through the elevator carrying feathered costumes, bottles, and the bright, tired confidence of people who had finished working and wanted the rest of the night to belong to them. Some of the guests disappeared into private rooms with their partners. Others stayed at the bar telling stories filthy enough to make a priest develop an urgent appointment.

There was cocaine at the far end of the party. There were men acting as if cocaine had personally invented their business plans. There were women rolling their eyes at those men and choosing better company. I had a drink, a pool cue, my brother beside me, and no desire to spend the next morning explaining to Shawna why the ceiling had become interesting.

A woman in silver boots leaned against our table and looked at Tank.

"You're the groom."

He nodded.

"Yeah."

"You look nervous."

"Nigga, people keep noticing."

She smiled.

"Good. Means you know the size of what you're getting."

Tank looked toward the elevator.

Rosa's laugh floated up from below.

The nigga smiled without thinking about it.

"Yeah," he said. "I do."

At the pool table, Anton challenged me to a game.

I accepted because, nigga, a king ought to provide recreational disappointment to his friends.

He was good. Better than I expected. The big man moved around the table with delicate care, lining up shots as if he apologized to the balls before making them obey him.

Tank watched from a chair.

"This nigga got little hands hidden inside the big ones."

Anton smiled.

"Precision is not limited by size."

"That's what I tell Rosa."

The whole table groaned.

"Nigga!" I shouted.

"What? I meant dancing!"

Nobody believed him, including the nigga who had said it.

I won the game with a shot that sent the last ball cleanly into the corner while the cue ball stopped exactly where I wanted it. Anton looked at the table, then at me, and bowed with exaggerated despair.

"Is there anything?"

"Nigga, I still buy the wrong butter occasionally."

"A comforting flaw."

"Don't spread it around."

Tank laughed and reached into his jacket.

A folded paper fell out onto the chair beside him.

I saw it but thought nothing of it.

That was how the trouble started.

Porsche came upstairs looking for a list of song requests. Victor had connected his improved karaoke machine to the stage speakers and announced that he could make any man sound magnificent, a claim I found both interesting and redundant.

"Where's the new song?" Porsche asked.

Tank was at the bar.

Cassius pointed toward the folded paper on the chair.

"There, perhaps."

Perhaps.

Nigga, that word has injured more evenings than cheap tequila.

Porsche took the paper to Victor. Victor read the first line, smiled, and decided it was clearly an emotional number. He handed it to the keyboard player, who began finding chords under it.

Then the lights changed.

The stage microphone came alive.

"Ladies and gentlemen," Victor announced, "a new song from Captain Aiden, prepared especially for the groom."

I turned from the pool table.

"Nigga, what?"

The crowd cheered.

Tank looked at me from the bar, confused.

I looked at Victor.

Victor held up the paper.

Nigga, the man had the confidence of a superhero and the information of a drunk wedding guest. A dangerous combination.

Porsche pushed a microphone into my hand.

"Go. They love you."

"Those are separate issues."

The keyboard player began.

I stepped onto the stage because a nigga can only explain confusion so loudly before a crowd decides it is part of his introduction.

The first line appeared on the screen behind me.

I KNOW HOW TO STAY.

I stared.

The second line followed.

I STAYED IN ROOMS WHERE LEAVING WOULD HAVE BEEN SMARTER.

I looked at Tank.

His face changed.

Nigga, those were his vows.

His private words for Rosa, folded in his pocket while he tried to become the man who could say them out loud without shaking.

Victor had put them on a twelve-foot screen with a slow jam behind them.

Tank started toward the stage.

I lifted my hand.

Not at him.

At the keyboard player.

"Different song."

The musician blinked.

"Captain?"

"Different song, nigga. Give me something with an ass on it."

The drummer laughed and changed the beat.

I took the paper from Victor, folded it, and put it inside my jacket.

Then I turned back toward the crowd.

"Y'all know my brother?"

They cheered.

"Nigga's getting married."

Louder.

"Which means the rest of us are going to have to stop borrowing his shirts without asking Rosa where the good laundry lives."

Tank stopped halfway to the stage.

The crowd laughed.

I began talking over the beat.

Not his vows.

My own ridiculous shit.

"That's my nigga by the bar, looking like a bank vault learned to love. That nigga got a ring, got a woman, got a reason to stop pretending the sofa is a bed. Rosa said dance, the nigga said which direction. Rosa said blue, the nigga bought the ocean a sample card."

The audience howled.

Tank covered his face.

"Nigga, this man stole a boat with his girlfriend beside him and still found time to argue about cake. That's commitment. That's range. That's a nigga who knows love comes with refreshments."

Rosa appeared in the elevator doorway.

Shawna stood beside her.

Both women looked at Tank.

Then at me onstage.

The drummer gave me a flourish.

I pointed at my brother.

"He got hands like trouble and a heart like somebody left the porch light on. He'll drag a nigga out of a fire, then ask whether anybody saved his good jacket. He'll fight the world, but Rosa says sit and the nigga discovers furniture immediately."

Tank laughed despite himself.

Rosa put both hands over her mouth.

I let the beat run beneath the next words.

"That's my brother. That's the nigga. The one who came. The one who stayed. The one I'm standing beside when the whole city watches him get the best thing he ever asked for."

I raised my glass.

"To Tank."

The room rose.

Every nigga at every table stood, cheering, glasses in the air.

Tank looked at me.

The anger had not vanished. I could still see it under the embarrassment, under the love. That was fair. Something private had nearly been taken from him in a room full of people he wanted to trust.

I came off the stage and put the folded paper in his hand.

"Let's talk."

We went onto the quieter side terrace.

The city glowed below us. Music moved through the glass doors behind us. Tank held the paper between two fingers like it might bite him if he looked at it too long.

"You read it?" he asked.

"The first two lines. Same as everybody."

"I didn't give it to you."

"I know."

"Nigga, I been working on that."

"I know."

He looked at me.

"Then why—"

"Porsche thought it was the song list. Cassius guessed. Victor got enthusiastic. A whole chain of niggas with confidence and no fucking evidence."

Tank breathed out.

The explanation did not magically make the feeling leave.

I let him stand with it.

After a while he unfolded the paper.

His own handwriting filled the page, big and careful. Some words crossed out. Others written above them. A man who had never needed help making his fists understood trying to choose exactly what his heart ought to sound like.

"I don't want it to sound like you," he said.

I looked at him.

"Good."

"Everybody expects some big shit when we talk. Some line. Some thing they can yell back. I don't want to get up there and sound like a nigga trying to perform my own wife."

Nigga, that hit me cleanly.

I put my glass on the railing.

"Then don't."

He looked down at the page.

"What if I forget?"

"You know her."

"What if I can't say it?"

"She's gonna be standing right there. Talk to Rosa. Let the rest of us be furniture."

He smiled faintly.

"You gonna manage furniture?"

"Nigga, for five minutes. Because I love you. Don't exploit it."

He laughed.

The terrace door opened.

Victor stepped out with Porsche and Cassius behind him. All three looked sober in the specific way people become sober when they realize a joke nearly cost somebody something they cannot replace with a better bottle.

"Tank," Victor said, "I am sorry. I should have asked."

Porsche nodded.

"Me too."

Cassius put a hand over his heart.

"I guessed. Poorly."

Tank looked at them.

Then at the paper.

"Niggas," he said, "y'all had my wedding vows on a karaoke screen."

Nobody defended it.

For a second the city hummed beneath us.

Then Tank started laughing.

Not because it had never mattered.

Because it still mattered, and the three niggas in front of him knew that now, and nobody was asking him to pretend otherwise.

"I KNOW HOW TO STAY," he sang badly in Victor's dramatic voice.

Porsche doubled over.

Cassius covered his face.

Victor looked mortified, then began laughing too.

"The chord progression was tasteful," he said weakly.

"Nigga, the chord progression was about to get punched."

I laughed until my shoulder hurt.

Rosa came out onto the terrace.

She looked at the five of us.

"You finished?"

Tank straightened.

"Yeah."

She held out her hand.

"Good. I want to dance with the man from that song."

He looked at me.

I pointed toward her.

"Nigga, furniture time. Go."

He went.

We watched them through the doors as she pulled him into the music. He put the folded paper safely inside his jacket before taking her other hand.

Victor leaned beside me at the railing.

"You handled that well."

"Nigga, you almost made my brother marry a bass line."

He winced.

"Yes."

"Next time ask."

"There will not be a next time."

I looked at him.

He considered our history.

"Next time I will ask."

"There you go. Growth."

Inside, Shawna caught my eye and lifted her hand.

I left the niggas on the terrace and went to my wife.

"Nice song," she said.

"Freestyle."

"I noticed. You mentioned yourself less than usual."

"Nigga, it was difficult."

She laughed and put her arms around me.

We danced while Tank and Rosa moved beside us, while the band played, while the city shone below a rooftop full of grown people telling outrageous stories and trying, in their own loud ways, to be good company for the people they had chosen.

Later, Tank handed me the folded vows.

I shook my head.

"Keep them."

He smiled.

"I got what I need."

He tapped his chest once.

Then he looked across the room at Rosa.

Nigga, I believed him.

## 21. Something Old, Something Loud

Marcellus made our wedding rings in a room that smelled of polished wood, hot metal, and the excellent coffee he refused to let Tank touch with sugar.

"Nigga," Tank said, looking into the cup, "why it taste like a serious decision?"

"Because you drink syrup," Marcellus replied.

Rosa laughed and took the cup from her fiancé.

"Give him something sweet before he proposes to the biscuit tray."

We sat around the jeweler's worktable while morning light came through the windows. Outside, Vegas prepared for the wedding with the patience of a city that had already decided patience was somebody else's problem. Florists called. Drivers called. A man from the sound crew called to ask whether the Sky High choir required separate support for the bass section because one member could accidentally levitate equipment when enthusiastic.

Rosa said yes, then demanded to know why nobody had asked that question before ordering the stage.

My wife sat beside me, turning our original wedding ring around her finger.

"We keeping those," I said.

"Of course."

"Nigga, I survived too much for a trade-in policy."

She smiled.

"The new ones go with them."

Marcellus set two narrow bands on the velvet between us. Mine was white gold with a thin blue line through the center. Shawna's matched it, finer at the edges, bright enough to catch the light when she moved without trying to compete with the ring she already wore.

Inside mine, tiny letters read:

I CAME BACK.

Inside hers:

I WAS HERE.

I looked at her.

She held my gaze.

Nigga, I had crossed continents looking for ways to say more, and my wife had put the whole fucking thing inside four words.

"You choose that?" I asked.

She nodded.

"You like it?"

I tried to make a joke.

Nothing came.

Shawna smiled, softer now.

"There he is."

Tank leaned forward.

"What mine say?"

Rosa covered her ring with one hand.

"You find out at the wedding."

"Nigga, I need time to prepare emotionally."

"You had months."

"I used them on flowers."

Marcellus laughed and brought out their rings. Tank's was broad, dark gold, built for a hand that had never encountered a delicate situation it could not accidentally turn into furniture. Rosa's held a small blue stone surrounded by warm gold, a ring that looked good beside both a microphone and a fist.

She stared at it.

Tank stared at her staring.

Nigga, that was his favorite part of being rich. Not the price. The second before the woman he loved found her voice again.

"Baby," she said quietly.

"Yeah?"

"You did good."

The nigga looked down at his coffee like he needed somewhere private to put his face.

I put a hand on his shoulder.

"Don't fall apart before the fitting. We need your measurements stable."

He laughed and shoved my hand away.

After they left to argue with the tailor, Shawna took Dante's watch off her wrist and laid it beside the rings.

Marcellus picked it up carefully.

"The clasp?"

"A little loose," she said. "After the bridge."

He examined it beneath the lamp.

I watched his hands move over the watch he had known in a different part of the story, before I stood inside it wearing a dead man's cross and wanting a living woman's whole heart.

The old jealousy did not rise.

That surprised me for half a breath.

Then I realized it had been quiet for a long time and I had finally stopped listening for it.

Shawna looked at me.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"Nigga, that's not your nothing face."

I touched the cross beneath my shirt.

"I was thinking about the first night. That watch on your wrist."

She smiled faintly.

"You thought it meant I was leaving."

"I thought a lot of stupid shit with excellent confidence."

"Past tense?"

"Nigga, let me grow for a minute."

She laughed.

Marcellus took the watch into the adjoining workroom, leaving us alone at the table.

Shawna rested her head against my shoulder.

"I'm wearing it tomorrow."

"I know."

"And your rings."

"I know that too."

"And a dress you're going to embarrass yourself about."

I turned toward her.

"Nigga, why you hide the important information at the end?"

She kissed me.

The watch ticked softly from the other room while Marcellus worked. It was an ordinary sound now. A little machine keeping time. No accusation. No contest. Just something a woman I loved had carried through days I could not change and into a morning where she had already chosen where to sit.

I put my arm around her.

"You think he would've liked me?" I asked.

She considered it seriously.

Then she smiled.

"He would have thought you were unbearable."

"Nigga, fair."

"And he would have laughed."

"At me?"

"With you. Eventually. After you stopped introducing yourself to every mirror."

"That's an important professional relationship."

She laughed against my chest.

I held her there until Marcellus returned.

He handed back the watch, repaired and shining.

Then he opened a small box of his own.

Blue Mercy lay inside.

The stone caught the light with that deep blue fire I had seen men lose their minds trying to own. It had crossed prisons, marriages, lies, dead hands, rich rooms. Now it rested in the palm of the man whose love had given it meaning before any of those niggas tried to put a price on it.

"You wearing it?" I asked.

He nodded.

"At the wedding."

"Good."

"I have kept it in the pouch long enough."

He slid the ring onto his finger. It fit. The old man's hand trembled slightly, then steadied.

Shawna reached across and touched it.

"Beautiful."

"She was," he said.

We did not correct him.

He took Celeste's letter from a drawer. The paper had been folded and unfolded so many times its creases seemed part of the handwriting. He looked at her name at the bottom, smiled to himself, and put it back beside a photograph.

Then he closed the drawer.

"Now," he said, "show me what you intend to wear with my work."

Nigga, the man had returned to his profession. I respected the shift.

The afternoon fitting took place at the mansion because the tailor had looked at the guest list and decided his shop was not structurally prepared.

Tank stood on a low platform in a blue suit while three people circled him with pins. He held his arms out like a dangerous angel waiting for somebody to finish making wings.

"Too tight?" the tailor asked.

Tank flexed.

A seam made a small sound.

The tailor closed his eyes.

"Please do not answer physically."

I laughed from the next platform.

"Nigga, he asked."

My own suit was midnight blue, dark enough to look black until the light found it. The jacket fit around the sling Vega still insisted I wear when I was not pretending the doctor could not see me. A narrow opening inside kept the badge where I could reach it, because Knox said she refused to attend a wedding where her best officer had to undress before becoming a problem.

The tailor adjusted my collar.

Then he stepped back.

Then farther back.

"What?" I asked.

"I need perspective."

"Nigga, it's a suit."

"On you, Captain, it has become an event."

Tank pointed at him.

"That nigga understands the assignment."

Rosa came in to check the colors.

She saw Tank.

Stopped.

Then put both hands over her mouth.

Tank looked down at himself, alarmed.

"Baby?"

She shook her head.

The nigga stepped off the platform so fast the tailor nearly fainted.

"What's wrong?"

"Nothing," she said through her fingers. "You look—"

She could not finish.

Tank went still.

Then he smiled, slow and astonished.

I looked away before the moment became something I had stolen by watching too closely.

On the terrace, Knox and Seraphine shared a bottle of wine while discussing the logistics of putting a floating choir over a city full of fireworks enthusiasts.

"They will remain at a sensible altitude," Seraphine said.

Knox looked at me through the open doors.

"My understanding of sensible has suffered recently."

"The captain does encourage revision."

"That's one word."

They laughed together. Two women who had spent years commanding rooms found it pleasant to sit in one where nobody needed rescuing for at least twenty minutes.

Magnolia and Bernard argued over table placements. Cassius and Inez arrived with both fathers, who immediately began correcting each other's memories of old races. Mercedes and Porsche brought a guest list covered in lipstick marks and changes. Liora called from the First Dance to say the airship was ready. Sienna's musicians rehearsed in the garden. June and Adrian arrived late, tired, and smiling like two niggas hiding a mechanical surprise.

Shawna remained upstairs.

I tried to go find her.

Rosa blocked the stairs.

"No."

"This my house."

"And that dress is none of your business until tomorrow."

"Nigga, I'm the groom."

"That's why you under restriction."

Tank came up beside me.

"We could go through the balcony."

Rosa looked at him.

He stepped backward.

"I was identifying a security concern."

I laughed so hard the tailor shouted from the other room that my shoulders were moving again.

That night, after the guests left and the house quieted, Shawna came downstairs wearing one of my shirts.

No wedding dress.

No jewels except the rings she already wore and the watch ticking on her wrist.

She sat beside me on the sofa and put her feet in my lap.

"You ready?"

I looked at her.

Nigga, I had been ready in a motel with a bullet in my side. Ready in a hospital while pretending pain did not frighten me. Ready on a floating school, on a racecourse, on a broken bridge with my hands refusing to work.

But that night I was ready in a quieter way.

No gun in my hand.

No door to break.

Just the woman, the house, and the next morning.

"Yeah," I said.

She smiled.

"Me too."

We stayed on the sofa until the city lights went soft beyond the windows, and for once I let tomorrow arrive without trying to beat it there.

## 22. Two Weddings and the Whole Fucking World

On the morning of the wedding, Tank forgot how to tie a tie.

This nigga had driven through gunfire, carried grown men out of burning rooms, stolen a boat under an emperor's palace, and stood beside me while the world repeatedly attempted to become inconvenient. Now he held a strip of blue silk like somebody had handed him a venomous snake with a dress code.

"Brother."

I looked at him.

"Nigga, you shaking."

"The fabric slippery."

"Your hands slippery?"

"Don't start."

I took the tie and fixed it around his neck.

The room was quiet except for the distant sound of musicians warming up in the garden. Sunlight came through the curtains. Our suits hung perfectly. Our shoes shone. Nobody had called to report an aircraft losing an engine.

That last fact felt like a wedding gift from the universe.

Tank looked at himself in the mirror.

Then at me standing behind him.

"We really doing this."

"Nigga, they rented chairs. We committed."

He laughed, then swallowed hard.

"I used to think getting through the night was the whole thing."

"I know."

"Then another night. Then another. You get enough of them together, you start calling it a life because nobody told you there was more."

I straightened his collar.

He watched my hands in the mirror.

"Then she looked at me like I was somebody she might want around in the morning."

Nigga, my brother's voice broke on morning.

I put both hands on his shoulders.

"She does."

He nodded.

"Yeah."

"And you ain't got to win her again every time the sun comes up. Just be there when it does."

Tank looked at me.

"That sound like something Shawna told you."

"Nigga, I cite my sources privately."

He laughed and hugged me.

Carefully. Vega had threatened everybody about the shoulder.

When he let go, I handed him his jacket.

"Come on. Your woman waiting."

The garden had become a city made of flowers.

Blue roses climbed white arches. Long tables glittered under hanging lights. Beyond them, the First Dance floated above the grounds, its painted heart renewed in gold. Sky High's choir stood on a broad platform beneath the airship, every singer firmly instructed to keep both feet where the music director could see them. Cars lined the drive in colors that made the sunset look underfunded.

The Last Word waited near the entrance.

Rebuilt.

Dark blue. Polished. Its silver letters shining.

June stood beside it with Adrian, both dressed beautifully, both looking like they had slept three hours and considered the result worth it.

I stopped.

"Nigga."

June smiled.

"Wedding gift."

"You fixed it."

"I improved it. Fixed would imply accepting the original driver behavior."

Shawna's name had been engraved on the passenger-side sill.

I ran my hand over it.

Adrian nodded.

"She brought it home as often as you did."

Nigga, I could not argue with excellence that precise.

I hugged them both.

Then Rosa's voice came from somewhere inside the house.

"If the men are crying over cars, tell them to save something for the women!"

Tank stood straighter.

"Yes, baby!"

The guests rose when we entered the garden.

Not because anybody asked them to. Because every nigga there had apparently agreed that watching us walk between those flowers deserved a standing event. Cops saluted. Drivers cheered. Professors applauded. Sex workers whistled louder than all of them and improved the occasion immediately.

Principal Mercer already had a handkerchief pressed to his face.

"He hasn't even done anything yet," Professor Halcyon whispered.

"He's arrived," Mercer said, voice breaking. "He so rarely did."

Professor Lorne nodded with grave academic pride.

"And yet, look at the outcome."

I heard every word.

"Niggas, I graduated once. Let it rest."

Mercer began crying harder.

Tank bent over laughing.

Knox stood near the front in a white uniform. Seraphine sat beside her, elegant and calm, though I saw both women watching the floating choir with the alertness of people who had learned music could become an emergency in my vicinity.

Marcellus held the rings.

Blue Mercy shone on his hand.

Magnolia and Bernard sat together under the shade of a flowering tree. Vesper sat beside them. Noor and Salma had brought their mother, who looked at the two captains, then at my suit, and declared she understood why they had both crossed a desert to attend.

"Mother," Noor murmured.

"I am old, not blind."

Shawna's friends laughed from the next row.

Nigga, everybody had brought their whole selves. I wanted it that way.

The music changed.

Tank stopped breathing.

I felt it beside me.

"Nigga," I whispered, "you need air for vows."

He did not answer.

Rosa appeared at the garden doors.

Her dress was ivory with a blue lining that flashed when she moved. No giant veil hiding her face. No attempt to make her look like a woman who had never lived before this morning. She looked like Rosa: beautiful, bold, nervous beneath the boldness, walking toward the man who had learned every version of her laugh and wanted the rest of them.

Shawna walked beside her.

My wife wore blue silk, pale at the shoulders and deepening toward the hem, with a narrow white wrap over one arm. Her wedding rings shone on one hand. Dante's watch shone on the other. She looked at me as she came down the aisle, and every room I had ever entered without her became suddenly difficult to remember.

Tank made a small sound.

I made a worse one.

The nigga turned toward me just long enough to whisper, "You too?"

"Nigga, look at them."

"I am."

"Then mind your own collapse."

We both laughed through eyes that had become inconveniently wet.

Rosa reached Tank.

He took her hands like he had been given something fragile and then remembered she would beat his ass for thinking that.

"You look—"

"I know," she whispered, smiling.

He laughed.

"Yeah."

Shawna came to my side and slipped her hand into mine.

The officiant began.

He was an older man Rosa had chosen because he could speak warmly without sounding like he was selling furniture. He looked at the crowd, the airship, the fleet of cars, the two captains in the front row, the jeweled king standing as best man, and took one deep breath before deciding to keep the introduction short.

A wise nigga.

When it was time for Tank's vows, my brother unfolded a sheet of paper.

His hands shook.

Rosa waited.

He looked at the page.

Then folded it again.

"I wrote a lot," he said.

The crowd laughed gently.

"Aiden said some of it sounded like I was buying a refrigerator."

"Nigga, the warranty language was concerning," I said.

Rosa laughed and squeezed his hands.

Tank took a breath.

"I know how to stay," he told her. "I stayed for people who didn't deserve it. Stayed in rooms where leaving would've been smarter. Stayed because I thought leaving made a man weak."

He looked into her face.

"But with you, staying don't feel like proving something. It feels like getting something. A morning. A song. You cussing at me because I put the wrong shirt in the wash. You standing in the kitchen eating cake with a fork you pretend you ain't using."

Rosa wiped her cheek with the back of one hand.

"I don't promise I'm gonna become smooth," Tank said. "These niggas know me. I can't lie in front of this many witnesses."

The garden laughed.

"I promise you won't have to wonder where I am when you call. I promise I will learn the dance. I promise I'm gonna be there when the music stops too."

His voice broke.

"And I promise every good thing I get, my first thought is gonna be, Rosa should have some of this."

Nigga, I looked away at the flowers and found no help there.

Rosa held his face between her hands.

"You big beautiful man," she whispered.

Then she began her vows.

"I had people listen to me sing and never hear a fucking word I said afterward. You heard me when I was tired. You heard me when I was angry. You heard me say I wanted the green shoes and came back with three pairs because you forgot which green."

Tank laughed.

"They all looked right."

"They did."

She smiled through the tears.

"I promise to tell you what I want. I promise not to make you guess when the truth would be kinder. I promise to keep dancing with you even when you try to count the steps out loud."

"That helps me."

"I know, baby."

The whole garden seemed to lean toward them.

"And I promise that when somebody asks who my husband is, I'm gonna point at you with my whole fucking hand. No little embarrassed finger. That man. That beautiful, loyal, loud, impossible man. Mine."

Tank closed his eyes.

One tear ran down his face.

Rosa kissed it away before the officiant could get to the next instruction.

Nobody objected.

The rings came from Marcellus's hands.

Tank read the words inside his.

STAY FOR THE LAST SONG.

He looked at Rosa.

Her ring read:

I'M STILL DANCING.

Nigga, that old jeweler had no respect for anybody trying to remain composed.

They exchanged the rings.

They said yes.

They kissed.

The garden erupted.

The choir rose a foot off the platform in excitement. Seraphine lifted one finger. Every singer came back down immediately without missing the note.

Knox watched, impressed.

"Excellent control."

"Practice," the dean said.

Tank lifted Rosa off the ground.

She laughed against his mouth and told him not to wrinkle the dress.

He put her down as carefully as he had ever handled anything in his life.

Then he turned toward me.

Nigga, my brother was married.

I hugged him hard enough for Vega to make a disapproving sound from the front row.

"We did it," he whispered.

"You did it."

"Nigga, you stood here. That counts."

I held him another second.

Then Shawna took my hand.

Our turn.

We did not need a second grand entrance. She removed the white wrap from her arm and let Rosa place it around her shoulders. The music softened. The guests sat. The same garden held a different quiet as my wife and I stood beneath the arch.

I looked at her.

The first wedding had felt like grabbing happiness before the world could close its fist.

This one felt like opening my hand and finding she had chosen to remain inside it.

The officiant asked whether we wished to renew the promises already made.

"Nigga," I said softly, looking only at her, "more than anything."

Shawna smiled.

"Yes."

I took both her hands.

"The first time I married you, I thought I had to promise the whole world because I didn't know what else a man could give a woman like you. Houses. Cars. Money. A city if I could find one with poor supervision."

The guests laughed.

"I still like giving you those things. I'm not about to embarrass myself by pretending I stopped enjoying being rich."

Shawna laughed, bright and familiar.

"But you met me in the parts I couldn't buy. The hospital. The car after the lightning. The bridge when my hands wouldn't work. You were there when being Aiden didn't feel like enough for Aiden."

Her eyes shone.

"And every time I got scared you might finally see all of me, you looked closer. Nigga, you looked closer and stayed."

I swallowed.

"So I promise this. When I say home, I mean where you can find me. When I say forever, I mean the next morning too. When I say I'm the greatest man alive—"

The crowd began laughing before I finished.

"—I mean I'm gonna spend every fucking day giving you new evidence."

Shawna laughed through tears.

"I knew you'd get that in."

"Baby, the vows got standards."

She squeezed my hands.

Then she spoke.

"You came into my life loudly."

Tank nodded from beside us.

"Very loudly."

"You were jealous, ridiculous, brave, and convinced a mansion could solve a conversation."

"Sometimes it helps," I said.

"Sometimes it does."

She smiled.

"You never became easy. I didn't marry you because I thought you would. I married you because beneath all that noise was a man who would hear me when I said my own name. A man who learned I could carry a past and still choose a future. A man who comes back."

She touched the new band in Marcellus's hand.

"I promise to keep choosing you on purpose. I promise to tell you when you're being unbearable."

"Nigga, that's been consistent."

"I promise to laugh when you're funny and when you're so full of yourself I need the relief. I promise to sing in the house even when you insist on joining the chorus."

"The public appreciates it."

"The public isn't married to you."

The garden laughed.

She stepped closer.

"And I promise you will never have to compete with a ghost for a place that already belongs to you. You are my husband. My living, impossible husband. I am here."

Nigga, I could not have answered if the whole world had offered me another crown.

I kissed her hands.

We exchanged the new rings beside the old.

I CAME BACK.

I WAS HERE.

Then the officiant said we could kiss, which was kind of him, given the evidence that we had never intended to wait for permission.

The choir sang.

The guests stood.

My wife put both hands on my face and kissed me beneath the blue roses while the city, the sky, and every nigga I loved made enough noise to let the dead know we were still doing all right down here.

## 23. Niggalicious

Tank began his wedding toast by calling me a motherfucker and immediately received a standing ovation from the people who knew me best.

"Sit down," Rosa told them, laughing. "Let the man develop his argument."

My brother stood beneath a canopy of lights with a glass in one hand and the microphone in the other. His tie had loosened. His new ring shone when he moved. Behind him, the First Dance floated against the night sky, its windows bright with guests looking down at the garden.

"I had a speech," he said.

"You had several," I called.

"Nigga, because you kept editing them."

"One of them threatened the guests."

"Only the ones who didn't bring gifts."

The tables roared.

Shawna leaned against me, laughing into my shoulder. Rosa stood beside Tank with her glass raised and the expression of a woman who had chosen exactly this man with full knowledge of the available evidence.

Tank looked around the garden.

"I been trying to figure out what you call a nigga like my brother. Captain ain't enough. King ain't enough. Husband only covers the part Shawna tolerates."

"Barely," she said.

"This nigga walks into a room and the room starts behaving like it got lucky."

People laughed and pointed toward me.

I lifted my glass.

"Architecture recognizes quality."

Tank shook his head.

"See? Nigga can't even receive a compliment without expanding it. So I had to invent a word."

Porsche stood at the next table.

"You did not invent that word."

Tank turned.

"Nigga, sit down. This my toast."

"And my word."

"What word?" Rosa asked, delighted.

Tank lifted the microphone.

"Niggalicious."

The garden exploded.

Mercedes bent over the table laughing. Victor looked at Cassius, who repeated the word slowly like a man testing whether a new engine note pleased him. Knox put her wine down before she spilled it. Principal Mercer began applauding with the solemn enthusiasm of a teacher witnessing an important contribution to language.

Porsche pointed at Tank.

"I said that on the airship!"

"You said the cake looked delicious."

"I said the nigga carrying the cake looked niggalicious."

Rosa turned toward her husband.

Tank blinked.

"Me?"

"Nigga, who else was carrying half a bakery up the stairs?"

He considered this new information.

Then smiled.

Rosa slapped his arm lightly.

"Stay married in your face."

"I am. I'm just linguistically appreciated."

I stood.

The crowd cheered before I spoke, which I considered a very efficient arrangement.

"Niggas," I said, "why y'all arguing about who invented a word for something I already am?"

Shawna covered her face.

Tank pointed at me with the microphone.

"That. That right there. That's the fucking condition."

"Niggalicious," Cassius agreed.

"Severely," Victor added.

"Possibly congenital," Vega said from her table.

The doctor had spoken so dryly that it took half the garden a second to collapse laughing.

I looked at her.

"Nigga, you finally giving me a diagnosis I enjoy."

"Do not let it interfere with wearing the sling."

Shawna stood beside me and raised her glass.

"To the men we married. Loudly, deliberately, and with every opportunity to read the warning signs."

Rosa lifted hers.

"We read them."

"We liked the font," Shawna said.

The women at the nearest tables cheered loud enough to make the choir above us turn around.

Tank raised his glass again.

"To my brother. To my wife. To every nigga who came home."

I looked around the garden.

At Victor with his arm around an old academy friend. At Cassius and Inez touching knees beneath the table. At June and Adrian, too tired to stop smiling. At Vesper laughing beside Magnolia. At Bernard looking up at the airship as if a night this beautiful might finally belong to him too. At Marcellus wearing Blue Mercy in the light.

I raised my glass.

"To coming home."

Everybody drank.

Then Rosa took the microphone from Tank.

"And now," she said, "my husband dances."

The big nigga looked at me like I might produce a legal exemption.

I shook my head.

"Nigga, jurisdiction ends at the dance floor."

She led him into the open space between the tables.

The band began softly.

Tank placed one hand at her waist. She put hers on his shoulder. For the first few steps he looked down. Rosa lifted his chin with one finger.

"Here," she whispered.

He looked at her.

The next step came easier.

Then another.

Nigga, my brother danced.

Not perfectly. Not like a man who had secretly been a professional all along. Like Tank, who had practiced because Rosa wanted it and trusted her enough to stop protecting himself from being seen trying.

She smiled at him with her whole face.

The crowd quieted around them.

I watched the big dangerous nigga turn gently beneath the lights and felt something in my chest settle into a place it had been looking for since the first night he stood beside me.

Shawna took my hand.

"Our turn."

I went with her.

She put her arms around my neck, careful of the shoulder. I held her close, the new ring against her back, the old one beside it. Her dress moved around our feet. The band found a melody I knew because I had heard her hum it in our house when she thought nobody was listening.

"You chose this?" I asked.

"You know it."

"Nigga, I know you."

She smiled.

"That's the idea."

We moved slowly. No stunts. No need to make the whole garden discover gravity again. I could hear her breathing near my ear. I could feel the watch against my shoulder. I could see Tank and Rosa turning beside us, laughing when he stepped the wrong way and she guided him back without making it matter.

For once, being the greatest man in the room did not require me to be the loudest thing in it.

Then the song ended and Tank shouted, "Niggalicious!" directly into the quiet.

Everybody laughed.

Nigga, peace had its limits.

The party grew.

Mercedes and Porsche took over the stage for a performance involving Sienna's violin, a bass line, and enough confidence to make three millionaires forget what they had been saying. Shawna sang with Rosa. Victor joined the choir for one song and accidentally lifted his chair off the ground during the final note. Seraphine looked at him. The chair returned immediately.

Cassius asked Inez to dance.

She told him to keep up.

The nigga looked delighted to receive a challenge he intended to spend his life losing beautifully.

Esteban and Nero stood beside the dance floor arguing over which of their children had inherited the better sense of rhythm. Neither seemed interested in the fact that both children were currently doing better than their fathers had demonstrated all evening.

Captain Lionel Graves found Knox beside the dance floor with two glasses in his hands and a blue rose between his teeth.

She looked at the flower.

"You realize everybody here is armed. They could end this embarrassment for you."

He offered her a glass and took the rose from his mouth.

"I have faced worse odds for your attention."

"Nigga," I called, "the man's consistent."

Knox looked at me over her shoulder, but she was smiling when she turned back to him. Graves tucked the rose into the ribbon at her wrist. She let him. Then she took his hand and led him into the music like the whole department could survive ten minutes without her watching its favorite problem.

Seraphine raised her glass as they passed.

"Excellent partner selection, Chief."

"Under continuing assessment," Knox said.

Graves pulled her close. Whatever answer he whispered made her laugh against his shoulder.

At the next table, Isolde took Marcellus's hand and examined Blue Mercy in the light.

"You wore it," she said.

He nodded.

"I wanted to."

"Good. Now bring the rest of yourself onto the floor."

The old jeweler looked alarmed. "There are witnesses."

"There were witnesses thirty-five years ago. You were less cautious then."

She stood, her dress moving around her ankles, and held out her hand. Marcellus took it. They began with the old seven-turn dance, the one their younger selves had carried all the way to the island vault. He remembered the first turn. She guided the second. On the third he laughed, surprised by his own feet, and Isolde kissed his cheek without losing the rhythm.

Nigga, the ring shone on his hand while he held a living woman close. Nothing on that hand had to disappear for the music to begin.

Magnolia danced with Bernard.

Slowly at first. Her cane rested against a chair. He held her hand with the shy attention of a man who had once thought the part of his life containing new music might be finished.

She said something to him.

He laughed.

Nigga, that was enough of their conversation for me to be glad I had lived to see it.

June came to our table carrying a set of keys.

I held out my hand.

She moved them away.

"Not yours."

"Nigga, that sentence hurts."

She gave them to Professor Lorne.

The professor blinked.

"My convertible?"

"Repaired. Better steering. New paint. Try not to let the captain use it as a teaching aid again."

Lorne looked at the keys, then at me.

"It did produce an extraordinary practical lesson."

Mercer began applauding again.

Halcyon took his glass away.

"Percival, breathe between achievements."

The principal nodded, overcome.

I leaned toward Shawna.

"Nigga, I should've attended more classes. These people love me."

She kissed my cheek.

"That's probably why you remain impressive to them."

The wedding cake arrived at midnight.

It was taller than Tank.

Nigga, I wish I could tell you I had opposed this. I had not. When the pastry chef asked how much cake we wanted, Tank said everybody, and I said make sure, which apparently constituted an architectural brief.

Nine tiers. Blue flowers made of sugar. White pillars. Two little couples on the top, both grooms rendered handsomely enough that I considered tipping the artist twice. The cake rolled into the garden on a reinforced platform while the Sky High cook walked beside it with the terrified pride of a man escorting a cathedral through traffic.

The crowd applauded.

Then one wheel struck the edge of a paving stone.

The platform tilted.

The cake began to lean.

Tank moved.

I moved.

Nigga, we had faced emperors, planes, guns, and collapsing bridges. Nothing had united us faster than seeing Rosa's cake consider the ground.

Tank caught the platform's lower edge. I caught the upper support with my good arm. Shawna and Rosa grabbed the tablecloth before it could pull the base sideways. Anton appeared behind Tank and lifted the other side like the laws of pastry had become a personal favor.

The cake steadied.

The little Aiden on top leaned forward.

I caught it before it fell.

The entire garden lost its fucking mind.

"That nigga saved himself!" Porsche shouted.

"At miniature scale!" Cassius added.

"Consistent across conditions," Professor Halcyon said, laughing so hard she had to wipe her glasses.

Vega pointed at my shoulder.

I held up the tiny groom.

"Medical emergency."

She looked at Rosa's face.

Then at the cake.

"I will allow that one."

We cut the first slices together.

Tank fed Rosa a bite with the concentration of a man handling an explosive device made of happiness. She fed him back, wiped icing from his mouth, and kissed him before he could make a joke about portion size.

Shawna held my slice up.

"Open."

I obeyed.

She smiled.

"Excellent husband. Follows instructions."

"Nigga, when the instruction is cake."

She kissed the icing from the corner of my mouth.

The fireworks began above the garden.

Blue. Gold. White.

The First Dance floated beneath them with its windows full of light. Music rose from the stage. Cars gleamed along the drive. Police and criminals danced together without anybody pretending the world had become simple because we had finally arranged a good night inside it.

Near the end, Tank found me by the fountain.

His tie hung loose. Rosa's lipstick marked his cheek. He held two glasses and handed me one.

"Brother."

"Husband."

The nigga smiled so wide I almost laughed before he spoke.

"I like how that sounds."

"Get used to it."

We stood together, watching our wives laugh beside the dance floor.

Tank lifted his glass toward them.

"We did all right."

"Nigga, we did magnificent."

He shook his head.

"Nah. New word."

I looked at him.

He looked back, completely serious for exactly half a second.

"Niggalicious."

I laughed until the water in the fountain seemed to laugh with me.

Then my wife called my name.

Rosa called his.

And both of us went.

## 24. Ten Toes Down, and Then Breakfast

Six months after the wedding, my wife sent me out for butter.

"Just butter," she said.

I looked at her across the kitchen.

"Nigga, why you emphasizing just?"

"Because last time I asked for lemons, you came back owning part of a restaurant."

"They had excellent lemons."

She pointed a wooden spoon at me.

"Butter."

"Salted?"

"Yes."

"Look at us communicating."

She laughed and kissed me before I could turn shopping into a speech.

The morning was warm. The house smelled of coffee. Outside, the white horse stood by the fence, watching a gardener arrange flowers with the bored authority of a nigga who had never once needed to earn his breakfast. My shoulder had healed. My arm had healed. Vega had cleared me for ordinary activity while refusing to define ordinary in a way I could use against her later.

The Last Word waited in the drive.

Blue paint. Silver lettering. Shawna's name inside the passenger door.

I got behind the wheel, put on my sunglasses, and started the engine.

Nigga, there are men who leave the house.

Then there is the way I leave the house.

The gardener looked up and smiled.

"Morning, Captain."

"Morning. You need anything?"

"The roses are arriving this afternoon."

"Good. Get extra."

"Your wife already did."

I grinned.

The nigga had no idea how much that answer pleased me.

I drove through the gates with a grocery list containing one word and absolutely no reason to expect the city to behave itself.

Tank called before I reached the first light.

"Brother."

"Husband."

He still laughed when I called him that.

"Rosa says come by tonight. She trying a new song."

"Nigga, last time she tried a song, you cried into a bowl of pasta."

"The sauce was hot."

"Emotionally?"

"You bringing Shawna or not?"

"We'll be there."

"Good. Also, I got a new car."

"Nigga, why you hiding the news behind dinner?"

"Rosa says I'm supposed to lead with relationships."

In the background, she shouted, "I said stop introducing the car before me!"

I laughed all the way through the green light.

At the bakery, two men were robbing the register.

Nigga, two grown motherfuckers in black masks stood between me and salted butter at nine-fifteen in the morning.

One held a gun. The other held a pastry bag.

I stopped in the doorway.

The woman behind the counter looked at me.

Then at them.

Then she sighed with such relief that the nigga holding the gun turned around to see what she had discovered.

"Everybody stay—"

He stopped.

I took off my sunglasses.

His friend looked up from the pastry bag.

"Nigga."

"Yeah," I said. "Morning."

The gunman's eyes widened above the mask.

"Aiden?"

"Captain, while you doing that."

The other man lowered the bag.

"Nigga, I told you we should've gone across town."

"You told me the croissants were good!"

"They are good! That doesn't make this nigga less here!"

I looked at the baker.

"You all right?"

She nodded.

"They haven't hurt anybody."

"Good. Let's keep that little achievement intact."

I held out my hand.

The gunman stared at it.

"What?"

"Nigga, give me the gun."

His friend nodded urgently.

"Give the nigga the gun."

"Shut up."

"You shut up. That's the nigga from the bridge."

I waited.

The gunman looked at the photograph of me beside the register. The baker had put it there after I paid for a year's worth of pastries for the officers working night shifts. In the photograph I held a croissant like a man presenting an important discovery to science.

The nigga looked from the photograph back to me.

"You really live here."

"Nigga, what you think I do? Hover over the city between incidents?"

His friend began laughing nervously.

The gunman handed me the weapon.

Then a third man burst out of the back room.

Of course there was a third nigga. Bad planning loves company.

He saw me, saw his friends surrendering, and ran straight through the side door.

I looked at the two men in front of me.

"Stay."

They stayed.

The baker reached beneath the counter and brought out the butter.

"I'll hold this."

"Appreciate you."

I ran outside.

The third man jumped into a stolen delivery car and pulled away hard enough to scatter a row of empty crates. I got into the Last Word, hit the lights, and followed.

Nigga, my wife had given me one item.

One.

The delivery car turned onto the boulevard. Ahead, a slow procession of trucks moved toward the civic plaza. Workers were bringing in equipment for a public celebration I had forgotten to put on my calendar because apparently the city kept finding new reasons to honor me without checking whether I had breakfast plans.

On the largest truck stood a covered statue.

I recognized the shape beneath the sheet.

"Nigga," I muttered.

The thief swerved between the trucks.

I followed, close enough to see him looking at me in the mirror with growing spiritual concern.

He took the next turn too fast.

His car clipped the statue truck's rear corner.

The straps snapped.

The sheet flew off.

A twenty-foot bronze Aiden rolled backward onto its transport platform, one enormous arm pointing at the sky.

Nigga, I looked excellent.

The truck driver braked.

The statue slid toward the open end.

The thief's car stopped beneath its outstretched boot.

He looked up.

Then at me pulling alongside.

Then up again.

"You gotta be fucking kidding me," he said.

I lowered my window.

"Nigga, even my statue caught you."

The statue's boot settled against his hood with a deep metallic groan. The front of the delivery car folded enough to trap it in place. The thief sat frozen behind the windshield while the largest version of my shoe in existence held him politely against the road.

Nobody was hurt.

Several people were already filming.

The nigga opened his door very slowly and raised both hands.

"I surrender."

"To which one of me?"

He stared.

I pointed up at the statue.

"Nigga, jurisdiction complicated today."

The crowd began laughing.

Knox arrived in her own car five minutes later.

She looked at the bronze boot on the stolen vehicle.

Then at me.

Then at the sculptor standing nearby with both hands pressed to his head.

"Captain," she said, "I am glad to see you contributing even while stationary."

"Efficient department."

The thief looked between us.

"Y'all always like this?"

Knox put a hand on his shoulder.

"Unfortunately for your morning, yes."

She took him away.

The sculptor approached me, trembling.

"The heel may be damaged."

I looked up at my bronze face.

"Nigga, the cheekbones survived. We're ahead."

He laughed, then almost cried, then asked whether I would stand beside the statue for a photograph before the recovery crew moved it.

I did.

The crowd cheered.

Somebody shouted, "Niggalicious!"

Three other niggas shouted it back.

I pointed toward them.

"Educated citizens."

My phone rang.

Shawna.

I answered.

"Baby."

"Butter."

"I got it."

"I'm watching a twenty-foot version of you arrest a man on my phone."

"Then you understand the delay."

"Aiden."

"Salted. I remembered."

She tried not to laugh.

I heard her fail.

Nigga, that sound could still make a whole city move to the background.

I went back to the bakery.

Knox's officers had taken the first two men away. The baker stood behind the counter with the butter wrapped in paper and a bag of pastries beside it.

"For your wife," she said.

"She sent me for one thing."

"Tell her I insisted."

"Nigga, excellent witness."

The woman laughed.

I paid, left more than the bill required, and drove home without purchasing the bakery, the block, or any additional part of municipal government.

Growth, if a nigga wanted to call it that.

At the house, Shawna stood in the kitchen wearing one of my shirts and an expression she had clearly been practicing since the video appeared.

I held up the butter.

She looked at it.

Then at the pastries.

Then at me.

"You made it."

"Nigga, against all odds."

She came around the counter and kissed me.

Not because the city had cheered.

Not because a statue of me now required a new heel.

Because I had come through the door and she wanted me close.

I put the groceries down and held her until the pan on the stove reminded us breakfast still existed.

We ate on the terrace.

The garden moved in the breeze. The white horse grazed beyond the fence. Somewhere inside, my phone kept filling with photographs of bronze greatness and one very frightened thief.

I left it there.

Shawna buttered her toast and watched me over her coffee.

"What?" I asked.

"You look happy."

I considered making a joke.

Then I let the simple thing stay simple for one breath.

"I am."

She smiled.

After breakfast, we opened the messages from our friends.

Rosa sent a recording of the new song. Tank could be heard humming badly in the background until she laughed and made him start again.

Cassius and Inez sent a photograph from their racing garage, both fathers standing behind them arguing over a car nobody had asked them to fix. Their first team driver had won a race that morning. Cassius wrote that victory tasted better when the woman beside him stole his champagne afterward.

Liora sent the First Dance above the sea, full of paying passengers and musicians on their way to Sienna's opening festival. The heart remained on the side. Tank had agreed to share the naming rights with love in general.

June sent the rebuilt Crownless Hotel's front doors. Bernard stood between the two courtyard palms with Magnolia's hand in his. Her cane leaned against his leg. The new sign gleamed behind them.

Vesper sent a photograph from the Blue House. Bastien sat beside Madame Caron, looking annoyed by the camera and pleased by everything else. Noor and Salma had come for dinner with their mother. Nobody in the picture appeared to be awaiting permission to leave.

Victor sent a picture of my academy portrait. The faculty had made it larger.

Nigga, I approved.

Marcellus sent no photograph. He called.

He had opened the workshop early. Sunlight was good at that hour, he said. Blue Mercy shone on his hand while he worked. Celeste's letter remained in the drawer where he could reach it. He had begun teaching two grown apprentices who asked good questions and held their tools badly, a combination he described with obvious delight. Isolde taught dancing in the room above the workshop and came downstairs to steal his coffee, correct his posture, and kiss him before the apprentices could pretend they had not noticed.

"Come by next week," he told us. "I have something for the house."

"Nigga, we got enough jewels."

He laughed.

"A clock. You two are always late."

Shawna took the phone to defend herself.

I listened to them argue and leaned back in my chair.

Gideon and Orson were in prison. Their cases had ended months earlier. Zero lay in a grave in the desert, named plainly, with no throne above him and no unfinished business beneath the stone. The people who had followed him had made their choices, served their sentences, changed their work, or gone home. None of them was waiting in a dark room to become the last page of my life.

The last page was here.

My wife on the terrace.

My brother calling about dinner.

My city loud beyond the walls.

Butter on the table.

Aight, my nigga. Now look at us.

That nigga Tank got a ring on his hand and a woman who makes him dance. That nigga Victor still thinks he can beat me at something, and I love the nigga enough to let him keep trying. Cassius got Inez beside him, and if that nigga acts surprised one more time when happiness climbs into the passenger seat, I'm charging him for the lesson. Marcellus got his stone, his letter, his good light in the morning. Nigga, the old man got mornings.

Look at my people. My niggas got keys. My niggas got places to put their shoes down without wondering who might make them run. Rosa got a stage and a husband who learns the words. Mercedes and Porsche got a room with their names over the door, and niggas better behave inside it. June got engines worth arguing with. Liora got a whole fucking sky that doesn't belong to an emperor. Vesper got friends who can tell her when she's being difficult and stay for dinner afterward.

And me?

Nigga, look at me.

I'm still the man who likes the loud car. Still the nigga who sees a crown and wants to know how it looks. Still the captain who should occasionally be supervised by somebody with better judgment and smaller ambitions for a grocery run. I got guns in the safe, money in places a nigga could get lost trying to count, and a city that put my face in bronze before asking whether bronze could handle the responsibility.

I did not become quiet. Nigga, you know me better than that.

I became somebody with a reason to hear the door open.

Because that's my wife coming out onto the terrace now. That's Shawna saying my name. Nigga, the way she says it still does something money never learned. She doesn't say king. She doesn't say captain. She says Aiden like the whole loud motherfucker fits inside a word she can carry without getting tired.

I get up.

She puts her hand in mine.

"What you smiling at?" she asks.

"Nigga," I tell her, "I'm thinking about how good your taste is."

She laughs. The same woman. The same laugh. New morning.

That's my heart, my nigga. Not somewhere precious where nobody can touch it. Right here, warm hand in my hand, telling me I bought too many pastries while eating the second one.

Ten toes down for the niggas who came when I called.

Ten toes down for the women who called me on my shit and loved me with their eyes open.

Ten toes down in the kitchen, in the driveway, beside my brother, beside my wife. Nigga, standing is easy when you finally know where you want to stay.

I came back.

She was here.

And the rest of the morning belonged to us.

Aiden.

Ten toes down. Forever, my nigga.
